Dear Director Nagle: 
The Muscogee (Creek) Nation (MCN) appreciates the invitation and opportunity to engage in consultation 
regarding the United States Environmental Protection Agency's (USEPA) Proposed Revisions to the 
Federal Water Quality Standards Regulations to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights. Through the consultation 
process it is the goal of the MCN that meaningful discussion, progressive thought, and robust conversation 
on Tribal sovereign rights to protect the land, air, and water resources within Tribal Reservations will help 
to improve the human health and environment of ALL citizens within those Tribal Reservations. 
The MCN supports the USEPA's proposed changes to the Water Quality Standards (WQS) Regulation at 
40 CFR Part 131 "to explicitly and sustainably protect tribal reserved rights in state waters." Additionally, 
the MCN requests that the USEP A strongly considers including the requirement language of "MUST work 
with Tribal Nations in the State o f  Oklahoma" regardless of Section 10211(a) of the Safe, Accountable, 
Flexible, Efficient Transportation Equity Act of 2005 (SAFE TEA) or similar requests from the State. This 
important requirement for Tribal input and coordination during the review process of state WQS 
submissions shall be an important step in Tribal natural resource protection and preservation within the 
MCN Reservation on issues of water quality standards and Tribal protection of reserved rights. 
Historic Background 
The MCN is a federally recognized Native American tribe in Oklahoma. The tribe's traditional homelands 
include portions of Oklahoma, Alabama, Georgia, and Florida, and their culture is closely tied to the waters 
and land of these regions.

Attention: Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791 
 
The Oregon Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ) appreciates the opportunity to provide 
comments on the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) proposal to protect tribal reserved rights in 
water quality standards. In addition to EPA’s federal tribal trust responsibilities, DEQ is committed to 
Government-to-Government consultation with tribes as relates to the establishment of WQS and other 
topics of mutual interests. We support the development of a rule to ensure that state and federal water 
quality standards will protect tribal rights. DEQ believes the proposed rule will benefit from several 
clarifications to make the rule more clear and provide a basis upon which the rule’s requirements can be 
feasibly implemented by EPA, the states, and the tribes: 
1. The rule needs to clearly define unsuppressed rights and how those will be determined. 
2. The statement in the rule requiring protection of “the health of the right holders to at least the 
same risk level as provided to the general population of the state” seems to be inconsistent with 
the explanation in EPA’s presentation provided to the states on 1/24/2023. DEQ recommends 
EPA clarifies the rule to be consistent with its presentation on 1/24/2023 as summarized below: 
• 
Establish acceptable risk (e.g., cancer risk level) for tribal members whose exercise of reserved 
rights may put them at greater risk than the general population, e.g., due to higher rates of fish 
consumption.  
• 
Specify that tribal members exercising applicable reserved rights should be exposed to no greater 
than a 1 in 100,000 cancer risk, which EPA’s guidance recommends for the general population. 
• 
Specify that the appropriate cancer risk level must be paired with an appropriate fish consumption 
rate. 
Please contact Connie Dou at (503)853- 6517 or Debra Sturdevant at 503-229-6691 if you have any 
questions regarding these comments. 
Sincerely,  
 
Connie Dou 
Water Quality Program Manager

To Whom It May Concern: 
 
Maine Rivers, a Maine nonprofit organization devoted to the health 
of Maine’s rivers, submits this comment on the EPA Notification of 
Consultations and Coordination on Potential Revisions to the 
Federal Water Quality Standards Regulations to protect Tribal 
Reserved Rights, Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791.  
 
The rule proposed by EPA would revise the Water Quality Standards 
at 40 CFR part 131, to create a regulatory framework that would be 
applied case-specifically to ensure protection of resources reserved 
to Tribes. 
 
Maine Rivers believes that clarity in the adoption and application of 
the federal WQCs to rivers, streams and other waters in Maine in the 
context of Tribal reserved rights would be a step forward, given the 
extensive Tribal lands in this State. We believe the key to 
compliance is transparency in the adoption of rules especially on the 
context of complex constitutional and treaty obligations. For these 
reasons, Maine Rivers supports the proposed rule.

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791-0157 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791 ---
To Whom It May Concern:
I thank you kindly for the opportunity to comment on the proposed rule EPA-HQ-OW-
2021-0791-0001. As an undergraduate 4th year student studying environmental science and 
conservation, my opportunities and provided course material have helped demonstrated a need to 
prompt environmental and ecological literacy that is digestible for future generations. The 
opportunity to discuss the importance of the lack of access to high-quality health-promoting 
infrastructure that has led to negative burdens on tribal communities intergenerationally is 
crucial. I would like to respond to your stated request for comment regarding Water Quality 
Standards Regulatory Revisions to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights, and the continuous 
marginalization and disproportionate impacts on indigenous communities within the United 
States.
Indigenous communities around the world have significantly suffered disproportionately 
from the impacts of climate change. I have had the wonderful opportunity to discuss and learn
about environmental injustices throughout the United States in my courses and was provided the 
opportunity to learn about the struggle for justice from Dr. Sacoby Wilson. I would like to bring 
to the agency’s attention the necessary revisions in relation to water quality standards, especially 
due to the social determinant of COVID-19. The water crises that tribal communities face are a 
direct reflection of colonization and ethical inequity for BIPOC communities. Water values are a 
political construct that reflects social dynamics. Extractivisim on natural resources, the impact of 
climate change, as well as poor sanitation mean that indigenous communities no longer have 
access to safe drinking water. To dismiss the traditional lifestyles and culture of indigenous 
communities is to dismiss their health and safety as we continue to alter our planet. 
I want to mainly focus on Executive Order 13045 – the Protection of Children from 
Environmental Health and Safety Risks. Poor water quality is noted to have significant impacts 
on human health. Persistent heavy metal contaminations exist within the Navajo Nation and 
adjacent reservation boundaries. The very digestion and inhalation of their public water lead to 
hypertension, cancer, cardiovascular diseases, and much more. However, opportunities to present 
water and wastewater infrastructure improvements are lengthy and exceedingly difficult. The 
BIA requires environmental assessments to be done before a ROW is allotted. Additionally, a 
legacy of inadequate environmental enforcement contributes to the expenses and operations of 
water infrastructure. For instance, the river source water for the Crow Agency water treatment 
plant has microbial contamination – there is no agency taking responsibility for inspecting the 
home septic systems on the Reservation, and the current technology provided cannot effectively 
handle changes due to climate change. More attentive measures are necessary rather than hopeful 
writing and words. Tribes lack the legal authority to create water districts, and the lack of 
ownership of major infrastructure cannot be upgraded or replaced through grants.  It is noted that 
the budget constraints in Crow result in understaffed water/wastewater plants, repairs that go 
beyond local expertise, and other difficult roadblocks.  
In summary, the supervision of water quality and sanitation on Indigenous Peoples’ land 
is critical to improving health disparities. Domestic water access in the United States is directly 
related to structural racism and needs further protection. Maintaining effective water 
infrastructure remains limited due to financial, technical, and administrative challenges that need 

to be reviewed thoroughly to engage in protecting marginalized communities. Please see below 
for additional details and pertinent literature.
Sincerely,
A Pace University Student

Re: 
Comments on EPA Proposed Clean Water Act Water Quality Standards Regulatory 
Revisions to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights, Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791 
Administrator Regan: 
Earthjustice files the following comments on behalf of the Mille Lacs Band of Ojibwe, the 
Bay Mills Indian Community, the Quinault Indian Nation, the Red Lake Band of Chippewa 
Indians, the Chickaloon Village Traditional Council, the Orutsararmiut Native Council, and the 
Swinomish Indian Tribal Community (collectively, the “Commenters”) on the Environmental 
Protection Agency’s (“EPA”) Clean Water Act Water Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions to 
Protect Tribal Reserved Rights (“Proposed Rule”).  87 Fed. Reg. 74361 (Dec. 5, 2022).  Protecting 
water quality is essential to protecting treaty rights and other reserved rights.  We strongly support 
EPA’s efforts to ensure protection of tribal reserved rights and offer the following comments for 
further consideration to help ensure effectiveness of the final rule. 
I. 
INTRODUCTION AND BACKGROUND 
The Mille Lacs Band of Ojibwe (Band) is a federally-recognized American Indian Tribe 
located in east-central Minnesota, with adjudicated reserved rights by retaining “[t]he privilege of 
hunting, fishing, and gathering the wild rice, upon the lands, the rivers and the lakes included in 
the territory ceded” in the 1837 Treaty of St. Peters (7 Stat. 536) and in the 1842 Treaty of La 
Pointe (7 Stat. 591) ceded territories in Minnesota, Wisconsin, and Michigan.  As a member of the 
Great Lakes Indian Fish and Wildlife Commission (GLIFWC), the Band coordinates with other 
member tribes and with the States in co-managing treaty-protected resources.  Additionally, the 
Band’s citizens “who possess a valid Tribal identification card from a federally recognized Tribe 
located in Minnesota are deemed to have a license to harvest wild rice anywhere within the State 
of Minnesota” per Minnesota Wild Rice Regulations. 
The Bay Mills Indian Community (Bay Mills) is a federally recognized American Indian 
Tribe and part of the Anishinaabe cultural-linguistic group. The Anishinaabe have inhabited what 
is today called Michigan since time immemorial and have relied on the Great Lakes ecosystem 

 
 
2 
 
and the Straits of Mackinac for their livelihood. The 1836 Treaty of Washington, (7 Stat. 491 
(1836)), ceded vast acres of land to the United States and guaranteed Bay Mills the right to hunt, 
fish, gather, and continue living as Anishinaabe in the ceded territory. 
Quinault Indian Nation is a federally recognized Indian tribe that occupies a reservation on 
the Olympic Peninsula in Washington state that includes over 200,000 acres of mostly forested 
land, thirty miles of undeveloped Pacific Coast beach lands, and thousands of miles of rivers and 
streams.  Quinault Indian Nation is a signatory to the Treaty of Olympia (1856) in which it reserved 
the right to take fish at its “usual and accustomed fishing grounds and stations” and the privilege 
of hunting and gathering, among other rights, in exchange for ceding lands it historically roamed 
freely.  12 Stat. 971 (1856).  Stewardship of natural resources is a paramount duty for the Quinault, 
as is protection of its homelands, on which its people have lived since time immemorial.  The 
Quinault have been called the Canoe people because of the primacy of the ocean, bays, estuaries, 
and rivers to every aspect of tribal life. 
The Red Lake Band of Chippewa Indians is a federally recognized Indian tribe that now 
occupies the Red Lake Reservation in Northern Minnesota. The Red Lake Reservation is the only 
closed Native American reservation in the United States, where there has never been allotment of 
tribal lands; where all land is held in common by the members; and where there is no non-Native 
ownership on the Red Lake Reservation. Red Lake also owns additional restored ceded lands in 
the approximate amount of 250,000 acres. The Band has been a party to multiple major treaties 
that impact Anishinaabe Territory, beginning with the 1825 Treaty of Prairie du Chien, the 1837 
Treaty of St. Peters, the Old Crossing Treaty of 1863, and additional treaties through 1904.  Red 
Lake members have historically depended, and continue to depend, on the natural freshwaters of 
Red Lake which lies both within the formal reservation and on ceded lands adjacent to it for their 
sustenance and economic livelihood.  Red Lake tribal members currently hunt large and small 
game, fish for many species of fish, and gather wild rice, edible plants, medicinal plants and other 
plant and animal species throughout the Red Lake Reservation, and on the lands that were ceded 
to the United States. 
Chickaloon Village Traditional Council (CVTC) is the governing body of Chickaloon 
Native Village (CNV), a federally recognized Ahtna Dene Tribal Government in Alaska that 
possesses all the inherent powers of a sovereign nation. CNV has not ceded, terminated, 
extinguished, or relinquished their original, possessory, and Indigenous rights or ancestral 
jurisdiction to any individual person, entity, or government. CNV’s ancestral territory and 
customary area of use encompasses much of Southcentral Alaska and extends from the Wrangell 
St. Elias Mountains and Copper River Watershed to the Talkeetna and Chugach Mountains and 
Upper Cook Inlet.  This territory includes countless watersheds, rivers, streams, lakes, and 
wetlands stewarded by CNV Tribal Citizens for thousands of years. CNV’s traditional area of 
influence overlaps neighboring Dena’ina Dene and Ahtna Dene federally recognized Tribes. CNV 
has a responsibility to steward and protect the environment, cultural resources, and the health of 
Tribal Citizens and community members in perpetuity.  
Orutsararmiut Native Council (ONC) is a federally recognized tribe located in the Yukon-
Kuskokwim region in Southwest Alaska. The ONC Tribal Council is the governing body of the 
Native Village of Bethel, the hub of the region. ONC’s mission is to promote the general welfare, 

 
 
3 
 
enhance independence, encourage self-sufficiency/self-motivation, enhance quality of life, and 
preserve cultural and traditional values of the Tribe, and to exercise tribal authority over resources 
through educational, economic, and social development opportunities. The Tribe is located along 
the Kuskokwim River, a resource of major cultural importance to the Tribe and the entire region. 
The ONC Tribal Council has a fundamental responsibility for protecting the ways of life and the 
health of its Tribal citizens and community members, which depend upon the region’s abundant 
fish, wildlife, and other natural resources. 
Since time immemorial, the Swinomish Indian Tribal Community and its forebears (Tribe) 
have occupied lands and waters in the northern Puget Sound region. Salmon and other fish 
(including shellfish) have played a central and enduring role in the Tribe’s subsistence, culture, 
identity and economy. In 1855, the Tribe signed the Treaty of Point Elliott with the United States. 
One of the core rights reserved by the Treaty is the right to take fish in its adjudicated usual and 
accustomed fishing areas and hunt and gather on open and unclaimed lands, which include, among 
others, the Skagit and Samish River basins and their tributaries and the lands and waters of northern 
Puget Sound. United States v. Washington, 459 F. Supp. 1020, 1049 (W.D. Wash. 1975). Water 
quality impairment harms salmon, other aquatic species, and terrestrial species and their habitats 
and therefore impairs the Tribe’s federal treaty rights.  
II. 
BACKGROUND ISSUES RELATED TO THE PROPOSED RULE  
A. 
Federal Trust Responsibility and EPA Requirements 
The federal government’s trust responsibility to tribes cannot be delegated to states or any 
other entity.  With this proposed rule, EPA makes great strides in recognizing that water quality 
can have significant impacts on tribal reserved rights and resources.  However, the proposed rule 
invites states to make determinations on tribal reserved rights.  EPA cannot delegate any of its 
duties or responsibilities that it holds under the federal trust responsibility to states or state 
agencies.  Ultimately, the duty to ensure that state water quality standards (WQS) are actually 
protective of tribal reserved rights rests with the EPA and the federal government.  A system 
involving state evaluation of whether tribal reserved rights are present in state waters, and state 
determinations of whether state WQS need to be revised to protect tribal reserved rights, inherently 
includes risk that states will make decisions on tribal reserved rights that exceed their authority, 
impermissibly curtail tribal rights, and potentially are inconsistent with federal law other state or 
tribal requirements.  EPA must ensure that it is involved throughout the entirety of the process and 
that it is not delegating final decision-making authority on tribal reserved rights to states.   
EPA has a duty to protect tribal reserved rights regardless of whether they are reserved 
expressly or implicitly, or whether they are reserved by treaty, statute, executive order, or other 
source of federal law.  Although the proposed rule includes this in the definition of a tribal reserved 
right, EPA must ensure that the implementation and application of this definition does not require 
tribes to litigate or otherwise adjudicate whether reserved rights exist, or whether those rights 
apply, if not already clear.  States cannot require a tribe to litigate or adjudicate a tribal reserved 
right as part of the process of setting WQS.   

 
 
4 
 
EPA must also clarify its role in and process for facilitating information sharing between 
tribes and states and mediating differences between tribes and states.  Historically, many tribes 
have had difficulty working with state agencies and the process can be fraught.  The proposed rule 
invites tribes to provide data or other information to be evaluated by states as they develop or 
revise state WQS.  EPA, as both federal trustee to tribes and reviewer of state WQS, must have a 
defined role in resolving potential conflicts so as to ensure that tribal reserved rights are protected 
throughout the process.   
EPA must outline how sensitive information, including Indigenous Knowledge (IK), will 
be used and protected throughout the process.  Historically, tribes have been reluctant to share data 
with states due to state disclosure laws or other state failures to protect tribal information.  We 
suggest a potential solution to this issue is that data from work performed under Clean Water Act 
Section 106 funding should be made public, even to the states, but data from work performed with 
tribal funds should be kept private, as part of a tribe’s intellectual property.  EPA should require 
states to develop protocols and procedures for how it will protect sensitive information as part of 
the process of developing or revising WQS.  Although the proposed rule suggests that EPA and 
states “should discuss in advance how the information will be shared and potentially used in the 
WQS context,” 87 Fed. Reg. at 74367, n.48, EPA must make this a requirement.  Without assured 
protections for sensitive tribal information, tribal input into state WQS development will be 
inhibited.  Federal agencies are currently in the process of seeking information about gathering, 
protecting, 
and 
applying 
IK 
to 
federal 
decision-making 
processes. 
 
See, 
e.g., 
https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2022/12/OSTP-CEQ-IK-Guidance.pdf.  Those 
processes and procedures can and should be followed by states to increase consistency, 
transparency and efficiency. 
B. 
Tribal Considerations 
EPA must consider the practical impacts that tribes will face throughout the process.  Tribes 
may not have readily available data, or the funding or staff necessary to gather relevant data on 
existing water quality or what level of water quality is required to protect tribal reserved rights.  
EPA must acknowledge and address this data and funding gap that tribes may face as the proposed 
rule is implemented.  EPA must also make explicit that if a tribe does not participate in the initial 
process for state revisions of WQS, that it is not later precluded from doing so.  Tribes may need 
time to gather both current and historical data to submit to EPA and states, especially on evolving 
issues such as climate change.  
C. 
Implementation and Enforcement 
EPA must clarify how it will review state implementation and enforcement of WQS 
developed to protect tribal reserved rights.  Developing WQS that protect tribal reserved rights is 
only useful if states are actually implementing and enforcing those standards.  In the past, tribes 
have had difficulty getting states to consider their requests for protection of off-reservation aquatic 
resources, and in getting states to apply those protections comprehensively.  There is potential for 
states and tribes to have conflicting data, conflicting priorities in protecting waterbodies, different 
standards for similar designated uses, and different models of how changes in water quality will 
impact tribal reserved resources.  Ideologically, states and tribes may differ on how climate change 

 
 
5 
 
will impact water resources and tribal reserved rights, and how those resources should be managed.  
States already have a mechanism through variances to avoid meeting WQS set to protect 
designated uses.  40 C.F.R. §131.14.  See also Upper Missouri Waterkeeper v. EPA, 15 F.4th 966, 
975 (9th Cir. 2021) (finding that approved variances “replace[] the base water quality standard 
with the most rigorous standard that can feasibly be attained”).  EPA must ensure that these 
mechanisms are not abused such that water quality continues to deteriorate and erode tribal 
reserved rights.  One solution is for states and tribes to co-manage waters where tribal rights exist.     
III. 
COMMENTS ON THE PROPOSED RULE 
A. 
Determining the Tribal Reserved Right 
EPA acknowledges that it may be a complex inquiry to determine if tribal rights apply in 
waters subject to state WQS, and if so, the nature of those rights and where they apply. 87 Fed. 
Reg. 74367.  EPA also acknowledges that tribal reserved rights can be derived from multiple 
sources, including treaties, statutes, executive orders, and other sources of federal law.  Id. at 
74366.  While we support EPA’s efforts to acknowledge tribal reserved rights and the need for 
protection of those rights in water and water dependent resources, EPA must also acknowledge 
that the nature and scope of those rights have often been the subject of decades-long court battles.  
In some instances, controversies have resulted in violence against tribal members attempting to 
exercise their rights.  Tribal rights to and use of off-reservation resources is an issue that is far 
from settled, and while we support EPA’s proposed rule, implementation may result in further 
controversy and litigation. 
EPA needs to recognize that determination of the scope and location of a right, as well as 
how the right is exercised, may in some areas be extremely controversial and met with state or 
inter-tribal resistance.  Tribes may have very good reasons to protect information such as cultural 
uses of certain water bodies, location of certain plants or other species, and may be averse to 
agreeing to a limited definition or scope of a right.  Establishment of a system where a state 
government attempts to define, at least in part, the scope of a tribal treaty right, may well have 
unintended negative consequences, including inconsistency with federal law or federal 
adjudications.  Often, tribal rights have been diminished or curtailed by state actors, and it may be 
difficult for tribes, particularly small tribes or those that are not well-resourced, to enter into 
protracted negotiations with state officials in the event of a disagreement between state and tribal 
officials as to the scope, location and nature of a right.  EPA should consider providing a dispute 
resolution mechanism, policy or set of guidelines for when states and tribes disagree as to the 
scope, location and type of tribal reserved right, and the level of protections required to protect 
those rights and resources.  Minor modifications to the dispute resolution provisions at 40 C.F.R. 
§ 131.7 could potentially provide a solution to this issue. 
We also note the possibility that the tribal outreach process could differ state by state.  EPA 
should require a certain minimum threshold for states engaging in outreach to right holders, such 
as requiring states to adhere to a certain uniform process or policy for outreach and recordkeeping 
requirements.  Requiring a uniform process will help to ensure consideration of tribal reserved 
rights even if a state government is hostile to tribal rights.  This will also make the process more 
efficient for right holders in the event that submissions to multiple states are necessary. This will 

 
 
6 
 
also help to minimize incidences where state political changes result in changes to the level or 
scope of protection for tribal reserved rights. 
In addition to the rights to hunt, fish, and gather, tribal reserved rights may include 
agricultural, ceremonial and cultural uses.  We also note that the canons of construction of Indian 
law dictate that EPA must consider that tribes likely believed at the time treaties were signed that 
the reserved resources would be useable – i.e., fish that are safe to eat, water that is safe to drink 
and bathe in, and plants that are not genetically modified. See, e.g., U.S. v. Winans, 198 U.S. 371 
(1905); Washington v. Washington State Commercial Passenger Fishing Vessel Ass’n, 443 U.S. 
658 (1979).  
B. 
Determining the Level of Water Quality 
1. 
Information Related to Unsuppressed Use 
EPA proposes to require that state WQS, to the extent supported by available data and 
information, be established to protect the exercise of tribal reserved rights unsuppressed by water 
quality or availability of the resource.  EPA requests comment on whether additional language 
should be included in the final rule specifying the considerations for determining unsuppressed 
WQS.  
States should be required to consider available data and information including tribally 
produced historical data about resource abundance and location, historical and current tribal uses 
of resources, and Traditional Ecological Knowledge (TEK).  In considering the information 
underlying the WQS, EPA should give equal weight to tribally produced data, articles, or reports.  
This includes TEK or other forms of IK that may not have been considered or included in previous 
state reviews of WQS.  EPA must also weigh tribally produced data, information, or reports equally 
with state-produced data or information when resolving conflicts.  
As mentioned above, federal agencies currently are developing best practices for obtaining, 
protecting, and applying IK to federal decision-making.  States should be required to follow a 
standard process for investigating, keeping and applying IK in a way that is protected and is 
consistent with the federal standards developed.  Without a standard process or procedure, tribes 
may be reluctant to commit the time and resources necessary to gather and provide sensitive 
information to states, particularly if there is no guarantee that sensitive cultural information will 
be protected from Freedom of Information Act requests, that tribal information and knowledge 
will be appropriately considered applied, or that tribally compiled data will not be rejected as 
unusable or minimized.  Thus, it is important for tribes and states to have a common understanding 
of how information will be gathered, protected, and applied in this process, and for that process to 
be uniform across the states. 
Monitoring and year-over-year data gathering needed to establish appropriately protective 
WQS is a long-term and potentially costly process.  Meaningful tribal involvement will require 
staff and resources to ensure tribes have the ability to engage over the long term.  Establishing 
protective WQS has the potential to be particularly complex if there is a goal of reestablishing uses 
lost due to pollution or degradation or restoring damaged or diminished resources.  EPA should 

 
 
7 
 
consider, and provide, the level of support in terms of staffing, funding and research that will be 
necessary for tribes to fully participate in the development of adequately protective WQS.  
Similarly, states should be required to provide relevant information to tribes as needed when doing 
so will assist in the process of WQS development necessary for protection of reserved rights and 
restoration of resources to a level that will support the exercise of those rights.  
EPA has stated that where information is conflicting, there are gaps in information and/or 
a difference of opinion exists between the state and one or more tribes about the level of water 
quality necessary to protect a reserved right, EPA will take action based on the best available 
information in the same way that EPA currently makes WQS decisions in these circumstances in 
other contexts, e.g., determining whether criteria are scientifically defensible in situations where 
there is conflicting science, there are gaps in the science, and/or there are different conclusions 
among stakeholders.  When making decisions under these circumstances, EPA also should 
consider the extent to which the tribal reserved rights have already been diminished, the years and 
decades where tribals citizens were prevented from exercising reserved rights, the tribes whose 
rights were terminated or not federally recognized, and take into consideration the circumstances 
surrounding the conflicting information or why informational gaps exist.  EPA should err on the 
side of protectiveness and restoration of a resource, as contemplated by the CWA itself. 
EPA notes that there may be situations where existing water quality is lower than necessary 
to allow for right holders to fully exercise their tribal reserved rights.  87 Fed. Reg. 74368.  EPA 
also notes that an unsuppressed level should balance heritage use of a resource with what is 
currently reasonably achievable for a particular waterbody.  Id. at 74369.  States and tribes may 
differ with regard to what is currently reasonably achievable.  Tribal cultural practices and resource 
management approaches often dictate a longer-term and more comprehensive approach than those 
selected by state or federal governments.  Tribal practices may emphasize preservation of a 
resource over development or economic use of a resource.  Tribal preferences may be to avoid 
degradation of water or water-dependent resources at all costs.  Accordingly, this could be an area 
of ongoing controversy or disagreement between state and tribal governments that share rights to 
certain resources. 
Where feasible, state and tribal co-management of aquatic and aquatic-dependent resources 
could be the most fruitful and efficient approach to protection and restoration of waters and 
resources that have been degraded or damaged to the point where tribal uses are no longer being 
practiced.  For example, this approach may be successful for specific areas or shared waterbodies.  
EPA also should consider co-management frameworks where multiple tribes have reserved rights 
to a waterbody, or where tribes have rights to inter-state resources or waterbodies.  For example, 
for GLIFWC member tribes, limited co-management is already exercised in accordance to the 
Voigt Decision.  Lac Courte Oreilles (LCO) v. Voigt (LCO I), 700 F.2d 341, 365 (7th Cir. 1983).  
However, the tribal role in co-management may be increased, as equity in co-management has the 
potential to encourage efficiency and a common approach to protecting the health of the entire 
watershed. 

 
 
8 
 
2. 
Health Criteria 
Proposed 40 C.F.R. § 131.9(a)(2) would require that the health of right holders be protected 
to at least the same risk level as the general population of the state would have been protected, had 
the general population been the “target population” for water quality protections in the waters at 
issue.  EPA anticipates the primary application of this provision to be in using a cancer risk level 
appropriate for a general population, i.e., at least 10-5, along with a fish consumption rate that 
reflects the reserved right for the purpose of calculating human health criteria.  
We support a practice of erring on the side of protectiveness, particularly if EPA is 
requiring WQS to be set at a level to protect unsuppressed use of a resource by right holders.  EPA 
must consider that some tribal or subsistence-based practices result in exposure to toxins from 
multiple pathways.  Uses in addition to hunting, fishing and gathering include cultural, ceremonial 
and agricultural uses—for example, bathing, drinking or engaging in ceremonies at certain waters 
or with certain species.  Accordingly, a 10-6 acceptable cancer risk rate with an appropriate fish 
consumption rate may be more appropriate.  We also encourage EPA to require consideration of 
these circumstances and uses in any future updates or revisions to the EPA 2000 Methodology for 
Deriving Ambient Water Quality Criteria for the Protection of Human Health; the National 
Environmental Justice Advisory Council 2002 publication Fish Consumption and Environmental 
Justice; and the 1985 Guidelines for Deriving Numerical National Water Quality Criteria for the 
Protection of Aquatic Organisms and Their Uses. 
C. 
Revising Water Quality Standards 
The proposed rule provides three options for states to revise WQS if needed to ensure 
protection of tribal reserved rights via designated uses, protective criteria, or antidegradation 
provisions.  The final rule should reflect that the preferred avenue for states to protect tribal 
reserved rights is by adopting designated uses specific to tribal reserved rights.  Establishing 
designated uses that clearly encompass tribal reserved rights ensures that states are actively 
considering tribal reserved rights as part of their water quality programs, rather than assuming that 
tribal reserved rights will be considered under some other designated use(s).  Even if attainment is 
not currently feasible, the states can still set designated uses as aspirational.  Indeed, the purpose 
of the CWA is to restore and revive water bodies and states must actively work towards that goal.   
In establishing designated uses specific to tribal reserved rights, states should also consider 
adopting or incorporating designated uses that tribes may have established as part of their own 
EPA approved WQS.  EPA should also weigh tribal designated uses when reviewing state WQS 
as part of the determination of whether the proposed state WQS are protective of tribal reserved 
rights.  Tribes with EPA-approved programs may have already collected data necessary to protect 
important or relevant resources.   
States may also adopt protective criteria but can do so in addition to adopting a designated 
use protective of tribal reserved rights.  Associating protective criteria with an already existing 
designated use may not ensure that tribal reserved rights are specifically contemplated and 
protected throughout the state process.  EPA should not allow states to rely solely on 
antidegradation policy options as a mechanism to protect tribal reserved rights in lieu of 

 
 
9 
 
establishing tribal reserved rights designated uses.  States are already required to have 
antidegradation policies in place to ensure that state water quality does not backslide.  Adopting 
designated uses that focus specifically on tribal rights would help ensure that tribal resources are 
protected through state programs, including through antidegradation measures.  
EPA has requested comments on whether and how states can revise designated uses, as 
provided by § 131.10, while also ensuring the protection of tribal reserved rights.  We recommend 
adding language to § 131.9 stating that a state may not remove a use where a waterbody is subject 
to tribal reserved rights unless it can demonstrate that all tribes whose rights are impacted consent 
in writing to removal of the use, and that any tribal consent to the removal of the use may include 
conditions (e.g., revisiting the use attainability analysis at regular intervals, revitalization efforts 
for other waterbodies or resources, co-management, or other collaborative efforts).  We also 
recommend that language should be added to § 131.9 stating that a state must demonstrate that 
where it seeks to apply a variance under § 131.14 or permit compliance schedule under § 131.15 
impacting tribal reserved rights, the state has conducted timely outreach efforts to tribes whose 
rights are impacted, obtained written consent from the tribe(s), and has implemented reasonable 
conditions as requested by the right holders.  The state or the right holder should have a provision 
to be able to seek EPA involvement and final approval. 
IV. 
OTHER ISSUES 
EPA recognizes its obligations to work with both federally recognized tribes and all other 
Indigenous peoples.  87 Fed. Reg. 74377, n.88.  Accordingly, the definition of “Indian Tribe” at 
40 C.F.R. § 131.3(l), “any Indian Tribe, band, group, or community recognized by the Secretary 
of the Interior and exercising governmental authority over a Federal Indian reservation,” should 
be revised because there are federally recognized tribes and Indigenous groups who do not have 
governmental authority over a Federal Indian reservation but who may nevertheless retain use 
rights entitled to protection under the proposed rule.   
We note that the bulk of the tribal responses to comments on EPA’s initial request for 
comment and tribal consultation pertain to regions where tribal off-reservation treaty rights have 
already been adjudicated.  However, there are a number of states where tribes or Indigenous 
communities exist whose off-reservation use rights have not been adjudicated, whose treaties were 
not ratified, and whose uses have not been protected by states. Further, even in states where off-
reservation treaty rights have been adjudicated, not all areas of the state may have been 
adjudicated.  Those rights and uses are still entitled to protection under the CWA. 
Per 40 C.F.R. § 131.3(f) and § 131.12(a)(2), any use actually attained in a water body on 
or after November 28, 1975 is entitled to protection.  The fact that tribal uses have not been 
recognized or protected by states does not negate the existing rule, and the proposed rule only 
highlights that both existing and historical uses of state-regulated waters by Indigenous people 
must be recognized and incorporated into state WQS.

Proposed Rule on Water Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions To Protect Tribal Reserved 
Rights, 87 Fed. Reg. 74361 (Tribal Rights Rule). The proposed Tribal Rights Rule would apply 
to all states, including Maine, that administer or oversee water quality programs. It sets forth a 
new uniform regulatory approach requiring the protection of tribal reserved rights and 
contemplates consideration and implementation by states of new or revised provisions in their 
water quality standards (WQS). 
Application of the Tribal Rights Rule, which adopts a similar approach to the one EPA 
abandoned in prior WQS litigation with the State, in Maine is both unnecessary and ineffective. 
The State of Maine, through a productive collaboration with EPA and the federally recognized 
tribes in Maine,1  and as a matter of voluntary state environmental regulatory policy, has already 
adopted similar state law provisions that were approved by EPA Region 1. These Maine WQS

The Maine Settlement Acts are unique.
 Maine has a nationally unique tribal-state 
relationship set forth in two statutes: the Maine Implementing Act (MIA), 30 M.R.S. §§ 6201-
6214 (2011 & Supp. 2022), and the Maine Indian Land Claims Settlement Act (MICSA), 25 U.S.C.

that establishes the general application of state law on tribal lands and delineates the areas of tribal 
jurisdiction.3

The Tribal Rights Rule would not apply in Maine. EPA's Tribal Rights Rule represents a 
proposed "uniform approach for establishment of WQS" with respect to tribal rights through 
"rulemaking rather than during review of individual state action" on a case-by-case basis in response 
to individual state WQS submissions. 87 Fed. Reg. at 74366. Such an approach is antithetical to 
core provisions of the Settlement Acts. Under the Acts, Maine has statewide environmental 
regulatory jurisdiction, including in all tribal areas, and the State's environmental and natural 
resource laws apply uniformly to the Tribes and their members, lands, and natural resources to the 
same extent as any other Maine citizens, lands, and natural resources. 30 M.R.S. §§ 6202, 6204; 
25 U.S.C. §§ 1721(b), 1725(a); Johnson, 498 F.3d at 42-46 (affirming Maine's statewide 
environmental regulatory jurisdiction). The proposed Tribal Rights Rule, however, creates a new 
tribal-specific framework that, most prominently with the addition of proposed § 131.9, requires 
state protection of tribal reserved rights and may require new or revised state WQS to protect such 
rights. This is contrary to the Settlement Act provisions requiring the uniform application of 
Maine's environmental and natural resource laws without regard to tribal status. 
It is also contrary to additional MICSA provisions that would bar application of the entirety 
of the Tribal Rights Rule with respect to Maine. The rule's new uniform regulatory approach to 
evaluating tribal rights would create special and heightened status, rights, and protections for the 
Tribes and their members, and Congress has not specifically made such provisions applicable in 
Maine. 25 U.S.C. §§ 1725(h), 1735(b).9  Moreover, any new or revised Maine WQS that EPA

Dear Administrator Regan: 
The North Dakota Department of Environmental Quality' (NDDEQ) appreciates the opportunity 
to comment on the proposed revisions to the Water Quality Standards (40 C.F.R. pt. 131) to protect 
Tribal Reserved Rights. See 87 Fed. Reg. 74361 (proposed Dec. 5, 2022) (to be codified at 40 
C.F.R. pt. 131) (Proposed Rule). NDDEQ, which has the authority for implementing North 
Dakota's Water Quality Standards (WQS) as required by 33 U.S.C. § 1313, supports engaging 
tribes in the standard-setting process. However, the Proposed Rule is not the appropriate 
mechanism to do so. It will not "provide clarity, transparency, and predictability" but will instead 
create confusion and chaos. 87 Fed. Reg. at 74366. 
NDDEQ therefore requests that the 
Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) reject the Proposed Rule. 
I. 
The Proposed Rule cannot be implemented. 
The Proposed Rule cannot be implemented because the foundational step of the rule is impossible 
to execute. Under the Proposed Rule, states must first determine if tribal reserved rights apply in 
waters subject to state WQS. 87 Fed. Reg. at 74367. EPA acknowledges that this "may be a 
complex inquiry," but fails to recognize that making this determination is beyond the scope of 
authority and outside the expertise of both EPA and NDDEQ. Id. NDDEQ is not aware of anything 
in the Clean Water Act (CWA), 33 U.S.C. § 1251 et seq., that gives it — or EPA — the authority to 
determine tribal reserved rights. NDDEQ and EPA are environmental experts, not Indian law 
experts. 
Treaty rights are socially, politically, and legally complex issues. EPA's overly simplistic directive 
that states should just ask the right holder ignores the reality that states may have no idea who 
possible right holders are, particularly for tribes that are no longer located in the state, and that 
NDDEQ also supports and joins the comments submitted by the Association of Clean Water 
Administrators.

determining tribal reserved rights. EPA, Summary Report of Tribal Consultation for the Proposed 
Rule: Water Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights (Oct. 
2021),https ://www.epa. gov/system/files/documents/2022-1 1/summary-report-trib al-consultation-
proposed-rule-wqs.pdf. Neither EPA nor NDDEQ is the proper entity to make a determination in 
the event of a treaty dispute. 
Not only would the Proposed Rule require NDDEQ to undertake a task certain to fail, but it would 
also harm the relationship between the State of North Dakota and the tribes. NDDEQ strives to 
have a good working relationship with its tribal counterparts. Putting NDDEQ in the middle of 
possible treaty disputes would injure this relationship. The Proposed Rule will harm state-tribal 
relations. 
11. 
The Proposed Rule is unnecessary. 
When developing WQS, NDDEQ already determines the level of water quality necessary to 
protect aquatic life and users of the resource. See 40 C.F.R. § 131.6. Like all states, NDDEQ 
conducts a triennial review of its WQS that includes the opportunity for public comment. See 40 
C.F.R. § 131.20. If NDDEQ is aware of a tribal reserved right, it will ensure that use is protected 
during its triennial review of its WQS. If there is a tribal reserved right that NDDEQ is unaware 
of, a right holder can bring that to NDDEQ's attention during the triennial review or by simply 
contacting NDDEQ. 
As EPA recognizes, "fflor many aquatic and aquatic-dependent resources that tribes have rights 
to fish, hunt or gather, the existing Federal WQS regulations already require states to provide a 
level of protection consistent with this proposed rulemaking." 87 Fed. Reg. at 74370. EPA 
identifies two categories that may require revisions to a state's WQS: fish consumers and wild 
rice. Id. at 74371. But it is not necessary to revise the existing Federal WQS regulations to address 
these two circumstances. If a population is more vulnerable due to cultural difference (e.g., above 
average consumption of aquatic organisms) or physically (e.g., child, youth, or sex), there is 
authority under 40 C.F.R. § 131.4(a) to write WQS more stringent than required by CWA Sections 
101(a)(2) or 304(a). 
In its Proposed Rule, which requires that WQS must protect the health of the right holders to the 
same risk level as provided to the general population of the state, EPA gives the impression that it 
does not believe states develop WQS protective of everyone regardless of their geographic 
location. 87 Fed. Reg. at 74366. This is inaccurate and disrespectful to state partners. 
III. 
The Proposed Rule is an unfunded mandate. 
EPA states, "[t]his action does not contain any unfunded mandate as described in [the Unfunded 
Mandates Reform Act] UMRA, 2 U.S.C. 1531-1538 . . . ." Id. at 74375. However, if adopted the 
2 

proposed revisions and additions to 40 C.F.R. pt. 131 would require investing a substantial increase 
of labor and expertise in the WQS review process, with no mechanism to pay for it. 
For example, as proposed, the revisions would require: (1) the state to determine if a Tribal 
Reserved Right applies to a state water; (2) the nature of the right (i.e., a fishing right, a hunting 
right, a resource gathering right); (3) where the right applies (i.e., to a specific set of waterbodies 
or to waters generally within a broad geographic area); and (4) how the right is exercised by the 
right holders (e.g., for subsistence purposes). 
States would then have to develop WQS to protect any tribal reserved rights that were determined 
to be applicable. This would require determining the level of water quality necessary to protect 
users of the resource and/or the aquatic or aquatic-dependent resource itself, based on available 
data. This level of water quality is to be determined by applying proposed 40 C.F.R. § 131.9(a)(1) 
& (2) by requiring the state to: (1) determine the level of water quality needed to protect the right; 
(2) accounting for suppression effects and protecting right holders to the same risk levels as the 
general population. 87 Fed. Reg. at 74366. 
IV. 
Conclusion 
NDDEQ urges EPA to reject the Proposed Rule. The Proposed Rule cannot be implemented, and 
is unnecessary and unfunded. Where tribal reserved rights require additional consideration of the 
appropriate WQS for relevant waters, EPA should work with the states and tribes, using the 
existing tools available under the Federal WQS regulations. 
Sincerely, 
L. David Glatt, 
Director

RE:   
Comments on Environmental Protection Agency Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791 -- 
Water Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights (Proposed 
Rule) 
Dear Administrator Regan, 
These comments are submitted on behalf of the Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe, Port Gamble 
S’Klallam Tribe, and Suquamish Indian Tribe (collectively, “the Tribes”) in response to the 
Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA’s) “Water Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions to Protect 
Tribal Reserved Rights (Proposed Rule),” 87 Fed. Reg. 74,361 (Dec. 5, 2023). The Tribes sincerely 
appreciate EPA’s efforts to “provide a nationally applicable regulatory framework to ensure that [water 
quality standards (WQS)] protect applicable reserved rights.” Id. at 74,366. We agree with EPA that the 
proposed rule will provide “clarity, predictability, and transparency,” and that there is an urgent need for 
this. Id. EPA’s efforts to propose a “uniform approach for establishment of WQS where tribal reserved 
rights apply and [to] clearly [lay] out how EPA will review such WQS” is appreciated. Id. Not only will 
this ensure a consistent approach across regions, but it will also ensure more durable decisions that do not 
become easily subject to whims of changing administrations. While these comments suggest several 
improvements—some crucial—to the proposed rule (“Reserved Rights Rule” or “rule”), the Tribes 
generally support the rule and look forward to working with EPA and Washington to implement it.  
I.  
THE TRIBES AND THEIR CITIZENS DEPEND ON CLEAN WATER FOR THE FREE 
AND SAFE EXERCISE OF THE RESERVED RIGHTS AT THE HEART OF THEIR 
CULTURES, ECONOMIES, AND CEREMONIAL LIFE.  
 
The Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe, Port Gamble S’Klallam Tribe, and Suquamish Indian Tribe are 
fishing tribes. Since time immemorial, fishing has been the foundation on which their cultures, 
economies, and ceremonial life were based. In 1855, when the Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe and Port 
Gamble S’Klallam Tribe entered the Treaty of Point No Point1 and the Suquamish Indian Tribe entered 
the Treaty of Point Elliott2 with the United States, sacred promises were made between sovereign nations. 
These three Tribes and others ceded hundreds of thousands of acres of their homelands, while reserving 
 
1 12 Stat. 933. 
2 12 Stat. 927. 

 
 
 
 
Page 2 of 32 
 
certain rights to themselves. Chief among the rights reserved—and persistently defended by the Tribes—
is the right to continue taking fish and shellfish as they always had throughout their usual and accustomed 
fishing grounds (U&A), as well as to hunt and gather across open and unclaimed lands in their ancestral 
territory. Article 4 of the 1855 Treaty of Point No Point and Article 5 of the 1855 Treaty of Point Elliott 
state: 
The right of taking fish at usual and accustomed grounds and stations is further secured to 
said Indians, in common with all citizens of the United States; and of erecting temporary 
houses for the purpose of curing; together with the privilege of hunting and gathering 
roots and berries on open and unclaimed lands. 
With this treaty language, these three Tribes, like other Treaty Tribes in Western Washington, reserved to 
themselves fundamental rights that they had exercised since time immemorial. The Treaties were intended 
to allow the Tribes and their citizens to continue their ways of life in the face of white settlement, both at 
that time and in perpetuity, in large part by continuing robust tribal harvest of fish in off-reservation 
marine waters and freshwater rivers and lakes, as well as hunting and gathering in open and unclaimed 
lands. And in addition to extinguishing tribal land claims to pave the way for orderly non-native 
settlement, the treaty-makers’ recognition of these reserved rights secured for the United States, as 
instructed by their superiors in Washington, D.C., the crucial practical benefit of not having to pay for the 
Indians’ perpetual subsistence.  
The United States, for its part, made promises in the Treaties that were designed to endure 
forever. By making these promises, the United States took on trust obligations to the Tribes. The United 
States Government, as Trustee for the Tribes, has a sacred responsibility to protect the Tribes’ access to 
clean water in order to ensure these sacred rights can be exercised fully forever. Fish are of central 
importance to the Tribes’ culture, economies, ceremonies and diets. The United States Supreme Court has 
recognized the central importance of fishing for tribes:  it is “not much less necessary to the existence of 
the Indians than the air they breathed.” United States v Winans, 198 U.S. 371, 381 (1905). Likewise, as 
discussed in greater detail in Section III.B. below, the Supreme Court has long held that when land has 
been reserved to a tribe, a reservation of water sufficient to meet the purposes of the reservation is 
implied. Winters v. United States, 207 U.S. 564, 576-77 (1908). A reserved right to take fish also 
impliedly reserves water necessary to fulfill that purpose, that is, water sufficient to keep streams suitable 
for fish reproduction and tribal harvest. E.g., United States v. Adair, 723 F.2d 1394, 1414-15 (9th Cir. 
1983) (tribe reserved the waters needed to “secure to the Tribe a continuation of its traditional . . . fishing 
lifestyle”); Kittitas Reclamation District v. Sunnyside Valley Irrigation District, 763 F.2d 1032, 1033-34 
(9th Cir. 1985) (water withdrawals that would destroy salmon eggs before they could hatch enjoined to 
protect treaty fishing right); Colville Confederated Tribes v. Walton, 647 F.2d 42, 47-48 (9th Cir. 1981) 
(implied reservation of water to preserve tribe’s replacement fishing grounds); Dep’t of Ecology v. 
Yakima Reservation Irrig. Dist. (Aquavella II), 121 Wash. 2d 257, 276-77 (Wash. 1993) (implied 
reservation of instream water to fulfill treaty right to take fish). 
 
Despite the promises made, the Tribes’ way of life is now severely threatened. Rivers, streams, 
bays, straits, lakes, and wetlands across the State of Washington—and throughout the Tribes’ off-
reservation usual and accustomed fishing grounds and open and unclaimed hunting and gathering lands—
are polluted and subject to fish advisories that warn people not to eat fish they catch lest they risk cancer 
and other diseases. Tribal members are left with the dilemma of whether to continue sustenance fishing 
and imperil their health, or to forgo sustenance fishing and imperil their culture. In waters in which Tribes 

 
 
 
 
Page 3 of 32 
 
reserved, through Treaties, their right to continue fishing as they had since time immemorial, tribal 
members should not be subjected to such a dilemma. Wildlife populations that the Tribes are dependent 
on are at risk from dehydration, illness, and death when drinking polluted waters. These waters and rights 
are entitled to protection under federal law, including under the Clean Water Act, which recognizes that 
tribal fishing, hunting, and gathering is the kind of use entitled to protection through appropriate water 
quality standards.  
 
Like other Treaty Tribes of Western Washington, the Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe, the Port 
Gamble S’Klallam Tribe, and the Suquamish Indian Tribe ceded most of their land but reserved their 
rights by treaty to fishing, hunting, and gathering. Today, over 150 years after signing the Treaty of Point 
No Point and the Treaty of Point Elliott, the Tribes retain deep cultural and economic ties to the 
surrounding waters and to their fisheries. The Lower Elwha Reservation and adjacent tribal trust lands 
comprise 1,017 acres with roughly 900 acres along the Elwha River, where it flows into the Strait of Juan 
de Fuca, and the Port Gamble Reservation comprises roughly 1,788 acres on Port Gamble Bay. The 
waters around these respective reservations constitute a core area for each Tribe, but both Tribes also 
depend heavily on harvest of fish, shellfish, and other aquatic resources throughout the larger, shared 
U&A. More than 150 Port Gamble tribal members and 100 Lower Elwha tribal members earn all or a 
portion of their livelihood working as commercial salmon and shellfish fishers. The Suquamish Indian 
Tribe is located on the Port Madison Indian Reservation along the shores of Puget Sound and is 
comprised of 7,657 acres. Because there are no large rivers in Suquamish’s territory, the Suquamish 
Indian Tribe is one of the few Western Washington Tribes who historically and currently travels to and 
covers a vast fishing area to harvest marine resources within its U&A. More than 140 Suquamish tribal 
members earn all or a portion of their livelihood working as commercial salmon and shellfish fishermen. 
Within their respective U&A, the Tribes that share the U&A are entitled to take half the harvestable fish 
and shellfish. In addition, each Tribe conducts fisheries throughout the shared U&A to obtain fish for 
ceremonial use (including funerals, weddings, and honoring and gifting observances, as well as other 
ceremonies and practices), and subsistence harvests from the Tribes’ U&A are a key element of the diet 
of many tribal members. These treaty rights continue to be of central spiritual, cultural, subsistence and 
economic importance to the Tribes. Indeed, they are central to the Tribes’ identity, and in reserving these 
rights, the Tribes reserved their lifeways.  
II. 
EPA’S PROPOSAL TO PROTECT TRIBAL RESERVED RIGHTS THROUGH WATER 
QUALITY STANDARDS IS CONSISTENT WITH—AND DEMANDED BY—BOTH 
FEDERAL INDIAN LAW AND THE CLEAN WATER ACT. 
Clean water is necessary to support tribal lifeways. It is a matter of vital importance to all people 
of the State of Washington, and of particularly vital importance to the Tribes, whose cultural, spiritual and 
subsistence practices require consuming much higher levels of aquatic species—including fish, wildlife, 
and plants that are vulnerable to toxic chemicals—than the general population. In order to safely eat fish 
and to ensure fish populations are of harvestable size, the habitat upon which they depend must be clean 
and protected. Ancient tribal customs and traditions reflect this reality by proscribing waste, regulating 
distribution of the catch to ensure appropriate upstream sharing and perpetuation of the fish runs, and 
discouraging water pollution. Modern tribal fisheries management, under which the Tribes are recognized 
co-managers with the State of Washington, builds on these traditions. Tribes are at the forefront of sound 
hatchery practices, habitat restoration, and cleanup of toxic contamination of fresh and marine waters. 
Although highly dependent on clean water, until very recently, EPA and the State of Washington 

 
 
 
 
Page 4 of 32 
 
had not considered the Tribes’ reserved rights when developing water quality standards, and therefore, the 
Tribes historically have not been afforded the full protection of the Clean Water Act. In turn, this has 
placed the burden of western development and industry on the Tribes, forcing them to choose between 
engaging in cultural and subsistence practices or sacrificing the health and welfare of tribal elders, tribal 
children, and other tribal members. As our Trustee, the U.S. Government must meet its trust obligation to 
the Tribes and ensure that stringent water quality standards are promulgated to ensure the protection of 
our reserved rights across our usual and accustomed areas and open and unclaimed lands.  
A.  
EPA’s Description of Tribal Reserved Rights and the Federal Indian Law That 
Requires Their Protection Is Accurate. 
The Tribes appreciate EPA’s commitment to doing that through promulgation of the Reserved 
Rights Rule. EPA is correct that “tribal reserved rights to resources are an intrinsic part of tribal life and 
are of deep cultural, economic, and subsistence importance to tribes.” 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,363. In the 
preamble to the proposed rule, the agency describes well the origin and sources of reserved rights, such as 
the right to take fish off-reservation that was reserved by many tribes in the Pacific Northwest. Id. at 
74,363-64. The agency also correctly acknowledges that “tribal reserved rights encompass subsidiary 
rights that are not explicitly addressed in treaty or statutory language but are necessary to render those 
rights meaningful.”3 Id. at 74,364 (citing United States v. Winans, 198 U.S. 371, 381 (1905); United 
States v. Washington, 853 F.3d 946, 966 (9th Cir. 2017), aff’d, 138 S.Ct. 1832 (per curiam)).  
Chief among these implied, subsidiary rights—for EPA’s purposes—is the reality that the 
environment must be of sufficient quality to ensure the subject of the right—whether it be fish, shellfish, 
beaver, muskrat, seaweed, wild rice, fiddlehead ferns, and many other aquatic or aquatic-dependent 
species—can thrive and remain available for tribal members to use, and to do so safely. Without the clean 
water that allows this, many usufructuary rights reserved by tribes would be rendered worthless. E.g., 
Winans, 198 U.S. at 381 (the right of taking fish at usual and accustomed areas necessarily included the 
right of access to those areas as “[n]o other conclusion would give effect to the treaty”); United States v. 
Washington, 853 F.3d at 965 (“The Indians reasonably understood Governor Stevens to promise not only 
that they would have access to their usual and accustomed fishing places, but also that there would be fish 
sufficient to sustain them.”); see also Letter from Hilary C. Tompkins, Solicitor, Dep’t of Interior, to Avi 
Garbow, General Counsel, EPA, regarding Maine’s WQS and Tribal Fishing Rights of Maine Tribes (Jan. 
30, 2015) (Attachment 1) (“Tribal fishing rights encompass subsidiary rights that are not explicitly 
included in treaty or statutory language but are nonetheless necessary to render them meaningful.”).  
EPA’s role as trustee, moreover, carries with it the duty and power to protect tribal reserved 
rights. United States v. Kagama, 118 U.S. 375, 383-84 (1886). The trust responsibility imposes upon the 
 
3 Related to this, the Tribes note a slight overstatement in EPA’s explanation of how this rule may prove to benefit 
tribes without federally reserved rights or resources in locations to which those rights do not extend. At page 74,378 
of the preamble, EPA writes, “It is EPA’s expectation that many of the coordination and collaboration processes that 
will be developed to implement this rule will also lead to better protection of aquatic and aquatic-dependent 
resources not referenced in treaties and similar instruments.” While the Tribes appreciate the sentiment and this 
likely benefit of the rule, the language is overinclusive. Reserved rights do not necessarily need to be “referenced in 
treaties and similar instruments” since they can arise by implication. Such rights must necessarily be included within 
the scope of the Reserved Rights Rule. 

 
 
 
 
Page 5 of 32 
 
United States and all its agencies the obligation to follow “the most exacting fiduciary standards” in 
dealing with the tribes, including in the protection of tribal rights and property. Seminole Nation v. United 
States, 316 U.S. 286, 296-97 (1942); Parravano v. Babbitt, 70 F.3d 539, 546-47 (9th Cir. 1995) 
(recognizing the United States’ trust obligation to protect impliedly reserved fishing rights). Consistent 
with this relationship of trust, federal courts require that ambiguities in federal laws regarding tribes must 
be construed in the tribes’ favor. E.g., Minnesota v. Mille Lacs Band of Chippewa Indians, 526 U.S. 172, 
200 (1999).  
EPA has long recognized these duties. See, e.g., EPA, Policy for the Administration of 
Environmental Programs on Indian Reservations (Nov. 8, 1984), available at 
http://www.epa.gov/sites/production/files/2015-04/documents/indian-policy-84.pdf; EPA Policy on 
Consultation and Coordination with Indian Tribes at 3 (May 4, 2011), available at 
https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2013-08/documents/cons-and-coord-with-indian-tribes-policy.pdf 
[hereinafter EPA Consultation Policy] (“EPA recognizes the federal government’s trust responsibility, 
which derives from the historical relationship between the federal government and Indian tribes as 
expressed in certain treaties and federal Indian law.”). In fact, the agency commemorated the 30th 
anniversary of, and reaffirmed, its 1984 Indian Policy, indicating that EPA should use its authority to 
protect tribal rights and resources when it is within its discretion to do so. See EPA Administrator 
McCarthy, Memorandum Commemorating the 30th Anniversary of EPA’s Indian Policy at 1 (Dec. 1, 
2014), available at https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2015-
05/documents/indianpolicytreatyrightsmemo2014.pdf. And just last year, EPA again formally reaffirmed 
the EPA Policy for the Administration of Environmental Programs on Indian Reservations, stating “the 
EPA reiterates its recognition that the United States has a unique legal relationship with tribal 
governments based on the Constitution, treaties, statutes, executive orders and court decisions. . . . The 
reaffirmation of the 1984 Indian Policy articulates the importance of the EPA’s tribal programs and our 
relationship with tribal governments. . . . It is an important time in our partnership with tribes as the EPA 
builds on past successes and strives to meet current and future environmental challenges with tribes.” 
Michael S. Regan, Reaffirmation of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s Indian Policy (Sept. 30, 
2021), https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2021-09/oita-21-000-6427.pdf. EPA itself has 
described its “fundamental objective in carrying out its responsibilities in Indian country” as “to protect 
human health and the environment.” EPA Consultation Policy at 3; EPA, EPA Policy on Consultation 
and Coordination with Indian Tribes: Guidance for Discussing Tribal Treaty Rights at 2, available at 
https://www.epa.gov/sites/production/files/2016-
02/documents/tribal_treaty_rights_guidance_for_discussing_tribal_treaty_rights.pdf (acknowledging 
“implied right to sufficient water quantity or water quality to ensure that fishing is possible” attendant to 
reserved rights).  
For many years and on many occasions, EPA has recognized these fundamental obligations to 
tribes in its decision making and defense of its decisions regarding water quality. E.g., EPA, Mem. in 
Supp. of Mot. for Summ. J. at 16, Montana v. U.S. Env’t Prot. Agency, 941 F. Supp. 945 (D. Mont. 1996) 
(“Tribes require clean water for a domestic water supply and to maintain fish, aquatic life and other 
wildlife for both subsistence and cultural reasons . . . In short, clean water is a crucial resource that plays a 
central role in Tribal culture. Because clean water has a direct effect on the . . . health and welfare of . . . 
Tribes that is serious and substantial, . . . Tribes have a strong interest in regulating on-reservation water 
quality.”); Revision of Certain Federal Water Quality Criteria Applicable to Washington, 80 Fed. Reg. 
55,063, 55,066 (Sept. 14, 2015) (“[M]any tribes hold reserved rights to take fish for subsistence, 
ceremonial, religious, and commercial purposes, including treaty-reserved rights to fish at all usual and 

 
 
 
 
Page 6 of 32 
 
accustomed fishing grounds and stations . . . . Such rights include not only a right to take those fish, but 
necessarily include an attendant right to not be exposed to unacceptable health risks by consuming those 
fish.”); State Program Requirements: Approval of Application by Maine to Administer the National 
Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) Program, 68 Fed. Reg. 65,052, 65,056 (Nov. 18, 2003) 
(“Clearly, the physical setting of the southern tribes in such close proximity to important rivers makes 
surface water quality important to them and their riverine culture.”); Promulgation of Certain Federal 
Water Quality Standards Applicable to Maine, 81 Fed. Reg. 92,466, 92,479 (Dec. 19, 2016) (“[T]he 
Tribes’ ability to take fish for their sustenance . . . would be rendered meaningless if it were not supported 
under the CWA by water quality sufficient to ensure that tribal members can safely eat the fish for their 
own sustenance.”). But until now, EPA’s commitment to these obligations has varied across EPA regions 
and across different administrations. See, e.g., 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,364-65, 74,370 (describing human 
health criteria decisions in Washington and Maine). 
The Tribes are pleased to support EPA in its decision to bring greater clarity and transparency to 
its Clean Water Act oversight obligations and agency decision making by codifying the simple yet 
fundamental rights and obligations described both here and in the preamble to the Reserved Rights Rule 
(87 Fed. Reg. at 74,363-66). This will bring consistency in CWA Section 303(c) oversight and decision 
making that implicates treaties and other sources of federal law reflecting reserved rights. EPA correctly 
states: “Tribal reserved rights to aquatic resources could be impaired by water quality levels that limit 
right holders’ ability to utilize their rights . . . . In exercising its CWA section 303(c) authority, EPA has 
an obligation to ensure that its actions are consistent with treaties, statutes, executive orders, and other 
sources of Federal law reflecting tribal reserved rights.” 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,364. By promulgating the 
Reserved Rights Rule, EPA will finally codify what it has long acknowledged: that tribes require clean 
water sufficient to support the tribal resources and uses that are the subject of their reserved rights, and 
that the Clean Water Act must be applied to ensure that protection.  
B.  
The Clean Water Act Has Not Adequately Protected Tribal Reserved Rights to Date 
But Can and Must Do So Now. 
The proposed Reserved Rights Rule does not come a moment too soon. Although the Clean 
Water Act recently celebrated its 50th anniversary, it has failed to meet its objectives in many waters in 
which tribes hold reserved rights that depend on clean water. A recent ProPublica article made waves in 
the Pacific Northwest and highlights the problem. See Tony Schick and Maya Miller, The U.S. Promised 
Tribes They Would Always Have Fish, but the Fish They Have Pose Toxic Risks, PROPUBLICA (Nov. 22, 
2022), available at https://www.propublica.org/article/how-the-us-broke-promise-to-protect-fish-for-
tribes (Attachment 2). The article describes toxics testing of fifty salmon purchased from Native 
fishermen for thirteen metals and two classes of chemicals, which was commissioned by Oregon Public 
Broadcasting and ProPublica. The testing revealed “concentrations of [mercury and polychlorinated 
biphenyls (PCBs)] in the salmon that the EPA and both Oregon and Washington’s health agencies deem 
unsafe at the levels consumed by many of the 68,000-plus Native people who are members of tribes living 
in the Columbia River Basin today.” Id. In the wake of the article, lawmakers have called for policy 
changes and additional funding. Maya Miller and Tony Schick, Toxic Salmon Reporting ‘Deeply 
Troubling,’ Lawmaker Says, Demanding Changes to Protect Pacific Northwest Tribal Health, 
PROPUBLICA (Dec. 14, 2022), available at https://www.propublica.org/article/toxic-salmon-columbia-
river-basin-lawmaker-response (Attachment 3). But notwithstanding lawmakers’ seeming surprise, the 
problems in the Columbia River have been known for a long time and are well-documented. E.g., EPA, 
Columbia River Basin: State of the River Report for Toxics (Jan. 2009), available at 

 
 
 
 
Page 7 of 32 
 
https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/documents/columbia_state_of_the_river_report_jan2009.pdf 
(Attachment 4) (Section 5.0: Status and Trends for Mercury, DDT, PCBs, and PBDEs). Yet, the effects of 
this pollution on Columbia Basin tribes and tribal health have been allowed to continue.  
This is commonplace. Across the region, tribes suffer from these same types of gaps in Clean 
Water Act protection and enforcement. For instance, we have known for many years that stormwater 
pollution has had lethal effects on coho salmon to which tribes have treaty-reserved rights throughout the 
Pacific Northwest. Instead of immediately requiring more effective stormwater infrastructure and best 
management practices to address the issue, much time was spent on identifying the specific culprit. Sarah 
McQuate, Tire-Related Chemical is Largely Responsible for Adult Coho Salmon Deaths in Urban 
Streams, UW News (Dec. 3, 2020), available at https://www.washington.edu/news/2020/12/03/tire-
related-chemical-largely-responsible-for-adult-coho-salmon-deaths-in-urban-streams/ (Attachment 5). It 
is good that we now know 6PPD-quinone’s identity and its toxicity, so that tire manufacturers can be 
pressed to replace that additive with a non-toxic substitute. See, e.g., Zhenyu Tian et al., 6PPD-Quinone: 
Revised Toxicity Assessment and Quantification with a Commercial Standard, 9 ENVIRONMENTAL 
SCIENCE & TECHNOLOGY LETTERS 140 (2022) (Attachment 6). However, if the Clean Water Act were 
geared more toward protecting tribal resources, it may have forced more rapid stormwater improvements 
even in the face of some uncertainty about the specific chemical’s identity.4 And now that we do know 
the lethal effects of this chemical on coho—and tribal reserved rights that depend on coho—the Clean 
Water Act requires immediate action. The same is true of other known pollutants that impede tribal 
reserved rights, such as PFAS, Environmental Working Group, Eating One Freshwater Fish Equals A 
Month Of Drinking ‘Forever Chemicals’ Water, ScienceBlog (Jan. 17, 2023), 
https://scienceblog.com/536016/eating-one-freshwater-fish-equals-a-month-of-drinking-forever-

(Attachment 11), and any other pollutants that depress the population of aquatic and aquatic-dependent 
resources for which tribes reserved rights. Despite five decades of Clean Water Act implementation, 
tribes and their members are still burdened by legacy and ongoing pollution that impedes full exercise of 
their rights and diminishes their health. The proposed rule can force swifter and more protective action 
than we’ve seen in the past. And it must. 
As EPA has long acknowledged, “‘[a]ny specific treaty requirements have the force of law,’ and 
 
4 The problem with stormwater is not limited to 6PPD-quinone. For example, the map described here shows multiple
