Page 8 of 32 
 
therefore, ‘State water quality standards will have to meet any treaty requirements.’” 87 Fed. Reg. at 
74,366 (citing 48 Fed. Reg. 51,400, 51,412 (Nov. 8, 1983)). However, whereas EPA previously declined 
to explicitly require States to adopt standards that meet treaty requirements” in its 1983 WQS regulations 
because such issues had been “adequately resolved . . . without the need for regulatory language,” 
experience since that time makes clear that regulatory language is urgently needed for states to understand 
their obligations with respect to the intersection of U.S.-Indian treaties and water quality standards in 
order to protect tribal reserved rights from the persistent and detrimental effects of water pollution. We 
believe that the Reserved Rights Rule has the potential, after accounting for the other comments made 
herein, to bring transparency and clarity to these issues in the revision and approval processes for state 
water quality standards. Beyond the ineffective implementation of the Clean Water Act described above, 
the Tribes have suffered the whiplash of inconsistent federal positions on tribal reserved rights and have 
been forced to devote considerable resources to ensuring their rights are protected. A recent example is 
the decades-long fight regarding the human health criteria (HHC) in Washington, including the rollbacks 
of the last administration. Our Tribes were dismayed by how long it took to get more protective HHC in 
place, as well as EPA’s abandonment of its trust obligations and adherence to the law in the last 
administration. We appreciate EPA’s recent restoration of the more protective HHC in Washington and 
support EPA’s efforts to develop a more durable and consistent federal policy for the future.  
In particular, we support the proposed rule’s commitment to the establishment of WQS that 
protect “[t]he exercise of tribal reserved rights unsuppressed by water quality or availability of the 
aquatic or aquatic-dependent resource” and “the health” of tribal members exercising reserved rights. 87 
Fed. Reg. at 74,378 (proposed 40 C.F.R. § 131.9(a)(1)-(2)) (emphasis added). While at times the 
preamble seems somewhat narrowly focused on toxics (e.g., human health criteria), we appreciate that the 
language of the rule itself is sufficient to encompass what should be two main drivers of the WQS: human 
health and habitat health that allows for healthy and abundant populations of species that are the subject 
to tribal reserved rights. This is crucial to ensuring an effective rule that does not only reach toxic 
pollution (such as in the Washington Department of Ecology’s upcoming revision of its aquatic life toxics 
criteria), but also reaches pernicious water quality problems like nutrient and temperature pollution that 
depress aquatic-dependent populations of species important to the exercise of tribal reserved rights, 
particularly in the era of climate change. In short, the Tribes believe wholeheartedly that 40 C.F.R. § 
131.9 should be amended to ensure that WQS “must protect tribal reserved rights applicable to waters 
subject to such standards,” and believe the Reserved Rights Rule should be finalized as quickly as 
possible and no later than the end of this year. 
The proposed Reserved Rights Rule is entirely consistent with—and even demanded by—the 
Clean Water Act, and it is well within the broad scope of EPA’s statutory authority under the Act. The 
overarching commitment of the Clean Water Act is to “restore and maintain the chemical, physical, and 
biological integrity of the Nation’s waters.” 33 U.S.C. § 1251(a). To that end, Congress established a 
national policy that “the discharge of toxic pollutants in toxic amounts be prohibited” and directed that 
water quality be sufficient to protect and allow the propagation of fish, shellfish, and wildlife safe for 
human consumption by July 1, 1983. See id. § 1251(a)(2), (3). The Act is designed to ratchet down the 
level of pollution over time to allow for ever safer use of the water until all uses are protected and remain 
protected. While the date for accomplishing these goals has long since passed, EPA’s efforts through this 
proposed rule help to ensure the Act’s polices are finally fulfilled as it relates to protecting tribal reserved 
rights wherever they exist in the waters and wetlands of Washington State. 
 
Water quality standards are the foundation of the Clean Water Act’s water quality-based control 

 
 
 
 
Page 9 of 32 
 
program. They define goals for a water body by designating the uses that water body supports or should 
support (“designated uses”); set water quality criteria designed to protect those uses and measure progress 
made (“criteria”); and establish anti-degradation policies, so that existing uses and water quality necessary 
to support those uses are protected and so that bodies with very high quality water do not become 
impaired. In order to attain the Act’s goals and to protect the uses of water, the Act imposes an obligation 
on states, with EPA acting in an oversight role, to develop water quality standards comprised of 
designated uses and narrative or numeric water quality criteria sufficient to protect uses such as fishing. 
Id. § 1313(a)-(b). Specifically, Clean Water Act section 303 directs states with delegated authority to do 
the following when they adopt or revise water quality standards for waters of the United States. 33 U.S.C. 
§ 1313.  
Whenever the State revises or adopts a new standard, such revised or new standard shall 
be submitted to the Administrator. Such revised or new water quality standard shall 
consist of the designated uses of the navigable waters involved and the water quality 
criteria for such waters based upon such uses. Such standards shall be such as to protect 
the public health or welfare, enhance the quality of water and serve the purposes of this 
chapter. Such standards shall be established taking into consideration their use and value 
for public water supplies, propagation of fish and wildlife, recreational purposes, and 
agricultural, industrial, and other purposes, and also taking into consideration their use 
and value for navigation. 
Id. § 1313(c)(2)(A) (emphasis added). As EPA notes in the preamble, whatever WQS a state might adopt 
must not affect or impair the provisions of any treaty of the United States under section 511 of the Act. 87 
Fed. Reg. at 74,364-65; see also 33 U.S.C. § 1371 (“[The Act] shall not be construed as . . . affecting or 
impairing the provisions of any treaty of the United States.”). 
 
While states have the first shot at promulgating protective, science-based water quality standards, 
EPA is obligated under the Act to review and to disapprove a state’s efforts if they fall short of meeting 
the requirements of the Act. Id. § 1313(a)-(c). Furthermore, EPA has independent authority to ensure that 
a state’s standards are up to date and adequate to meet the Act’s requirements. Id. § 1313(c). Thus, where 
a state fails to act in accordance with the statute, EPA is obligated to fulfill the state’s traditional role of 
issuing standards that comply with the Act. In other words, EPA is correct that “the statute’s structure and 
objectives for the establishment and oversight of WQS, including the discretion afforded to EPA, provide 
ample room for the agency to consider and give effect to all applicable reserved rights.” 87 Fed. Reg. at 
74,365. As EPA notes, it has exercised this authority with regard to the human health criteria in 
Washington and Maine before, and as noted in the previous section, those actions and this are consistent 
with long-standing EPA policy regarding tribal rights and resources. 
III. 
COMMENTS ON SPECIFIC SECTIONS OF THE PROPOSED RESESERVED RIGHTS 
RULE AND ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS POSED BY EPA IN THE PREAMBLE  
 
In this section, the Tribes provide comments on specific statements in the Federal Register notice 
and proposed rule language, as well as respond to questions specifically raised by EPA regarding the 
proposed rule. 
A. 
EPA Must Require States To Protect Tribal Reserved Rights By Employing All 
Three Components of Water Quality Standards. 

 
 
 
 
Page 10 of 32 
 
 
The Federal Register notice indicates that after a state has determined that tribal reserved rights 
exist in the waters over which it has Clean Water Act jurisdiction and the level of water quality necessary 
to protect those rights, “states would be required to revise their WQS if needed to ensure protection of 
those rights using designated uses, criteria and/or antidegradation as described at proposed 40 CFR 
131.9(c).” 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,371. The proposed regulatory language is: 
(c) In order to meet the requirements in paragraph (a) of this section, States must: (1) 
Designate uses consistent with § 131.10 that either expressly incorporate protection of the 
tribal reserved rights or encompass such rights; and (2) Establish water quality criteria 
consistent with § 131.11 to protect tribal reserved rights; and/or (3) Use applicable 
antidegradation requirements consistent with § 131.12 to maintain and protect water 
quality that protects tribal reserved rights. 
The Tribes support specific regulatory language directing states to promulgate each component of water 
quality standards in order to meet the requirements in paragraph (a) of proposed 40 C.F.R. § 131.9 
(“Water quality standards must protect tribal reserved rights applicable to waters subject to such 
standards.”). However, as described below, the Tribes believe that the regulatory language should be 
stated only in the conjunctive (“and”)—without use of the phrase “and/or” between subsections (2) and 
(3)—in order to comport with the requirements of the Clean Water Act and its existing implementing 
regulations, as well as to best meet the goals of the Reserved Rights Rule. Consequently, in response to 
EPA’s query “whether the following two options related to Tier 2 and Tier 3 could be used to protect 
tribal reserved rights in lieu of the options identified in proposed 40 CFR 131.9(c)(1) and (2) and 
explained earlier in this section,” 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,371 (emphasis added), the answer is “no.” However, 
by adding some more specifics about how a state might use or modify its antidegradation policy to protect 
tribal reserved rights in already high quality waters (Tier 3 and potentially Tier 2), we believe that 
antidegradation policies are a legitimate and helpful way for states to protect tribal reserved rights in high 
quality waters in addition to establishing designated uses and water quality criteria for them.  
1. 
Water Quality Standards Include Three Components, and EPA Cannot Rely 
Solely on States’ Antidegradation Policies to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights. 
 
The proposed rule suggests one option to protect tribal reserved rights, either alone or in 
combination with others, is for states to revise their antidegradation policies. 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,371; id. at 
74,378 (proposed 40 C.F.R. § 131.9(c)(2)) (“and/or”). Reliance solely on antidegradation policies, while 
not utilizing the other options EPA proposes, does not meet the plain language of the Clean Water Act 
and will not adequately protect tribal reserved rights. EPA should only be considering the use of 
antidegradation policies in addition to protective designated uses and water quality criteria. 
 
The proposed rule’s preamble explains that the core components of water quality standards are 
designated uses, water quality criteria, and antidegradation requirements. 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,362 (citing 
33 U.S.C. § 1313(c)(3)). As explained above, EPA is required to protect reserved rights; forgoing the use 
of two of the three water quality standards core components does not make sense and would not comply 
with EPA’s obligation to protect reserved rights. Importantly, it also would not meet the plain language of 
the Act, which requires that states’ “revised or new water quality standard shall consist of the designated 
uses of the navigable waters involved and the water quality criteria for such waters based upon such 
uses.” 33 U.S.C. § 1313(c)(2)(A) (emphasis added). The use of “and/or” (both the conjunctive and 
disjunctive) at proposed 40 C.F.R. § 131.9(c) suggests that states could meet the requirements of the 

 
 
 
 
Page 11 of 32 
 
Clean Water Act either by completing all three components (designated uses and criteria and 
antidegradation) or by using only its antidegradation policy to meet the requirements of the Act.5 A 
disjunctive regulatory list (“or”) would seemingly allow a state to avoid submitting designated uses and 
criteria in its new or revised WQS and is therefore inconsistent with the plain statutory language.6   
 
Beyond the statutory imperatives, the current implementing regulations also would not permit 
sole reliance on antidegradation policies to protect tribal reserved rights in many cases. “Where existing 
water quality standards specify designated uses less than those which are presently being attained, the 
State shall revise its standards to reflect the uses actually being attained.”7 40 C.F.R. § 131.10(i) 
(emphasis added); see also Idaho Mining Ass’n v. Browner, 90 F. Supp. 2d 1078, 1081 (D. Idaho 2000). 
There is no dispute that tribal exercise of reserved rights is and has been occurring at waters under state 
jurisdiction throughout the country. Consequently, where a state has not yet designated tribal reserved 
right uses for water bodies in which tribes are currently exercising tribal reserved rights (at whatever level 
 
5 We do not interpret the proposed rule language as allowing either 1) designated uses and antidegradation policy, 
but no criteria; or 2) criteria and antidegradation policy, but no designated uses. If EPA intended either such option 
to be available to states, it is not clear from the regulatory language’s use of the conjunctive between (1) and (2) and 
the conjunctive/disjunctive between (2) and (3). We have not suggested alternative language due to our belief that 
only the conjunctive “and” should follow each subpart. 
6 EPA notes in the preamble that the “proposed rulemaking would complement the existing regulatory requirements 
set forth in EPA’s WQS regulation. In certain circumstances, these existing requirements may already be operating 
to ensure water quality levels are protective of particular tribal reserved rights.” 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,371. In theory, 
this is true, and in many cases, EPA is correct that already promulgated designated uses (such as “fishing” or 
“wildlife”) may encompass tribal reserved rights and that criteria may exist that are intended to protect those 
designated uses. However, as suggested by the articles discussed in section II.B. above, the agency and states cannot 
assume that their existing WQS are getting the job done even where tribal reserved rights might conceptually fall 
within those WQS. In the preamble, 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,371, EPA states: “EPA’s identification of two categories of 
circumstances where compliance with the proposed rulemaking is most likely to necessitate new or revised WQS is 
consistent with input from tribes during pre-proposal consultation, which focused primarily on protection of fish 
consumers and protection of wild rice. EPA requests comment on whether there are other instances where WQS 
may need to be adjusted to protect tribal reserved rights consistent with this proposed rulemaking. This request for 
comment includes, but is not limited to, whether there are tribal reserved rights to aquatic or aquatic-dependent 
resources that may require more stringent criteria than otherwise required to protect applicable designated uses in 
order to comply with this proposed rulemaking and whether there are differential health risks for right holders 
associated with activities other than fish consumption such that new or revised criteria may be necessary to comply 
with this proposed rulemaking.” Based on our experience, we have to disagree that the scope of likely revisions is so 
narrow. States, in consultation with tribes, will need to take a hard and fresh look at their WQS, including each of 
the specific things listed in EPA’s query, to see whether they are actually protecting tribal reserved rights (including 
harvestable populations of aquatic and aquatic-dependent species), even if their WQS theoretically should have been 
doing so all along. 
7 “Designated uses” are defined as “those uses specified in water quality standards for each water body or segment 
whether or not they are being attained.” 40 C.F.R. § 131.3(f). “Existing uses” are defined as “those uses actually 
attained in the water body on or after November 28, 1975, whether or not they are included in the water quality 
standards.” Id. § 131.3(e) (emphasis added).

of use),8 it must do so, and the final Reserved Rights Rule should not introduce confusion about that.9 In 
addition, “States may adopt sub-categories of a use and set the appropriate criteria to reflect varying needs 
of such sub-categories of uses, for instance, to differentiate between cold water and warm water 
fisheries.” 40 C.F.R. § 131.10(c). So, for example, if a water body has been used for both sport and tribal 
reserved rights fishing, a designated use of “fishing” may incorporate both existing uses, but the criteria 
must be set at protective enough levels to protect the tribal reserved fishing right. 40 C.F.R. § 
131.11(a)(1) (“States must adopt those water quality criteria that protect the designated use. Such criteria 
must be based on sound scientific rationale and must contain sufficient parameters or constituents to 
protect the designated use. For waters with multiple use designations, the criteria shall support the most 
sensitive use.”). If the Reserved Rights Rule allows a state an “option” to use designated uses/criteria or 
its antidegradation policy, EPA risks causing confusion as to the state’s obligations under these regulatory 
provisions, which the agency does not propose to amend. States therefore should revise their designated 
uses (and accompanying criteria) to reflect the exercise of reserved rights use, in addition to protections 
afforded by antidegradation policies. The Reserved Rights Rule should be clear on this in the preamble, 
response to comments, and regulatory text. Specifically, “and/or” should be changed to “and” in the final 
40 C.F.R. § 131.9. 
2. 
State Antidegradation Policies Are Insufficient to Protect Tribal Reserved 
 
Rights On Their Own. 
 
Antidegradation policies can provide protections for high water quality that has not been 
degraded or has already been achieved, 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,363, but they offer no mandatory protections 
for enhancing degraded water quality to levels that can support the unsuppressed exercise of reserved 
rights. Consequently, the use of the antidegradation policy—even a strong policy—could only help 
protect tribal reserved rights in a very limited subset of waters of any given state. Where there are high 
quality waters, they should be protected under Tier 3 already, but certainly they should be afforded that 
 
8 As suggested in the preamble, this is underinclusive of the water bodies in which tribal reserved rights may apply 
and require WQS adjustments since water pollution and depressed populations of tribal resources may have 
prevented tribal use of a water body in which a tribe continues to have rights. 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,370 (“EPA 
anticipates that the circumstances where WQS may need to be adjusted to protect tribal reserved rights would fall 
primarily into two categories: . . . 2. Where a reserved rights is not already accounted for as a designated or presently 
attained use for a waterbody, but that waterbody could be reasonably be expected to support that right in the future 
(e.g., if restoration efforts are underway).”). However, in cases where tribal reserved rights have been exercised 
(even if not to their full extent), these provisions of the implementing regulations are another action-forcing element 
to ensure they are included in designated uses and protected by appropriate water quality criteria. 
9 To be clear, discussion of “existing uses” in this paragraph is in regard to the action-forcing obligation under 
EPA’s regulations with respect to designated uses, which is separate and apart from the Tier 1 antidegradation 
protections for “existing uses.” The Tier 1 antidegradation policy requires all “[e]xisting instream water uses and the 
level of water quality necessary to protect the existing uses shall be maintained and protected.” 40 C.F.R. §

allowable under the antidegradation policy which would partially or completely eliminate any existing use whether

quality” is not sufficient to protect tribal reserved rights. 

 
 
 
 
Page 13 of 32 
 
protection wherever tribal reserved rights apply. We therefore strongly support the sentiments and goals 
driving EPA’s statement in the preamble that: “in situations where a waterbody’s existing water quality 
exceeds the levels that protect tribal reserved rights, these options would provide a mechanism to 
maintain high water quality and provide a margin of safety that would afford the water body increased 
resilience to potential future stressors, including climate change. Protecting such high-quality waters 
would potentially be more cost-effective and resource-efficient than investing in long-term restoration or 
remedial actions in the future.” 87 Fed. Reg. 74,371. Our Tribes and others in western Washington have 
been adamant and vocal that it is imperative that water quality in our usual and accustomed areas be 
protected where the water is of high quality or restored where the water has been degraded. EPA’s 
statement is consistent with the Tribes’ former objective. Our concern, however, is that the 
antidegradation policy should not be available to states as a sole option for protecting tribal reserved 
rights in their water quality standards.  
 
For various reasons, the Clean Water Act’s antidegradation requirements have not been used 
successfully to implement the Act’s purpose to “restore and maintain the chemical, physical, and 
biological integrity of the Nation’s waters.” 33 U.S.C. § 1251(a). In 2013, EPA stated:  
EPA indicated in its 1998 ANPRM that “on a national scale, antidegradation is not being 
used as effectively as it could be,” a concern that continues today and is echoed by 
stakeholders who have identified antidegradation as an underused component of water 
quality protection. . . . [T]he EPA received substantial feedback from stakeholders that 
existing CWA antidegradation regulatory provisions and related guidance have not been 
fully successful in ensuring consistent and effective implementation of Tier 2 high quality 
water protections.  
Water Quality Standards Regulatory Clarifications, 78 Fed. Reg. 54,518, 54,526 (proposed Sept. 4, 2013) 
(to be codified at 40 C.F.R. pt. 131). Similarly, in 1998, EPA explained: 
In sum, EPA’s current thinking is that the antidegradation policy is significantly 
underused as a tool to attain and maintain water quality and plan for and channel 
important economic and social development that can impact water quality. EPA believes 
this is especially true for nonpoint source run-off. 
Water Quality Standards Regulation, 63 Fed. Reg. 36,742, 36,780 (proposed July 7, 1998). Numerous 
commentators have recognized these issues as well, including problems stemming from overly broad 
federal requirements for states and lack of EPA authority to review designations beyond broad language; 
ineffective or even no classification designations; minimal use of Outstanding National Resource Water 
designations; lack of nonpoint source pollution regulation and thus no nonpoint triggering of 
antidegradation reviews; and elevation of or deference to economic considerations. See, e.g., Katherine A. 
Zogas, The Clean Water Act’s Antidegradation Policy: Has It Been “Dumped”?, 42 J. MARSHALL L. 
REV. 209, 227-28 (2008) (Attachment 12); John A. Chilson, Keeping Clean Waters Clean: Making the 
Clean Water Act’s Antidegradation Policy Work, 32 U. MICH. J.L. REFORM 545, 548, 553-64 (1999) 
(Attachment 13); Kent Modesitt, Antidegradation: A Lost Cause or the Next Cause, 2 U. DENV. WATER 
L. REV. 189, 220-22 (Spring 1999) (Attachment 14); see also The Antidegradation Policy, 2 PUB. NAT. 
RESOURCES L. § 19:13 (2nd ed.) (“Indeed, the entire antidegradation policy of some states is so vague as 
to be virtually meaningless.”) (Attachment 15). 

 
 
 
 
Page 14 of 32 
 
The proposed rule’s suggested options and regulatory text do not address these problems but will 
likely exacerbate them as applied to protecting tribal reserved rights. The one provision of proposed 
regulatory text at 40 C.F.R. § 131.9(c)(3) is too vague to ensure protection or meaningful review. It does 
not include the limitations on the antidegradation policy described in the preamble of the rule, limitations 
that would be necessary in order to protect tribal reserved rights when applying the antidegradation 
policy. See 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,371 (discussion of “Option 1” and “Option 2” for implementing 
antidegradation requirements to protect tribal reserved rights through use of Tier 3 and Tier 2 
designations). The preamble’s discussion and suggested alternatives do not offer any solace as: 1) the 
preamble is not enforceable and 2) it itself does not contain any mandatory protective requirements. 
EPA’s decades of experience should make clear that protecting tribal reserved rights cannot be left solely 
to the whims of the states’ antidegradation policies and decisions without firm requirements and 
guidance. Moreover, it is not clear how the sole use of antidegradation policies would help waters that are 
currently impaired improve water quality to allow for the full exercise and enjoyment of reserved rights. 
Nor is it clear how the use of antidegradation policies would protect against harm to reserved rights from 
nonpoint source discharges. 
To conclude, the agency should modify proposed 40 C.F.R. § 131.9(c)(2) to use “and” instead of 
“and/or,” thus requiring the use of antidegradation policies in addition to protective designated uses and 
criteria, rather than potentially instead of those requirements.10 The agency should also include mandatory 
and more specific regulatory language about how antidegradation policies must be implemented to protect 
tribal reserved rights, providing particular detail and emphasis regarding “Option 1.” 
3. 
EPA Should Utilize Tier 3 for Outstanding National Resource Waters to 
Protect Reserved Rights. 
Notwithstanding our objections to giving states an option to only use its antidegradation policy to 
protect tribal reserved rights and our concern regarding the lack of prescriptive language in the proposed 
regulatory text regarding how to use pertinent aspects of the antidegradation policy in waters with tribal 
reserved right, the Tribes do see a role for some aspects of antidegradation policies in the protection of 
tribal reserved rights. In 2021, EPA provided notice that it was considering proposing “Assignment of 
Tier 3 antidegradation protection (i.e., requirement to maintain and protect current and future improved 
water quality) in waters where tribal reserved rights apply and where current water quality is sufficient to 
protect those rights.” Deborah G. Nagle, Notification of Consultation and Coordination on Potential 
Revisions to the Federal Water Quality Standards Regulations to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights (June 
11, 2021). This idea appears akin to “Option 1” suggested by EPA in the preamble, 87 Fed. Reg. at 
74,371, although without any regulatory text implementing the option, see id. at 74,378 (proposed 40 
C.F.R. § 131.9(c)(3)). 
Tier 3 protections apply to Outstanding National Resource Waters, which are generally 
exceptional, important, unique, or sensitive ecologically, or offer unique or important recreational uses. 
 
10 As discussed above, the proposed text at the end of § 131.9(c)(1) “and” combined with the proposed text at the 
end of § 131.9(c)(2) “and/or”, create ambiguity which of these three provisions will be required and which EPA 
would allow to be optional. The Tribes believe that § 131.9(c)(1) [designated uses], (c)(2) [criteria], and (c)(3) 
[antidegradation] should all be required or better yet, (c)(3) [antidegradation] should be moved into a separate 
subsection and include more detailed requirements. 

 
 
 
 
Page 15 of 32 
 
Tier 3 protects against any permanent degradation to these important waters; only a temporary, short-
term, and limited change in the water quality of a Tier 3 water is allowed; for example, for construction 
activities. Given the well-documented importance of tribal reserved rights, see id. at 74,363, and EPA’s 
trust responsibility to protect these rights, see Michael S. Regan, Reaffirmation of the U.S. Environmental 
Protection Agency’s Indian Policy (Sept. 30, 2021), https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2021-
09/oita-21-000-6427.pdf, it is important to ensure these waters are maintained and protected. The Tribes 
believe that high quality waters with reserved rights are a good fit for protection as Outstanding National 
Resource Waters and supports EPA’s proposed Option 1, subject to the other comments and 
qualifications stated in these comments. EPA should operationalize this option with strong regulatory 
language rather than merely describing the option in the preamble. 
Given the well-documented history of minimal ONRW designation, see, e.g., John A. Chilson, 
Keeping Clean Waters Clean: Making the Clean Water Act’s Antidegradation Policy Work, 32 U. MICH. 
J.L. REFORM 545, 547 (1999) (Attachment 13), relying on the states to designate ONRWs is insufficient. 
EPA should set up a process by which tribes can directly nominate to EPA high quality waters in areas 
where they hold reserved rights to be designated as ONRWs. That way, EPA can ensure that tribal 
nominations are given full consideration and not lost in the state process. 
4. 
Without Stronger Language, Tier 2 Is Insufficient to Protect Reserved 
Rights. 
The Tribes are concerned about the suggested “Option 2,” which would let states utilize Tier 2 
protections to limit the lowering of water quality in high quality waters (that exceed Clean Water Act 
section 101(a) uses) to protect applicable reserved rights. 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,371 (citing 40 C.F.R. § 
131.12(a)(2)). Tier 2 allows lowering of water quality “only in a few extraordinary circumstances where 
the economic and social need for the activity clearly outweighs the benefit of maintaining water quality 
above that required for ‘fishable/swimmable’ water, and both cannot be achieved.” EPA, Water Quality 
Standards Handbook, Chapter 4: Antidegradation, at 9 (2012). Specifically, EPA describes Option 2 as: 
“States could amend their antidegradation policy and/or other legally binding procedures to include a 
provision that ensures that any lowering of water quality in a high-quality water that is authorized by the 
state, in accordance with 40 CFR 131.12(a)(2), results in water quality that continues to protect applicable 
reserved rights.” 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,271.  
To begin, the Tribes assume that EPA intends for Tier 2 to be used only where water quality 
exceeds the quality necessary for the full unsuppressed use of tribal reserved rights, and not just Clean 
Water Act section 101(a) designated uses. However, that is not clear from the proposed language and 
preamble, so should be clarified. And the Tribes note, as explained above, that this option would not help 
waters whose quality is below the level necessary for the unsuppressed use of reserved rights. 
Fundamentally, the Tribes are concerned with how even the best-intentioned states might weigh 
important economic or social development in the area against maintaining high water quality that protects 
tribal reserved rights. If given the option, we are not confident that the reserved rights sacred to a tribe 
would prove more consequential to the state than other policy goals it must weigh, at least not 
consistently. And as explained above, without specific regulatory language, it is not clear how Option 2 
would actually be implemented or enforced to ensure a thumb on the scale in favor of tribal reserved 
rights. The bottom line is that EPA would need to include strong mandatory language in the regulatory 
text itself if this is offered as a potential measure of protection to states. And it should not be available as 

 
 
 
 
Page 16 of 32 
 
a sole measure of protection. 
Tier 2’s exceptions allowing some level of water quality degradation of a high-quality water 
based on economic and social considerations are distressing where reserved rights are at issue. Water 
contamination threatens traditional Indian lifeways, including longstanding traditions of fishing and fish 
consumption that are central to many tribes’ cultural identity and that make individual tribes distinct as 
people. Further, many tribes are connected to particular waters for cultural, spiritual, or other reasons (and 
others’ fishing rights are limited to certain grounds by treaty), so tribal members cannot simply move 
their fishing to another location to avoid contamination or lowered water quality. The benefits of 
protecting high water quality to tribes in terms of public health, environmental, cultural, and other gains 
are difficult, and in many cases impossible, to monetize or quantify. EPA has correctly recognized that 
“cultural impacts to tribes and the furtherance of the United States’ treaty obligations to tribes—are an 
example of the type of societal value that cannot be monetized.”11 Supplemental Finding That It Is 
Appropriate and Necessary To Regulate Hazardous Air Pollutants  From Coal- and Oil-Fired Electric 
Utility Steam Generating Units, 81 Fed. Reg. 24,420, 24,429 n.18 (April 25, 2016); see also 87 Fed. Reg. 
at 74,374 (qualitatively describing variety of unique benefits from proposed rule). Most of the benefits 
from high water quality to tribal health, subsistence, fishing rights, and cultural identity defy full 
calculation. See, e.g., Cass R. Sunstein, The Limits of Quantification, 102 CALIF. L. REV. 1369, 1380-85 
(2014) (Attachment 17); United States v. Washington, 384 F. Supp. 312, 404 (W.D. Wash. 1974) (“[T]he 
treaty rights . . . are unique and the damages which have been or will be sustained are not susceptible of 
definite monetary determination.”); see also 2019 NCAI et al. Comments on MATS Rule Reconsideration 
of Supplemental Finding and Residual Risk at 10-13 (Attachment 18). States, with their own objectives, 
are unlikely to want—or even be able—to successfully evaluate a tribal member’s ability to continue to 
engage in the fishing culture practiced since time immemorial by her ancestors, and to pass those 
traditions on to her children. But that does not mean that these core values can be excluded when 
weighing whether lowering water quality is necessary to accommodate important economic or social 
development or choosing from a range of practicable alternatives that would prevent or lessen the 
 
11 Even economists that have attempted to place a value on subsistence fishing have acknowledged that such

on the accuracy of the analysis, we note the Army Corps of Engineers stated:

degradation.12  
Because of this problem, the Tribes do not support the use of Tier 2, at least as the sole protective 
measure, for tribal reserved rights. Should EPA move forward with utilizing Tier 2 as an option in 
combination with other requirements, EPA should incorporate additional language that assures these 
important tribal interests are prioritized to assure they are properly accounted for and protected. EPA and 
states should recognize that a state’s evaluation must begin from a balance favoring protecting water 
quality and reserved rights that otherwise may not get captured in the state’s economic balancing. 
B. 
Description of Definition of “Tribal Reserved Rights” Is Underinclusive 
EPA requested comment on whether additional types of reserved rights should be included 
beyond fishing, gathering of aquatic plants, and hunting for aquatic dependent animals in its definition of 
“tribal reserved rights.” See 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,367 (“Examples of tribal reserved rights as defined in this 
proposed rulemaking include but are not limited to the rights to fish; gather aquatic plants; and to hunt for 
aquatic-dependent animals. EPA requests comment on whether there are additional types of tribal 
reserved rights that it should consider.”). The answer is yes. While tribal reserved rights certainly extend 
to each of the already enumerated rights, tribes reserved more water-dependent rights than those 
specifically listed in the Federal Register notice. While the actual language proposed for the definition at 
40 C.F.R. § 131.3(r) would encompass these rights, the supporting materials—including the preamble to 
the final rule and the response to comments—should include a more comprehensive list of rights covered 
by the rule. EPA should also make clear that this definition of “tribal reserved rights” applies only to this 
rule as tribes have other reserved rights that extend beyond aquatic and aquatic-dependent resources. 
Ultimately, it may not be possible for all types of aquatic and aquatic-dependent tribal reserved rights to 
be explicitly highlighted in this administrative record, but common ones should be and EPA should make 
clear that just because a right has not been listed in the preamble or response to comments does not mean 
that it is not covered by the rule.    
Many tribes engage in water-dependent ceremonies and cultural events in which tribal members 
come into direct contact with water, such as during canoe journeys, boat dances, sweat lodges, and in-
water ceremonies. Poor water quality can directly affect those ceremonies and cultural events. For 
instance, the Suquamish Indian Tribe recently settled a Clean Water Act action against King County, 
Washington, which was prompted, in part, by untreated sewage discharges from a county wastewater 
treatment plant on the opposite side of Puget Sound that reached Suquamish shores just as tribal members 
from across Puget Sound were arriving during the annual Canoe Journey. Washing stations had to be set 
up, so that the Tribe’s guests could clean themselves after paddling through contaminated off-reservation 
 
12 We note that even EPA has had difficulty with the concept of taking qualitative benefits properly into account 
when engaged in economic analyses during certain administrations. EPA recently acknowledged this failing itself. 
See EPA, National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants: Coal- and Oil-Fired Electric Utility Steam 
Generating Units – Revocation of the 2020 Reconsideration, and Affirmation of the Appropriate and Necessary 
Supplemental Finding (pre-publication version) at 86, available at 
https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2023-
02/6716.2_MATS%20A_N_Final%20Rule_20230213_SPPD.admin__0.pdf (“The decision framework in the 2020 
Final Action, however, did not give ‘less weight’ to these factors – it effectively gave them none.”). Given even the 
federal Trustee’s track record with these types of issues, relying on states to protect tribal reserved rights using Tier 
2 protections provides little comfort. 

 
 
 
 
Page 18 of 32 
 
waters and stepping into fouled waters on the reservation’s shores. See, e.g., Lynda V. Mapes, Suquamish 
Tribe Intends to Sue King County after 2019 Tribal Canoe Journey Marred by Wastewater Spill, 
SEATTLE TIMES (July 23, 2020), available at https://www.seattletimes.com/seattle-
news/environment/suquamish-tribe-intends-to-sue-king-county-after-2019-tribal-canoe-journey-marred-
by-wastewater-spill/ (Attachment 19) (including photographs showing tribal members in water around 
canoe). While portions of this example took place on the Tribe’s reservation, where currently only EPA 
has authority to set WQS, the entirety of the example is representative of the type of harm that poor water 
quality can have on reserved ceremonial and cultural uses that may take place in waters where a state has 
authority to set WQS. 
Tribes across the country also have reserved water rights that must be protected. In Winters v. 
United States, the Supreme Court recognized that when land has been reserved to a tribe, a reservation of 
water sufficient to meet the purposes of the reservation is implied. 207 U.S. 564, 576-77 (1908); see also, 
e.g., Cappeart v. United States, 426 U.S. 128, 139 (1976); Arizona v. California, 373 U.S. 546, 597-602 
(1963); Agua Caliente Band of Cahuilla Indians v. Coachella Valley Water Dist., 849 F.3d 1262, 1270 
(9th Cir. 2017) (“[T]he primary purpose underlying the establishment of the reservation was to create a 
home for the Tribe, and water was necessarily implicated in that purpose.”). In many cases, the water 
reserved by a tribe originates outside of its reservation and flows downstream to the reservation. The 
Winters reserved water right entitles the tribe to a quantity of water sufficient to meet the purposes of the 
reservation, but the water must also be of sufficient quality to meet the purposes. Cohen’s Handbook of 
Federal Indian Law—the seminal treatise in the field—states as follows:  
To meet federal purposes, Indian reserved water rights should be protected against . . . 
impairments of water quality, as well as against diminutions in quantity. . . . Fulfilling the 
purposes of Indian reservations depends on the tribes receiving water of adequate quality 
as well as sufficient quantity. . . . The quality of the water necessary for [tribal] uses may 
vary from the high quality needed for human consumption to a lesser quality for fish and 
wildlife habitat to an even lower quality for irrigation. Each use, however, requires water 
that is appropriate quality to support that use.  
The quality and quantity of water may be directly related. This interrelationship is most 
evident in the case of a reserved right to water for fisheries preservation. The right 
reserved is that amount of water necessary to maintain the fishery. The fishery consists 
not only of the fish themselves, but also of the conditions necessary to their survival. 
Thus, habitat protection is an integral component of the reserved right. In order to protect 
the fishery habitat, tribes should have a right not only to a sufficient amount of water, but 
also to water that is of adequate quality. 
COHEN’S HANDBOOK OF FEDERAL INDIAN LAW § 19.03[9], at 1236 (Nell Jessup Newton ed., 2012) 
(footnotes and citations omitted). In the Federal Register notice, EPA indicates that “[t]ribal reserved 
rights as defined in this proposed rulemaking generally do not address the quantification of Winters 
rights.” 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,363. However, as noted above, the quality and quantity of water may be 
directly related. For instance, for a tribe with a Winters reserved water right that requires water sufficient 
to support fishing on a reservation, what happens upstream of the reservation with respect to water 
quantity may diminish water quality both outside and within the reservation. A good example is 
temperature impacts from upstream diversions. A stream may become water quality impaired for 
temperature if too much water has been diverted from the stream; in turn, this may affect fish dependent 

 
 
 
 
Page 19 of 32 
 
on cold water both outside and within the tribe’s reservation. This is an increasingly important issue in 
light of increased pressures from climate change, as EPA generally acknowledges. See 87 Fed. Reg. at 
74,366. In that case, the “tribal reserved right” in this rule should include the Tribe’s Winters reserved 
water right to protect the water quality before it reaches the reservation, even if the quantity of water is 
also implicated. Moreover, sometimes protection of the Winters reserved water right will have nothing to 
do with quantity. For instance, if a tribe has a Winters reserved water right for economic development, 
drinking water, or some other purpose, an upstream state must protect the water quality required to meet 
each such use before the water to which the tribe is entitled reaches the reservation, which may include 
more protective criteria to preventing pollutants from being discharged upstream of the reservation that 
would impair the Winters right.13  
At proposed 40 C.F.R. § 131.3(r), the rule defines “tribal reserved rights” as “any rights to 
aquatic and/or aquatic-dependent resources reserved or held by tribes, either expressly or implicitly, 
through treaties, statutes, executive orders, or other sources of Federal law.” This language is broad 
enough to encompass ceremonial uses and Winters reserved water rights, as it must. However, EPA’s 
decision not to include “water” itself among the list of enumerated examples of tribal reserved rights (87 
Fed. Reg. at 74,367) and its statement that the definition generally does not include quantification of 
Winters rights (87 Fed. Reg. at 74,363) could be used to suggest that Winters rights need not be protected 
under the rule. This cannot be, and the preamble and response to comments for the final rule must make it 
clear that the water quality needed for Winters reserved water rights to fulfill the purposes of a reservation 
must be maintained or achieved. The same is true for ceremonial uses of water wherever tribes reserved 
such rights in areas where states or EPA may promulgate water quality standards. 
In EPA’s description of the “tribal reserved rights” definition, the agency notes that the proposed 
definition “does not apply to unratified treaties or reserved rights that have been abrogated or otherwise 
superseded.” 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,366. The Tribes do not take exception to this language but note for the 
record that many states do not seem to understand or accept that only Congress has the authority to 
abrogate a reserved right and that any such abrogation must be explicit. E.g., United States v. Dion, 476 
U.S. 734, 738-39 (1986) (“We have required that Congress’ intention to abrogate Indian treaty rights be 
clear and plain.”); Washington v. Wash. Com. Passenger Fishing Vessel Ass’n, 443 U.S. 658, 690 (1979) 
(“Absent explicit statutory language, we have been extremely reluctant to find congressional abrogation 
of treaty rights. . . .”). While some states may wish that treaties or other sources of reserved rights did not 
exist or claim that circumstances have changed such that the reserved rights have been relinquished, EPA, 
in coordination with affected rights holders, will need to ensure that such erroneous positions are provided 
no credence.14 If a state asserts abrogation of a tribal reserved right as a basis for not protecting it in its 
 
13 Similar arguments can be made that some waters outside of the waters in which a tribe might hold its reserved 
fishing rights may still require more protective WQS to protect tribal reserved rights where such waters are 
necessary to support the right. For instance, anadromous salmon and steelhead travel away from tribal usual and 
accustomed areas at points in their life cycles. Habitat on which they depend when they are outside of the U&A 
should still be sufficiently protective so as not to undermine the tribal reserved right when they return to or pass 
through the U&A. 
14 In the preamble, EPA posits a question regarding whether in a situation in which “a waterbody may not be able to 
support a reserved right to an aquatic and/or aquatic-dependent resource because attaining that use in that waterbody 
is not currently feasible,” the state could revise its designated uses to remove the tribal reserved rights use following 
a use attainability analysis. 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,372. We do not believe either EPA or the state would have that 
option. While such an administrative action would have no legal bearing on the tribe’s reserved rights, Clean Water

authority supporting its position rather than shifting the burden to the tribe to prove that there is no such 
authority.  
C. 
The “Right Holder” Definition Is Acceptable But Its Use Does Not Make Sense at 
One Point in the Proposed Regulatory Language. 
EPA proposes to define “right holders” at 40 C.F.R. § 131.3(s) as “tribes holding rights to aquatic 
and/or aquatic-dependent resources pursuant to an applicable treaty, statute, executive order, or other 
source of Federal law.” 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,366, 74,378. The Tribes do not object to this definition but 
note that use of the term “right holder” does not make sense in at least one circumstance in which it has 
been used in the regulatory scheme. At 40 C.F.R. § 131.9(a)(2), the proposed language states that WQS 
must be established to protect “[t]he health of the right holders to at least the same risk level as provided 
to the general population of the State.” It would be better to use another term besides “right holders” in 
this instance since EPA presumably means individual tribal members rather than a tribe in this provision. 
A phrase such as “right holder’s members” or “right holder’s population” could be substituted in this 
provision. In other instances, such as the information sharing provision at 40 C.F.R. § 131.6(g)(1) and the 
tribal consultation provision at 40 C.F.R. § 131.9(b), the use of the term “right holders” makes sense as 
these activities would involve the affected tribe. The Tribes also note that the definition of “right holders” 
could be shortened to: “tribes holding tribal reserved rights,” assuming the agency does not make any 
changes to the definition of “tribal reserved rights” proposed for 40 C.F.R. § 131.3(r). As it stands now, 
the language in 40 C.F.R. § 131.3(s) is somewhat redundant to the definition at § 131.3(r). 
D. 
The Types of Historic Information to Determine the Level of Water Quality 
Necessary to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights Should Include Indigenous Traditional 
Ecological Knowledge, and Funding Should Be Provided to Ensure Sufficient Data 
and Information Is Available to Support Protective WQS.  
EPA has requested comment on the types of information that states and EPA should consider in 
determining the level of water quality necessary to protect tribal reserved rights. EPA writes:  
Determining the level of water quality necessary to protect any aquatic or aquatic-
 
Act actions should not be taken that suggest a right no longer exists or create confusion for the public in that regard. 
Instead, the CWA should only be”[striving] for attainment of such uses to protect a tribal reserved right consistent 
with the obligations of treaties and other Federal Laws.” Id. Further, where some level of reserved right use, even if 
severely suppressed, is being attained, the state would have no authority to remove that existing use under EPA’s 
existing implementing regulations. 40 C.F.R. §131.10(g) (“States may designate a use, or remove a use that is not an 
existing use, if the State conducts a use attainability analysis . . . .”). In short, if a tribe has reserved rights in a water 
body in which a state has jurisdiction to set WQS, that reserved right must be a designated use, and EPA should not 
afford the state an opportunity or any authority to remove that designated use unless and until Congress explicitly 
and plainly abrogates that right. In extremely limited circumstances, a WQS variance that conforms to the 
requirements in 40 C.F.R. § 131.14 may be available. However, as EPA is well aware, “[w]here a State adopts a 
WQS variance, the State must retain, in its standards, the underlying designated use and criterion addressed by the 
WQS variance.” 40 C.F.R. § 131.14(a)(2). Any such variance would need to be approved by EPA after consultation 
with right holders. As the Tribes’ trustee, we expect that EPA would adhere to the right holder’s position on the 
variance.

weighing multiple lines of evidence. However, this endeavor will largely mirror the 
process states already follow in developing their WQS. Examples of such evidence 
include fish consumption rate surveys, studies or accounts of heritage fish consumption 
rates, peer-reviewed articles or reports on the types and levels of pollutants that can
