87 Fed. Reg. at 74,368 (emphasis added). The Tribes agree that each of these categories of information is 
an appropriate type of information for states and EPA to consider in determining the level of water quality 
necessary to protect tribal reserved rights (i.e., in setting criteria). In addition, however, we emphasize the 
need for states and EPA to consider Indigenous Traditional Ecological Knowledge (ITEK) in their 
development of water quality standards. Further, some level of funding must be made available by the 
federal government to ensure that the requirement in proposed 40 C.F.R. § 131.9(a) indicating that states 
and EPA must rely on “available data and information” to establish WQS that protect 1) the exercise of 
tribal reserved rights unsuppressed by water quality or aquatic-dependent resource availability and 2) 
tribal member health can be fulfilled. Otherwise, there is a risk that relevant information may not be 
readily available, which may derail urgently needed improvements in water quality. 
 
 
1. 
Indigenous Traditional Ecological Knowledge (ITEK) 
On November 15, 2021, the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP) and 
the White House Council on Environmental Quality (CEQ) jointly released a memorandum that commits 
to elevating Indigenous Traditional Ecological Knowledge (ITEK) in federal scientific policy processes. 
Office of Science and Technology Policy, Council on Environmental Quality Indigenous Traditional 
Ecological Knowledge and Federal Decision Making (Nov. 15, 2021) [2021 White House 
Memorandum], available at https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2021/11/111521-OSTP-
CEQ-ITEK-Memo.pdf. This memorandum formally recognized ITEK as one of many bodies of 
knowledge that are valuable to improving policy making and recognizes that its inclusion in federal 
policy making is “[c]onsistent with the Administration’s additional commitment to scientific integrity and 
knowledge and evidence-based policymaking.” Id. at 1. On November 30, 2022, the White House 
followed up on this memorandum with “Guidance for Federal Departments and Agencies on Indigenous 
Knowledge” (https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2022/12/OSTP-CEQ-IK-Guidance.pdf) 
and an associated memorandum on “Implementation of Guidance for Federal Departments and Agencies 
on Indigenous Knowledge” (https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2022/12/IK-Guidance-
Implementation-Memo.pdf). These documents are “intended to promote and enable a government-wide 
effort to improve the recognition and inclusion of Indigenous Knowledge” in “research, policy, and other 
decision making,” including review and approval of state water quality standards. Nov. 30, 2022 
Implementation of Guidance Memorandum at 1; see also November 30, 2022 Guidance Memorandum at 
4-5 (“Indigenous Knowledge can provide accurate information, valuable insights, and effective practices 
that complement practices and knowledge derived from other approaches. For example, at times 
Indigenous Knowledge holders have observed early and accurate detection of environmental changes, 
such as interconnected patterns of species, signs of drought, or impacted water quality.”). 
The 2021 White House Memorandum defined “ITEK [as] a body of observations, oral and 
written knowledge, practices, and beliefs that promote environmental sustainability and the responsible 

 
 
 
 
Page 22 of 32 
 
stewardship of natural resources through relationships between humans and environmental systems.” Id. 
at 2. As far as we are aware, EPA has not yet adopted its own definition of ITEK, but it has employed the 
U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service’s definition in prior guidance: 
Also called by other names including Indigenous Knowledge or Native Science, 
(hereafter, TEK) refers to the evolving knowledge acquired by indigenous and local 
peoples over hundreds or thousands of years through direct contact with the environment. 
This knowledge is specific to a location and includes the relationships between plants, 
animals, natural phenomena, landscapes and timing of events that are used for lifeways, 
including but not limited to hunting, fishing, trapping, agriculture, and forestry. TEK is 
an accumulating body of knowledge, practice, and belief, evolving by adaptive processes 
and handed down through generations by cultural transmission, about the relationship of 
living beings (human and non-human) with one another and with the environment. It 
encompasses the world view of indigenous people which includes ecology, spirituality, 
human and animal relationships, and more. 
EPA Re: “Considering Traditional Ecological Knowledge (TEK) During the Cleanup Process (Jan. 3, 
2017), available at https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2020-
10/documents/considering_traditional_ecological_knowledge_tek_during_the_cleanup_process_updated_
link.pdf (quoting Sarah Rinkevich et al., Traditional Ecological Knowledge for Application by Service 
Scientists Fact Sheet, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Native American Program. (Feb. 2011)). As 
suggested by the definitions above, ITEK has been identified with several names, including “Traditional 
Ecological Knowledge” (TEK) and “Indigenous Knowledge,” but all retain a common theme: Indigenous 
knowledge systems are based on intense, place-based observations that have evolved, and continue to 
evolve, over millennia. Indigenous knowledge survives and adapts as it is passed from one generation to 
the next through the exercise of cultural practices.  
Increasingly, non-Indigenous scientists and policy makers recognize the importance of ITEK in 
decision-making, including the connections it demonstrates between biological, physical, cultural, and 
spiritual systems. The White House recognizes ITEK “as one of the many important bodies of knowledge 
that contributes to the scientific, technical, social, and economic advancements of the United States and to 
our collective understanding of the natural world.” 2021 White House Memorandum at 1. Likewise, 
EPA’s 2014 Policy on Environmental Justice for Working with Federally Recognized Tribes and 
Indigenous People (https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2017-10/documents/ej-indigenous-policy.pdf), 
“encourages as appropriate and to the extent practicable and permitted by law, the integration of 
Traditional Ecological Knowledge into the agency’s environmental science, and policy decision-making 
processes to address environmental justice concerns and facilitate program implementation.” Id. at 3. 
Certainly, ITEK must be considered in determining the level of water quality necessary to protect “tribal 
reserved rights” under the rule.  
 
EPA must be mindful that tribes may have confidentiality concerns with respect to ITEK and 
other types of tribal history and knowledge. As EPA acknowledged in its 2014 Environmental Justice 
Policy (page 3), “The EPA considers confidentiality concerns regarding information on sacred sites, 
cultural resources, and other traditional knowledge, as permitted by law. The EPA acknowledges that 
unique situations and relationships may exist in regard to sacred sites.” Before seeking ITEK from “right 
holders,” EPA should, at a minimum, observe the cautions laid out in the Nov. 30, 2022 White House 
Guidance (pages 15-16) regarding conducting an initial meeting, so that ITEK holders are aware of how 

 
 
 
 
Page 23 of 32 
 
the information will be used and the extent to which it can be made available to states or the public at 
large. Likewise, it should provide guidance and a process for states to use in handling such information. 
2.  
Federal Funding 
Ensuring that the type of information necessary to meet the requirements of proposed 40 C.F.R. § 
131.9(a) (“to the extent supported by available data and information”) takes resources. It is not cheap or 
easy to complete things like fish consumption surveys, toxicology studies, interviews with tribal elders to 
record ITEK and oral histories, etc. Both tribes and states are likely to require resources in order to ensure 
that the information EPA is calling for is available and does not present an unintended barrier to 
promulgation and approval of WQS that actually protect tribal reserved rights. A good example of the 
type of study that could inform unsuppressed levels of fish consumption is the Wabanaki Traditional 
Cultural Lifeways Exposure Pathway Scenario (July 2009), available at 
https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2015-08/documents/ditca.pdf (Attachment 20). The Wabanaki 
study was funded by EPA through a Direct Implementation Tribal Cooperative Agreement, peer-
reviewed, and specifically designed for use in reviewing and developing water quality standards. It 
provides a numerical representation of the environmental contact, diet, and exposure pathways of people 
fully using natural resources and pursuing traditional cultural lifeways. Wabanaki Study at 7-10; see also 
81 Fed. Reg. 23,239, 23,246 (April 20, 2016) (quoting purpose of study as “to describe the lifestyle that 
was universal when resources were in better condition and that some tribal members practice today (and 
many more that are waiting to resume once restoration goals and protective standards are in place)”). The 
study breaks down consumption levels based on the estimated range of diets that reflect three traditional 
lifestyle modes reflective of different habitat types. Another good example of this type of EPA-tribal 
funding partnership is the fish consumption survey completed for the Columbia Basin Treaty Tribes by 
the Columbia River Inter-Tribal Fish Commission (CRITFC), which was a project funded through a 
cooperative agreement between CRITFC and the EPA’s Office of Policy, Planning and Evaluation. 
CRITFC, A Fish Consumption Survey of the Umatilla, Nez Perce, Yakama, and Warm Springs Tribes of 
the Columbia River Basin: Technical Report 94-3 (Oct. 1994), available at https://www.critfc.org/wp-
content/uploads/2015/06/94-3report.pdf (Attachment 21). We request that EPA discuss in its response to 
comments how the agency intends and plans to ensure that federal funding is available to help tribes 
gather or develop the information necessary to ensure rapid progress on WQS improvements is not 
thwarted by a lack of available information. Further, EPA should ensure that it does not set too onerous a 
threshold for the data and information required to meet the language of 40 C.F.R. § 131.9(a) (“available 
data and information”) in either practice or guidance documents that would prevent improvements on a 
prompt timeline. 
E. 
EPA Is Correct to Account for Suppression Effects Explicitly in the Language of the 
Proposed Rule.  
The Tribes wholeheartedly agree with EPA that the WQS must be set to protect the exercise of 
tribal reserved rights unsuppressed by water quality or the availability of the resource at issue. Without 
such a provision, water quality standards will only protect the unsatisfactory status quo in which tribal 
members consume fish at rates far below heritage rates of consumption when fish and shellfish were more 
abundant and tribal members did not need to be fearful of eating too much seafood due to toxic 
contamination. This is the present circumstance throughout much, if not all, of the Tribes’ usual and 
accustomed areas. In 40 C.F.R. § 131.9(a), EPA proposes the following language:  

 
 
 
 
Page 24 of 32 
 
(a) Water quality standards must protect tribal reserved rights applicable to waters 
subject to such standards. To protect tribal reserved rights, water quality standards must, 
to the extent supported by available data and information, be established to protect: 
(1) The exercise of tribal reserved rights unsuppressed by water quality or availability of 
the aquatic or aquatic-dependent resource; and 
(2) The health of the right holders to at least the same risk level as provided to the 
general population of the State. 
87 Fed. Reg. at 74,378. We believe this proposed regulatory language does a good job of pointing out—
and requiring states to address—the problem of suppression, both in terms of the effects of depressed 
supplies of aquatic resources resulting from degraded water quality and the effects of contamination on 
tribal member health. “EPA request[ed] comment on whether additional language should be included in 
the final rule specifying the considerations for determining unsuppressed WQS.” 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,369. 
While we do not have specific suggestions for more detail in the proposed regulatory language itself, we 
do believe it will be incumbent upon EPA to ensure its guidance documents, including documents such 
EPA’s Methodology for Deriving Ambient Water Quality Criteria for the Protection of Human Health 
(2000), are updated to be consistent with the CWA’s implementing regulations. Moreover, specific 
guidance documents may be required to implement this new rule, and consistent application of this 
provision may benefit especially from such guidance. 
 
Related to tribal reserved fishing rights, the National Environmental Justice Council explains: “A 
‘suppression effect’ occurs when a fish consumption rate (FCR) for a given population, group, or tribe 
reflects a current level of consumption that is artificially diminished from an appropriate baseline level of 
consumption for that population, group, or tribe. The more robust baseline level of consumption is 
suppressed, inasmuch as it does not get captured by the FCR.” NEJAC, Fish Consumption and 
Environmental Justice, at 43-45 (Nov. 2002) (Attachment 22). We have attached the comments from both 
the Northwest Indian Fish Commission (Attachment 23 at 33, 36, 71, 76) and Ridolfi Environmental 
(Attachment 24 at 7-9) regarding the Washington human health criteria, which discuss the effects of 
suppression on contemporary fish consumption surveys and the need to determine and use heritage rates 
in establishing WQS. The Federal Register notice indicates that EPA is not necessarily proposing to 
return waterbodies to a “condition that existed at the time a reserved right was established, 87 Fed. Reg. at 
74,366-67, citing the Grand Coulee Dam as the type of condition that revised WQS are not able to fully 
account for due to the dam’s depletion of fish populations available for tribal member consumption. Id. 
However, “the regulation is intended to result in WQS that protect reasonably anticipated future uses, 
taking into account factors that may have substantially altered a water body,” id. at 74,367. The Federal 
Register notice also notes, “the unsuppressed level or use of a resource should account for situations 
where restoration efforts are planned or underway (e.g., efforts to improve habitat or reduce 
contamination), such that it would be reasonable to expect the opportunities for use of the resource to 
increase in the future.” Id. at 74,369. While we agree with this latter sentiment, EPA must not allow 
legacy pollution and levels of pollution to be locked in place just because there is long-standing 
infrastructure or industrial use that has depleted the quality of water in a water body. Dams come down 
(just look at the Elwha River) and legacy pollution can be cleaned up and habitat restored (each of our 
Tribes is involved in various Trustee Council processes to address Natural Resource Damages, for 
example), so we are discomforted by the idea that historic wrongs may be built into a diminished baseline 
from which the level of protection necessary for the tribal reserved right WQS will be assessed. As the 

 
 
 
 
Page 25 of 32 
 
agency acknowledges, EPA should be forcing action rather than reinforcing an existing suppressed use or 
“set[ting] in motion a ‘downward spiral’ of further reduction/suppression.” Id. at 74,369. As a trustee with 
fiduciary obligations to the tribes, EPA must apply its authority to prompt restoration, not maintain the 
status quo. 
EPA notes that determining levels for the unsuppressed exercise of tribal reserved rights would 
need to be based on “available data and information” without specifying what types of data and 
information states or EPA may rely on. 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,378. In an earlier section, we note the types of 
information that might be used, but we do want to make clear that this proposal calls for caution. For 
example, as described above, contemporary fish consumption surveys may indicate lower rates of fish 
consumption than historic levels or the levels to which those exercising reserved rights are entitled. 
Consequently, as suggested above, EPA should include language in the rule, preamble, response to 
comments, and guidance documents that would require states and EPA to rely on available ITEK, other 
tribal accounts of unsuppressed rates, historical or anthropological reports of the exercise of tribal 
reserved rights, or studies of the historical exercise of tribal reserved rights, so that WQS do not end up 
protecting only for a suppressed status quo. If these types of information are available, they should 
supersede other available data or information.15 If these types of information are not available at the time 
of a triennial review, as suggested above, EPA should make grants or other funding available for studies 
of the unsuppressed exercise of tribal reserved rights to be completed before the next triennial review, so 
that suppression effects can be corrected.  
IV. 
TRIBAL CONSULTATION AND PRACTICALITIES OF RULE IMPLEMENTATION 
We conclude with one of our—if not the—greatest concerns about the proposed Reserved Rights 
Rule. As described at the outset of this letter, when our ancestors entered treaties with the Federal 
government in 1855, we gave up vast swaths of our ancestral territory while reserving certain essential 
rights to ourselves in order to perpetuate our existence then and forever. As sovereigns, the off-
reservation usufructuary rights that our forebears fought hard to reserve—and which we continue every 
day to fight hard to protect for the generations to come—are some of our most sacred and fundamental 
rights. We know these rights better than anyone else. We can speak authoritatively to these rights when 
others cannot. While we deeply appreciate EPA’s efforts through this proposed rule to protect our 
reserved rights, the proposed rule is flawed in the process it describes for determining if and where tribal 
reserved rights apply, and with whom it places that power. The rule must be corrected on this score before 
 
15 In the Federal Register notice, EPA writes, “Where information is conflicting, there are gaps in information, 
and/or a difference of opinion exists between the state and one or more tribes about the level of water quality 
necessary to protect a reserved right, EPA will take action based on the best available information in the same way 
that EPA currently makes WQS decisions in these circumstances in other contexts, e.g., determining whether criteria 
are scientifically defensible in situations where there is conflicting science, there are gaps in the science, and/or there 
are different conclusions among stakeholders. EPA requests comment on whether there are other factors it should 
consider when making decisions under these circumstances.” 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,371. We do not generally have a 
concern about this approach, except that where there is conflicting information about which a tribe would know 
more than a state (e.g., the existence and level of use of the tribe’s own reserved rights) or where there is “a 
difference of opinion . . . between [a] state and one or more tribes about the level of water quality necessary to 
protect a reserved right,” EPA should defer to, or at least weigh more heavily, the tribal position in that 
circumstance. The failure to do so may run afoul of EPA’s trust responsibility and obligations under the Clean Water 
Act and federal Indian law to ensure that tribal reserved rights are protected. 

 
 
 
 
Page 26 of 32 
 
it is finalized. 
 
The proposed rule requires that EPA consult with tribes (“right holders”) in association with the 
agency’s review of a state’s water quality standards. The proposed language at 40 C.F.R. § 131.9(b) 
states, “In reviewing State water quality standards submissions under this section, EPA will initiate tribal 
consultation with the right holders, consistent with applicable EPA tribal consultation policies, in 
determining whether State water quality standards protect applicable tribal reserved rights in accordance 
with paragraph (a) of this section.” 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,378. The Tribes appreciate this commitment to 
tribal consultation in EPA’s review of the standards a state submits for approval, and we want to see this 
explicit commitment to consultation in the final rule (and other rules EPA is promulgating). However, we 
are concerned that the tribal consultation described in the regulatory language itself comes too late in the 
process if it only occurs after a state has already gone through its rulemaking process and submitted such 
standards to EPA for approval. If a state does not have and use the requisite information from affected 
tribes much earlier in the process, this could result in costly, lengthy delays that could have been avoided 
had an affected tribe been consulted earlier, as well as the state being less inclined to willingly incorporate 
tribal information after it has already completed its administrative process. Consequently, we believe that 
the affirmative duty for EPA to consult should be maintained in the final language of the rule, but it 
should be expanded to require early (and frequent) consultation with the right holders. We understand 
from EPA’s preamble and from government-to-government consultation that EPA appreciates the need 
for early and frequent consultation with tribes and to provide direction and guidance to states, but that 
understanding should be made a requirement in the regulatory text. Compare 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,372 
(“EPA makes itself available to engage early and often to provide support when states are adopting and 
revising WQS. . . . EPA intends to support states by providing input and information on any tribal 
reserved rights and the level of water quality to protect those rights. As previously mentioned, EPA is also 
available to facilitate dialogue between states and tribes.”), with 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,378 (proposed § 
131.9(b) requiring no early consultation with tribes or states), and id. (proposed § 131.20 describing state 
review and triennial review with no reference to consultation with EPA or tribes). 
 
The language at 40 C.F.R. § 131.6(g)(1) in which EPA proposes the following language 
regarding the minimum requirements for a state’s water quality standards submission does not assuage the 
concern: 
Where applicable, information which will aid the agency in evaluating whether the 
submission protects tribal reserved rights consistent with § 131.9, including: 
(1) Information about the scope, nature, and current and past use of the tribal reserved 
rights, as informed by the right holders; and 
(2) Data and methods used to develop the water quality standards. 
87 Fed. Reg. at 74,378 (emphasis added). In fact, it causes us quite a bit of consternation, as does the 
process described (but not required) in the preamble at pages 74,367-68. Most fundamentally, the 
italicized phrase is too vague regarding tribes’ role and does not require the state to actually use the 
information provided by tribes regarding their own reserved rights. We are very concerned that states—
which frequently have the least incentive to recognize tribal reserved rights and are frequently outright 
hostile to such rights—will be opining on the existence, scope, nature, and current and past use of tribes’ 
most sacred rights without being required to accept the affected tribe’s or even the federal trustee’s 

 
 
 
 
Page 27 of 32 
 
description and assessment of these rights. We understand that states with delegated Clean Water Act 
authority over waters in which tribes hold reserved rights must have some role in developing the WQS to 
protect that use of waters over which they have jurisdiction. However, we do not believe that states can or 
should be in the driver’s seat with respect to the analysis of the topics included in proposed 40 C.F.R. § 
131.6(g)(1). While certainly not true of all states, in enough, it will put the fox in charge of the hen house, 
such that this provision is not workable from our perspective. Instead, the federal trustee, after working 
closely with an affected tribe (and the Department of Interior, if needed), must take a much more active—
and binding—role in this process in order to ensure that tribes’ sovereign interests and sacred rights are 
protected. Once the tribal reserved rights are appropriately characterized by the appropriate actors (the 
tribe, first and foremost), at that point, we could see states properly exercising their delegated authority to 
set designated uses, criteria, and antidegradation policy. We request that the final language of the rule 
reflect these comments through more detailed and binding regulatory provisions that put tribes in charge 
of characterizing their own rights. At the very least, the language of 40 C.F.R. § 131.6(g)(1) should be 
stripped down to its bare minimum, so that states (as opposed to tribes or EPA) are not charged with 
characterizing the “scope, nature, and current and past use of tribal reserved rights.” Changing that 
provision to “(1) Information about tribal reserved rights, as provided by the right holders” would provide 
us considerably more comfort about how the process might work and what its ultimate outcome might 
be.16 
Even if we could abide the placement of authority to assess tribal reserved rights in states’ hands 
(which we cannot), the proposed regulatory language is not prescriptive enough about what a state must 
do to ensure that it has appropriate information from a tribe—or that it uses it. In theory, the “as informed 
by the right holders” language above would suggest to a state that it should engage in government-to-
government consultation with tribes holding tribal reserved rights in order to ensure it has sufficient 
information about the existence, scope, nature, and current and past use of tribal reserved rights to know 
where and how to protect them through the state’s WQS. However, without more explicit, mandatory 
language, we are skeptical that robust consultation with tribes will be the outcome of this language in 
most states, particularly those that do not have an existing government-to-government consultation policy 
(or where the policy is underdeveloped or underutilized in practice). As EPA is well aware, the 
relationship between states and tribes can be fraught and very adversarial at times. Even where a tribe and 
a state have a decent, or even a very good, relationship, they may not be able to agree on what level of 
water quality will actually protect the tribal reserved rights. Consequently, we recommend more direct 
and robust regulatory language that explicitly requires states to consult with tribes at the outset of and 
 
16 At the end of its description of the process for “Determining if Tribal Reserved Rights Apply,” EPA indicates that 
“[i]n addition to seeking input from potential right holders, EPA will also consider other sources of information 
regarding applicable tribal reserved rights including the language of the treaties, statutes, or Executive orders and 
relevant judicial precedent.” 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,368. We note that in many cases this should be the starting and end 
point of the analysis. For instance, the United States v. Washington case area covers nearly the entire geographic 
scope of western Washington. One tribe or another has adjudicated usual and accustomed areas throughout the case 
area, and neither the State of Washington nor EPA needs to—or should—try to reinvent the wheel. Mere reference 
to the judicial opinions and findings of fact made in that case should be sufficient support for recognition of the 
tribal reserved rights that need to be protected. Other pertinent sources of information that are not listed in this 
passage include legislative history and prior federal actions in which an agency has already recognized the need to 
protect tribal reserved rights, such as prior Department of Interior or Bureau of Indian Affairs analyses or past EPA 
decisions. Good examples are the very materials that EPA cites in this preamble related to the human health criteria 
processes in Washington and Maine.  

 
 
 
 
Page 28 of 32 
 
throughout its revision process to determine whether, where, and how tribal reserved rights will be 
affected by the WQS, as well as language that establishes a presumption in favor of the use of a tribe’s 
own assessment of its rights when EPA reviews a state’s WQS submission. In addition to strengthening 
the proposed regulatory language, the Tribes suggest that EPA prepare guidance explaining how a state 
should engage in government-to-government consultation with a tribe; the value and need to accept 
Indigenous Traditional Ecological Knowledge as relevant, reliable information; and the sensitivities and 
need for careful handling of some such information and knowledge.  
Other issues that are not accounted for in the regulatory language include: How will EPA protect 
tribes from state analyses of reserved rights that may be unsupported by law, the subject of litigation, or in 
need of update due to new information? How will EPA ensure that the wishes of a tribe that does not want 
its reserved rights to be assessed by a state at all or put in issue in a Clean Water Act administrative 
process are respected? What happens when a state ignores the information provided by a tribe or the 
federal trustee? Moreover, while the preamble notes, “where information is conflicting, there are gaps in 
information, and/or a difference of opinion exists between the state and one or more tribes about the level 
of water quality necessary to protect a reserved right, EPA will take action based on the best available 
information in the same way that EPA currently makes WQS decisions in these circumstances in other 
contexts,” 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,371, this may be cold comfort during certain administrations’ review of 
state water quality standards, as we saw in the human health criteria rollbacks of the last administration. 
As with preparation of materials required to determine the level of protection for tribal reserved 
rights, we are also concerned about the resources it is likely to take tribes to engage with states regarding 
the very existence of their rights. At 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,375, EPA asks for comment on the following 
conclusion, “While tribal right holders would not be direct respondents, EPA acknowledges that the 
proposed regulation would require that state submissions be informed by the right holders. EPA believes 
this would not lead to increased burden on right holders because the proposed rule would not require 
additional coordination beyond that which already occurs during WQS public participation processes and 
EPA’s consultations with tribal governments.” We disagree with this statement. While it is true that we 
and many other tribes actively participate in existing WQS public participation processes and while we 
welcome this rule, there is no question that there will be additional burdens on us and other tribes as a 
result of it. It takes time and money to engage in administrative processes, and it takes even more time 
and money to engage in administrative processes where sovereigns do not agree. In order to support 
protective criteria, we are likely to need to conduct or commission fish consumption surveys and other 
materials to establish the level of water quality necessary to protect our rights. Likewise, with respect to 
designated uses and other aspects of WQS, while we are hopeful (and expect) that Washington’s current 
Governor, Attorney General, and Department of Ecology Director will work cooperatively with our tribes 
to ensure protection of tribal reserved rights, we have no guarantee that that will be the case with future 
political leaders. After all, even with the current political actors, we had to go to the United States 
Supreme Court in 2018 to protect—and have the State accept—subsidiary aspects of our reserved fishing 
rights. With respect to characterization and geographic location of tribal reserved rights, this rule may 
necessitate additional time and cost associated with leadership-to-leadership meetings between tribes, 
states, and EPA; preparation of comments and legal analyses; and potentially even legal action. We 
therefore again request that the Federal government provide funding to help tribes engage in this process. 
Finally, EPA proposes to modify 40 C.F.R. § 131.20 to require that a state’s “triennial review 
process include an evaluation of whether there are tribal reserved rights applicable to waters subject to the 
state’s WQS and whether WQS need to be revised to protect those rights.” 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,367, 

 
 
 
 
Page 29 of 32 
 
74,378-79 (proposed § 131.20(a)). We understand that states will need a little time to implement this rule 
as practical matter and agree that the triennial review is a good way to first incorporate the Reserved 
Rights Rule’s requirements. Of course, EPA is aware that triennial reviews can sometimes be delayed and 
some are currently in process. While a gradual process may be ok (or even beneficial) in some 
circumstances), states are on notice now that a final rule is on its way, so they should begin thinking about 
whether any WQS revisions they are currently undertaking implicate tribal reserved rights. For instance, 
the Washington State Department of Ecology is currently going through revision of its aquatic life toxics 
criteria. As a result of this Federal Register notice and its experience with the human health criteria, the 
state is aware that it has obligations to set those criteria in a manner that protects tribal reserved rights. 
We do not think that potentially less protective criteria should be grandfathered in, as it were, just because 
the revision process began before the Reserved Rights Rule has been completed. A similar example might 
be where a state already has adopted a sustenance fishing designated use (like the State of Maine for 
certain waters), the state should ensure that any criteria it revises be sufficient to protect tribal reserved 
rights in those waters, regardless of when this rule is finalized.  
. 
. 
. 
To conclude, the Tribes thank EPA for recognizing the need and doing the work to ensure that 
water quality standards protect tribal reserved rights and the people who depend on exercise of their rights 
for their health and well-being, livelihoods, culture, religion, and community cohesion. We encourage you 
to move swiftly to finalize the proposed rule, but to do so with the comments made here firmly in mind. 
We do not believe EPA should finalize a rule that would allow the omission of certain components of 
WQS or that would put a state in the position of defining the scope, nature, or current or past use of a 
tribe’s reserved rights is appropriate, and we look forward to EPA refining the final rule and preamble to 
address these concerns. The Tribes also appreciate EPA’s efforts to engage in meaningful government-to-
government consultation with respect to agency rulemakings like this, which were either pro forma or 
non-existent under the prior administration. We are available and more than happy to discuss this matter 
further should you have any questions about our comments or would like to discuss possible resolutions 
to any potential problems we have identified in the proposed rule. You may contact Jane Steadman at 
jsteadman@kanjikatzen.com or 206-344-8100 with any questions you might have or to coordinate further 
discussion with our Tribes.

RE: Potential Revisions to Federal Water Quality Standards Regulations to Protect Tribal 
Reserved Rights 
 
Dear Ms. Brundage: 
 
Thank you for the opportunity to submit comments as a follow up to our consultation on January 
23, 2023.  The Squaxin Island Tribe supports the Environmental Protection Agency’s (“EPA”) 
proposed amendments to the Clean Water Act (“CWA”) water quality standards (“WQS”) 
regulation because they expressly recognize that state water quality standards are subject to the 
reserved rights of tribal nations and the EPA’s fiduciary duty to protect these rights.   
 
The Squaxin Island Tribe is a federally recognized Indian tribe located in Southern Puget Sound 
in Mason County, Washington with treaty rights to harvest fish and shellfish, “at their usual and 
accustomed fishing places in the shallow bays, estuaries, inlets and open Sound of Southern Puget 
Sound and in the freshwater streams and creeks draining into those inlets.”1  (Figure 1)  The Tribe’s 
cultural and economic well-being depend upon clean water to support abundant and sustainable 
fisheries.  Thus, the Tribe has vital interests in ensuring that laws and regulations intended to 
protect water quality and related aquatic habitat, are implemented and enforced, so that it can 
continue to exercise its federal treaty rights.  
 
The Squaxin Island Tribe is uniquely positioned to offer a perspective on water quality.  The 
Tribe’s location at the south end of Puget Sound, where pollutants discharged from all parts north 
accumulate, makes water quality standards in all areas of the sound especially critical to the 
Squaxin Island Tribe.  An example of this cumulative impact is the effect of nutrient pollution on 
dissolved oxygen levels.  Nutrient discharge by wastewater treatment plants exacerbates algae 
blooms, which leads to low dissolved oxygen conditions.  Oxygen depletion is especially severe 
in shallow inlets, such as those found in South Puget Sound, and thus has a disproportionate impact 
on water quality in the Tribe’s “Usual and Accustomed” places (“U&A”) (Figure 2).  Elevated
                                                           
1 See generally United States v. Washington, 384 F.Supp. 312, 378 (W.D. Wash. 1974); United States v. 
Washington, 459 F.Supp. 1020 (W.D. Wash. 1978). 

Tribal Reserved Water Rights 
Squaxin Island Tribe to EPA 
February 21, 2023 
2 
 
levels of dissolved oxygen impact the behavior and movement of adult salmon, which has a 
negative effect on Tribal fisheries.  Harmful effects of low marine dissolved oxygen also include 
acidification, which can prevent shellfish and other marine organisms from forming shells; shifts 
in the number and types of bottom-dwelling invertebrates; increases in abundance of macroalgae, 
which can impair the health of eelgrass beds; seasonal reduction in fish habitat and intensification 
of fish kill events; and potential disruption of the entire food web.  Protective dissolved oxygen 
standards and enforcement of nutrient discharge limitations are a prime example of how WQS can 
protect tribal reserved rights.  
 
Water quality standards can also protect tribal reserved rights by ensuring the safety of both 
shellfish and finfish consumption.  Fecal coliform bacterial standards and fish consumption rates 
are set by the State of Washington through rules in the Washington Administrative Code (WAC-
173-201A-210 and WAC 173-2-1A-240).  Consideration of tribal reserved rights would secure 
regulations that limit fecal coliform bacteria in saltwater and reduce exposure to toxic substances 
through fish consumption.  For example, standards set by the State of Washington currently 
assume a fish consumption rate of 175 grams per day.  This consumption rate reflects a 2012 
compromise.  However, the Tribe expects that the fish consumption rate should be increased over 
time to 330 grams per day to reflect the true fish consumption rate of tribal members.  In doing so, 
the State would be protecting tribal reserved rights with water quality standards.   
 
For the above reasons, EPA’s proposal is positive.  However, it does raise some concerns that we 
would like the agency to consider and address as it moves forward with rulemaking. The EPA 
must clarify that tribes, not states, dictate where reserved rights are exercised and where treaty-
reserved resources exist.  Without this clarity, the state may decline to recognize resources that are 
critical to the Squaxin Island Tribe’s exercise of its reserved rights and thus fail to enact 
appropriately protective WQS.  The Squaxin Island Tribe reserves its fishing rights both on 
reservation and, importantly, throughout its U&A.  Perpetually establishing and defending these 
rights with the state would be both contrary to the law and a drain on the Tribe’s limited resources.  
The proposed rule must create an assumption that the Tribe’s assertions regarding where reserved 
rights are exercised and where treaty-reserved resources exist are conclusive.   
 
The EPA must clearly establish that the proposed rule covers connected waters that support the 
habitat of treaty-reserved resources.  As described above, the Squaxin Island Tribe exercises its 
reserved rights in interconnected waters and ecosystems that depend on healthy water quality from 
upstream sources.  Some of these water bodies may not include designated beneficial uses that 
cover treaty-reserved resources, however, these waters play a critical role in supporting the habitat 
of treaty-reserved resources and the sustainable exercise of those reserved rights.  The proposed 
rule must clarify that WQS developed to protect treaty-reserved resources and rights apply both 
within the location of place-based rights as well as in adjacent and connected waters.   
 
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on Tribal Reserved Water Rights.

proposed Water Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights 
rulemaking as outlined in the December 5, 2022 Federal Register Notice. WSEO also supports 
and joins the comments from Wyoming Governor Mark Gordon and the Wyoming Department 
of Environmental Quality in whole. 
Wyoming holds title to water within its borders in a sovereign capacity as representative of all 
the people for the purpose of guaranteeing that the common rights of all are equally protected. 
Wyo. Const. art. 8 § 1; art. 1 § 31; Merrill v. Bishop, 287 P.2d 620, 625 (Wyo. 1955); See also 
Farm Inv. Co. v. Carpenter, 61 P. 258, 265 (Wyo. 1900). Wyoming constitutional and statutory 
provisions charge the State Engineer and the State Board of Control with the supervision, 
appropriation, distribution, and diversion of surface and groundwater use within the state. Wyo. 
Const. art. 8 §§ 2, 5; See, e.g., Wyo. Stat. Ann. §§ 41-4-502 through -511. The need for the state 
to control the use of its limited and precious water resources compelled Wyoming's 
Constitutional declaration of water ownership, and its history of water law and water 
administration that has since developed. 
Wyoming's Environmental Quality Act, under which Wyoming regulates water quality, further 
respects the diversion and use of water, as well as the State Engineer and State Board of 
Control's authority over those activities. "Nothing in this act shall be construed to supersede or 
abrogate any valid water right. It is recognized that diversion of water caused by the exercise of a 
valid water right is an allowable practice." Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 35-11-302(c). "Nothing in this 

act:...Limits or interferes with the jurisdiction, duties or authority of the state engineer, the state 
board of control..." Wyo. Stat. Ann. § 35-11-1104(a)(iii). 
The Clean Water Act (CWA) provides that it is the "policy of Congress to recognize, preserve, 
and protect the primary responsibilities of States to . . . plan the development and use of land and 
water resources." 33 U.S.C. § 1251(b). Additionally, the CWA states: "It is the policy of 
Congress that the authority of each State to allocate quantities of water within its jurisdiction 
shall not be superseded, abrogated or otherwise impaired by this chapter. It is the further policy 
of Congress that nothing in this chapter shall be construed to supersede or abrogate rights to 
quantities of water which have been established by any State." 33 U.S.C. § 1251(g). As 
recognized by the CWA, Wyoming has an important, sovereign interest in protecting its ability 
to plan for the use of its limited water resources, and to allocate its waters for those uses 
according to state law. The proposed rule does not give sufficient weight and deference to state 
interests, needs, priorities, and concerns. In Wyoming, where water scarcity is pervasive, it is 
important that any rule also explicitly acknowledge the primary and often exclusive role of the 
States in allocating and administering rights to the use of water under authorities to which the 
Congress has a long history of deference. 
Due in part to the widely variable nature of tribal reserved rights, the proposed rule is so vague 
and ambiguous that it is impossible to predict the full extent of its impact on Wyoming's 
exclusive authority to allocate and administer quantities of water within its jurisdiction. EPA 
acknowledges the complexity of determining the nature and geographic scope of tribal reserved 
rights, and whether they even apply in water subject to state water quality standards. At the same 
time, EPA offers no helpful guidance about making those determinations other than requiring 
engagement with potential right holders. Those potential right holders, and EPA itself, have no 
authority to determine the nature or geographic scope of tribal reserved rights outside of 
established and legally binding methods of review, as laid out in a multitude of court decisions. 
Further, no consideration is given to the holders of other lawful rights that may be impacted by 
the rule's application. In fact, EPA acknowledges its uncertainty regarding the outcome of the 
proposed rule's application. The proposed rule establishes newly created, potentially far-reaching 
consequences and concepts which are undefined and subject to agency discretion. The rule 
threatens to impair—not recognize, preserve, and protect—Wyoming's ability to plan for the use 
of its limited water resources, and to allocate its waters for those uses according to state law. 
The proposed rule was also created without state consultation. Like other states, Wyoming plays 
a significant role in ensuring effective implementation of the CWA. Our co-regulator status, 
shared by the other states and many tribes, elevates Wyoming and other co-regulators above the 
multitude of stakeholders now engaged in the public review process. It is imperative that with a 
rulemaking process of this magnitude, which directly impacts the states' implementation of 
CWA programs, that significant input and review be provided to co-regulator entities on the 
substance of the proposed rule before it is drafted. However, Wyoming and other states were not 
included in this rulemaking process in any meaningful way. 

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the proposed rule, and we ask that EPA withdraw 
it due to its deficiencies.

,JC,te

Re: NWIFC Comments on Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791, Proposed Water Quality 
Standards Regulatory Revisions to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights 
 
Dear Mr. Regan: 
 
Thank you for the opportunity to provide comments on the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency 
(EPA) proposed Water Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights, 87 
Fed. Reg. 74361 (Dec. 2022).  The Northwest Indian Fisheries Commission1 (NWIFC) supports EPA’s 
commitment to honor its trust obligation to tribal nations with the proposed amendments to 
federal water quality standards (WQS) regulations to explicitly protect aquatic and aquatic-
dependent treaty reserved resources.  The amendments make clear that state water quality 
standards must be stringent enough to protect treaty-reserved rights and resources.  The proposed 
rule is an acknowledgement that the health, welfare, and culture of tribal communities in western 
Washington depend on functioning aquatic ecosystems and healthy harvestable populations of 
salmon, shellfish and other species.  The rule is also borne from the understanding that water 
quality continues to decline, is threatened by development, polluted by runoff and a warming 
climate, and therefore, WQS must be protective of treaty resources and those exercising their 
treaty-reserved rights.  Undoubtedly, new information about existing and emerging threats from 
toxic chemicals and warming waters will require revisions to state WQS to ensure tribal members 
and resources are adequately protected.  This rule proactively addresses the need for states to 
consider treaty rights when setting WQS.  NWIFC supports EPA’s initiative, and we offer the 
following comments to help strengthen the intent and implementation of the rule.  
 
EPA’s Authority  
The heart of EPA’s proposed rule is the addition of §131.9 to the WQS regulations.  This addition 
would require that WQS “protect tribal reserved rights applicable to the waters subject to such 
standards.”  This requirement is supported by proposed §131.5, which requires EPA to disprove 
WQS revisions that do not meet the requirements of §131.9.

Suquamish, Swinomish, Tulalip, and Upper Skagit.

NWIFC supports these provisions because they are consistent with EPA’s federal trust responsibility 
to the tribes comprising the NWIFC.  Where a tribal nation has reserved treaty rights, the federal 
government has a duty to protect those rights.2  
 
Definition of Tribal Reserved Rights 
In §131.3, EPA defines “tribal reserved rights” as “any rights to aquatic and/or aquatic-dependent 
resources reserved or held by tribes, either expressly or implicitly, through treaties, statutes, 
executive orders, or other sources of Federal law.”  We agree with EPA’s proposed definition, but 
recommend that the definition be prefaced with, “for the purposes of this Rule,” to clarify that it 
does not encompass rights to other, non-aquatic resources.  The treaty tribes in western 
Washington also reserved rights to hunt and gather, including in areas that are adjacent to waters 
covered by the proposed rule.  Many of these species could be considered “aquatic-dependent;” 
deer need clean water to drink, and plants need fresh water to grow.  We recommend EPA clarify 
the definition of “aquatic-dependent.”  
 
Protection of Treaty Rights  
Proposed §131.9(a) would require that, “to the extent supported by available data and information, 
to protect applicable tribal reserved rights WQS must be established to protect: 1) The exercise of 
tribal reserved rights unsuppressed by water quality or availability of the aquatic or aquatic-
dependent resource; and 2) The health of the right holders to at least the same risk level as 
provided to the general population of the State.”  
 
NWIFC agrees that that tribal reserved rights must be protected at levels unsuppressed by water 
quality or the availability of the resource.  Virtually all tribal reserved resources exist today at 
suppressed levels due to degraded habitat, including poor water quality.  As a result, the exercise of 
treaty rights has been suppressed throughout the tribes’ usual and accustomed (U&A) fishing areas, 
with many U&A’s no longer supporting treaty resources.  EPA suggests that in determining the level 
of protection required, states should balance heritage use of a resource with what is currently 
reasonably achievable for a particular waterbody.  We disagree.  This language appears to 
contradict EPA’s objective to prevent suppressed use to be hardwired into WQS or to exacerbate a 
downward spiral of reserved resources.  Nor does it reflect EPA’s fiduciary trust obligation to fully 
protect treaty resources.   
 
Historic use of treaty resources, including when the treaties were signed, is the restoration 
benchmark that tribes strive to achieve and reflects full protection when these rights were truly 
unsuppressed.  When tribes ceded the lands that now comprise western Washington and reserved 
their right to fish, hunt, and gather, it did so with the expectation that there would be fish, game, 
and berries to harvest.  The treaty right is meaningless without resources to harvest and gather.  
Under the U.S. Constitution, treaties are defined as the “supreme law of the land,” which trumps 
state law in the event of a conflict.  There was little conflict in western Washington in the early life 
of the Stevens treaties because there were plentiful fishery resources, few non-Indian fishermen, 
 
2 Parravano u. Babbitt, 70 F.3d 539, 547 (9th Cir. 1995) ("[T]he Tribes' federally reserved fishing rights are accompanied by a 
corresponding duty on the part of the government to preserve those rights.")

and habitats were largely intact.  Since that time, however, treaty rights are being rendered 
meaningless because the federal and state governments continue to allow salmon habitat to be 
damaged and destroyed faster than it can be restored.  Unfortunately, this trend is not showing 
signs of improvement and is leading to the failure of salmon recovery in western Washington.  
Through the Treaty Rights at Risk Initiative, tribes have called on their federal trustee to assume 
control and responsibility for salmon recovery and to lead a more coordinated effort among federal 
agencies.  EPA’s proposed rule is a positive step in this direction.  
 
We also note some waters may not include designated beneficial uses that support treaty-reserved 
resources, like salmon rearing, spawning or migration, but may play a critical role in supporting the 
habitat of treaty resources and the sustainable exercise of treaty rights by tribal members.  Many 
NWIFC member tribes exercise their rights in interconnected waters and ecosystems that depend 
on healthy water quality from upstream sources.  EPA should clarify that WQS developed to protect 
treaty-reserved resources and rights apply both within the location of place-based rights as well as 
in adjacent and connected waters, as determined by tribes.  
 
The language in §131.9(a)(1) appears to prevent states from using the absence of a treaty resource 
in a waterbody due to a passage barrier (such as a culvert or dam) as a reason to reduce the level of 
protection in WQS, which we support.  However, EPA caveats §131.9(a)(1) with the following 
language: “WQS must protect reasonably anticipated future uses of water, not the condition of the 
water that existed when the reserved right was established.”  While EPA’s assertion may be a 
practical acknowledgment that some waters will not currently support treaty rights, nor do so in the 
near future, this caveat does not reflect NWIFC’s viewpoint on past, present or future uses of water, 
the level of restoration needed to restore conditions to a level that supports and sustains treaty 
resources, or the timeframe in which restoration may occur.  Tribes take a multi-generational 
approach to resource management.  Further, treaties are to be interpreted in the favor of tribes, as 
they would have understood them at the time the treaties were made, and any ambiguities in their 
interpretation should be construed favorably to tribes.3 
 
In general, NWIFC supports the protection of tribal reserved rights so that the health of tribal 
members will not be subject to greater risk level than the general population, as described in 
§131.9(a)(2).  This will require the mean use of a 10-6 risk level, not the “at least to the 10-5” 
referenced in the proposed rule.  WQS, including human health criteria to protect tribal members 
exercising their treaty rights, must reflect the level of protection deemed necessary by those 
holding the right and the needs of the resource.   
 
As you are aware, NWIFC and its member tribes fought EPA’s 2019 rollback of Washington’s Human 
Health Criteria that EPA issued in 2016 because it did not reflect an adequate level of protection for 
tribal members consuming fish and shellfish.  In determining the level of protection for treaty 
resources and right holders, states and EPA should rely on fish consumption surveys, accounts of

historic fish consumption rates through consultation with tribes, interviews with tribal elders and 
historians (with permission), and research about emerging threats to aquatic and aquatic-
dependent species. 
 
Proposed §131.9(b) provides: “In reviewing State water quality standards submissions under this 
section, EPA will initiate tribal consultation with the right holders, consistent with applicable EPA 
tribal consultation policies, in determining whether State water quality standards protect applicable 
tribal reserved rights in accordance with paragraph (a) of this section.” 
 
We support early and frequent consultation between EPA and tribes.  We also remind EPA that 
merely listening to tribal perspectives does not constitute adequate consultation.  EPA, as federal 
trustee, must also act to protect treaty resources. 
 
NWIFC also supports the requirement in §131.9 (c) that WQS must designate uses and establishes 
appropriate water quality criteria to protect those uses.  To be clear, the exercise of treaty rights 
constitutes an existing use; therefore, those rights must be fully protected, and no degradation of 
water quality is permitted. 
 
Minimum Requirements for Water Quality Standards Submissions 
Under §131.6, EPA proposes that where tribal reserved rights apply to WQS being submitted for 
review and approval, states must include: 1) Information about the scope, nature, and current and 
past use of the tribal reserved rights, as informed by the right holders; and 2) Data and methods 
used to develop the WQS.  Additionally, EPA is revising the triennial review process to include an 
evaluation of whether there are tribal reserved rights applicable to waters subject to the state's 
WQS and whether WQS need to be revised to protect those rights.  To ensure that tribes with 
reserved rights are engaged in the process of determining whether reserved rights apply, § 131.6 
would require that WQS submissions to EPA include information about tribal reserved rights “as 
informed by the right holders,” where applicable. 
 
The NWIFC generally support these provisions of the proposed rule.  We recommend that 
Traditional Ecological Knowledge (TEK) is incorporated as required information in defining the 
reserved right.  EPA had demonstrated a willingness to utilize TEK in decision-making during the 
remediation of contaminated lands.4  
 
While EPA’s intent to encourage active engagement with the tribes by the states is well-meaning, 
we are concerned this provision leaves determination of the existence of treaty rights and the 
standards necessary for their protection to the thoroughness of a state’s consultation efforts with 
those holding the reserved rights.  There are numerous examples where states have failed to 
consult with tribes on actions harmful to treaty resources.  Tribes determine where their treaty 
rights are exercised and where treaty-reserved resources exist, not states.  As co-managers, tribes 
 
4 U.S. Environmental Protection Agency; Memorandum “Considering Traditional Ecological Knowledge (TEK) During the Cleanup

determine where, how, and when treaty resources are sustained and harvested.  Tribe’s exercise 
their rights on their reservations and at all “usual and accustomed” places, which can cover an 
extensive geographic area, crossing multiple state and federal jurisdictions.   
 
Further, treaty right holders may want information about where treaty rights are exercised, or how 
treaty resources are used for cultural purposes, kept confidential.  Section 131.6(g) should allow for 
this information to be kept confidential at the right holder’s request.  As outlined in the proposed 
rule, EPA’s role in the determination of the applicability of treaty rights appears more like that of a 
facilitator for tribal and state engagement, and not that of a federal trustee.  We recommend that 
the proposed rule include a dispute resolution process which rights holders can request to engage 
directly with the EPA Administrator.  Should a dispute arise about whether treaty rights apply to a 
waterbody, or the level of protection needed to protect the right, EPA would be expected to consult 
with the tribes and disapprove any weakening of WQS where treaty rights are currently exercised or 
will be exercised in the future.   
 
Use Attainability Analysis and Tribal Reserved Rights 
EPA requested comments on whether and how states can revise designated uses, as provided by 40 
CFR 131.10 while also ensuring the protection of tribal reserved rights.  As noted above, the 
exercise of treaty rights must be considered an existing use, practiced since time immemorial, and 
certainly when the Clean Water Act was enacted.  Therefore, use attainability analysis (U.A.A.) is 
not appropriate for revising WQS in waters identified by treaty right holders as a place where treaty 
rights are, or will be, exercised.  Therefore, U.A.A. should be prohibited in these waters.  
 
Conclusion 
In closing, we appreciate EPA’s initiative to protect treaty rights through revision of federal WQS 
regulations.  The proposed rule will help address current and emerging threats to water quality and 
treaty-reserved resources.  We trust our comments will be useful as EPA finalizes the rule.  If you 
have any questions, please contact Greg Haller, Environmental Protection Policy Analyst, at 
ghaller@nwifc.org.   
 
 
Sincerely,

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791-0231 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791 ---
1 
 
Tribal Treaty Right Effect Determination Process  
 
Version: July 27, 2020 
 
 
What is the purpose of this document?   
 
As part of the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE), Seattle District’s permit application review 
process, we notify Tribes of proposed activities occurring within waters of interest to federally 
recognized Tribes, and request Tribal notification of any concerns or comments regarding the 
proposed activity’s effects.  If a Tribe has concerns regarding the proposed Department of the Army 
(DA) regulated activity, we will encourage the applicant and Tribe to work together to resolve those 
concerns, to the extent both the applicant and Tribe are amenable to that approach.   
 
Should a Tribe have unresolved concerns that rise to the level where the Tribe objects to USACE 
authorization of the activity on the basis that it would violate a Tribe’s reserved treaty right, the 
Tribe notifies the Seattle District of the Tribe’s objection.  In making a permit decision, the USACE 
must ensure it does not authorize an activity that would result in a violation of a Tribal treaty right.  
 
This document provides general information about the review process of the Seattle District once a 
Tribe notifies the agency of an objection to authorize a proposed activity because the Tribe is 
concerned the proposed activity would impermissibly infringe a Tribe’s treaty right.  
 
What effect would a Tribal objection based on tribal treaty rights have on the Seattle District’s 
permit decision? 
 
When presented with such an objection from a Tribe, the Seattle District considers project-specific 
information to determine whether the proposed activity under the USACE’s regulatory jurisdiction 
would result in an impermissible abrogation of the treaty right.   The USACE both recognizes its 
obligation to uphold Tribal treaty rights and that the applicant is entitled to a timely decision 
regarding its permit application.  In conducting this effects determination, the USACE is neither a 
proponent nor opponent for a permit application. 33 C.F.R § 320.1(4).  
 
If the USACE was to make a determination and finding that DA authorization of the applicant’s 
proposed activity would impermissibly infringe on a reserved treaty right, the USACE would need 
substantial evidence from an objecting Tribe to rebut the presumption that approval of the DA 
permit would not be contrary to the public interest. The applicant is afforded an opportunity to 
review and respond to the Tribe’s submission, and to submit evidence. The USACE must examine 
the specific facts of the situation in the context of existing information, law, and policy to determine 
whether the proposed project would abrogate a treaty right. In doing this, the USACE does not 
conduct a balancing test. If information before the Agency demonstrates the specific proposed 
project before the Agency would obstruct, eliminate, or interfere with the objecting Tribe’s access to 
its Usual and Accustomed fishing grounds and stations to such an extent the Tribe’s reserved treaty 
fishing right will be impermissibly impaired, the USACE does not have the authority to issue a 
permit for the project in the absence of a specific statutory authorization.  See Northwest Sea Farms 
v. United State Army Corps of Engineers, 931 F. Supp. 1515 (W.D.Wash. 1996).  If, however, the 
USACE determines that DA authorization of the proposed activity would not abrogate a treaty right, 

2 
 
the Corps would continue the full evaluation of the permit application notwithstanding the objection 
from the tribe.  
 
 
What information might assist Seattle District in determining whether an activity would 
abrogate a treaty right? 
 
As the Tribe has unique access to relevant information regarding the scope of its interest that would 
potentially be affected by the proposed DA regulated activity and how the proposed project would 
physically obstruct access to tribal Usual and Accustomed (U&A) places, an objecting Tribe with 
treaty-reserved fishing rights bears the burden of raising, and, thereafter, presenting, information to 
the agency sufficient to sustain an objection to the issuance of a proposed permit. In the absence of a 
raised and sustained objection, the Corps will presume the granting of a permit would not abrogate a 
treaty right.  
 
 
The Seattle District must have sufficient evidence to evaluate whether the proposed activity’s 
interference with a treaty right is of the type that would abrogate the right.  Potentially relevant 
information regarding the scope of the tribe’s interest includes: the specific proposed project’s 
effect(s) on the Tribe’s reserved treaty right regarding: (1) the geographic right of access to the 
Tribe’s U&A fishing places, (2) degradation of fish runs and habitat, (3) other treaty issues, as 
applicable.   
 
This determination must evaluate the specific treaty right alleged to be at risk of impairment by the 
proposed project by the applicant.  First, a treaty right must be established in the project area.  The 
Seattle District is in interested in the Tribe’s historic, present, and proposed use of the project site, 
and will also look to specific treaties and adjudicated treaty rights determinations, if available, 
regarding the project location.  Second, the Seattle District is interested in understanding the nature 
of the proposed activity’s effect(s) on the Tribe’s treaty rights.  Third, the Seattle District will 
consider other information provided by the Tribe in order to evaluate the extent of potential 
impact(s) to the Tribe’s treaty right, and whether the identified impacts impermissibly infringe on 
the treaty right.  The USACE may also choose to seek out additional information from public 
sources or third parties regarding certain topics, such as fish conservation matters or applicable 
regulatory parameters.  The applicant may choose to present evidence to respond to submissions by 
the tribe, but is under no obligation to add to the record.  
 
 
Documentation to support this fact specific inquiry may include, but is not necessarily limited to: 
 
 Affidavits/declarations from Tribal members explaining, as applicable: 
1. How often, and, when, Tribal harvesting at the location in question has occurred; and if it 
is intended to occur in the future? 
2. Type of fishing/harvesting method(s) involved in fishing/harvesting from the site, e.g., dip 
net, reef net, drift net etc. 
3. How would Tribal access to fishing/harvesting sites be affected by the proposed project? 
What standoff distance(s) would the tribe need to maintain from the proposed project, and, 
why; as well as how many acres of fishing (for that species) with that specific fishing 
method would become inaccessible or impaired?  

3 
 
4. Information about the applicable conservation and/or management plans regarding the 
fishery in and around the project area. 
 Drawing/map showing location of the fishing activity in relation to the proposed permit activity.   
 Videos/photos of the fishing/harvesting activity at or around the project site. 
 
What are the next steps after this information is provided to the Seattle District? 
 
The information provided to the Seattle District will be shared with the permit applicant.  The permit 
applicant will be afforded the opportunity to respond to the materials provided by the Tribes in 
support of a treaty right.  If the permit applicant chooses to respond, the response will be shared with 
the Tribe asserting the treaty right.  The scope of the USACE’s inquiry into an allegation of a treaty 
rights abrogation on the basis that the proposed project presents a physical bar of access to tribal 
U&A places, is focused upon an evaluation of the relevant and material facts submitted into the 
administrative record by the parties.  The USACE may also choose to seek information from public 
sources and third parties, such as fish conservation programs or applicable regulatory 
parameters.The end goal of this process is that the Seattle District obtains information necessary to 
complete our fact-specific analysis, and renders a decision that complies with all legal requirements 
and standards.  
 
If there is not sufficient evidence available to the USACE to demonstrate that DA authorization 
of the proposed activity would result in an impermissible abrogation of the treaty right because of 
the extent it physically impairs or obstructs the Tribe’s access to it’s U&A grounds and stations,, the 
USACE will continue to process the permit application in accordance with the agency’s 
implementing regulations.    The USACE will then next determine if there are other aspects of the Tribe’s 
objection  to evaluate, and may seek out further information from both the Tribe and applicant in regards to 
other aspects of the effects of the proposed permit application on the Tribe’s treaty right. The USACE will 
not conclude its public interest review until it has resolved any Tribal objection that authorizing the 
applicant’s proposal would be an abrogation of a reserved treaty right. If, however, the Seattle 
District determines a Tribal objection to DA authorization of the proposed activity has been raised 
and substantiated with project-specific information, the Seattle District may not authorize the 
proposed activity, in the absence of specific statutory authorization.

EPA Region 10 Tribal Operations Committee (RTOC)
