Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians Comments Page 10 of 29 
executive orders, and other sources of Federal law reflecting tribal reserved rights.” 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,364. By 
promulgating the Reserved Rights Rule, EPA will finally codify what it has long acknowledged: that tribes require 
clean water sufficient to support the tribal resources and uses that are the subject of their reserved rights, and that 
the Clean Water Act must be applied to ensure that protection.  
B.  
The Clean Water Act Has Not Adequately Protected Tribal Reserved Rights to Date But Can 
and Must Do So Now. 
The proposed Reserved Rights Rule does not come a moment too soon. Although the Clean Water Act 
recently celebrated its 50th anniversary, it has failed to meet its objectives in many waters in which tribes hold 
reserved rights that depend on clean water. At the outset of this letter, we detailed the types of water pollution 
problems we have had throughout waters in which we hold reserved rights. Unfortunately, we are not alone. Across 
the nation, tribes suffer from these same gaps in Clean Water Act protection and enforcement. Despite five decades 
of Clean Water Act implementation, tribes and their members are still burdened by legacy and ongoing pollution 
that impedes full exercise of their rights and diminishes their health. The proposed rule can force swifter and more 
protective action than we’ve seen in the past. And it must. 
As EPA has long acknowledged, “‘[a]ny specific treaty requirements have the force of law,’ and therefore, 
‘State water quality standards will have to meet any treaty requirements.’” 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,366 (citing 48 Fed. 
Reg. 51,400, 51,412 (Nov. 8, 1983)). However, whereas EPA previously declined to explicitly require States to 
adopt standards that meet treaty requirements” in its 1983 WQS regulations because such issues had been 
“adequately resolved . . . without the need for regulatory language,” experience since that time makes clear that 
regulatory language is urgently needed for states to understand their obligations with respect to the intersection of 
U.S.-Indian treaties and water quality standards in order to protect tribal reserved rights from the persistent and 
detrimental effects of water pollution. We believe that the Reserved Rights Rule has the potential, after accounting 
for the other comments made herein, to bring transparency and clarity to these issues in the revision and approval 
processes for state water quality standards. Beyond the ineffective implementation of the Clean Water Act 
described above, the Band has suffered the whiplash of inconsistent federal positions on tribal reserved rights and 
has been forced to devote considerable resources to ensuring its rights are protected. A recent example is the fight 
regarding the human health criteria (HHC) in Maine, including the last administration’s reversal in position. The 
Band was offended by EPA’s abandonment of its trust obligations and adherence to the law in the last 
administration when it essentially abandoned defense of the federally promulgated HHC. We therefore support 
EPA’s efforts to develop a more durable and consistent federal policy for the future.  
In particular, we support the proposed rule’s commitment to the establishment of WQS that protect “[t]he 
exercise of tribal reserved rights unsuppressed by water quality or availability of the aquatic or aquatic-dependent 
resource” and “the health” of tribal members exercising reserved rights. 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,378 (proposed 40 
C.F.R. § 131.9(a)(1)-(2)) (emphasis added). While at times the preamble seems somewhat narrowly focused on 
toxics (e.g., human health criteria), we appreciate that the language of the rule itself is sufficient to encompass what 
should be two main drivers of the WQS: human health and habitat health that allows for healthy and abundant 
populations of species that are the subject to tribal reserved rights. This is crucial to ensuring an effective rule that 
does not only reach toxic pollution, but also reaches pernicious water quality problems like nutrient and 
temperature pollution that depress aquatic-dependent populations of species important to the exercise of tribal 
reserved rights, particularly in the era of climate change. In short, the Band believes wholeheartedly that 40 C.F.R. 
§ 131.9 should be amended to ensure that WQS “must protect tribal reserved rights applicable to waters subject to 
such standards,” and believes the Reserved Rights Rule should be finalized as quickly as possible and no later than 
the end of this year. 
The proposed Reserved Rights Rule is entirely consistent with—and even demanded by—the Clean Water 
Act, and it is well within the broad scope of EPA’s statutory authority under the Act. The overarching commitment 
of the Clean Water Act is to “restore and maintain the chemical, physical, and biological integrity of the Nation’s 
waters.” 33 U.S.C. § 1251(a). To that end, Congress established a national policy that “the discharge of toxic 
pollutants in toxic amounts be prohibited” and directed that water quality be sufficient to protect and allow the 

 
88  Bell Road   Littleton, Me  04730   www.maliseets.com 
 
Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians Comments Page 11 of 29 
propagation of fish, shellfish, and wildlife safe for human consumption by July 1, 1983. See id. § 1251(a)(2), (3). 
The Act is designed to ratchet down the level of pollution over time to allow for ever safer use of the water until all 
uses are protected and remain protected. While the date for accomplishing these goals has long since passed, EPA’s 
efforts through this proposed rule help to ensure the Act’s polices are finally fulfilled as it relates to protecting 
tribal reserved rights wherever they exist in the waters and wetlands of Maine. 
 
Water quality standards are the foundation of the Clean Water Act’s water quality-based control program. 
They define goals for a water body by designating the uses that water body supports or should support (“designated 
uses”); set water quality criteria designed to protect those uses and measure progress made (“criteria”); and 
establish anti-degradation policies, so that existing uses and water quality necessary to support those uses are 
protected and so that bodies with very high-quality water do not become impaired. In order to attain the Act’s goals 
and to protect the uses of water, the Act imposes an obligation on states, with EPA acting in an oversight role, to 
develop water quality standards comprised of designated uses and narrative or numeric water quality criteria 
sufficient to protect uses such as fishing. Id. § 1313(a)-(b). Specifically, Clean Water Act section 303 directs states 
with delegated authority to do the following when they adopt or revise water quality standards for waters of the 
United States. 33 U.S.C. § 1313.  
Whenever the State revises or adopts a new standard, such revised or new standard shall be 
submitted to the Administrator. Such revised or new water quality standard shall consist of the 
designated uses of the navigable waters involved and the water quality criteria for such waters 
based upon such uses. Such standards shall be such as to protect the public health or welfare, 
enhance the quality of water and serve the purposes of this chapter. Such standards shall be 
established taking into consideration their use and value for public water supplies, propagation of 
fish and wildlife, recreational purposes, and agricultural, industrial, and other purposes, and also 
taking into consideration their use and value for navigation. 
Id. § 1313(c)(2)(A) (emphasis added). As EPA notes in the preamble, whatever WQS a state might adopt must not 
affect or impair the provisions of any treaty of the United States under section 511 of the Act. 87 Fed. Reg. at 
74,364-65; see also 33 U.S.C. § 1371 (“[The Act] shall not be construed as . . . affecting or impairing the 
provisions of any treaty of the United States.”). 
 
While states have the first shot at promulgating protective, science-based water quality standards, EPA is 
obligated under the Act to review and to disapprove a state’s efforts if they fall short of meeting the requirements 
of the Act. Id. § 1313(a)-(c). Furthermore, EPA has independent authority to ensure that a state’s standards are up 
to date and adequate to meet the Act’s requirements. Id. § 1313(c). Thus, where a state fails to act in accordance 
with the statute, EPA is obligated to fulfill the state’s traditional role of issuing standards that comply with the Act. 
In other words, EPA is correct that “the statute’s structure and objectives for the establishment and oversight of 
WQS, including the discretion afforded to EPA, provide ample room for the agency to consider and give effect to 
all applicable reserved rights.” 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,365. As EPA notes, it has exercised this authority with regard to 
the human health criteria in Washington and Maine before, and as noted in the previous section, those actions and 
this are consistent with long-standing EPA policy regarding tribal rights and resources. 
III. 
COMMENTS ON SPECIFIC SECTIONS OF THE PROPOSED RESESERVED RIGHTS RULE 
AND ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS POSED BY EPA IN THE PREAMBLE  
 
In this section, the Band provides comments on specific statements in the Federal Register notice and 
proposed rule language, as well as responses to questions specifically raised by EPA regarding the proposed rule. 
A. 
EPA Must Require States To Protect Tribal Reserved Rights By Employing All Three 
Components of Water Quality Standards. 
 
The Federal Register notice indicates that after a state has determined that tribal reserved rights exist in the 
waters over which it has Clean Water Act jurisdiction and the level of water quality necessary to protect those 
rights, “states would be required to revise their WQS if needed to ensure protection of those rights using designated 

 
88  Bell Road   Littleton, Me  04730   www.maliseets.com 
 
Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians Comments Page 12 of 29 
uses, criteria and/or antidegradation as described at proposed 40 CFR 131.9(c).” 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,371. The 
proposed regulatory language is: 
(c) In order to meet the requirements in paragraph (a) of this section, States must: 
(1) Designate uses consistent with § 131.10 that either expressly incorporate protection of the tribal 
reserved rights or encompass such rights; and 
(2) Establish water quality criteria consistent with § 131.11 to protect tribal reserved rights; and/or 
(3) Use applicable antidegradation requirements consistent with § 131.12 to maintain and protect 
water quality that protects tribal reserved rights. 
The Band supports specific regulatory language directing states to promulgate each component of water quality 
standards in order to meet the requirements in paragraph (a) of proposed 40 C.F.R. § 131.9 (“Water quality 
standards must protect tribal reserved rights applicable to waters subject to such standards.”). However, as 
described below, the Band believes that the regulatory language should be stated only in the conjunctive (“and”)—
without use of the phrase “and/or” between subsections (2) and (3)—in order to comport with the requirements of 
the Clean Water Act and its existing implementing regulations, as well as to best meet the goals of the Reserved 
Rights Rule. Consequently, in response to EPA’s query “whether the following two options related to Tier 2 and 
Tier 3 could be used to protect tribal reserved rights in lieu of the options identified in proposed 40 CFR 
131.9(c)(1) and (2) and explained earlier in this section,” 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,371 (emphasis added), the answer is 
“no.” However, by adding some more specifics about how a state might use or modify its antidegradation policy to 
protect tribal reserved rights in already high quality waters (Tier 3 and potentially Tier 2), we believe that 
antidegradation policies are a legitimate and helpful way for states to protect tribal reserved rights in high quality 
waters in addition to establishing designated uses and water quality criteria them.  
1. 
Water Quality Standards Include Three Components, and EPA Cannot Rely Solely 
on States’ Antidegradation Policies to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights. 
 
The proposed rule suggests one option to protect tribal reserved rights, either alone or in combination with 
others, is for states to revise their antidegradation policies. 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,371; id. at 74,378 (proposed 40 
C.F.R. § 131.9(c)(2)) (“and/or”). Reliance solely on antidegradation policies, while not utilizing the other options 
EPA proposes, does not meet the plain language of the Clean Water Act and will not adequately protect tribal 
reserved rights. EPA should only be considering the use of antidegradation policies in addition to protective 
designated uses and water quality criteria. 
 
The proposed rule’s preamble explains that the core components of water quality standards are designated 
uses, water quality criteria, and antidegradation requirements. 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,362 (citing 33 U.S.C. § 
1313(c)(3)). As explained above, EPA is required to protect reserved rights; forgoing the use of two of the three 
water quality standards core components does not make sense and would not comply with EPA’s obligation to 
protect reserved rights. Importantly, it also would not meet the plain language of the Act, which requires that states’ 
“revised or new water quality standard shall consist of the designated uses of the navigable waters involved and the 
water quality criteria for such waters based upon such uses.” 33 U.S.C. § 1313(c)(2)(A) (emphasis added). The use 
of “and/or” (both the conjunctive and disjunctive) at proposed 40 C.F.R. § 131.9(c) suggests that states could meet 
the requirements of the Clean Water Act either by completing all three components (designated uses and criteria 
and antidegradation) or by using only its antidegradation policy to meet the requirements of the Act.8 A disjunctive

2) criteria and antidegradation policy, but no designated uses. If EPA intended either such option to be available to states, it is 
not clear from the regulatory language’s use of the conjunctive between (1) and (2) and the conjunctive/disjunctive between (2) 
and (3). We have not suggested alternative language due to our belief that only the conjunctive “and” should follow each 
subpart.

Beyond the statutory imperatives, the current implementing regulations also would not permit sole reliance

and has been occurring at waters under state jurisdiction throughout the country. Consequently, where a state has 
not yet designated tribal reserved right uses for water bodies in which tribes are currently exercising tribal reserved 
rights (at whatever level of use),11 it must do so, and the final Reserved Rights Rule should not introduce confusion 
about that.12 In addition, “States may adopt sub-categories of a use and set the appropriate criteria to reflect varying

response to comments, and regulatory text. Specifically, “and/or” should be changed to “and” in the final 40 C.F.R.

2. 
State Antidegradation Policies Are Insufficient to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights On 
Their Own. 
 
Antidegradation policies can provide protections for high water quality that has not been degraded or has 
already been achieved, 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,363, but they offer no mandatory protections for enhancing degraded 
water quality to levels that can support the unsuppressed exercise of reserved rights. Consequently, the use of the 
antidegradation policy—even a strong policy—could only help protect tribal reserved rights in a very limited 
subset of waters of any given state. Where there are high quality waters, they should be protected under Tier 3 
already, but certainly they should be afforded that protection wherever tribal reserved rights apply. We therefore 
strongly support the sentiments and goals driving EPA’s statement in the preamble that: “in situations where a 
waterbody’s existing water quality exceeds the levels that protect tribal reserved rights, these options would 
provide a mechanism to maintain high water quality and provide a margin of safety that would afford the water 
body increased resilience to potential future stressors, including climate change. Protecting such high-quality 
waters would potentially be more cost-effective and resource-efficient than investing in long-term restoration or 
remedial actions in the future.” 87 Fed. Reg. 74,371. The Band has been adamant and vocal that it is imperative 
that water of high quality be protected and water with degraded quality be restored. EPA’s statement is consistent 
with the Band’s former objective. Our concern, however, is that the antidegradation policy should not be available 
to states as a sole option for protecting tribal reserved rights in their water quality standards.  
 
For various reasons, the Clean Water Act’s antidegradation requirements have not been used successfully 
to implement the Act’s purpose to “restore and maintain the chemical, physical, and biological integrity of the 
Nation’s waters.” 33 U.S.C. § 1251(a). In 2013, EPA stated:  
EPA indicated in its 1998 ANPRM that “on a national scale, antidegradation is not being used as 
effectively as it could be,” a concern that continues today and is echoed by stakeholders who have 
identified antidegradation as an underused component of water quality protection. . . . [T]he EPA 
received substantial feedback from stakeholders that existing CWA antidegradation regulatory 
provisions and related guidance have not been fully successful in ensuring consistent and effective 
implementation of Tier 2 high quality water protections.  
Water Quality Standards Regulatory Clarifications, 78 Fed. Reg. 54,518, 54,526 (proposed Sept. 4, 2013) (to be 
codified at 40 C.F.R. pt. 131). Similarly, in 1998, EPA explained: 
In sum, EPA’s current thinking is that the antidegradation policy is significantly underused as a 
tool to attain and maintain water quality and plan for and channel important economic and social 
 
completely eliminate any existing use whether or not that use is designated in a State’s water quality standards.”). As discussed 
below, the “absolute floor of water quality” is not sufficient to protect tribal reserved rights.

development that can impact water quality. EPA believes this is especially true for nonpoint source 
run-off. 
Water Quality Standards Regulation, 63 Fed. Reg. 36,742, 36,780 (proposed July 7, 1998). Numerous 
commentators have recognized these issues as well, including problems stemming from overly broad federal 
requirements for states and lack of EPA authority to review designations beyond broad language; ineffective or 
even no classification designations; minimal use of Outstanding National Resource Water designations; lack of 
nonpoint source pollution regulation and thus no nonpoint triggering of antidegradation reviews; and elevation of 
or deference to economic considerations. See, e.g., Katherine A. Zogas, The Clean Water Act’s Antidegradation

Policy, 2 PUB. NAT. RESOURCES L. § 19:13 (2nd ed.) (“Indeed, the entire antidegradation policy of some states is 
so vague as to be virtually meaningless.”) (Attachment 12). 
The proposed rule’s suggested options and regulatory text do not address these problems but will likely 
exacerbate them as applied to protecting tribal reserved rights. The one provision of proposed regulatory text at 40 
C.F.R. § 131.9(c)(3) is too vague to ensure protection or meaningful review. It does not include the limitations on 
the antidegradation policy described in the preamble of the rule, limitations that would be necessary in order to 
protect tribal reserved rights when applying the antidegradation policy. See 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,371 (discussion of 
“Option 1” and “Option 2” for implementing antidegradation requirements to protect tribal reserved rights through 
use of Tier 3 and Tier 2 designations). The preamble’s discussion and suggested alternatives do not offer any solace 
as: 1) the preamble is not enforceable and 2) it itself does not contain any mandatory protective requirements. 
EPA’s decades of experience should make clear that protecting tribal reserved rights cannot be left solely to the 
whims of the states’ antidegradation policies and decisions without firm requirements and guidance. Moreover, it is 
not clear how the sole use of antidegradation policies would help waters that are currently impaired improve water 
quality to allow for the full exercise and enjoyment of reserved rights. Nor is it clear how the use of antidegradation 
policies would protect against harm to reserved rights from nonpoint source discharges. 
To conclude, the agency should modify proposed 40 C.F.R. § 131.9(c)(2) to use “and” instead of “and/or,” 
thus requiring the use of antidegradation policies in addition to protective designated uses and criteria, rather than 
potentially instead of those requirements.13 The agency should also include mandatory and more specific regulatory 
language about how antidegradation policies must be implemented to protect tribal reserved rights, providing 
particular detail and emphasis regarding “Option 1.” 
3. 
EPA Should Utilize Tier 3 for Outstanding National Resource Waters to Protect 
Reserved Rights. 
Notwithstanding our objections to giving states an option to only use its antidegradation policy to protect 
tribal reserved rights and our concern regarding the lack of prescriptive language in the proposed regulatory text 
regarding how to use pertinent aspects of the antidegradation policy in waters with tribal reserved right, the Band 
does see a role for some aspects of antidegradation policies in the protection of tribal reserved rights. In 2021, EPA 
provided notice that it was considering proposing “Assignment of Tier 3 antidegradation protection (i.e., 
requirement to maintain and protect current and future improved water quality) in waters where tribal reserved 
rights apply and where current water quality is sufficient to protect those rights.” Deborah G. Nagle, Notification of 
Consultation and Coordination on Potential Revisions to the Federal Water Quality Standards Regulations to

optional. The Band believes that § 131.9(c)(1) [designated uses], (c)(2) [criteria], and (c)(3) [antidegradation] should all be 
required or better yet, (c)(3) [antidegradation] should be moved into a separate subsection and include more detailed

Protect Tribal Reserved Rights (June 11, 2021). The Band submitted comments on this notice and explained its 
general support for this proposal. Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians Comments on EPA’s Notification of 
Consultation and Coordination on Potential Revisions to the Federal Water Quality Standards Regulations to 
Protect Tribal Reserved Rights, at 6-7 (Sept. 13, 2021) (Attachment 13). This idea appears akin to “Option 1” 
suggested by EPA in the preamble, 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,371, although without any regulatory text implementing the 
option, see id. at 74,378 (proposed 40 C.F.R. § 131.9(c)(3)). 
Tier 3 protections apply to Outstanding National Resource Waters, which are generally exceptional, 
important, unique, or sensitive ecologically, or offer unique or important recreational uses. Tier 3 protects against 
any permanent degradation to these important waters; only a temporary, short-term, and limited change in the water 
quality of a Tier 3 water is allowed; for example, for construction activities. Given the well-documented 
importance of tribal reserved rights, see id. at 74,363, and EPA’s trust responsibility to protect these rights, see 
Michael S. Regan, Reaffirmation of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s Indian Policy (Sept. 30, 2021), 
https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2021-09/oita-21-000-6427.pdf, it is important to ensure these waters 
are maintained and protected. The Band believes that high quality waters with reserved rights are a good fit for 
protection as Outstanding National Resource Waters and supports EPA’s proposed Option 1, subject to the other 
comments and qualifications in these comments. EPA should operationalize this option with strong regulatory 
language rather than merely describing the option in the preamble. 
Given the well-documented history of minimal ONRW designation, see, e.g., John A. Chilson, Keeping 
Clean Waters Clean: Making the Clean Water Act’s Antidegradation Policy Work, 32 U. MICH. J.L. REFORM 545, 
547 (1999) (Attachment 10), relying on the states to designate ONRWs is insufficient. EPA should set up a process 
by which tribes can directly nominate to EPA high quality waters in areas where they hold reserved rights to be 
designated as ONRWs. That way, EPA can ensure that tribal nominations are given full consideration and not lost 
in the state process. 
4. 
Without Stronger Language, Tier 2 Is Insufficient to Protect Reserved Rights. 
The Band is concerned about the suggested “Option 2,” which would let states utilize Tier 2 protections to 
limit the lowering of water quality in high quality waters (that exceed Clean Water Act section 101(a) uses) to 
protect applicable reserved rights. 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,371 (citing 40 C.F.R. § 131.12(a)(2)). Tier 2 allows lowering 
of water quality “only in a few extraordinary circumstances where the economic and social need for the activity 
clearly outweighs the benefit of maintaining water quality above that required for ‘fishable/swimmable’ water, and 
both cannot be achieved.” EPA, Water Quality Standards Handbook, Chapter 4: Antidegradation, at 9 (2012). 
Specifically, EPA describes Option 2 as: “States could amend their antidegradation policy and/or other legally 
binding procedures to include a provision that ensures that any lowering of water quality in a high-quality water 
that is authorized by the state, in accordance with 40 CFR 131.12(a)(2), results in water quality that continues to 
protect applicable reserved rights.” 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,271.  
To begin, the Band assumes that EPA intends for Tier 2 to be used only where water quality exceeds the 
quality necessary for the full unsuppressed use of reserved rights, and not just Clean Water Act section 101(a) 
designated uses. However, that is not clear from the proposed language and preamble, so should be clarified. And 
the Band notes, as explained above, that this option would not help waters whose quality is below the level 
necessary for the unsuppressed use of reserved rights. 
Fundamentally, the Band is concerned with how even the best-intentioned states might weigh important 
economic or social development in the area against maintaining high water quality that protects tribal reserved 
rights. If given the option, we are not confident that the reserved rights sacred to a tribe would prove more 
consequential to the state than other policy goals it must weigh, at least not consistently. And as explained above, 
without specific regulatory language, it is not clear how Option 2 would actually be implemented or enforced to 
ensure a thumb on the scale in favor of tribal reserved rights. The bottom line is that EPA would need to include 
strong mandatory language in the regulatory text itself if this is offered as a potential measure of protection to 
states. And it should not be available as a sole measure of protection. 

 
88  Bell Road   Littleton, Me  04730   www.maliseets.com 
 
Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians Comments Page 17 of 29 
Tier 2’s exceptions allowing some level of water quality degradation of a high-quality water based on 
economic and social considerations are distressing where reserved rights are at issue. Water contamination 
threatens traditional Indian lifeways, including longstanding traditions of fishing and fish consumption that are 
central to many tribes’ cultural identity and that make individual tribes distinct as people. Further, many tribes are 
connected to particular waters for cultural, spiritual, or other reasons (and others’ fishing rights are limited to 
certain grounds by treaty), so tribal members cannot simply move their fishing to another location to avoid 
contamination or lowered water quality. The benefits of protecting high water quality to tribes in terms of public 
health, environmental, cultural, and other gains are difficult, and in many cases impossible, to monetize or quantify. 
EPA has correctly recognized that “cultural impacts to tribes and the furtherance of the United States’ treaty 
obligations to tribes—are an example of the type of societal value that cannot be monetized.”14 Supplemental 
Finding That It Is Appropriate and Necessary To Regulate Hazardous Air Pollutants  From Coal- and Oil-Fired 
Electric Utility Steam Generating Units, 81 Fed. Reg. 24,420, 24,429 n.18 (April 25, 2016); see also 87 Fed. Reg. 
at 74,374 (qualitatively describing variety of unique benefits from proposed rule). Most of the benefits from high 
water quality to tribal health, subsistence, fishing rights, and cultural identity defy full calculation. See, e.g., Cass 
R. Sunstein, The Limits of Quantification, 102 CALIF. L. REV. 1369, 1380-85 (2014) (Attachment 15); United 
States v. Washington, 384 F. Supp. 312, 404 (W.D. Wash. 1974) (“[T]he treaty rights . . . are unique and the 
damages which have been or will be sustained are not susceptible of definite monetary determination.”); see also 
2019 NCAI et al. Comments on MATS Rule Reconsideration of Supplemental Finding and Residual Risk at 10-13 
(Attachment 16). States, with their own objectives, are unlikely to want—or even be able—to successfully evaluate 
a tribal member’s ability to continue to engage in the fishing culture practiced since time immemorial by her 
ancestors, and to pass those traditions on to her children. But that does not mean that these core values can be 
excluded when weighing whether lowering water quality is necessary to accommodate important economic or 
social development or choosing from a range of practicable alternatives that would prevent or lessen the 
degradation.15  
Because of this problem, the Band does not support the use of Tier 2, at least as the sole protective 
measure, for tribal reserved rights. Should EPA move forward with utilizing Tier 2 as an option in combination 
with other requirements, EPA should incorporate additional language that assures these important tribal interests

B. 
Description of Definition of “Tribal Reserved Rights” Is Underinclusive. 
EPA requested comment on whether additional types of reserved rights should be included beyond fishing, 
gathering of aquatic plants, and hunting for aquatic dependent animals in its definition of “tribal reserved rights.” 
See 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,367 (“Examples of tribal reserved rights as defined in this proposed rulemaking include but 
are not limited to the rights to fish; gather aquatic plants; and to hunt for aquatic-dependent animals. EPA requests 
comment on whether there are additional types of tribal reserved rights that it should consider.”). The answer is 
yes. While tribal reserved rights certainly extend to each of the already enumerated rights, tribes reserved more 
water-dependent rights than those specifically listed in the Federal Register notice. While the actual language 
proposed for the definition at 40 C.F.R. § 131.3(r) would encompass these rights, the supporting materials—
including the preamble to the final rule and the response to comments—should include a more comprehensive list 
of rights covered by the rule. EPA should also make clear that this definition of “tribal reserved rights” applies only 
to this rule as tribes have other reserved rights that extend beyond aquatic and aquatic-dependent resources. 
Ultimately, it may not be possible for all types of aquatic and aquatic-dependent tribal reserved rights to be 
explicitly highlighted in this administrative record, but common ones should be and EPA should make clear that 
just because a right has not been listed in the preamble or response to comments does not mean that it is not 
covered by the rule.  
Many tribes engage in water-dependent ceremonies and cultural events in which tribal members come into 
direct contact with water, such as during canoe journeys, boat dances, sweat lodges, bathing, and in-water 
ceremonies. Poor water quality can directly affect those ceremonies and cultural events. As described in Section I, 
the Band’s members engage in various water-based ceremonies like this. One example is the sweat lodges that 
Maliseets hold to heal and honor the spirit, in which they rely on water from the river, which is poured on heated 
stones to generate steam. Uses like this must be protected by the Reserved Rights Rule. 
Tribes across the country also have reserved water rights that must be protected. In Winters v. United 
States, the Supreme Court recognized that when land has been reserved to a tribe, a reservation of water sufficient 
to meet the purposes of the reservation is implied. 207 U.S. 564, 576-77 (1908); see also, e.g., Cappeart v. United 
States, 426 U.S. 128, 139 (1976); Arizona v. California, 373 U.S. 546, 597-602 (1963); Agua Caliente Band of 
Cahuilla Indians v. Coachella Valley Water Dist., 849 F.3d 1262, 1270 (9th Cir. 2017) (“[T]he primary purpose 
underlying the establishment of the reservation was to create a home for the Tribe, and water was necessarily 
implicated in that purpose.”). In many cases, the water reserved by a tribe originates outside of its reservation and 
flows downstream to the reservation. The Winters reserved water right entitles the tribe to a quantity of water 
sufficient to meet the purposes of the reservation, but the water must also be of sufficient quality to meet the 
purposes. Cohen’s Handbook of Federal Indian Law—the seminal treatise in the field—states as follows:  
To meet federal purposes, Indian reserved water rights should be protected against . . . impairments 
of water quality, as well as against diminutions in quantity. . . . Fulfilling the purposes of Indian 
reservations depends on the tribes receiving water of adequate quality as well as sufficient 
quantity. . . . The quality of the water necessary for [tribal] uses may vary from the high quality 
needed for human consumption to a lesser quality for fish and wildlife habitat to an even lower 
quality for irrigation. Each use, however, requires water that is appropriate quality to support that 
use.  
The quality and quantity of water may be directly related. This interrelationship is most evident in 
the case of a reserved right to water for fisheries preservation. The right reserved is that amount of 
water necessary to maintain the fishery. The fishery consists not only of the fish themselves, but 
also of the conditions necessary to their survival. Thus, habitat protection is an integral component 
of the reserved right. In order to protect the fishery habitat, tribes should have a right not only to a 
sufficient amount of water, but also to water that is of adequate quality. 

 
88  Bell Road   Littleton, Me  04730   www.maliseets.com 
 
Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians Comments Page 19 of 29 
COHEN’S HANDBOOK OF FEDERAL INDIAN LAW § 19.03[9], at 1236 (Nell Jessup Newton ed., 2012) (footnotes and 
citations omitted). In the Federal Register notice, EPA indicates that “[t]ribal reserved rights as defined in this 
proposed rulemaking generally do not address the quantification of Winters rights.” 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,363. 
However, as noted above, the quality and quantity of water may be directly related. For instance, for a tribe with a 
Winters reserved water right that requires water sufficient to support fishing on a reservation, what happens 
upstream of the reservation with respect to water quantity may diminish water quality both outside and within the 
reservation. A good example is temperature impacts from upstream diversions. A stream may become water quality 
impaired for temperature if too much water has been diverted from the stream; in turn, this may affect fish 
dependent on cold water both outside and within the tribe’s reservation. This is an increasingly important issue in 
light of increased pressures from climate change, as EPA generally acknowledges. See 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,366. In 
that case, the “tribal reserved right” in this rule should include the Tribe’s Winters reserved water right to protect 
the water quality before it reaches the reservation, even if the quantity of water is also implicated. Moreover, 
sometimes protection of the Winters reserved water right will have nothing to do with quantity. For instance, if a 
tribe has a Winters reserved water right for economic development, drinking water, or some other purpose, an 
upstream state must protect the water quality required to meet each such use before the water to which the tribe is 
entitled reaches the reservation, which may include more protective criteria to preventing pollutants from being 
discharged upstream of the reservation that would impair the Winters right.16  
At proposed 40 C.F.R. § 131.3(r), the rule defines “tribal reserved rights” as “any rights to aquatic and/or 
aquatic-dependent resources reserved or held by tribes, either expressly or implicitly, through treaties, statutes, 
executive orders, or other sources of Federal law.” This language is broad enough to encompass ceremonial uses 
and Winters reserved water rights, as it must. However, EPA’s decision not to include “water” itself among the list 
of enumerated examples of tribal reserved rights (87 Fed. Reg. at 74,367) and its statement that the definition 
generally does not include quantification of Winters rights (87 Fed. Reg. at 74,363) could be used to suggest that 
Winters rights need not be protected under the rule. This cannot be, and the preamble and response to comments for 
the final rule must make it clear that the water quality needed for Winters reserved water rights to fulfill the 
purposes of a reservation must be maintained or achieved. The same is true for ceremonial uses of water wherever 
tribes reserved such rights in areas where states or EPA may promulgate water quality standards. 
In EPA’s description of the “tribal reserved rights” definition, the agency notes that the proposed definition 
“does not apply to unratified treaties or reserved rights that have been abrogated or otherwise superseded.” 87 Fed. 
Reg. at 74,366. The Band does not take exception to this language but note for the record that many states do not 
seem to understand or accept that only Congress has the authority to abrogate a reserved right and that any such 
abrogation must be explicit. E.g., United States v. Dion, 476 U.S. 734, 738-39 (1986) (“We have required that 
Congress’ intention to abrogate Indian treaty rights be clear and plain.”); Washington v. Wash. Com. Passenger 
Fishing Vessel Ass’n, 443 U.S. 658, 690 (1979) (“Absent explicit statutory language, we have been extremely 
reluctant to find congressional abrogation of treaty rights. . . .”). While some states may wish that treaties or other 
sources of reserved rights did not exist or claim that circumstances have changed such that the reserved rights have 
been relinquished, EPA, in coordination with affected rights holders, will need to ensure that such erroneous 
positions are provided no credence.17 If a state asserts abrogation of a tribal reserved right as a basis for not 
 
16 Similar arguments can be made that some waters outside of the waters in which a tribe might hold its reserved fishing rights 
may still require more protective WQS to protect tribal reserved rights where such waters are necessary to support the right. 
For instance, the life cycle of fish may include the fish spending time in habitat outside of areas in which a tribe holds reserved 
rights. However, that habitat should still be sufficiently protective so as not to undermine the tribal reserved right once the fish 
(or population of fish) enters or returns to an area in which the tribe holds the right. 
17 In the preamble, EPA posits a question regarding whether in a situation in which “a waterbody may not be able to support a 
reserved right to an aquatic and/or aquatic-dependent resource because attaining that use in that waterbody is not currently 
feasible,” the state could revise its designated uses to remove the tribal reserved rights use following a use attainability 
analysis. 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,372. We do not believe either EPA or the state would have that option. While such an 
administrative action would have no legal bearing on the tribe’s reserved rights, Clean Water Act actions should not be taken 
that suggest a right no longer exists or create confusion for the public in that regard. Instead, the CWA should only be 
“[striving] for attainment of such uses to protect a tribal reserved right consistent with the obligations of treaties and other 
Federal Laws.” Id. Further, where some level of reserved right use, even if severely suppressed, is being attained, the state

protecting it in its water quality standards, the burden must be on the state to provide explicit, clear, and plain 
Congressional authority supporting its position rather than shifting the burden to the tribe to prove that there is no 
such authority.  
C. 
The “Right Holder” Definition Is Acceptable But Its Use Does Not Make Sense at One Point 
in the Proposed Regulatory Language. 
EPA proposes to define “right holders” at 40 C.F.R. § 131.3(s) as “tribes holding rights to aquatic and/or 
aquatic-dependent resources pursuant to an applicable treaty, statute, executive order, or other source of Federal 
law.” 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,366, 74,378. The Band does not object to this definition but notes that use of the term 
“right holder” does not make sense in at least one circumstance in which it has been used in the regulatory scheme. 
At 40 C.F.R. § 131.9(a)(2), the proposed language states that WQS must be established to protect “[t]he health of 
the right holders to at least the same risk level as provided to the general population of the State.” It would be better 
to use another term besides “right holders” in this instance since EPA presumably means individual tribal members 
rather than a tribe in this provision. A phrase such as “right holder’s members” or “right holder’s population” could 
be substituted in this provision. In other instances, such as the information sharing provision at 40 C.F.R. § 
131.6(g)(1) and the tribal consultation provision at 40 C.F.R. § 131.9(b), the use of the term “right holders” makes 
sense as these activities would involve the affected tribe. The Band also notes that the definition of “right holders” 
could be shortened to: “tribes holding tribal reserved rights,” assuming the agency does not make any changes to 
the definition of “tribal reserved rights” proposed for 40 C.F.R. § 131.3(r). As it stands now, the language in 40 
C.F.R. § 131.3(s) is somewhat redundant to the definition at § 131.3(r). 
D. 
The Types of Historic Information to Determine the Level of Water Quality Necessary to 
Protect Tribal Reserved Rights Should Include Indigenous Traditional Ecological 
Knowledge, and Funding Should Be Provided to Ensure Sufficient Data and Information Is 
Available to Support Protective WQS.  
EPA has requested comment on the types of information that states and EPA should consider in 
determining the level of water quality necessary to protect tribal reserved rights. EPA writes:  
Determining the level of water quality necessary to protect any aquatic or aquatic-dependent 
resource or users of that resource can be a complex endeavor that involves weighing multiple lines 
of evidence. However, this endeavor will largely mirror the process states already follow in 
developing their WQS. Examples of such evidence include fish consumption rate surveys, studies 
or accounts of heritage fish consumption rates, peer-reviewed articles or reports on the types and 
levels of pollutants that can adversely affect the resource in question, and monitoring data 
reflecting historic and/or current water quality. EPA requests comment on the types of historic 
information that states and EPA should consider. 
87 Fed. Reg. at 74,368 (emphasis added). The Band agrees that each of these categories of information is an 
appropriate type of information for states and EPA to consider in determining the level of water quality necessary 
to protect tribal reserved rights (i.e., in setting criteria). In addition, however, we emphasize the need for states and 
EPA to consider Indigenous Traditional Ecological Knowledge (ITEK) in their development of water quality 
 
would have no authority to remove that existing use under EPA’s existing implementing regulations. 40 C.F.R. §131.10(g) 
(“States may designate a use, or remove a use that is not an existing use, if the State conducts a use attainability analysis . . . 
.”). In short, if a tribe has reserved rights in a water body in which a state has jurisdiction to set WQS, that reserved right 
should be a designated use, and EPA should afford the state no opportunity or authority to remove that designated use unless 
and until Congress explicitly and plainly abrogates that right. In extremely limited circumstances, a WQS variance that 
conforms to the requirements in 40 C.F.R. § 131.14 may be available. However, as EPA is well aware, “[w]here a State adopts 
a WQS variance, the State must retain, in its standards, the underlying designated use and criterion addressed by the WQS 
variance.” 40 C.F.R. § 131.14(a)(2). Any such variance would need to be approved by EPA after consultation with right 
holders. As the tribes’ trustee, we expect that EPA would adhere to the right holder’s position on the variance.

standards. Further, some level of funding must be made available by the federal government to ensure that the 
requirement in proposed 40 C.F.R. § 131.9(a) indicating that states and EPA must rely on “available data and 
information” to establish WQS that protect 1) the exercise of tribal reserved rights unsuppressed by water quality or 
aquatic-dependent resource availability and 2) tribal member health can be fulfilled. Otherwise, there is a risk that 
relevant information may not be readily available, which may derail urgently needed improvements in water 
quality. 
 
 
1. 
Indigenous Traditional Ecological Knowledge (ITEK) 
On November 15, 2021, the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP) and the White 
House Council on Environmental Quality (CEQ) jointly released a memorandum that commits to elevating 
Indigenous Traditional Ecological Knowledge (ITEK) in federal scientific policy processes. Office of Science and 
Technology Policy, Council on Environmental Quality Indigenous Traditional Ecological Knowledge and Federal 
Decision Making (Nov. 15, 2021) [2021 White House Memorandum], available at 
https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2021/11/111521-OSTP-CEQ-ITEK-Memo.pdf. This 
memorandum formally recognized ITEK as one of many bodies of knowledge that are valuable to improving 
policy making and recognizes that its inclusion in federal policy making is “[c]onsistent with the Administration’s 
additional commitment to scientific integrity and knowledge and evidence-based policymaking.” Id. at 1. On 
November 30, 2022, the White House followed up on this memorandum with “Guidance for Federal Departments 
and Agencies on Indigenous Knowledge” (https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2022/12/OSTP-CEQ-
IK-Guidance.pdf) and an associated memorandum on “Implementation of Guidance for Federal Departments and 
Agencies on Indigenous Knowledge” (https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2022/12/IK-Guidance-
Implementation-Memo.pdf). These documents are “intended to promote and enable a government-wide effort to 
improve the recognition and inclusion of Indigenous Knowledge” in “research, policy, and other decision making,” 
including review and approval of state water quality standards. Nov. 30, 2022 Implementation of Guidance 
Memorandum at 1; see also November 30, 2022 Guidance Memorandum at 4-5 (“Indigenous Knowledge can 
provide accurate information, valuable insights, and effective practices that complement practices and knowledge 
derived from other approaches. For example, at times Indigenous Knowledge holders have observed early and 
accurate detection of environmental changes, such as interconnected patterns of species, signs of drought, or 
impacted water quality.”). 
The 2021 White House Memorandum defined “ITEK [as] a body of observations, oral and written 
knowledge, practices, and beliefs that promote environmental sustainability and the responsible stewardship of 
natural resources through relationships between humans and environmental systems.” Id. at 2. As far as we are 
aware, EPA has not yet adopted its own definition of ITEK, but it has employed the U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service’s 
definition in prior guidance: 
Also called by other names including Indigenous Knowledge or Native Science, (hereafter, TEK) 
refers to the evolving knowledge acquired by indigenous and local peoples over hundreds or 
thousands of years through direct contact with the environment. This knowledge is specific to a 
location and includes the relationships between plants, animals, natural phenomena, landscapes 
and timing of events that are used for lifeways, including but not limited to hunting, fishing, 
trapping, agriculture, and forestry. TEK is an accumulating body of knowledge, practice, and 
belief, evolving by adaptive processes and handed down through generations by cultural 
transmission, about the relationship of living beings (human and non-human) with one another and 
with the environment. It encompasses the world view of indigenous people which includes 
ecology, spirituality, human and animal relationships, and more. 
EPA Re: “Considering Traditional Ecological Knowledge (TEK) During the Cleanup Process (Jan. 3, 2017), 
available at https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2020-
10/documents/considering_traditional_ecological_knowledge_tek_during_the_cleanup_process_updated_link.pdf 
(quoting Sarah Rinkevich et al., Traditional Ecological Knowledge for Application by Service Scientists Fact Sheet, 
U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Native American Program. (Feb. 2011)). As suggested by the definitions above, 

 
88  Bell Road   Littleton, Me  04730   www.maliseets.com 
 
Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians Comments Page 22 of 29 
“ITEK” has been identified with several names, including “Traditional Ecological Knowledge” (TEK) and 
“Indigenous Knowledge,” but all retain a common theme: Indigenous knowledge systems are based on intense, 
place-based observations that have evolved, and continue to evolve, over millennia. Indigenous knowledge 
survives and adapts as it is passed from one generation to the next through the exercise of cultural practices.  
Increasingly, non-Indigenous scientists and policy makers recognize the importance of ITEK in decision-
making, including the connections it demonstrates between biological, physical, cultural, and spiritual systems. The 
White House recognizes ITEK “as one of the many important bodies of knowledge that contributes to the 
scientific, technical, social, and economic advancements of the United States and to our collective understanding of 
the natural world.” 2021 White House Memorandum at 1. Likewise, EPA’s 2014 Policy on Environmental Justice 
for Working with Federally Recognized Tribes and Indigenous People 
(https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2017-10/documents/ej-indigenous-policy.pdf), “encourages as appropriate 
and to the extent practicable and permitted by law, the integration of Traditional Ecological Knowledge into the 
agency’s environmental science, and policy decision-making processes to address environmental justice concerns 
and facilitate program implementation.” Id. at 3. Certainly, ITEK must be considered in determining the level of 
water quality necessary to protect “tribal reserved rights” under the rule.  
 
EPA must be mindful that tribes may have confidentiality concerns with respect to ITEK and other types of 
tribal history and knowledge. As EPA acknowledged in its 2014 Environmental Justice Policy (page 3), “The EPA 
considers confidentiality concerns regarding information on sacred sites, cultural resources, and other traditional 
knowledge, as permitted by law. The EPA acknowledges that unique situations and relationships may exist in 
regard to sacred sites.” Before seeking ITEK from “right holders,” EPA should, at a minimum, observe the cautions 
laid out in the Nov. 30, 2022 White House Guidance (pages 15-16) regarding conducting an initial meeting, so that 
ITEK holders are aware of how the information will be used and the extent to which it can be made available to 
states or the public at large. Likewise, it should provide guidance and a process for states to use in handling such 
information. 
 
 
2.  
Federal Funding 
Ensuring that the type of information necessary to meet the requirements of proposed 40 C.F.R. § 131.9(a) 
(“to the extent supported by available data and information”) takes resources. It is not cheap or easy to complete 
things like fish consumption surveys, toxicology studies, interviews with tribal elders to record ITEK and oral 
histories, etc. Both tribes and states are likely to require resources in order to ensure that the information EPA is 
calling for is available and does not present an unintended barrier to promulgation and approval of WQS that 
actually protect tribal reserved rights. A good example of the type of study that could inform unsuppressed levels of 
fish consumption is the Wabanaki Traditional Cultural Lifeways Exposure Pathway Scenario (July 2009), 
available at https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2015-08/documents/ditca.pdf (Attachment 17). The Wabanaki 
study was funded by EPA through a Direct Implementation Tribal Cooperative Agreement, peer-reviewed, and 
specifically designed for use in reviewing and developing water quality standards. It provides a numerical 
representation of the environmental contact, diet, and exposure pathways of people fully using natural resources 
and pursuing traditional cultural lifeways. Wabanaki Study at 7-10; see also 81 Fed. Reg. 23,239, 23,246 (April 20, 
2016) (quoting purpose of study as “to describe the lifestyle that was universal when resources were in better 
condition and that some tribal members practice today (and many more that are waiting to resume once restoration 
goals and protective standards are in place)”). The study breaks down consumption levels based on the estimated 
range of diets that reflect three traditional lifestyle modes reflective of different habitat types. Another good 
example of this type of EPA-tribal funding partnership is the fish consumption survey completed for the Columbia 
Basin Treaty Tribes by the Columbia River Inter-Tribal Fish Commission (CRITFC), which was a project funded 
through a cooperative agreement between CRITFC and the EPA’s Office of Policy, Planning and Evaluation. 
CRITFC, A Fish Consumption Survey of the Umatilla, Nez Perce, Yakama, and Warm Springs Tribes of the 
Columbia River Basin: Technical Report 94-3 (Oct. 1994), available at https://www.critfc.org/wp-
content/uploads/2015/06/94-3report.pdf (Attachment 18). We request that EPA discuss in its response to comments 
how the agency intends and plans to ensure that federal funding is available to help tribes gather or develop the 
information necessary to ensure rapid progress on WQS improvements is not thwarted by a lack of available 

 
88  Bell Road   Littleton, Me  04730   www.maliseets.com 
 
Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians Comments Page 23 of 29 
information. Further, EPA should ensure that it does not set too onerous a threshold for the data and information 
required to meet the language of 40 C.F.R. § 131.9(a) (“available data and information”) in either practice or 
guidance documents that would prevent improvements on a prompt timeline. 
E. 
EPA Is Correct to Account for Suppression Effects Explicitly in the Language of the 
Proposed Rule.  
The Band wholeheartedly agrees with EPA that the WQS must be set to protect the exercise of tribal 
reserved rights unsuppressed by water quality or the availability of the resource at issue. Without such a provision, 
water quality standards will only protect the unsatisfactory status quo in which tribal members consume fish at 
rates far below heritage rates of consumption when fish were more abundant and tribal members did not need to be 
fearful of eating too much seafood due to toxic contamination. This is the present circumstance in the Band’s 
waters. In 40 C.F.R. § 131.9(a), EPA proposes the following language:  
(a) Water quality standards must protect tribal reserved rights applicable to waters subject to such 
standards. To protect tribal reserved rights, water quality standards must, to the extent supported by 
available data and information, be established to protect: 
(1) The exercise of tribal reserved rights unsuppressed by water quality or availability of the 
aquatic or aquatic-dependent resource; and 
(2) The health of the right holders to at least the same risk level as provided to the general 
population of the State. 
87 Fed. Reg. at 74,378. We believe this proposed regulatory language does a good job of pointing out—and 
requiring states to address—the problem of suppression, both in terms of the effects of depressed supplies of 
aquatic resources resulting from degraded water quality and the effects of contamination on tribal member health. 
“EPA request[ed] comment on whether additional language should be included in the final rule specifying the 
considerations for determining unsuppressed WQS.” 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,369. While the Band does not have specific 
suggestions for more detail in the proposed regulatory language itself, we do believe it will be incumbent upon 
EPA to ensure its guidance documents, including documents such EPA’s Methodology for Deriving Ambient Water 
Quality Criteria for the Protection of Human Health (2000), are updated to be consistent with the CWA’s 
implementing regulations. Moreover, specific guidance documents may be required to implement this new rule, 
and consistent application of this provision may benefit especially from such guidance. 
 
Related to tribal reserved fishing rights, the National Environmental Justice Council (NEJAC) explains: “A 
‘suppression effect’ occurs when a fish consumption rate (FCR) for a given population, group, or tribe reflects a 
current level of consumption that is artificially diminished from an appropriate baseline level of consumption for 
that population, group, or tribe. The more robust baseline level of consumption is suppressed, inasmuch as it does 
not get captured by the FCR.” NEJAC, Fish Consumption and Environmental Justice, at 43-45 (Nov. 2002) 
(Attachment 19). The Federal Register notice indicates that EPA is not necessarily proposing to return waterbodies 
to a “condition that existed at the time a reserved right was established, 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,366-67, citing the Grand 
Coulee Dam as the type of condition that revised WQS are not able to fully account for due to the dam’s depletion 
of fish populations available for tribal member consumption. Id. However, “the regulation is intended to result in 
WQS that protect reasonably anticipated future uses, taking into account factors that may have substantially altered 
a water body,” id. at 74,367. The Federal Register notice also notes, “the unsuppressed level or use of a resource 
should account for situations where restoration efforts are planned or underway (e.g., efforts to improve habitat or 
reduce contamination), such that it would be reasonable to expect the opportunities for use of the resource to 
increase in the future.” Id. at 74,369. While we agree with this latter sentiment, EPA must not allow legacy 
pollution and levels of pollution to be locked in place just because there is long-standing infrastructure or industrial 
use that has depleted the quality of water in a water body. Dams come down (just look at the Kennebec and 
Penobscot rivers) and legacy pollution can be cleaned up and habitat restored (see the Morningstar Road culvert 
replacement project on Moose Brook), so we are discomforted by the idea that historic wrongs may be built into a 
diminished baseline from which the level of protection necessary for the tribal reserved right WQS will be 

 
88  Bell Road   Littleton, Me  04730   www.maliseets.com 
 
Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians Comments Page 24 of 29 
assessed. As the agency acknowledges, EPA should be forcing action rather than reinforcing an existing suppressed 
use or “set[ting] in motion a ‘downward spiral’ of further reduction/suppression.” Id. at 74,369. As a trustee with 
fiduciary obligations to the tribes, EPA must apply its authority to prompt restoration, not maintain the status quo. 
EPA notes that determining levels for the unsuppressed exercise of tribal reserved rights would need to be 
based on “available data and information” without specifying what types of data and information states or EPA 
may rely on. 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,378. In an earlier section, we note the types of information that might be used, but 
we do want to make clear that this proposal calls for caution. For example, as described above, contemporary fish 
consumption surveys may indicate lower rates of fish consumption than historic levels or the levels to which those 
exercising reserved rights are entitled. Consequently, as suggested above, EPA should include language in the rule, 
preamble, response to comments, and guidance documents that would require states and EPA to rely on available 
ITEK, other tribal accounts of unsuppressed rates, historical or anthropological reports of the exercise of tribal 
reserved rights, or studies of the historical exercise of tribal reserved rights, so that WQS do not end up protecting 
only for a suppressed status quo. If these types of information are available, they should supersede other available 
data or information.18 If these types of information are not available at the time of a triennial review, as suggested 
above, EPA should make grants or other funding available for studies of the unsuppressed exercise of tribal 
reserved rights to be completed before the next triennial review, so that suppression effects can be corrected.  
F. 
The Reserved Rights Rule Must Apply Wherever a State Has Jurisdiction to Set WQS in 
Waters in Which a Tribe Holds Reserved Rights. 
It is important to make sure that tribal reserved rights are protected wherever they exist, including any 
place where a state or EPA has jurisdiction to set WQS. As described in detail in Section II.A., the Band holds 
reserved rights, at a minimum, on its trust lands and in its waters, including fishing, hunting, ceremonial, water, and 
other reserved rights. We continue to disagree with EPA’s determination that Maine has the right to set WQS in 
tribal waters, including the waters in and adjacent to the Houlton Band’s trust lands. However, as long as that 
interpretation is in place, EPA must ensure the rule extends to our waters. To avoid any uncertainty or ambiguity 
with respect to the Reserved Rights Rule’s application in Maliseet waters, we ask EPA to avoid the use of an “off-
reservation” shorthand. While the Band understands that the Reserved Rights Rule would most frequently apply to 
waters outside of Indian Country, as you are well aware, EPA’s determination that Maine has authority to set WQS 
within Maliseet waters is authority that other states do not enjoy with respect to the Indian Country within their 
boundaries. We believe the Federal Register notice for the proposed rule was careful to include all waters in which 
states are permitted to promulgate WQS, but we want to ensure that the final rule, preamble, and response to 
comments is equally careful. Using a shorthand like the rule applying “off-reservation” is not fully inclusive of all 
places where the Reserved Rights Rule would apply, and we are concerned that deviation from the careful language 
of the rule could be exploited. 
 
IV. 
TRIBAL CONSULTATION AND PRACTICALITIES OF RULE IMPLEMENTATION 
We conclude with one of our—if not the—greatest concerns about the proposed Reserved Rights Rule. We 
know our reserved rights better than anyone else. We can speak authoritatively to these rights when others cannot. 
 
18 In the Federal Register notice, EPA writes, “Where information is conflicting, there are gaps in information, and/or a 
difference of opinion exists between the state and one or more tribes about the level of water quality necessary to protect a 
reserved right, EPA will take action based on the best available information in the same way that EPA currently makes WQS 
decisions in these circumstances in other contexts, e.g., determining whether criteria are scientifically defensible in situations 
where there is conflicting science, there are gaps in the science, and/or there are different conclusions among stakeholders. 
EPA requests comment on whether there are other factors it should consider when making decisions under these 
circumstances.” 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,371. We do not generally have a concern about this approach, except that where there is 
conflicting information about which a tribe would know more than a state (e.g., the existence and level of use of the tribe’s 
own reserved rights) or where there is “a difference of opinion . . . between [a] state and one or more tribes about the level of 
water quality necessary to protect a reserved right,” EPA should defer to, or at least weigh more heavily, the tribal position in 
that circumstance. The failure to do so may run afoul of EPA’s trust responsibility and obligations under the Clean Water Act 
and federal Indian law to ensure that tribal reserved rights are protected. 

 
88  Bell Road   Littleton, Me  04730   www.maliseets.com 
 
Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians Comments Page 25 of 29 
While we deeply appreciate EPA’s efforts through this proposed rule to protect our reserved rights, the proposed 
rule is flawed in the process it describes for determining if and where tribal reserved rights apply, and with whom it 
places that power. The rule must be corrected on this score before it is finalized. 
 
The proposed rule requires that EPA consult with tribes (“right holders”) in association with the agency’s 
review of a state’s water quality standards. The proposed language at 40 C.F.R. § 131.9(b) states, “In reviewing 
State water quality standards submissions under this section, EPA will initiate tribal consultation with the right 
holders, consistent with applicable EPA tribal consultation policies, in determining whether State water quality 
standards protect applicable tribal reserved rights in accordance with paragraph (a) of this section.” 87 Fed. Reg. at 
74,378. The Band appreciates this commitment to tribal consultation in EPA’s review of the standards a state 
submits for approval and we want to see this explicit commitment to consultation in the final rule (and other rules 
EPA is promulgating). However, we are concerned that the tribal consultation described in the regulatory language 
itself comes too late in the process if it only occurs after a state has already gone through its rulemaking process 
and submitted such standards to EPA for approval. If a state does not have and use the requisite information from 
affected tribes much earlier in the process, this could result in costly, lengthy delays that could have been avoided 
had an affected tribe been consulted earlier, as well as the state being less inclined to willingly incorporate tribal 
information after it has already completed its administrative process. Consequently, we believe that the affirmative 
duty for EPA to consult should be maintained in the final language of the rule, but it should be expanded to require 
early (and frequent) consultation with the right holders. We understand from EPA’s preamble and from 
government-to-government consultation that EPA appreciates the need for early and frequent consultation with 
tribes and to provide direction and guidance to states, but that understanding should be made a requirement in the 
regulatory text. Compare 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,372 (“EPA makes itself available to engage early and often to provide 
support when states are adopting and revising WQS. . . . EPA intends to support states by providing input and 
information on any tribal reserved rights and the level of water quality to protect those rights. As previously 
mentioned, EPA is also available to facilitate dialogue between states and tribes.”), with 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,378 
(proposed § 131.9(b) requiring no early consultation with tribes or states), and id. (proposed § 131.20 describing 
state review and triennial review with no reference to consultation with EPA or tribes). 
 
The language at 40 C.F.R. § 131.6(g)(1) in which EPA proposes the following language regarding the 
minimum requirements for a state’s water quality standards submission does not assuage the concern: 
Where applicable, information which will aid the agency in evaluating whether the submission 
protects tribal reserved rights consistent with § 131.9, including: 
(1) Information about the scope, nature, and current and past use of the tribal reserved rights, as 
informed by the right holders; and 
(2) Data and methods used to develop the water quality standards. 
87 Fed. Reg. at 74,378 (emphasis added). In fact, it causes us quite a bit of consternation, as does the process 
described (but not required) in the preamble at pages 74,367-68. Most fundamentally, the italicized phrase is too 
vague regarding tribes’ role and does not require the state to actually use the information provided by tribes 
regarding their own reserved rights. We are very concerned that states—which frequently have the least incentive 
to recognize tribal reserved rights and are frequently outright hostile to such rights—will be opining on the 
existence, scope, nature, and current and past use of tribes’ most sacred rights without being required to accept the 
affected tribe’s or even the federal trustee’s description and assessment of these rights. We understand that states 
with delegated Clean Water Act authority over waters in which tribes hold reserved rights must have some role in 
developing the WQS to protect that use of waters over which they have jurisdiction. However, we do not believe 
that states can or should be in the driver’s seat with respect to the analysis of the topics included in proposed 40 
C.F.R. § 131.6(g)(1). While certainly not true of all states, in enough, it will put the fox in charge of the hen house, 
such that this provision is not workable from our perspective. Instead, the federal trustee, after working closely 
with an affected tribe (and the Department of Interior, if needed), must take a much more active—and binding—
role in this process in order to ensure that tribes’ sovereign interests and sacred rights are protected. Once the tribal 
reserved rights are appropriately characterized by the appropriate actors (the tribe, first and foremost), at that point, 

 
88  Bell Road   Littleton, Me  04730   www.maliseets.com 
 
Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians Comments Page 26 of 29 
we could see states properly exercising their delegated authority to set designated uses, criteria, and antidegradation 
policy. We request that the final language of the rule reflect these comments through more detailed and binding 
regulatory provisions that put tribes in charge of characterizing their own rights. At the very least, the language of 
40 C.F.R. § 131.6(g)(1) should be stripped down to its bare minimum, so that states (as opposed to tribes or EPA) 
are not charged with characterizing the “scope, nature, and current and past use of tribal reserved rights.” Changing 
that provision to “(1) Information about tribal reserved rights, as provided by the right holders” would provide us 
considerably more comfort about how the process might work and what its ultimate outcome might be.19 
Even if we could abide the placement of authority to assess tribal reserved rights in states’ hands (which 
we cannot), the proposed regulatory language is not prescriptive enough about what a state must do to ensure that it 
has appropriate information from a tribe—or that it uses it. In theory, the “as informed by the right holders” 
language above would suggest to a state that it should engage in government-to-government consultation with 
tribes holding tribal reserved rights in order to ensure it has sufficient information about the existence, scope, 
nature, and current and past use of tribal reserved rights to know where and how to protect them through the state’s 
WQS. However, without more explicit, mandatory language, we are skeptical that robust consultation with tribes 
will be the outcome of this language in most states, particularly those that do not have an existing government-to-
government consultation policy (or where the policy is underdeveloped or underutilized in practice). As EPA is 
well aware, the relationship between states and tribes can be fraught and very adversarial at times. Even where a 
tribe and a state have a decent, or even a very good, relationship, they may not be able to agree on what level of 
water quality will actually protect the tribal reserved rights. Consequently, we recommend more direct and robust 
regulatory language that explicitly requires states to consult with tribes at the outset of and throughout its revision 
process to determine whether, where, and how tribal reserved rights will be affected by the WQS, as well as 
language that establishes a presumption in favor of the use of a tribe’s own assessment of its rights when EPA 
reviews a state’s WQS submission. In addition to strengthening the proposed regulatory language, the Band 
suggests that EPA prepare guidance explaining how a state should engage in government-to-government 
consultation with a tribe; the value and need to accept Indigenous Traditional Ecological Knowledge as relevant, 
reliable information; and the sensitivities and need for careful handling of some such information and knowledge.  
Other issues that are not accounted for in the regulatory language include: How will EPA protect tribes 
from state analyses of reserved rights that may be unsupported by law, the subject of litigation, or in need of update 
due to new info? How will EPA ensure that the wishes of a tribe that does not want its reserved rights to be 
assessed by a state at all or put in issue in a Clean Water Act administrative process are respected? What happens 
when a state ignores the information provided by a tribe or the federal trustee? Moreover, while the preamble notes, 
“where information is conflicting, there are gaps in information, and/or a difference of opinion exists between the 
state and one or more tribes about the level of water quality necessary to protect a reserved right, EPA will take 
action based on the best available information in the same way that EPA currently makes WQS decisions in these 
circumstances in other contexts,” 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,371, this may be cold comfort during certain administrations’ 
review of state water quality standards, as we saw in the human health criteria rollbacks of the last administration. 
As with preparation of materials required to determine the level of protection for tribal reserved rights, we 
are also concerned about the resources it is likely to take tribes to engage with states regarding the very existence of 
their rights. At 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,375, EPA asks for comment on the following conclusion, “While tribal right 
holders would not be direct respondents, EPA acknowledges that the proposed regulation would require that state 
submissions be informed by the right holders. EPA believes this would not lead to increased burden on right 
 
19 At the end of its description of the process for “Determining if Tribal Reserved Rights Apply,” EPA indicates that “[i]n 
addition to seeking input from potential right holders, EPA will also consider other sources of information regarding applicable 
tribal reserved rights including the language of the treaties, statutes, or Executive orders and relevant judicial precedent.” 87 
Fed. Reg. at 74,368. We note that in many cases this should be the starting and end point of the analysis. Other pertinent 
sources of information that are not listed in this passage include legislative history and prior federal actions in which an agency 
has already recognized the need to protect tribal reserved rights, such as prior Department of Interior or Bureau of Indian 
Affairs analyses or past EPA decisions. Good examples are the very materials that EPA cites in this preamble related to the 
human health criteria processes in Maine and Washington.
