Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians Comments Page 27 of 29 
holders because the proposed rule would not require additional coordination beyond that which already occurs 
during WQS public participation processes and EPA’s consultations with tribal governments.” We disagree with 
this statement. While it is true that we and many other tribes actively participate in existing WQS public 
participation processes and while we welcome this rule, there is no question that there will be additional burdens on 
us and other tribes as a result of it. It takes time and money to engage in administrative processes, and it takes even 
more time and money to engage in administrative processes where sovereigns do not agree. In order to support 
protective criteria, we are likely to need to conduct or commission fish consumption surveys and other materials to 
establish the level of water quality necessary to protect our rights. With respect to characterization and geographic 
location of tribal reserved rights, this rule may necessitate additional time and cost associated with leadership-to-
leadership meetings between tribes, states, and EPA; preparation of comments and legal analyses; and potentially 
even legal action. We therefore again request that the Federal government provide funding to help tribes engage in 
this process. 
Finally, EPA proposes to modify 40 C.F.R. § 131.20 to require that a state’s “triennial review process 
include an evaluation of whether there are tribal reserved rights applicable to waters subject to the state’s WQS and 
whether WQS need to be revised to protect those rights.” 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,367, 74,378-79 (proposed § 
131.20(a)). We understand that states will need a little time to implement this rule as practical matter and agree that 
the triennial review is a good way to first incorporate the Reserved Rights Rule’s requirements. Of course, EPA is 
aware that triennial reviews can sometimes be delayed and some are currently in process. While a gradual process 
may be ok (or even beneficial) in some circumstances), states are on notice now that a final rule is on its way, so 
they should begin thinking about whether any WQS revisions they are currently undertaking implicate tribal 
reserved rights. We do not think that potentially less protective criteria should be grandfathered in, as it were, just 
because the revision process began before the Reserved Rights Rule has been completed. Where a state already has 
adopted a sustenance fishing designated use—as the state of Maine has for certain waters—the state should ensure 
that any criteria it revises be sufficient to protect tribal reserved rights in those waters, regardless of when this rule 
is finalized.

. 
. 
To conclude, the Band thanks EPA for recognizing the need to ensure that water quality standards protect 
tribal reserved rights and the people who depend on exercise of their rights for their health and well-being, 
livelihoods, culture, religion, and community cohesion. We encourage you to move swiftly to finalize the proposed 
rule, but to do so with the comments made here firmly in mind. We do not believe EPA should finalize a rule that 
would allow the omission of certain components of WQS or that would put a state in the position of defining the 
scope, nature, or current or past use of a Tribe’s reserved rights, and we look forward to EPA refining the final rule 
and preamble to address these concerns. The Band appreciates EPA’s efforts to restore meaningful government-to-
government consultation with respect to agency rulemakings like this, which were either pro forma or non-existent 
under the prior administration. We are available and more than happy to discuss this matter further should you have 
any questions about our comments or would like to discuss possible resolutions to any potential problems we have 
identified in the proposed rule. You may contact Jane Steadman at jsteadman@kanjikatzen.com or 206-344-8100 
with any questions you might have or to coordinate further discussion.

Water Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions To Protect Tribal Reserved

Dear Ms. Brundage, 
Thank you for providing Doyon, Limited (“Doyon”) the opportunity to submit the 
following comments on the Environmental Protection Agency’s (“EPA”) proposed revisions 
to the agency’s Clean Water Act water quality standards (“WQS”) regulations relating to 
protection of aquatic and aquatic-dependent resources reserved to Indian tribes. Water 
Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions To Protect Tribal Reserved Rights, 87 Fed. Reg. 74361 
(Dec. 5, 2022) (“Proposed Rule”).  
Doyon is one of the Alaska Native regional corporations established by Congress 
under the terms of the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act (“ANCSA”). Headquartered in 
Fairbanks, Doyon has more than 20,400 Alaska Native shareholders. Doyon is the largest 
private landowner in Alaska, with a land entitlement under ANCSA of more than 12.5 million 
acres. Doyon’s lands extend from the Brooks Range in the north to the Alaska Range in the 
south and from the Alaska-Canada border in the east to almost the Bering Sea in the west. 
Doyon’s mission is to continually enhance its position as a financially strong Native 
corporation to promote the economic and social well-being of its current and future 
shareholders, to strengthen its Native way of life, and to protect and enhance its land and 
resources.  
Doyon’s comments focus specifically on EPA’s and other federal agencies’ obligation 
to consult with ANCSA Corporations, which the Proposed Rule fails to address, and which is 
a critical tool for Doyon to carry out its mission. 
Under federal law, EPA is required to consult with ANCSA Corporations on the same 
basis as Indian tribes. In Executive Order (“EO”) 13175, Consultation and Coordination with 
Indian Tribal Governments, President Clinton required federal agencies to implement an 
effective process to ensure meaningful and timely consultation with tribes during the 
development of policies or projects that may have tribal implications. Such consultation is 
intended to ensure meaningful tribal participation in planning and decision-making 

2 
 
1 Doyon Place, Suite 300 | Fairbanks, Alaska 99701-2941 | (907) 459-2000 WWW.DOYON.COM 
 
processes for actions with the potential to affect tribal interests. Although EO 13175 itself 
applies specifically to federally-recognized tribal governments, pursuant to Public Law No. 
108-199, 118 Stat. 452, as amended by Public Law No. 108-447, 118 Stat. 3267, Congress 
specifically extended these obligations to ANCs, requiring the Office of Management and 
Budget (“OMB”) and all Federal agencies to “consult with Alaska Native corporations on the 
same basis as Indian tribes under Executive Order No. 13175.” Consolidated Appropriations 
Act, 2004, Pub. L. 108-199, Div. H § 161, 118 Stat. 3, 452 (2004), as amended by Consolidated 
Appropriations Act, 2005, Pub. L. 108-447, Div. H, Title V § 518, 118 Stat. 2809, 3267 (2004). 
In November 2009, President Obama signed a Memorandum for the Heads of 
Executive Departments and Agencies on Tribal Consultation, in which he emphasized his 
commitment to “regular and meaningful consultation and collaboration with tribal officials 
in policy decisions that have tribal implications including, as an initial step, through complete 
and consistent implementation of Executive Order 13175.” Following from this 
Memorandum, in July 2010, the Director of the Office of Management and Budget issued a 
Memorandum for the Heads of Executive Departments and Agencies, and Independent 
Regulatory Agencies on Guidance for Implementing E.O. 13175, “Consultation and 
Coordination with Indian Tribal Governments,” in order to “help Federal agencies to comply 
with their obligations to provide meaningful consultation and collaboration” and “to 
promote greater openness in government.” This guidance specifically recognized that “OMB 
and all Federal agencies “are required to “consult with Alaska Native corporations on the 
same basis as Indian tribes under Executive Order No. 13175.” 
In accordance with these mandates and guidance, EPA has developed Guiding 
Principles for Consulting with Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act (ANCSA) Corporations to 
“clarify how the [EPA] engages in consultation and coordination with Alaska Native Claims 
Settlement Act (ANCSA) corporations.” Under these Principles, “EPA recognizes its 
obligation [under federal law] to ‘consult with [ANCSA] corporations on the same basis as 
Indian tribes under Executive Order 13175.’” 
Unfortunately, while the Proposed Rule specifically addresses consultation with 
federally recognized Indian tribes, it fails to appropriately recognize its obligation to consult 
with ANCSA Corporations. Proposed section 131.9(b) provides that, “In reviewing State 
water quality standards submissions under this section, EPA will initiate tribal consultation 
with the right holders, consistent with applicable EPA tribal consultation policies, in 
determining whether State water quality standards protect applicable tribal reserved rights 
in accordance with paragraph (a) of this section.” 87 Fed. Reg. at 74378. The Proposed Rule 
further explains that: 
Although proposed 40 CFR 131.9(b) would specifically apply to EPA’s review of state 
WQS submissions, EPA intends, per its 2011 Policy on Consultation and Coordination 
with Tribes, the 2016 EPA Policy on Consultation and Coordination with Indian 
Tribes: Guidance for Discussing Tribal Treaty Rights, and applicable EPA regional 
consultation procedures, to initiate consultation with tribes in the geographic area 
where any WQS decision under EPA’s consideration may affect tribal interests, 
including reserved rights. EPA would consider all relevant information obtained 

3 
 
1 Doyon Place, Suite 300 | Fairbanks, Alaska 99701-2941 | (907) 459-2000 WWW.DOYON.COM 
 
through consultation to help ensure that the agency is fully informed before taking a 
WQS action. 
87 Fed. Reg. at 74372-73 (footnotes omitted).  
Just as they could affect the interests of Indian tribes in a particular geographic area, 
WQS submissions and WQS actions also could affect the interests of ANCSA Corporations in 
a particular geographic area. Any final rule, therefore, must similarly recognize EPA’s 
obligation to consult with ANCSA Corporations “on the same basis as Indian tribes,” 
reference applicable authorities, including EPA’s Guiding Principles for Consulting with 
Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act (ANCSA) Corporations, and commit to consultation with 
potentially impacted ANCSA Corporations before taking a WQS action. 
Doyon cannot overstate the importance of federal agencies’ obligations to consult 
with Doyon and other ANCSA Corporations regarding these and other activities under 
Executive Order No. 13175, as specifically extended to the ANCSA Corporations by Congress. 
Pursuant to Federal law and policy, EPA must ensure that ANCSA Corporations are provided 
the opportunity to meaningfully participate in WQS actions and other Federal agency 
decision-making processes that could impact our ability to fulfill the purposes for which we 
were established under ANCSA and to protect and advance the economic, social, and cultural 
interests of our shareholders. 
Thank you for your consideration of these comments.

Sarah E. Obed

RE: Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791; Water Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions to 
Protect Tribal Reserved Rights 
 
Dear Administrator: 
 
Gnoozhekaaning, “the Place of the Pike” or Bay Mills Indian Community (Bay Mills) is a federally 
recognized Indian Tribe and signatory to the Treaty of March 28, 1836 (7 Stat. 491) by which the right to 
hunt, fish, and gather on 13.8 million acres of what is now the State of Michigan, and on over 12.2 million 
acres of lakes Superior, Michigan and Huron was expressly reserved for all time. Bay Mills strongly 
supports EPA’s effort to recognize off-reservation tribal reserved rights and to revise federal water quality 
standards (WQS) regulations to protect them. These revisions represent the most definitive and impactful 
steps the agency has taken to fulfill its trust responsibilities to tribes. 
 
Bay Mills has the following comments, concerns, and answers to specific requested information: 
 
1. The proposed regulatory revisions will require states to undertake many actions, which include 
determining the level of water quality necessary to protect tribal reserved rights. These 
requirements will result in states gathering and interpreting tribal information. One of the biggest 
challenges and unknowns with this proposed revision is how tribally-supplied information will be 
incorporated into decision making. It is unclear whether tribal perspectives about their own 
reserved rights will be treated with the highest regard by states or EPA. Furthermore, it is not clear 
how the EPA will handle situations where tribes disagree with conclusions drawn by states 
regarding treaty protected resources. Bay Mill’s supports the comment letter provided by 
EarthJustice on behalf of several tribes, including Bay Mills, as it articulates in detail the potential 
issues with delegation to the States. 
 
2. Within the federal register notice, EPA requests additional information on types of reserved rights 
that should be considered in the revisions. Bay Mills will not quantify our reserved rights. Rather, 
it is important to recognize that tribal culture, natural resources and environmental health, and treaty 
rights are all intricately interwoven and interdependent. And, without clean water, none of these 
are sustainable. Bay Mills, therefore, reserves the right to clean water. We ask that EPA recognize 
the interconnectedness of our lifeway when acting to protect our tribally reserved rights. 
 
3. Bay Mills is a fishing community, and has relied on fishing for its subsistence and economic needs 
since time immemorial. EPA acknowledges that poor water quality disproportionally impacts tribal 

2 
 
communities like ours, whose lifeways rely heavily on fish consumption. Bay Mills fully supports 
EPA’s efforts to protect the health of our tribal citizens. Bay Mills is committed to work with EPA 
on this issue. 
 
4. Bay Mills also supports EPA’s effort to protect tribal reserved rights at levels unsuppressed by 
water quality. The application of these protections to waters where Bay Mills is actively attempting 
restoration of wild rice and fisheries will be of utmost importance. We understand the complexity 
of EPA’s approach to use historic and currently available data to balance heritage use of a resource 
with what is reasonably attainable today. 
 
5. Within the federal register notice, EPA requests additional information on what sources of 
information should be considered, including historic information, to quantify level of water quality 
necessary to protect tribal reserved rights. Tribal knowledge and tribal ecological knowledge should 
be at the apex of decision making regarding tribal reserved rights. In the least, tribal knowledge 
should never be discounted when determining the protection of tribal reserved rights. However, it 
remains unclear how EPA and states would treat tribal ecological knowledge with this regulatory 
revision. 
 
6. Furthermore, EPA requests information on what factors should be considered when there is 
conflicting science, there are gaps in science, and/or there are different conclusions among 
stakeholders. Likewise, tribes should have the ultimate voice in how their reserved rights are 
protected. 
 
7. Bay Mills supports the highest classification of protection for waters where we hold treaty rights. 
 
Bay Mills reiterates its support for the EPA’s effort to recognize off-reservation tribal reserved rights and 
to revise the federal WQS regulations to protect our treaty rights. Our treaty reserved rights and resources 
have experienced continual disregard and degradation after losing sole stewardship of our resources. The 
principle and goal set forth in this regulatory revision is long overdue. We look forward to working with 
EPA to ensure that our treaty reserved rights and resources are fully protected for perpetuity. 
 
Chi miigwetch (thank you), 
 
 
 
 
Whitney B. Gravelle 
President, Executive Council 
Bay Mills Indian Community

Re: Proposed Water Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights 
Dear USEPA, 
Buena Vista Rancheria of Me-Wuk Indians (BVR) is a federally recognized Native American 
Tribe located within the Mokelumne River Watershed of Northern California. Buena Vista 
Rancheria is writing to provide comments regarding the Proposed Water Quality Standards 
Regulatory Revisions to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights by EPA. BVR intends to reaffirm our 
interest in ongoing government to government consultation throughout EPA’s process to develop 
this new rule within 40 CFR Part 131.  
BVR thanks EPA for proposing this rule to protect tribal reserved rights related to water 
resources and create water quality standards to protect these rights. BVR; however, is concerned 
about scope of the proposed regulation as it is only protective of tribal water uses that are defined 
by the federal government as reserved rights and does not recognize water uses as identified by 
tribes themselves. There are many federally unrecognized tribes that will be left out by this rule 
and many tribal water uses that will be missed by only focusing on the reserved rights. Buena 
Vista Rancheria recommends this rule to better protect tribal water uses as described and 
determined by tribes.  
There are parallel processes taking place in the State of California where the State and Regional 
Water Boards are looking to designate Tribal Beneficial Uses of water to waterbodies and then 
adopt water quality standards to protect the tribal beneficial use. This pathway offers an 
alternative for Tribes to utilize as a means to protect human health regarding the use on a water 
body. Unfortunately, this mechanism is not available in all states; therefore, EPA should consider 
developing a secondary pathway to protect tribal uses of water either by to identifying tribal 
designated uses on a federal level, broaden this rule to include non-reserved rights, develop a 
rule to push States to adopt tribal beneficial uses, or some other mechanism.  

 
 
Buena Vista Rancheria of Me-Wuk Indians 
1418 20th Street Suite 200 
Sacramento, CA  95811 
Office 916.491.0011  
Fax 916.491.0012 
 
Furthermore, this rule does not clearly articulate who will be responsible for identifying tribal 
reserved rights, though it has been stated that this determination will be left to the states. There 
must be clear guidance, developed in consultation with tribes, to outline a process the federal 
government and/or states follow when identifying reserved rights. This process should require 
tribal consultation as a practice in identifying reserved rights to ensure tribal rights are protected. 
If a state does not recognize a tribe’s asserted reserved right, there must be a process to hold 
states accountable for recognizing and protecting a tribe’s right(s).  
In this process to identify reserved rights, pollutants of concern, and water quality standards 
needed to protect the right, tribes must be consulted and included throughout the entire process. 
This means open and transparent communication with tribes regarding the identification of 
reserved rights, on which water body, pollution contamination levels, scientific research, 
literature, and analyses used to develop a water quality standard to protect that use. It is 
important to note that although in some cases a single water quality standard may be protective 
across a state or region, the rule should allow for water quality standards to be tailored and 
specific to the reserved right on a case-by-case basis in consultation with the tribal reserve right 
holder.   
Currently, through various land back movements and government programs, tribes are acquiring 
new ownership and management over ancestral lands. This creates the need for an open and 
continual process for ongoing consultation and discussions with tribes. The historic and 
continuing uses section of the rule addresses the connections of tribes; however, it does not 
address revitalized connections. In California and in many other states tribes have been 
disconnected from their ancestral areas and are revitalizing their ceremonies and connections. 
This process must consider new or revitalized connections as well as continual uses of aquatic 
resources. 
Finally, BVR would like to ensure that the EPA and states are clear in understanding that they do 
not need to request culturally sensitive information about water uses, and must respect tribal 
confidentiality regarding water uses in identifying reserved rights, and working toward 
developing the standards to protect that right. Many of the sites are protected by the National 
Historic Preservation Act Section 106 and many other state laws. These laws require continual 
tribal consultation and consideration with regards to effects on the areas as well as confidentiality 
for sensitive information.  
Please reach out to Buena Vista Rancheria Staff for questions or clarification.

fishing and hunting on the said tract of land hereby intended to be conveyed."2 
The State has been the primary beneficiary of the Treaty of Big Tree along with the holder of the 
preemption rights, investor Robert Morris. The Nation received pennies per acre amid allegations 
of bribery of our traditional chiefs. Part of the reason our ancestors approved the Treaty was the 
reassurance the citizens of the Nation would retain the traditional hunting and fishing rights to our 
ceded territories, necessary for our survival.3  The bargained-for exchange, accounts for part of the 
almost unconscionably low purchase price of our ceded lands. However, the United States 
Supreme Court significantly curtailed the meaningful expression of our hunting and fishing rights 
in 1916 deciding that our reserved treaty rights did not withstand the State's interest in preserving 
fish and game resulting in Nation citizens being forced to abide by hunting and fishing regulations 
applicable to the general publie 
Accordingly, our ability to exercise our hunting and fishing rights that were retained in our ceded 
territory were significantly diminished to hunt and fish at the times and by the manners we were 
accustomed—under the fallacy our citizens would harm the wildlife and the State would protect 
it—with the approbation and acquiesce of the federal government. The current State regulations 
recommend to only eat a few of the smaller fish species up to 4 times a month, due to pollution.5 
The recommended consumption of most other fish species is even less including many species 
listed as "do not eat."6
 The State's exercise of jurisdiction has negatively impacted the fish, 
animals, plants, and waters of our Nation, which has further curtailed the exercise of our reserved 
treaty rights. Both the limitations placed on us from eating our traditional diets and any 
consumption of polluted fish have negatively impacted the health and well-being of our people. 
The Nation welcomes any measure to rectify the current situation including support for this 
Proposed Rule. It is imperative that the State be required to maintain water quality and fish 
populations that are safe to eat in sustenance quantities in waters where the Nation has reserved 
the right to fish pursuant to the Treaty of Big Tree. 
In the Proposed Rule, EPA explains that "by amending EPA's WQS regulations, rather than 
addressing [tribal reserved rights] on a case-by-case basis as state WQS are submitted for review 
[. . 1, EPA is proposing a uniform approach for establishment of WQS where tribal reserved rights 
apply and clearly laying out how EPA will review such WQS." 87 Fed. Reg. at 74366. The Nation 
supports EPA's approach. Requiring a uniform approach will help protect all Native nations, not 
just those in states more favorably disposed to recognizing reserved rights.

We also would like to point out that the extent of tribal reserved rights goes beyond EPA's 
definition of the term in new 40 C.F.R. § 131.3(r) as "rights to aquatic and/or aquatic-dependent 
resources reserved or held by tribes." We understand that the Proposed Rule is being promulgated 
under the Clean Water Act and therefore that it is tied to "waters of the United States." It bears 
keeping in mind, however, that the Nation has treaty rights to hunt that may extend beyond aquatic 
or aquatic-dependent resources, in the way contemplated under the Clean Water Act, although—
especially in the Seneca view—all life is dependent on water. The Nation's treaty rights also 
extend over resources not specifically discussed in the Proposed Rule, including various freshwater 
mussels and other culturally significant freshwater species, and plants used for medicinal and 
cultural purposes. 
The Nation also supports EPA's proposed addition of a new Section 131.9 to Title 40 of the Code 
of Federal Regulations. We support the proposed requirement in § 131.9(a)(1) that WQS must 
protect "the exercise of tribal reserved rights unsuppressed by water quality or availability of the 
aquatic or aquatic-dependent resource." We are concerned, however, that EPA's proposed 
interpretation of this requirement as being limited to protecting "reasonably anticipated future uses, 
taking into account factors that may have substantially altered a waterbody," Proposed Rule at 
74366-67, may result in undue limitations on tribal reserved rights. At a minimum, EPA should 
clarify that the concept of a reasonably anticipated future use most likely will change over time, 
and if uses expand — for example, due to the removal of dams impacting fisheries, which is already 
happening in parts of the country, cleanup of upstream polluted waters, or resource restoration 
projects — then the impacts on tribal reserved rights must be reevaluated. 
The Nation is also concerned as to the level of data the EPA will require to demonstrate 
unsuppressed uses. We understand the advantages of having underlying surveys and documents 
similar to the Wabanaki Traditional Cultural Lifeways Exposure Scenario to support claims to 
tribal reserved rights, but these take time to produce, and many tribes do not have the resources to 
conduct them. If there is a possibility for the EPA to identify funding, technical assistance, and 
other support to generate supporting data, that would be extremely valuable. Even if a Native 
nation chooses to do this work, its data sovereignty should be supported to decrease the 
exploitation by outside agencies. 
We request the language in the proposed section of § 131.9(a)(2) be clarified: "water quality 
standards must, to the extent supported by available data and information, be establish to protect: 
(2) The health of the right holders to at least the same risk level as provided to the general 
population of the State." At the consultation with EPA concerning the proposed rule, it was 
clarified that this would be a more protective standard for the cancer risk level of our citizens than 
being considered a highly exposed population. This is not the most natural reading of the Proposed 
Rule, and the Nation requests clarification so it is plain to all the standard is more protective of the 
rights holders. 
Page 3 of 5 

Proposed Rule § 131.9(b) provides: "In reviewing State water quality standards submissions under 
this section, EPA will initiate tribal consultation with the right holders, consistent with applicable 
EPA tribal consultation policies, in determining whether State water quality standards protect 
applicable tribal reserved rights in accordance with paragraph (a) of this section." The Nation 
strongly believes there should be a standard for consultation such as early and meaningful 
consultation imposed or a statutory deadline by which consultation with all right holders will 
commence. 
The Nation also supports the requirement in § 131.9(c) that WQS must designate uses and establish 
appropriate water quality criteria to protect those uses, pursuant to § 131.11. We agree that this 
process could involve creating a new designated use to protect the tribal reserved rights, with 
associated water quality criteria for that use, or developing revised criteria to protect the reserved 
right under an existing designated use, such as fishing, or both options. However, the Nation 
supports, that to protect tribal reserved rights, the antidegradation requirements referenced in § 
131.9(c)(3) should be required in addition to the designated uses and water quality criteria required 
in § 131.9(c)(1)-(2), not instead of those requirements. The regulatory text should say "and" 
instead of "and/or" when listing the requirements in § 131.9(c). The antidegradation options for 
Outstanding National Resource Waters and to ensure that any lowering of water quality will 
continue to protect tribal reserved rights (Options 1 and 2 in the Proposed Rule at 74371) can both 
be used to support designated uses and related water quality criteria that protect reserved rights. 
•
The Nation believes that narrative water quality criteria should be used only when numeric 
criteria cannot be established or to supplement numeric criteria, per existing § 131.11. 
Proposed Rule at 74368 says that "EPA is available to assist status in gathering more 
information, in coordination with the right holders, for future use" when data and 
information are not available or inconclusive. The Nation requests that this commitment to 
the regulation or in more formal guidance be include in the Proposed Rule. 
•
Additionally, information about key aquatic species of a Native nation could be provided, 
as EPA suggests (74368); however, the EPA must recognize the sovereignty of the Native 
nation and leave the decision to share that information, to the Nation. 
The Nation advocates for the inclusion of the new sentence in § 131.20(a), which requires a 
triennial review of WQS to "include evaluating whether there are tribal reserved rights applicable 
to State waters and whether water quality standards need to be revised to protect those rights 
pursuant to § 131.9." However, the only process specified for determining whether the WQS 
satisfy § 131.9 is the public participation required in existing § 131.20(b). The Nation requests that 
EPA provide a specific process to ensure that states do consult with Native nations. An early and 
meaningful, and deliberate partnership, not just a consultation should be required. States should 
engage in that process while they are reviewing their WQS, rather than leaving it up to EPA to 
determine whether there are tribal reserved rights at issue once the states have already submitted 
the WQS to EPA for review and approval, which is when § 131.9(b) is appropriate. Additionally, 
the EPA could also require that states contact all Native nations within their borders and 
neighboring jurisdictions, meet with them separately from the general public hearing provided in 
§ 131.20, and take their input into account when reviewing WQS.

Lastly, it is common knowledge that the triennial review process does not in regularly take place 
every three years. To guarantee that a review of WQS takes place in a timely fashion in response 
to these revised WQS regulations, another sentence should be added to § 131.20(a) to require that, 
within two years of the effective date of this rulemaking, all states must review and, if needed, 
revise their WQS to protect tribal reserved rights. These rights, which are protected not only by 
the Clean Water Act but by the Constitution, have been disregarded for centuries. 
In closing, the Nation requests all Native territory receive the same protection as lands with 
reserved rights. Less than approximately twenty percent of Native nations have WQS under the 
CWA. Native nations deserve the same downstream protection that is provided to states across the 
United States even if they do not have their own approved WQS or even Treatment as a State 
("TAS") status. That reflects, not only the difficulty of obtaining such status under the CWA, but 
the failure of the federal government in upholding their responsibility to Native nations. We look 
forward to changes made through legislation and rulemaking to rectify some of the difficulties in 
the TAS process going forward to help properly protect the waters of Native nations.

Dear Ms. Brundage: 
On behalf of the Puyallup Tribe of Indians, I write these comments in support of the Environmental 
Protection Agency's proposed revisions to the Federal Clean Water Act water quality standards 
(WQS) regulation to clarify and prescribe how WQS must protect aquatic and aquatic-dependent 
resources reserved to tribes through treaties, statutes, executive orders, or other sources of Federal 
law. Se, 87 Fed. Reg. 74361 (Dec. 5, 2022). 
To understand our perspective on this matter, we provide a brief description of the Puyallup Tribe 
and our history. 
I. 
Introduction 
A. Puyallup Tribe of Indians 
The Puyallup Tribe of Indians is a federally recognized Tribe located in Pierce County, Washington 
along the shores of Commencement Bay, a large inlet of Puget Sound. The Puyallup Tribe is a 
signatory to the Treaty of Medicine Creek, 10 Stat. 1132. Under this Treaty, the Tribe reserved the 
lands for its Reservation, which was established by two subsequent Executive Orders. Executive 
Order of January 20, 1857; Executive Order September 6, 1873. Over the next fifty years, 
notwithstanding the establishment of the Tribe's Reservation, the Tribe lost ownership to most of 
the land within its Reservation as a result of Acts of Congress authorizing and directing the 
allotment and sale of reservation land, court decisions and other private and federal actions. See 
H.R. Rep. No. 101-57, at 3 (1989). With the enactment of the Indian Reorganization Act, 25 U.S.C. 
§§ 461-479, the Tribe adopted a constitution and organized its Tribal government, which then set 
out to restore the Tribal land base and develop programs to better serve its tribal members. 
In 1983, the Tribe's title to the bed of the Puyallup River and adjacent exposed lands, including 
lands within the Port of Tacoma, was confirmed by the federal court. Puyallup Tribe v. Port of 
3009 E. Portland Ave. 
Tacoma, Washington 98404 
253/573-7800 

March O 1, 2023 
Page2 
Tacoma, 717 F.2d 1251 (9th Cir. 1983). This decision gave rise to an historic Settlement Agreement 
between the Tribe, the City of Tacoma, the Port of Tacoma, the State of Washington and the Federal 
Government, which was enacted by Congress. Puyallup Tribe of Indians Settlement Act of 1989, 
Public Law 101-41, 25 U.S.C. §§ 1773-et seq. (1989). The Settlement Act restored to the Tribe 
nearly 1000 acres ofland, including lands within the Port of Tacoma. Today the Puyallup 
Reservation is located in Pierce County, extends into King County, and includes areas within the 
City of Tacoma, all of Fife, and parts of several other municipalities and unincorporated areas. The 
Tribe has a membership of nearly 6000 people. 
In the Treaty of Medicine Creek, the Puyallup Tribe also reserved its right to fish in its usual and 
accustomed places, and to hunt and gather on opened and unclaimed lands. These rights were 
affirmed in numerous Supreme Court cases including Puyallup Tribe v. Department of Game, 391 
U.S. 392 (1968), Department of Game v. Puyallup Tribe, 414 U.S. 44 (1973), Puyallup Tribe v. 
Department of Game, 433 U.S. 165 (1977); and Washington v. Washington State Commercial 
Passenger Fishing Vessel Ass 'n, 443 U.S. 658 (1979). The Tribe, through its Fisheries Department 
and Shellfish Department, works in conjuncture with federal, state and other tribal agencies to 
ensure that the environment for its treaty protected resources (which includes not only the Puyallup 
River and its tributaries, but also large areas of the Puget Sound) is protected and preserved. This is 
necessary not only because Tribal members rely on these resources for economic support, but also 
because these resources and the environment in which they live serve as the foundation of the 
Puyallup Tribe's cultural and spiritual practices. 
B. Tribal Treaty Reserved Rights must be considered in establishing WQS 
The land and rights reserved for the Tribe are what our ancestors secured, so that our children and 
grandchildren would have a place to live, work, fish, pray and raise their families. If our 
Reservations and the places where we exercise our rights are not environmentally safe, then all that 
was reserved to us in the Treaties are in jeopardy. Thus, specific consideration of treaty reserved 
rights in aquatic and aquatic-dependent resources in establishing State (and Tribal) Water Quality 
Standards (WQS) is critical to ensure that we will continue to have the benefit of the bargain our 
ancestors struck with the United States. 
Treaty rights are inseparable from the natural environment on which Indian tribes rely for our 
wellbeing. Thus, as EPA undertakes to review and approve State WQSs, we have always asserted 
that the law requires that the EPA consider "What impacts will these standards have on tribes and 
are their specific treaty rights?" with the fundamental principle that Indian tribes' federally-
protected rights to their homelands and to hunt, fish, gather and pray can only be guaranteed when 
the natural world is healthy and safe enough to sustain those activities. Thus, we strongly support 
the EPA's effort to amend the WQS regulation to explicitly address how WQS must protect tribal 
reserved rights as to aquatic and aquatic-dependent resources. This will ensure a WQS process that 
is transparent and consistent for all stakeholders. 
Below we discuss in detail our comment on the proposed rule. 
II. Discussion of the proposed rule 
3009 E. Portland Ave. 
Tacoma, Washington 98404 
253/573-7800 

March 01, 2023 
Page 3 
1. Determining if Tribal Reserved Rights Apply 
The EPA requested comments on whether there are additional types of Tribal reserved rights that 
should be considered in addition to the rights to fish, gather aquatic plants, and to hunt for aquatic-
dependent animals. 87 Fed. Reg. 74367 (December 5, 2022). We would assert that all the species 
that we fish, hunt and gather are aquatic-dependent resources. Thus, in examining WQS standards 
we must consider not only fish and shellfish, but the terrestrial and waterfowl species that rely on 
our rivers and waterbodies to survive. 
We suggest EPA add one critical right and activity that is attendant to the exercise of our hunting, 
fishing and gathering rights which is the right to pray in these waters. See, Too Long Too Silent: The 
Threat to Cedar and Sacred Ways of the Skokomish, American Indian Culture Research Journal 
(1993). We have prayed and used our waters for religious purposes since the beginning of time, and 
it is important that this right be recognized as a use of these waters in setting WQS. These waters 
are for all intents and purposes our baptisteries and should be acknowledged as such. 
We are concerned that EPA is going to require Tribes to demonstrate where and how the right is 
exercised by the right holders. Id. While the preamble indicates that these inquiries are limited to 
specific water bodies or waters generally within a broad geographic area, and whether the right is 
for subsistence purposes, our experience with the Army Corps of Engineers teaches us that this 
could result in the EPA requiring Tribes to indicate the exact locations and times that we exercise 
our treaty rights, exactly how we do this, and for how long, and that a particular WQS is necessary 
to preserve the exercise of the right in a specific location. See, Tribal Treaty Rights Effects 
Determination, USACE Seattle District Policy (July 27, 2020) (Attached as Exhibit 1). Thus, we 
believe EPA should only require the nature of the right in broad geographic terms, or in the case of 
Tribes in the Northwest, our adjudicated Usual and Accustomed Areas ("U&A's"). We do not 
believe it is necessary to ask how the right is exercised as we see no relevancy of this question to 
establishing WQS. 
However, if the EPA is going to insist on this being a prong of the inquiry, we think the correct 
question is "Why is the right being exercised?" For Puyallup and other Tribes in the Northwest, we 
have a Treaty right to 50% of the harvestable fisheries species in our U&A's, we exercise this right 
both for commercial and subsistence purposes, and we gather other aquatic-dependent resources for 
subsistence and cultural purposes. Thus, the inquiry should be is the right a subsistence right, treaty 
commercial right, and/or for cultural purposes, and not how the right is exercised. Again, we rely on 
the waters of our territories for all these purposes and believe that the WQS should be based on an 
understanding that these activities and uses are coexistent with one another. 
2. 
Protecting Applicable Reserved Rights 
a. Determining the level of Water Quality Necessary to Protect the Right 
We agree with the Preamble's direction that States and Tribal right holders should establish lines of 
communications to develop WQS that are necessary to protect any aquatic or aquatic-dependent 
3009 E. Portland Ave. 
Tacoma, Washington 98404 
253/573-7800 

March 01, 2023 
Page4 
resources. Id. at 74368. This includes working with Tribal communities to gather accurate data on 
fish consumption rates, and utilization of aquatic-dependent resources (which again includes 
terrestrial resources and waterfowl), as well as the water itself (this includes not only for 
cultural/religious activities but uses for other activities like Tribal fish hatcheries, acclimation and 
rearing ponds, and related facilities). 
b. Accounting for Suppression Effects 
We agree with the change to §131.9(a)(l) that WQS must be established to "protect the 'exercise of 
the tribal reserved rights unsuppressed by water quality or availability of the aquatic or aquatic-
depended resource."' In 2013, a 135-acre tract ofland, the Redondo tract, where the Puyallup Tribal 
members exercise the right to harvest geoduck, was closed due to legacy arsenic contamination. 
This contamination resulted in China banning shellfish imports from the Northwest greatly 
impacting Tribal treaty commercial harvesters. This was because the State of Washington, unlike 
China, had not tested for inorganic arsenic, and had declared the Redondo tract safe for harvesting. 
Thus, our right to engage in our commercial treaty harvest was suppressed because the water quality 
was lower than necessary to engage in vital trade with a critical international partner. This also 
relates to the "why" the right is exercised, because once commercially harvested, these resources 
enter the international market, and we need these resources to meet the higher environmental 
standards of our trading partners. 
We endorse the Preamble's direction that States work with right holders to gather information about 
unsuppressed uses. Id. at 74369. This is consistent with the federal government's elevation of 
Traditional Ecological Knowledge in its decision making. 
c. Protecting Right Holders to the Same Risk Level as the General Populations. 
We also endorse the proposed rule treating Tribal members exercising reserved rights as a distinct, 
identifiable class of individuals holding legal rights to resources, whose reserved rights are unique 
to them and have a defmed geographic scope. Id. at 74370. This is critically important for deriving 
the human health water quality criteria, and as discussed above, for other purposes as well, 
including engaging in international trade. With regard to the human health criteria, for decades the 
fish consumption rate for the state of Washington was 6.5 grams per day (approximately 1 fish meal 
per month). It has been well established that tribal members consume fish in far larger quantities 
than one "fish meal" per month. Moreover, these criteria did not account for the consumption of 
other aquatic-dependent resources and other uses of the water itself. Nor did these criteria account 
for other risk factors that put tribal members, as an identifiable class, at a higher risk for cancer and 
other health conditions. Thus, the change to 13 l .9(a)(2) is vital to ensuring that WQS are based on 
actual data regarding the use of the water and aquatic and aquatic-dependent resources by Tribal 
right holders, as well as the recognized health risk factors that exist in tribal communities. 
d. Implementation of These Proposed Requirements. 
In the Preamble the EPA requests comment on whether there are instances beyond fish consumption 
and protection of wild rice where "WQS may need to be adjusted to protect tribal reserved rights 
3009 E. Portland Ave. 
Tacoma, Washington 98404 
253/573-7800 

March 01, 2023 
Page 5 
consistent with this proposed rulemaking." Id. at 74371. As we discussed, there are instances 
beyond fish consumption that necessitate more stringent criteria, in particular the commercial 
harvest and international trade of the resources. In addition, there is the consumption and use of 
aquatic-dependent resources, in particular aquatic-dependent vegetation, which we not only 
consume, but use for different cultural activities such as weaving; therefore, tribal members could 
be exposed to higher levels of toxins through skin absorption, and such a use would likely require a 
more stringent criterion. Finally, again we have prayed and used the waters in our territory for 
religious purposes since the beginning of time, and we need these waters to be available to use for 
these purposes, as it is vital to our tribal way of life. This use alone requires the most stringent WQS 
possible. 
EPA requested comment mi whether, in instances when there is conflicting information, gaps in 
information, or there is a difference of opinion between a State and Tribe, if there are other factors 
beyond the best available information to determine that a criteria is "scientifically defensible, that 
EPA should consider in resolving the conflict or disagreement." Id. at 74371. The scope of the best 
available information is critical, which is why the State and Tribal right holders must have a free 
and frank exchange of information. In addition, the best available information must include the 
Traditional Ecological Knowledge of the tribal people who have used and relied on the resources 
and waters for generations. This information must be accepted as real data and not be viewed as 
anecdotal or unreliable information. 
3. Options for Establishing WQS to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights 
We agree with the proposed rule designating Tribal reserved rights as an explicitly designated use, 
and where a use (i.e., fishing) is designated that the WQS be established to ensure that Tribes with 
reserved rights are protected to the level appropriate to protect the general population, are viable 
ways to proceed, and complement each other well in establishing WQS. To be sure, for waters 
where a particular use is not designated, it is important that all the tribal reserved rights be so 
designated, for example gathering cattails or other vegetation, in addition to fishing, and that the 
criteria be adjusted accordingly. And where a use is designated, i.e., fishing, requiring that the 
criteria must be adjusted to ensure to protect tribal member health. 
However, regarding the reliance on antidegradation, we agree that it is reasonable that WQS should, 
at a minimum, be established to ensure that the resources are maintained and not further degraded. 
But this must be the floor in setting WQS and cannot be the ceiling. Thus, this option cannot be to 
the exclusion of the other two options, but rather the baseline by which the other two options are 
implemented. We are also concerned with how this option is to be implemented in concert with 
§ 131.9( a)(l) which requires WQS to be established to protect the exercise of the tribal reserved 
rights unsuppressed by water quality or availability of the aquatic or aquatic-dependent resource. 
Id. at 74368. Certainly, preventing further damage is critical, but that alone will not be sufficient to 
preserving and restoring tribal reserved rights into the future. 
We believe the proposed rule must be clear that the States will likely need to combine these 
methods to protect tribal reserved rights. Thus, designating a water body as an ONRW to prevent 
3009 E. Portland Ave. 
Tacoma, Washington 98404

further degradation alone is not likely to protect tribal reserved rights, and that additional designated 
uses and corresponding criteria will likely be necessary. 
4. Use Attainability 
The preamble to the proposed rule requests comment on how States can revise their designated uses 
to ensure compliance with the revised§ 131.9. We agree that EPA should not modify §131.10 
( designated uses), but rather include in § 131.9 provisions that specify whether or how a State could 
revise designated uses to protect Tribal reserved rights. 
III. Conclusion 
We appreciate the opportunity to provide these comments and support EPA' s efforts to better 
protect Tribes' legally protected rights and resources, and thereby uphold the United States' 
responsibility under treaties, statutes and Executive Orders to Tribes throughout the country.

Tribal Treaty Right Effect Determination Process  
 
Version: July 27, 2020 
 
 
What is the purpose of this document?   
 
As part of the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE), Seattle District’s permit application review 
process, we notify Tribes of proposed activities occurring within waters of interest to federally 
recognized Tribes, and request Tribal notification of any concerns or comments regarding the 
proposed activity’s effects.  If a Tribe has concerns regarding the proposed Department of the Army 
(DA) regulated activity, we will encourage the applicant and Tribe to work together to resolve those 
concerns, to the extent both the applicant and Tribe are amenable to that approach.   
 
Should a Tribe have unresolved concerns that rise to the level where the Tribe objects to USACE 
authorization of the activity on the basis that it would violate a Tribe’s reserved treaty right, the 
Tribe notifies the Seattle District of the Tribe’s objection.  In making a permit decision, the USACE 
must ensure it does not authorize an activity that would result in a violation of a Tribal treaty right.  
 
This document provides general information about the review process of the Seattle District once a 
Tribe notifies the agency of an objection to authorize a proposed activity because the Tribe is 
concerned the proposed activity would impermissibly infringe a Tribe’s treaty right.  
 
What effect would a Tribal objection based on tribal treaty rights have on the Seattle District’s 
permit decision? 
 
When presented with such an objection from a Tribe, the Seattle District considers project-specific 
information to determine whether the proposed activity under the USACE’s regulatory jurisdiction 
would result in an impermissible abrogation of the treaty right.   The USACE both recognizes its 
obligation to uphold Tribal treaty rights and that the applicant is entitled to a timely decision 
regarding its permit application.  In conducting this effects determination, the USACE is neither a 
proponent nor opponent for a permit application. 33 C.F.R § 320.1(4).  
 
If the USACE was to make a determination and finding that DA authorization of the applicant’s 
proposed activity would impermissibly infringe on a reserved treaty right, the USACE would need 
substantial evidence from an objecting Tribe to rebut the presumption that approval of the DA 
permit would not be contrary to the public interest. The applicant is afforded an opportunity to 
review and respond to the Tribe’s submission, and to submit evidence. The USACE must examine 
the specific facts of the situation in the context of existing information, law, and policy to determine 
whether the proposed project would abrogate a treaty right. In doing this, the USACE does not 
conduct a balancing test. If information before the Agency demonstrates the specific proposed 
project before the Agency would obstruct, eliminate, or interfere with the objecting Tribe’s access to 
its Usual and Accustomed fishing grounds and stations to such an extent the Tribe’s reserved treaty 
fishing right will be impermissibly impaired, the USACE does not have the authority to issue a 
permit for the project in the absence of a specific statutory authorization.  See Northwest Sea Farms 
v. United State Army Corps of Engineers, 931 F. Supp. 1515 (W.D.Wash. 1996).  If, however, the 
USACE determines that DA authorization of the proposed activity would not abrogate a treaty right, 
Exhibit 1

2 
 
the Corps would continue the full evaluation of the permit application notwithstanding the objection 
from the tribe.  
 
 
What information might assist Seattle District in determining whether an activity would 
abrogate a treaty right? 
 
As the Tribe has unique access to relevant information regarding the scope of its interest that would 
potentially be affected by the proposed DA regulated activity and how the proposed project would 
physically obstruct access to tribal Usual and Accustomed (U&A) places, an objecting Tribe with 
treaty-reserved fishing rights bears the burden of raising, and, thereafter, presenting, information to 
the agency sufficient to sustain an objection to the issuance of a proposed permit. In the absence of a 
raised and sustained objection, the Corps will presume the granting of a permit would not abrogate a 
treaty right.  
 
 
The Seattle District must have sufficient evidence to evaluate whether the proposed activity’s 
interference with a treaty right is of the type that would abrogate the right.  Potentially relevant 
information regarding the scope of the tribe’s interest includes: the specific proposed project’s 
effect(s) on the Tribe’s reserved treaty right regarding: (1) the geographic right of access to the 
Tribe’s U&A fishing places, (2) degradation of fish runs and habitat, (3) other treaty issues, as 
applicable.   
 
This determination must evaluate the specific treaty right alleged to be at risk of impairment by the 
proposed project by the applicant.  First, a treaty right must be established in the project area.  The 
Seattle District is in interested in the Tribe’s historic, present, and proposed use of the project site, 
and will also look to specific treaties and adjudicated treaty rights determinations, if available, 
regarding the project location.  Second, the Seattle District is interested in understanding the nature 
of the proposed activity’s effect(s) on the Tribe’s treaty rights.  Third, the Seattle District will 
consider other information provided by the Tribe in order to evaluate the extent of potential 
impact(s) to the Tribe’s treaty right, and whether the identified impacts impermissibly infringe on 
the treaty right.  The USACE may also choose to seek out additional information from public 
sources or third parties regarding certain topics, such as fish conservation matters or applicable 
regulatory parameters.  The applicant may choose to present evidence to respond to submissions by 
the tribe, but is under no obligation to add to the record.  
 
 
Documentation to support this fact specific inquiry may include, but is not necessarily limited to: 
 
 Affidavits/declarations from Tribal members explaining, as applicable: 
1. How often, and, when, Tribal harvesting at the location in question has occurred; and if it 
is intended to occur in the future? 
2. Type of fishing/harvesting method(s) involved in fishing/harvesting from the site, e.g., dip 
net, reef net, drift net etc. 
3. How would Tribal access to fishing/harvesting sites be affected by the proposed project? 
What standoff distance(s) would the tribe need to maintain from the proposed project, and, 
why; as well as how many acres of fishing (for that species) with that specific fishing 
method would become inaccessible or impaired?

4. Information about the applicable conservation and/or management plans regarding the
fishery in and around the project area.
Drawing/map showing location of the fishing activity in relation to the proposed permit activity.
Videos/photos of the fishing/harvesting activity at or around the project site.
What are the next steps after this information is provided to the Seattle District? 
The information provided to the Seattle District will be shared with the permit applicant.  The permit 
applicant will be afforded the opportunity to respond to the materials provided by the Tribes in 
support of a treaty right.  If the permit applicant chooses to respond, the response will be shared with 
the Tribe asserting the treaty right.  The scope of the USACE’s inquiry into an allegation of a treaty 
rights abrogation on the basis that the proposed project presents a physical bar of access to tribal 
U&A places, is focused upon an evaluation of the relevant and material facts submitted into the 
administrative record by the parties.  The USACE may also choose to seek information from public 
sources and third parties, such as fish conservation programs or applicable regulatory 
parameters.The end goal of this process is that the Seattle District obtains information necessary to 
complete our fact-specific analysis, and renders a decision that complies with all legal requirements 
and standards.  
If there is not sufficient evidence available to the USACE to demonstrate that DA authorization 
of the proposed activity would result in an impermissible abrogation of the treaty right because of 
the extent it physically impairs or obstructs the Tribe’s access to it’s U&A grounds and stations,, the 
USACE will continue to process the permit application in accordance with the agency’s 
implementing regulations.    The USACE will then next determine if there are other aspects of the Tribe’s 
objection  to evaluate, and may seek out further information from both the Tribe and applicant in regards to 
other aspects of the effects of the proposed permit application on the Tribe’s treaty right. The USACE will 
not conclude its public interest review until it has resolved any Tribal objection that authorizing the 
applicant’s proposal would be an abrogation of a reserved treaty right. If, however, the Seattle 
District determines a Tribal objection to DA authorization of the proposed activity has been raised 
and substantiated with project-specific information, the Seattle District may not authorize the 
proposed activity, in the absence of specific statutory authorization.

Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) Comments on  
Water Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights 
 
Federal Register Vol. 87, No. 232 74361-74379 
 
Background 
 
On December 5, 2022, the U. S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) published for 
public comment a proposed rule to revise existing federal regulations for water quality 
standards (WQS) under the Clean Water Act (CWA). The revisions include new 
requirements for states to specifically protect tribal reserved rights for federally-
recognized tribes. Tribal reserved rights are defined in the proposal as “any rights to 
aquatic and/or aquatic-dependent resources reserved or held by tribes, either 
expressly or implicitly, through treaties, statutes, executive orders, or other sources of 
Federal law.”  The proposed rule includes extensive new requirements for states to 
engage and coordinate with federally-recognized tribes, ensure ongoing WQS review 
processes consider, and state-adopted WQS specifically protect, tribal reserved rights. 
EPA will consult with federally-recognized tribes on the protectiveness of state-
adopted standards, and may disapprove or promulgate standards to meet the 
requirements of the CWA.   
Federal WQS regulations codified at Title 40 Code of Federal Regulations (40 CFR) Part 
131 provide the framework and requirements for states to develop and submit WQS 
for EPA approval. WQS adopted by states must be submitted for EPA approval prior to 
use in CWA activities such as: assessments for CWA Sections 305(b) and 303(d), total 
maximum daily loads, CWA Section 401 certifications, CWA Section 404 permits for 
dredged or fill material, and permitting of wastewater discharges. Currently, these 
regulations do not include requirements for states to consider and adopt WQS 
specifically for the protection of tribal reserved rights.   
  
TCEQ offers the following recommendations as outlined below. 
 
 
Comments Regarding Water Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions to Protect 
Tribal Reserved Rights 
 
I.  Comments concerning scope and limitation of federal authority. 
A. The preamble and proposed rule revision should be revised to clearly 
indicate the scope and limitation of federal authority. Alternately, EPA may 
assume the responsibilities to implement these requirements as currently 
authorized.  EPA’s proposed revisions seem to delegate existing federal 
responsibilities to the states, by incorporating new requirements for states to 
consider and to protect treaty rights, rather than EPA, and circumvent 
established processes. Federal agencies (such as EPA) are required to consult 
with tribes on a government-government basis, pursuant to Executive Orders, 
Presidential  

TCEQ Comments  
Water Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights; 
Proposed Rule 
2 
 
 
memoranda, and other authorities, on policies that have tribal implications, 
including regulations or actions that have a substantial direct effect on one or 
more Indian tribes. In particular, the proposed requirements establish a 
separate process from the “Treatment as States” (TAS) policy established in 
accordance with Section 518 of the CWA. The TAS process established at CWA 
Section 518(e) authorizes EPA to treat an “Indian tribe as a State” for purposes 
of administering water quality standards. EPA’s implementing TAS policies 
recognize tribes as self-governed, self-determined, and sovereign. Although 
mechanisms exist for EPA to delegate such responsibility (upon authorization 
by tribal nations), as part of cooperative agreements, the proposed rulemaking 
unilaterally creates new requirements for states and circumvents these 
established processes. If the existing processes are ineffective, including 
existing federal authorities and authorizations, the preamble and rule should be 
revised to clearly explain why new requirements are needed, and clarify the 
scope and limitations of federal authority.    
Alternately, in lieu of rulemaking, EPA should assume these responsibilities to 
implement proposed requirements as part of their responsibilities already 
authorized by the U.S. Constitution and CWA, and memorialized in federal 
policies; including the identification of all tribal reserved rights. For example, 
EPA retains authority to implement the National Pollution Discharge Elimination 
System (NPDES) on tribal lands, regardless of a state’s delegation status to 
implement the NPDES program. EPA also has a primary role in consulting and 
coordinating with tribes. As stated in the preamble, EPA plans to coordinate 
with tribes during planned initial tribal consultation meetings with tribal 
reserved right holders, as specified in proposed 40 CFR §131.9(b), to determine 
whether state water quality standards protect applicable reserved rights. (See 
pages 74366 and 74367 in the FR.) Will EPA assume responsibility for 
identifying all tribal reserved rights in these consultation meetings, and then 
provide that detailed information to the appropriate states? Identifying and 
ensuring the protectiveness of tribal reserved rights, at the federal and tribal 
level, seems feasible given the existing federal regulatory framework. 
B. The definition of, and requirements to protect, tribal reserved rights needs 
clarification regarding their scope of applicability to water quality and water 
availability (quantity).  For example, does the definition of “tribal reserved 
rights” in proposed 40 CFR §131.3(r), as well as the proposed requirements to 
protect tribal reserved rights in 40 CFR §131.9, include sufficient water quantity 
to access and use fishing resources? Is water availability to access and use such 
resources within the scope of this regulation, if allocation of rights to state 
surface water is authorized and adjudicated within a state’s legal framework?  
1. If water availability is not explicitly included in the definition and 
protection of “tribal reserved rights,” the language should be revised to 
clearly allow for, and explain, the limits of the exclusion.  
2. If water availability is intended to be included in the definition and 
protection of “tribal reserved rights,” how is this new regulation 
consistent with Section 101(g) of the CWA, which clearly recognizes state 
primacy in allocation of state surface water? Including water availability  

TCEQ Comments  
Water Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights; 
Proposed Rule 
3 
 
 
has the potential to undermine Texas’ authority to allocate and manage 
its surface water resources.   
 
II.  Concerns regarding state resources to comply with the proposed requirements. 
A. Implementation of the new regulations will require legal and technical 
expertise that may not be available within existing state resources. TCEQ 
requests federal resources be made available to implement new 
requirements. If finalized as proposed, states will be required to identify any 
tribal reserved rights and document the scope, nature, and current and past use 
of the tribal reserved rights as informed by the right holders, as well as ensure 
WQS adopted by states are protective of tribal reserved rights. Specific legal and 
technical expertise will be needed to comply with these requirements, and to 
facilitate engagement and coordination with tribal right holders. Such expertise 
is not readily available within existing and limited state resources.  
 
Since the scope of this proposed regulation includes consideration of only 
federal sources of law and policies (statutes, treaties, executive orders, etc.), EPA 
should ensure federal resources to coordinate and implement these provisions 
are available to states, particularly the identification of any and all applicable 
tribal reserved rights, and other pertinent information to identify and apply 
these rights for purposes of water quality standards. Such resources may be 
available within the EPA’s American Indian Environmental Office, and each EPA 
Region’s Tribal Program, including Regional Tribal Operations Committees. It is 
foreseeable that EPA could lead regional consultation meetings with tribes, and 
also invite state representatives, so that all parties can hear directly from the 
tribes on what issues need to be addressed related to tribal reserved rights. At a 
minimum, TCEQ requests EPA identify the aquatic and/or aquatic-dependent 
resources to be considered, using their existing federal authority. Without direct 
consultation with tribes (which is the purview of EPA), states cannot know which 
specific aquatic and/or aquatic-dependent resources are important to specific 
tribes. Following EPA’s tribal consultation, a list of specific resources should be 
developed and provided to states in a timely manner to facilitate 
implementation of the rule.  
B. While EPA has emphasized they will work early and often with both tribes 
and states, it appears that the bulk of EPA’s consultation with tribes will 
occur without state participation, and after the state has adopted water 
quality standards revisions and submitted a rule package to EPA for review 
and approval.  EPA coordination with both states and tribes to identify any 
major issues with the state’s approach to protecting tribal rights should occur 
earlier in the rule revision process to help ensure that the state adopted 
revisions will meet tribal expectations and garner EPA approval. Coordination 
earlier, rather than after adoption, will help ensure scarce state and tribal 
resources are used most efficiently and effectively. Additionally, it is unclear 
how state participation and representation will be incorporated into EPA’s tribal 
consultation program. 

TCEQ Comments  
Water Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights; 
Proposed Rule 
4 
 
 
C. EPA’s economic analysis underestimates the burdens and costs to states. EPA 
has not identified the realm of applicable tribal reserved rights in each state. 
Thus, the administrative burden and cost of implementing these rules is 
unknown and not appropriately considered in the proposed economic analysis. 
Additionally, EPA did not take into consideration the costs associated with the 
engagement and completion of tribal coordination by states to inform required 
revisions. Some of these uncertainties are reflected in Table 2-3 of EPA’s 
Economic Analysis for Water Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions to Protect 
Tribal Reserved Rights (Proposed Rule), published to accompany the rule 
proposal, and with EPA’s inability to estimate costs to regulated entities. The 
costs of compliance by both states and regulated entities should be better-
estimated and quantified, the Economic Analysis revised accordingly, and 
finalization of the rule delayed until uncertainties are addressed.   
 
III.  Requests for clarity of key terms, and coordination within the existing regulatory 
framework to administer water quality standards.  
A. TCEQ requests EPA better-define or provide additional guidance regarding 
what is a “reasonably anticipated future use” and how to determine “heritage 
fish consumption rates.”  
Page 74367 of the rule preamble indicates “the regulation is intended to result 
in WQS that protect reasonably anticipated future uses, taking into account 
factors that may have substantially altered a waterbody,” however, there is no 
explicit requirement in revised 40 CFR Part 131 regarding “reasonably 
anticipated future uses.”  Current regulations require states to consider existing 
uses, thus the concept of “reasonably anticipated future uses” is not currently 
codified. EPA must clearly define this concept in rule (as “existing uses” are 
codified), or provide additional detailed guidance to determine and apply a 
“reasonably anticipated future use.” This clarification is needed particularly 
considering the current requirements to protect existing uses and water quality 
in accordance with 40 CFR Part 131. 
Additionally, in the rule preamble, EPA endeavors to ensure the level of water 
quality necessary to determine tribal resources “largely mirror the process 
states already follow,” and provide heritage fish consumption rates as an 
example. Although a footnote to EPA’s 2016 Guidance for Conducting Fish 
Consumption Surveys is provided in the preamble, the rule does not establish 
any nationally applicable thresholds. States without prior experience 
determining heritage rates and levels of suppression will encounter substantial  
uncertainty when attempting to comply with the new requirements, without 
additional clarification.     
 
B. TCEQ requests EPA clarify if the requirement of 40 CFR §131.9(a)(1) to 
protect the “exercise of tribal reserved rights unsuppressed by water quality 
or availability of the aquatic or aquatic-dependent resource” extends to other 
water quality standards requirements. These include requirements specified in

40 CFR §131.10(g) regarding designation and removal of uses; 40 CFR 
§131.12(a)(2)  
 
regarding antidegradation and allowances for the lowering of water quality; and

zones,  
low-flows and federal variances. Proposal of these revisions involving 
suppression of water quality or availability, without fully considering and

C. TCEQ requests EPA clarify how the proposed protections of tribal reserved 
rights should be coordinated with existing provisions regarding Use 
Attainability Analyses and Use and Value Demonstrations for non-Section 
101(a)(2) uses. On page 74372 of the preamble, EPA requests comment on 
whether and how states can revise designated uses, while also ensuring the 
protection of tribal reserved resources. In response to that question, TCEQ 
recommends tribal reserved rights be considered in a manner consistent with 
other existing uses to ensure proposed protections for tribal reserved rights are 
consistent, and do not conflict with, the existing regulatory framework of water 
quality standards. 
Revision of designated uses to ensure compliance with the Section 101(a)(2) goal 
of fishable -swimmable, “wherever attainable” is an essential component of 
water quality standards, and the overall management of surface water quality in 
accordance with the goals of the CWA. EPA must clarify how the proposed 
revisions can be coordinated with current procedures for revising existing uses, 
the milestone upon which the federal framework is based. If the proposed 
revisions cannot be coordinated with current provisions and existing uses, then 
it is doubtful the revisions can be appropriately administered within existing 
water quality standards programs.

To whom so ever it may concern
The requirements involve ensuring that the WQS are protective of tribal reserved rights, 
including the rights to fish, hunt, and gather, as well as other cultural and spiritual uses of the 
waters. The requirements also typically include provisions for meaningful tribal consultation and 
participation in the WQS development process. 
In addition, some states have adopted specific standards to protect the quality of water used by 
tribes for traditional and cultural purposes. In some states, the WQS regulatory revisions may 
also include special provisions designed to recognize tribal treaty and trust obligations, such as 
the obligation to provide safe drinking water for tribal members. Additionally, the regulatory 
revisions may include provisions that recognize the unique status of tribal governments and 
provide for tribal consultation and participation in WQS implementation, monitoring, and 
enforcement activities. Finally, some WQS regulatory revisions may provide for special 
procedures to ensure that tribal water quality is adequately protected and that any violations of 
tribal water quality standards are promptly addressed. 
These special procedures may include requirements to provide tribal members with timely notice 
of any water quality violations and/or to ensure that environmental enforcement actions are taken 
against violators of tribal water quality standards. Overall, the purpose of WQS regulatory 
revisions is to ensure that tribal reserved rights are adequately protected and that the water 
quality standards established by states are consistent with the special relationship between tribes 
and the federal government.
With Regards,
Saranya Madhira and Madison Christianson
