I.  Introduction 
 
On December 5, 2022, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) published a 
proposed rule titled, “Water Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions to Protect Tribal 
Reserved Rights.” 87 FR 74361 (Dec 5, 2022).  The proposal is intended to modify the 
Clean Water Act (CWA) water quality standards program, promulgated at 40 CFR Part 
131, to create additional requirements for states, tribes, and the federal government when 
promulgating water quality standards.  Water quality standards are the foundation for 
many other CWA programs, including impairment assessments, total maximum daily load 
(TMDL) development, section 401 certifications, effluent limits, and permitting decisions 
under the section 404 and section 402 National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System 
(NPDES) permit programs.   
 
The J.R. Simplot Company (Simplot) is a privately held, global agribusiness corporation 
based in Boise, Idaho.  Simplot is engaged in a number of businesses including vegetable 
and potato processing, farming, mining of phosphate and silica, fertilizer manufacturing, 
fertilizer distribution, ranching, beef cattle feedlots, beef processing, and other enterprises 
related to agriculture.  Simplot has operations throughout the United States, and has been 
a reliable domestic manufacturer and supplier of phosphate nutrients to American 
agriculture for over seven decades.  
  
Simplot’s operations are often subject to the requirements of the CWA, including section 
303 water quality standards and TMDLs; section 401 water quality certification; section 
311 oil spill prevention and response; section 404 dredge and fill permit; and section 402 
discharge permit programs; and, of course, every regulatory interaction with the CWA 
implicates the ever-changing regulatory definition of “waters of the United States” 
(WOTUS).  Thus, this rulemaking is of interest as it has a direct impact on the company’s 
United States operations. 
 
 
II.  Overview of comments  
  
Simplot is supportive of efforts to promote self-determination and economic prosperity 
among tribal communities in Idaho and across the country.  EPA’s proposed rule, though 
couched in those terms and presented as a move to lift up tribal communities, is replete 
with internal inconsistencies, could unlawfully establish an actionable trust obligation on 
the federal government and on states, and, if finalized as proposed, will create new 
burdens on state agencies, create new conflicts between sovereign states and tribal 
nations, and result in considerable new requirements upon the regulated community.  As 
demonstrated below, EPA proposed a rule that is exceeds its statutory authority and is 
not in accordance with the law.  Furthermore, the proposal lacks the scientific rigor 
required by the Clean Water Act in regards to the establishment of water quality 
standards. Simplot respectfully requests that EPA withdraw the proposed rule; engage 
meaningfully with states, who EPA readily acknowledges will bear the burden of any final 

Proposed Rule on WQS and Tribal Reserved Rights:  Comments by the J.R. Simplot Co. 
 
P a g e  5 | 30 
 
rule; engage meaningfully with the regulated community; consult with the U.S. Justice 
Department concerning the agency’s ability to create new trust obligations for itself and 
other sovereigns; and reconsider this unlawful effort to broaden the CWA well beyond its 
intended purpose.  
 
 
III. The proposed rule is unlawful 
 
The proposed rule contains numerous internal inconsistencies and legal flaws.  These 
are not minor flaws and, if the rule is finalized as proposed, are likely to result in litigation 
and a remand or vacatur of portions of the proposed rule, if not the rule in its entirety.  
There are very few, if any, changes EPA could make to the rule to minimize or mitigate 
the risk of litigation.  As drafted the proposed rule is arbitrary and capricious and unlawful 
under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA). 
 
 
a.  The proposed rule is expansive, but EPA has interpreted it narrowly and has 
failed to consider major aspects of the problems it would be creating 
 
The proposed rule would require states to protect tribal reserved rights when establishing 
water quality standards under the CWA.  The scant preamble, which amounts to less than 
18 pages, would lead a reader to believe that actual implementation of the rule would be 
quite narrow.  The preamble is inconsistent with the proposed regulatory text and must 
be rewritten to acknowledge the significant impacts this rule would have on water quality 
standards and other water management programs, which are overwhelmingly 
administered by the states.   
 
The proposed rule defines “tribal reserved rights” extremely broadly to mean “any rights 
to aquatic and/or aquatic-dependent resources reserved or held by tribes, either 
expressly or implicitly, through treaties, statutes, executive orders, or other sources of 
Federal law.”1 (emphasis added).  The preamble does explain that tribal reserved rights 
“include but are not limited to the rights to fish; gather aquatic plants; and to hunt for 
aquatic-dependent animals...”  This explanation is also extremely broad and does not 
explain the potential scope of such rights.  Tellingly, the agency requests comment on 
what other types of reserved rights it should consider, indicating that EPA does not know 
the extent of rights that could or would be protected under its own proposal.2  The 
preamble then claims that the proposal’s mandate that states and EPA protect these 
expansive reserved rights is likely to have limited application.  The agency’s narrow 
interpretation of its own proposal is unreasonable and fails to consider the very real 
likelihood that this rule would create chaos in the water quality standards program and 
likely generate decades-long litigation.  
 
 
1 Federal Register.  2022.  Vol. 87 (232) p.74,363 
2 Ibid p.74,367 

Proposed Rule on WQS and Tribal Reserved Rights:  Comments by the J.R. Simplot Co. 
 
P a g e  6 | 30 
 
The proposal asserts that EPA has only identified “two categories of circumstances where 
compliance with the proposed rulemaking is most likely to necessitate new or revised 
WQS...”3  First, for the development of human health criteria (HHC) that would incorporate 
the “unsuppressed fish consumption rate” and therefore be protective of subsistence 
fishers.  Second, where a reserved right is not already accounted for as a designated use 
or presently attained.4. The effect on HHC development is discussed further in Section 
IV. b and c below.   
 
Concerning designated uses and attainment, the proposal suggests that many states 
already protect tribal reserved rights through water quality standards that provide 
“protection and propagation of fish, shellfish, and wildlife and provide for recreation in and 
on the water.”5  EPA also points to the existing requirement that states adopt water quality 
standards to protect designated uses and states, “where a tribe has the right to hunt an 
aquatic-dependent species, for example, the species may already be protected in 
accordance with this proposed rulemaking by a state’s ‘wildlife’ designated use and 
associated criteria, such that this rulemaking would not require any additional protection 
of that species beyond what is already required under the CWA and EPA’s existing WQS 
regulation.”6  
 
EPA has no basis to make these statements because, elsewhere in the proposal, the 
agency admits that “it may be a complex inquiry to determine if tribal reserved rights apply 
in waters subject to state WQS” but that EPA can help states “determine if there are 
reserved rights, and whether and how they should be applied in the WQS context.”7  In 
other words, EPA has no idea what the substantive or geographic scope of reserved tribal 
rights is across the country, nor how such rights could be interpreted for purposes of 
establishing water quality standards.  Notably, EPA apparently intended to keep the 
proposed rule as broad as possible to capture as many potential rights claims as 
possible.8 The agency’s attempt to downplay the significance of mandating that states 
establish water quality standards to protect an undefined set of tribal reserved rights to 
an undefined standard is dishonest.  
 
The agency’s statements also presume that a tribe with reserved rights would agree that 
a state’s existing generic “wildlife” designated use would suffice to protect asserted 
reserved rights.  The likelihood of disagreement escalates when, as the rule would 
require, states must protect an historic “unsuppressed” expression of a reserved right, for 
example to hunt undefined aquatic-dependent species that may have been more 
abundant in prior generations.  This type of disagreement among sovereigns is likely play 
out in dozens of ways, over dozens of designated uses, in an untold number of

b. The proposal would broadly expand the federal government’s reach into state 
management of waters and other resources  
 
The elephant in the room is the agency’s unlawful failure to consider how this proposal 
would greatly expand EPA’s ability to regulate and interfere with a state’s management 
of water quantity, flow, and other resources.  Water quantity and flow are aspects of water 
management that have long been within the exclusive jurisdiction of states, not the federal 
government.  Disputes over water quantity and water rights in the western part of the 
country go back generations and there is no indication they will resolve any time soon.  
These longstanding disputes foreshadow the new water wars that will erupt from this 
proposal, if finalized.   
 
In one current example, the U.S. Solicitor General, on behalf of the U.S. Department of 
the Interior; Deb Haaland, Secretary of the Interior; the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation; and 
the Bureau of Indian Affairs, is seeking to overturn a decision that gives the Navajo Nation 
a breach of trust claim against the Federal government for its failure to provide sufficient 
water for the Navajo Nation to farm its reservation land.  The Navajo Nation’s claims are 
based on implied tribal reserved rights that it argues guarantee a certain quantity of water 
along the Colorado River. State of Arizona, et al., v. Navajo Nation, et al.; Department of 
Interior et al. v. Navajo Nation, et al. (Nos. 21-1484 and 22-51).  This case is set for oral 
argument before the U.S. Supreme Court on March 20, just two weeks after the public 
comment period closes on this proposed rule.  A handful of states have filed amicus briefs 
in support of the Federal government’s position because, if the Navajo Nation’s claims 
are upheld, the quantity of water available and the existing water rights held by those 
states and citizens along the Colorado River will be curtailed. 
 
The Navajo Nation case is critically relevant because it begs the question: what would 
preclude a tribe from asserting a reserved right for a sufficient quantity of flow within a 
waterway and seeking protection of that right through a state water quality standard?  A 
specific quantity of flow could serve a tribe’s reserved right to take a certain quantity or 
species of fish, hunt a large game animal that relies on certain species of fish, grow an 
aquatic-dependent crop such as wild rice, or provide sufficient drinking water to serve 
tribal needs.  According to the proposal, these uses need not be currently attainable, and 
the tribe may not have engaged in these practices in decades or generations due to social 
changes like the need for traditional employment. See e.g., EPA Guidance for Conducting

to incur costs, such as legal fees or costs to complete scientific studies to support their position on the 
scope and nature of their rights and/or water quality necessary to protect them.” EPA EA, November 
2022, 3.

Fish Consumption Surveys (2016).  The answer is, nothing in the proposal would preclude 
a tribe from making such claims, even on waters like the Colorado River that have 
longstanding water rights and related generational disputes.  Yet, the proposal does not 
mention any of these potential implications of the rule, nor does it examine the impact of 
the proposal on sovereign states.  
 
As the Navajo Nation case demonstrates, these are not far-fetched outcomes from the 
proposal.  If a tribe asserts an implied reserved right for fishing salmon, would EPA require 
a state to establish a designated use for “salmon fishing,” and require a specific seasonal 
or monthly flow rate?  For an asserted reserved right to grow wild rice, would EPA require 
the state to establish a “wild rice” designated use over a wet area of land and require a 
certain quantity of water flow over that land to grow the crop?  How would these flow and 
quantity-based “water quality standards” interact with the longstanding prior 
appropriations framework for water rights?  How would such standards affect long settled 
(or recently settled) claims for water rights, including in the West, South, Midwest, and 
Eastern United States?  If EPA failed to mandate certain flows or if a tribe disagreed with 
a flow volume that EPA mandates for an asserted reserved right, would that tribe initiate 
legal action arguing that that the state’s standards do not comply with the CWA, or worse 
that the state or EPA has breached its fiduciary duty to protect those reserved rights?  
EPA should also assume that other water users and rights holders, including other states, 
would be deeply involved in any process or dispute over quantity or flow requirements or 
diversions.  
 
The proposal does not indicate that EPA has considered any of these potential outcomes 
from its proposal.  Importantly, the agency’s obligation here is not just to consider and 
reflect on these potential outcomes but, should it proceed to finalize some version of this 
proposal, EPA must avoid interfering with longstanding water and land management 
duties and obligations that fall squarely within the authority and prevue of the states.  The 
failure to consider these major aspects is arbitrary and capricious and unlawful, and the 
proposal to interfere with existing water management programs, including water rights 
and appropriations, is not in accordance with law. 
 
 
c.  States and TAS tribes establish designated uses, not EPA 
 
The CWA requires states to adopt water quality standards, including designated uses, 
but the proposed rule would mandate states and treatment as states (TAS) tribes to adopt 
specific designated uses.  The CWA requires that state water quality standards “shall 
consist of the designated uses of the navigable waters involved and the water quality 
criteria for such waters based upon such uses” and they “shall be such as to protect the 
public health or welfare, enhance the quality of water.” See U.S.C. 1313(c)(2)(A).  When 
establishing water quality standards, states are also required to consider their “use and 
value for public water supplies, propagation of fish and wildlife, recreational purposes, 
and agricultural, industrial, and other purposes, and... their use and value for navigation.” 
Id. EPA’s regulations also provide, “[e]ach state must specify appropriate water uses to 
be achieved and protected.” 40 CFR 131.10(a). 

Proposed Rule on WQS and Tribal Reserved Rights:  Comments by the J.R. Simplot Co. 
 
P a g e  9 | 30 
 
 
The proposed rule would replace this state and TAS tribe authority and discretion with a 
mandate from EPA to adopt a specific designated use for state or tribal waters.  Not only 
is this contrary to the discretion that the CWA provides to states and TAS tribes, but the 
proposed provision would create internal inconsistences in the Code of Federal 
Regulations.  EPA has not identified any legal authority allowing it to mandate states to 
adopt certain designated uses, nor has the agency considered the resulting internal 
inconstancies in federal regulation.   
 
 
d.  It is unclear if the proposed rule would influence the pending Supreme Court 
decision or vice versa  
 
The proposal conspicuously fails to acknowledge the Navajo Nation case pending before 
the Supreme Court.  This is troubling for a number of reasons, but principally because 
EPA’s proposed preamble is substantively aligned with arguments the Navajo Nation 
makes in that case; arguments that the Federal government has strenuously refuted in 
its briefs.  It is unclear how EPA is able to propose a rule that directly contradicts legal 
arguments and positions that the U.S. Solicitor General is taking in a case before the 
Supreme Court.  EPA must explain how the federal government can file briefs before the 
Supreme Court disclaiming obligations to protect certain reserved rights and, literally at 
the same time, propose a rule requiring states and EPA to protect those same reserved 
rights.  EPA must also explain whether this proposal, if finalized, would provide the Navajo 
Nation the evidence it needs to prevail in the case.  EPA’s failure to consider the Navajo 
Nation case or explain how the proposed rule would affect the case is arbitrary and 
capricious and unlawful under the APA. 
 
 
e.  It is unclear if Winters implied rights are included in the rule  
 
The proposed rule defines “tribal reserved rights” to include rights held by tribes “either 
expressly or implicitly.” Proposed 131.3(r).  As explained in the proposal preamble,  
“Under Winters v. United States and its progeny, the establishment of a Federal 
reservation (Indian or otherwise) implicitly reserves sufficient water to accomplish the 
purposes of the reservation.  See 207 U.S. 564, 576 (1908); Cappaert v. United States, 
426 U.S. 128, 139 (1976); Arizona v. California, 373 U.S. 546, 597–602 (1963).”, fn 6. In 
other words, the Winters line of cases establishes implied reserved rights like those 
included in the proposed definition of “tribal reserved rights.”  However, the preamble also 
states that, “[t]ribal reserved rights as defined in this proposed rulemaking generally do 
not address the quantification of Winters rights.”10.  The regulatory text and the preamble 
are inconsistent and cannot be finalized as proposed. 
 
First, the agency has not explained what it means for the rule to “generally” not address 
Winters rights.  The preamble does not entirely reject Winters reserved rights, indicating 
 
10 Federal Register. 2022. Vol 87 (232), p.74,363. 

Proposed Rule on WQS and Tribal Reserved Rights:  Comments by the J.R. Simplot Co. 
 
P a g e  10 | 30 
 
that such rights would be covered by the proposed rule in some cases.  It is unclear under 
what circumstances the proposed rule would bring Winters rights into the CWA 
framework. Additionally, and perhaps more importantly, the proposed regulation does not 
exclude Winters rights from the definition of tribal reserved rights.  So, regardless of what 
the preamble would “generally” consider covered under the rule or not, the regulatory text 
explicitly includes implied rights, including Winters rights.  If the preamble text is 
inconsistent with the regulatory text, the regulation is what will control in any legal dispute.  
If EPA intends to exclude Winters rights from the definition of tribal reserved rights it must 
do so in the regulatory text, not the preamble.  If EPA does not intend to exclude Winters 
rights from this rulemaking, it must state this clearly in the final rule.  
 
The proposed rule is internally inconsistent and EPA’s failure to consider or explain 
whether or how the Winters implied rights would be incorporated into the CWA programs 
is arbitrary and capricious and unlawful under the APA. 
 
 
IV.  The proposed rule undercuts the use of science and rigorous scientific 
methods to develop water quality standards 
 
The existing CWA programs are more than sufficient to protect water quality, but EPA’s 
proposal fails to acknowledge the significant authority and discretion that states currently 
have to protect waters in their states.  The proposal has not provided any technical, 
scientific, water quality, or public health-based rationale for the proposed rule, nor has 
EPA explained why it no longer believes existing CWA programs and regulations are 
adequately protective of water quality.   
 
 
a. Proposed rule does not use scientific rigor to set water quality standards  
 
In most federal programs, including the water quality standards program, EPA prides itself 
on being a scientific institution, driven by the highest levels of scientific integrity to meet 
the Congressional charge of the various statutes it administers.  Should this proposal be 
finalized as proposed, EPA’s administration of the water quality standards program would 
shift from an orientation of the hard sciences (e.g., chemistry, biology) to one driven by 
social sciences (e.g., anthropology, and cultural and historic investigation).  This shift is 
not one Congress envisioned or authorized, and it would be inconsistent with other 
longstanding water quality standards regulations that EPA has not proposed to modify.  
The proposed rule is arbitrary and capricious and not in accordance with the law. 
 
Congress gave EPA many roles when it enacted the CWA, including obligations in 
CWA;11 
 
• Section 104 (to conduct and coordinate research, investigations, experiments, 
training, demonstrations, surveys, and studies relating to the causes, effects, 
 
11 See 33. U.S.C. §§ 1254, 1267, 1268, 1269, 1270, 1273, and 1314. 

Proposed Rule on WQS and Tribal Reserved Rights:  Comments by the J.R. Simplot Co. 
 
P a g e  11 | 30 
 
extent, prevention, reduction, and elimination of pollution; to develop and issue to 
states the “latest scientific knowledge available” regarding the presence of 
pesticides in water); 
• Sections 117, 118, 119, 120, 121 (to make scientific inquiry into water quality 
concerns in specific waters and watersheds); and  
• Section 304 (to develop and from time to time revise criteria for water quality 
“accurately reflecting the latest scientific knowledge…on the kind and extent of all 
identifiable effects on health and welfare…on the concentration and dispersal of 
pollutants, or their byproducts, through biological, physical, and chemical 
processes…on the effects of pollutants on biological community diversity, 
productivity, and stability…”).   
 
To implement these Congressional mandates and relevant to the proposed rule, EPA 
promulgated regulations that require water quality standards be based on "sound 
scientific rationale" and "scientifically defensible methods.”12  
 
Neither the CWA nor EPA’s regulations define the terms “sound scientific rationale” or 
“scientifically defensible methods.”  However, EPA has made clear that water quality 
standards are to be based on data and scientific information derived from the hard 
sciences, including chemistry and biology, with a focus on science, science policy, and 
risk management. See e.g., 2000 EPA Methodology for Deriving Ambient Water Quality 
Criteria for the Protection of Human Health (2000 Methodology) (“When EPA speaks of 
science or scientific analysis, it is referring to the extraction of data from toxicological or 
exposure studies and surveys with a minimum of judgment being used to make inferences 
from the available evidence.”); 2002 Human Health Criteria Recommendations (“Water 
quality criteria developed under section 304(a) are based solely on data and scientific 
judgments on the relationship between pollutant concentrations and environmental and 
human health effects. Section 304(a) criteria do not reflect consideration of economic 
impacts or the technological feasibility of meeting the chemical concentrations in ambient 
water.”); 2015 Human Health Criteria Recommendations (“EPA’s recommended water 
quality criteria are scientifically derived numeric values that EPA determines will generally 
protect aquatic life or human health from the adverse effects of pollutants in ambient 
water.”).  These documents demonstrate that the foundation for water quality standards 
is science-based.  
 
Additionally, although not directly on point, CWA section 311 defines the term “best 
available science” to mean “science that (A) maximizes the quality, objectivity, and 
integrity of information, including statistical information; (B) uses peer-reviewed and 
publicly available data; and (C) clearly documents and communicates risks and 
uncertainties in the scientific basis for such projects.”  See 33 U.S.C. §1321(a)(27)  An 
argument could be made that if Congress intended all CWA programs to adhere to this 
level of scientific rigor, it would have explicitly required it in the statute.  The 
counterargument is, Congress was very clear in section 311 what it thought “best 
available science” means and, although it did not define this term elsewhere in the CWA, 
this definition should be a starting point for how EPA interprets similar words and phrases

b.  Water quality data provide no to very limited support for fish consumption 
suppression concept  
 
In the proposed rule, EPA would require states to protect an “unsuppressed” expression 
of reserved rights, including an historic or “heritage” rate of fish consumption.  To the 
extent consumption is suppressed because of societal changes that have occurred since 
settlement, including the modern economy and the opportunity to purchase necessities, 
these considerations fall well outside of the CWA’s science-driven framework and would 
undermine the longstanding scientific basis of the water quality standards program. 
The concept of “suppression” is whether the levels of contamination in game fish 
“suppress” fish consumption rates – especially by tribes or sub-populations that might 
consume for fish than the general population.13  A similar concept is that historically 
subpopulations had higher fish consumption rates, but these “heritage rates” are no 
longer possible due to either “suppression” or lack of available fish.  The corollary is that 
by reducing contaminant levels in fish (via more stringent water quality standards) then 
“suppression” is decreased since more fish can be consumed safely and that improved 
water quality will result in more fish.  These concepts (theories) need to be rigorously 
tested by available data on contaminants in fish and water to determine if they are valid. 
 
To evaluate the concept of suppression, health-advisories for fish consumption in Idaho 
were reviewed.  As described in Appendix A, there is one state-wide advisory for bass 
consumption and 22 water body-specific advisories for consumption of various other 
species.  All these advisories are based on mercury, with two exceptions: 
 
• Lake Coeur d’Alene, which has advisories based on arsenic and lead in addition 
to mercury; and  
• East Mill Creek for selenium. 
 
A fish consumption advisory is based on when concentrations of a contaminant exceed 
risk thresholds based on consuming monthly 8.5 meals (4 ounces uncooked per meal) of 
fish per month.  This equates to a fish consumption rate of 32 grams per day.  The risk 
threshold is adjusted for sensitive populations (children and pregnant women); this may 
reduce the fish consumption.  It should be noted, as shown in Table 1 of Appendix A, for 
the general population more than 8.5 meals per month of fish can be eaten for most of 
the waters that have fish advisories.14  Thus, it is unlikely that fish contaminant 
concentrations have any measurable “suppression” effect on the consumption rates of 
 
13 The assumption is that the contaminants present in the fish came from the contaminants present in the 
water. 
14 This is equivalent to 32 grams/day of fish. 

Proposed Rule on WQS and Tribal Reserved Rights:  Comments by the J.R. Simplot Co. 
 
P a g e  13 | 30 
 
Idaho game fish.  Idaho’s human health water quality standards are based on fish 
consumption rate of 66.5 grams per day.   
 
What is the source of mercury that has resulted in these fish consumption advisories?  
The State of Idaho conducted a study looking at mercury concentrations in Idaho’s waters 
and fish, concluding that atmospheric deposition was responsible for mercury in Idaho’s 
waters.15  Specifically that air emission sources in eastern Oregon and northern Nevada 
were likely regional sources of airborne mercury being deposited in Idaho’s waters.16  
Such a finding is similar to other research.  Peterson, in a comprehensive look at mercury 
concentrations in fish throughout the West concluded “our findings suggest that 
atmospheric deposition is a key factor relative to fish tissue mercury concentrations 
across the western U.S.”17  Work conducted by Abbott et al. identified deposition of 
mercury coming from global (trans-Pacific), natural (volcanoes, naturally enriched 
substrates, geothermal areas, and regional wildfires) and anthropogenic (combustion, 
cement and mining) sources.18  In particular for Salmon Falls Creek Reservoir, Abbott 
concluded that regional sources of the atmospheric mercury were from natural sources 
and anthropogenic activities (mines in northern Nevada and combustion/cement sources 
in western Utah).  Thus, making changes in Idaho’s water quality standards will not affect 
these sources and will not change state-wide mercury concentrations in bass and similar 
fish. 
 
Finally, it needs to be noted that bass, perch, bullhead, walleye and a number of the other 
fish species listed in Appendix A for fish advisories are non-native fish.19  Thus, these fish 
species would not have been available for “heritage” consumption by tribal members.   
 
There have been documents prepared to try to determine “heritage” or “suppression 
rates.”  A review of such information prepared for a State of Idaho water quality 
rulemaking from 2014-2016 (see Appendix B) shows that information in such documents 
has not gone through a rigorous scientific validation process (similar to the process that 
current fish consumption rate studies go through) and thus is too speculative and 
unreliable in setting water quality standards.  We note that EPA has published protocols 
for conducting fish surveys and for quantifying fish consumption rates around the United 
States.20  These studies represent the most current and best available methods for 
quantifying fish consumption rates in setting human heath criteria.  The focus of these 
studies and methodologies is on obtaining objectively defensible fish consumption rates 
based on current and actual fish consumption.  Hypothetical fish consumption rates are

Moreover, use of suppression rates or heritage rates to set water quality standards is 
beyond the minimum requirements of the Clean Water Act.  EPA in this proposed 
rulemaking, defines “heritage rate” as:21 
 
“A heritage rate is the amount of fish consumed prior to non-Indigenous or

suppression rates that would warrant using such “data” in setting human health criteria.  
On the contrary, EPA has published national recommended human health criteria as well

that federal rules require that water quality criteria be based on “sound scientific rationale”

suppression rates in setting human health criteria is not scientifically defensible and there 
are no peer reviewed methodologies that support reliance upon this type of information.  
Accordingly, we believe that reliance upon suppression rates in setting water quality 
criteria would not be based on “sound scientific rationale” and as such do not meet the 
requirements of the Clean Water Act.

aquatic systems (dams, water use, natural changes, etc.) should be used to determine a

As EPA is aware, courts afford agencies a substantial degree of deference in the scientific 
methods relied upon or employed in determining appropriate regulatory standards.  See, 
e.g. League of Wilderness Defs.-Blue Mts. Biodiversity Project v. Allen, 615 F.3d 1122,

expertise in the social sciences or in conducting anthropological studies.  This means that 
EPA actions that are based on these concepts would not enjoy deference that the agency 
may otherwise receive for its science and technology-based agency actions. 
Courts have also acknowledged that EPA’s review of the scientific basis for a state’s 
water quality criteria is limited to determining compliance with the federal water quality 
standards.  If a state’s standards are more stringent than what the CWA requires, EPA 
may approve them without reviewing the scientific support for the increased standards.

Clean Water Act.).  Here, EPA is proposing to incorporate into the CWA’s water quality 
standards program new requirements for which there are no objective science-based 
standards.  If the proposed rule is finalized, there would be no clear federal minimum 
requirement for states to achieve.  To be clear, states are currently welcome to develop

c. EPA’s proposal for tribal subpopulations to be protected to the same risk as the 
general population is scientifically invalid.  
 
For the first time in the 50 years since EPA has been implementing the CWA, the 
proposed rule would require states and TAS tribes to use a particular cancer risk rate.  
The proposal provides no technical or public health support for this change in law and 
policy and provides no legal analysis or precedent showing that the CWA requires these 
changes.  The proposal also does not explain how these major changes will affect water 
quality standards that states must establish.   
 
Historically, states have had discretion to establish cancer risk rates within a range that 
EPA and other federal agencies have determined to be protective of human health.27  
Until this proposal, EPA’s longstanding recommendation has been that states and TAS 
tribes apply a 10-5 or 10-6 risk rate for the general population, and they can apply a higher 
standard of 10-7, but states must ensure that smaller subpopulations are protected to rate 
no lower than 10-4.28  
 
The proposed rule would require states and TAS tribes to set cancer risk rates for tribal 
subpopulations “to at least the same risk level as the general population of the state would 
have been protected…”29  In doing so, the proposal would strip states and TAS tribes of 
the discretion to make risk management and public health decisions.  Additionally, when 
a small subpopulation is protected to 10-5 or 10-6, the general population would actually 
be protected to a rate of 10-7 or 10-8 or higher.  These risk rates have largely been 
dismissed as unnecessarily protective, and EPA has never required the general 
population to be protected to these levels.  Notably, EPA has not provided any rationale 
to support the proposed mandate and has not made a determination that protection to 10-
4 creates an unacceptable human health risk to subpopulations.  EPA’s only justification 
for this change is the agency’s view that a tribe’s sovereign status requires that it be 
protected to the same degree as the general population.  This justification is not sufficient 
under the APA.   
 
EPA has not made a scientific, technical, public health, or legal finding that tribal 
subpopulations require a greater level of risk protection than afforded under EPA’s

longstanding recommendations.  EPA has not explained why it no longer believes that 
states and TAS tribes are capable of making risk-based decisions.  EPA has also not 
explained why the CWA would require tribal subpopulations to be protected to a greater 
degree than other high consuming subpopulations, for example, subsistence fishers of

Thus, in this proposed rule there is a serious technical error by EPA for the failure to 
recognize that risks vary among different members of the population; we all eat different 
amounts and kinds of fish.  Faced with this variation, public health policy makers must 
make decisions about the level of protection afforded different segments of the population 
(i.e., the average member of the population, more highly exposed individuals, highly 
exposed subpopulations).  EPA, up until this rulemaking, recognized this variation in 
potential risk and provided guidance on how to address it:   
 
“With AWQC derived for carcinogens based on a linear low-dose 
extrapolation, the Agency will publish recommended criteria values at a 10-
6 risk level. States and authorized Tribes can always choose a more 
stringent risk level, such as 10-7.  USEPA also believes that criteria based 
on a 10-5 risk level are acceptable for the general population as long as 
States and authorized Tribes ensure that the risk to more highly exposed 
subgroups (sport fishers or subsistence fishers) does not exceed the 10-4 
level.”  
 
It is important to recognize that risk varies across the general population and that this has 
implications for what target risk goals can be achieved.  At times a mentioned 
environmental justice goal is “equal protection” for everyone.  It is impossible for water 
quality criteria to provide equal protection for all of the population.  It is an incontrovertible 
fact that the more water a person drinks and the more fish a person consumes, the higher 
will be his or her exposure and lifetime risk.  For a given water quality criterion, each 
individual has a unique exposure and risk because each individual consumes different 
amounts of water and fish from waters regulated by the state over his or her lifetime.  As 
long as each chemical is regulated with a single state-wide criterion, and that criterion is 
not zero, these risks can never be made equal across the population.   
 
Figure 1 shows the risk distributions for the general, angler and two Idaho Indian tribes 
(the Nez Perce and Shoshone Bannock) populations exposed to a hypothetical water 
quality criterion with a concentration equal to X g/L.  This figure demonstrates the relative 
positions of the risk distributions for these four populations.30  While all four risk 
distributions overlap to a large extent, the bulk of the general population has the lowest 
risk, followed by the angler population, Shoshone Bannock population, and Nez Perce 
population, respectively.  These relative positions remain the same regardless of the 
concentration of the hypothetical water quality criterion to which the populations are

As another example, the Federal Register notice discusses a 865 gram per day fish 
consumption rate (FCR) for the Spokane Tribe.  If a water quality criterion is based on a 
cancer risk factor of 10-5 and a FCR of 865 g/d is adopted and applied to all waters, then 
the general public (who consume at 22.5 grams of fish per day – a 38.5x lower rate) will 
be protected at a 38.5x lower (more stringent) target risk level, 2.6 x 10-7.  So, the tribes 
will not be protected to the same level as the general population.  Such equal protection 
is impossible if the tribes are assumed to consume more fish than the general population.   
 
It is important to understand that criteria for carcinogens are based on chosen risk levels 
that inherently reflect, in part, the exposure parameters used to derive those values.  
Therefore, changing the exposure parameters also changes the risk. Specifically, the 
incremental cancer risk levels are relative, meaning that any given criterion associated 
with a particular cancer risk level is also associated with specific exposure parameter 
assumptions (e.g., intake rates, body weights).  When these exposure parameter values 
change, so does the relative risk.  For a criterion derived on the basis of a cancer risk 
level of 10-6 individuals consuming up to 10 times the assumed fish intake rate would not 
exceed a 10-5 risk level.  Similarly, individuals consuming up to 100 times the assumed 
rate would not exceed a 10-4 risk level.  Thus, for a criterion based on EPA’s default fish 
intake rate (17.5 gm/day) and a risk level of 10 -6, those consuming a pound per day (i.e., 
454 grams/day) would potentially experience between a 10-5 and a 10-4 risk level (closer 
to a 10-5 risk level).  (Note: Fish consumers of up to 1,750 gm/day would not exceed the 
10-4 risk level.  If a criterion were based on high-end intake rates and the relative risk of 
10-6, then an average fish consumer would be protected at a cancer risk level of 
approximately 10-8.  The point is that the risks for different population groups are not the 
same. 
 
The proposed rule is mixing up the concepts of “equal protection of all consumers” (an 
impossible goal, but one that is integral to and ingrained in environmental justice) and 
assigning to tribes a level of protection that has historically been assigned to the general 
population (with the consequence of protecting the general population at a level that is 
10-100x more stringent than the level used historically).  In short, the rule’s “logic” of 
providing tribes the same protect as the general population fatally flawed. 
 
From an implementation standpoint, EPA has also not provided any examples of how this 
risk level requirement could affect the stringency of water quality standards.  Observers 
can readily determine that requiring a cancer risk rate that is orders of magnitude more 
protective will result in water quality standards that are orders of magnitude more 
stringent.  EPA must explain that mandating that states promulgate extremely stringent 
water quality standards is likely to result in vast numbers of waters that do not meet the 
new stringent water quality standards.  This means states and TAS tribes would be 
required to develop and implement TMDLs for hundreds of newly impaired waters and 
establish effluent discharge limits at levels that are likely too low to be detectible with 
standard laboratory testing methods.  In short, the proposal could severely restrict or 
prohibit economic activity in large portions of a state TAS tribe’s territory.  EPA must 
acknowledge this likely outcome and provide a scientific, technical, public health, and

legal justification for the proposal and its failure to do so is unlawful and renders the 
proposed rule arbitrary and capricious. 
 
 
d.  The proposed rule creates new, ambiguous designated uses, for which the 
“science” to protect such “uses” is not established 
 
As a part of protecting tribal reserved rights, EPA is now expanding the concept of 
“presently attained use” to cover plants or other aquatic (non-fish, non-wildlife) resources. 
 
“For example, if a tribe has a right to gather an aquatic plant in a state 
waterbody and that use is presently attained, state WQS should already 
reflect that as a designated use, per 40 CFR 131.10(i), and thus this 
resource should be protected in accordance with proposed 40 CFR 
131.9(a).”31 
 
EPA then expands on this concept providing further information as to what is expected 
with these new designated uses. 
 
“… tribal reserved rights to aquatic or aquatic-dependent resources that 
may require more stringent criteria than otherwise required to protect 
applicable designated uses in order to comply with this proposed 
rulemaking and whether there are differential health risks for right holders 
association with activities other than fish consumption such that new or 
revised criteria may be necessary to comply with this proposed 
rulemaking.”32 
 
The issues with this proposed requirement for new designated uses for aquatic-
dependent resources (such as plants) are significant but can be summarized as follows: 
 
• Determining such uses would require tribes to provide information on the plants 
and other aquatic-dependent resources (non-fish) used to the states; and  
• The states would then have to determine what “criteria” would then be needed to 
maintain such resources. 
 
It is Simplot’s experience that tribal nations are often hesitant to share information on 
cultural practices.  Furthermore, if such information was provided to the states, it is not 
clear what information is available then to determine the appropriate criteria.  This 
requirement alone could result in substantial work as state environmental agencies work 
to determine the appropriate criteria for such aquatic-dependent “designated uses.” 
 
For illustrative purposes, let’s discuss an example.  Let’s say that a tribe gathers 
watercress for cultural purposes, from a nearby river on non-Indian land.  Thus, according

e.  The economic analysis does not reflect the scientific complexity of the 
proposed rule and fails to account for the costs to the regulated community and 
delegated state authorities.  
 
The economic analysis makes an attempt to estimate some of the work that will be 
required by the states and TAS tribes to implement the proposed rule.  However, EPA’s 
estimates fully fail to account for:  (a) the intensive “consultation” that will be required with 
tribes; (b) the development of additional technical work to try to estimate “suppressed 
FCR; (c) the recalculation of criteria based on changes to risk factors and FCRs; (d) the 
determination of which waters are now not meeting WQC based on the new calculated 
criteria including the costs associated with determining (i.e., monitoring, etc.); (e) the 
development of total maximum daily loads (TMDLs) for any waters that now do not meet 
any new criteria; (f) any new monitoring needed as to determining progress on TMDLs; 
and (g) major costs to the regulated community associated with new treatment 
requirements to meet more stringent standards (for which treatment technology may not 
be able to achieve) and additional monitoring/analytical costs (which will be very elevated 
by trying to achieve very low method detection limits, etc.). 
 
All of this work is based on the concept (theory) that setting new, more stringent criteria 
will result in more availability of fish or other aquatic-dependent resources and that tribes 
will have additional consumption of fish and other aquatic-dependent resources.  As 
described in Sections IV.b. and IV.c. of these comments, available data indicates that 
such outcomes are not likely.  The reality is that the new criteria will approach, be at, ore 
be less than current and available analytical detection methods.  In other words, actually 
being able to measure such small concentrations in water, fish and effluents may be very 
difficult.  Also, for most pollutants (like the mercury example discussed in Section IV.b),

V.  The proposal creates significant federalism conflicts that EPA has not 
acknowledged or considered and implicates the “major question” doctrine 
 
EPA has proposed to conclude that the rule “will not have substantial direct effects on the 
states, on the relationship between the national government and the states, or on the 
distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government.” 34  This 
proposed conclusion cannot be reasonably or objectively sustained.  Additionally, as an 
executive agency, EPA has only those powers given to it by Congress, and there is no 
evidence that Congress intended EPA to have the expansive powers in the proposal. 
 
When Congress enacted the CWA, it sought to “restore and maintain the chemical, 
physical, and biological integrity of the Nation’s waters” and simultaneously “recognize, 
preserve, and protect the primary responsibilities and rights of states” to mitigate pollution 
and direct development of land and water resources. 33 USC 1251(a), (b).  Indeed, the 
CWA is often referred to as a statute based on a cooperative federalism foundation that 
intends strong partnerships between “the States and the Federal Government.” See e.g., 
New York v. United States, 505 U.S. 144, 167 (1992), Arkansas v. Oklahoma, 503 U.S. 
91, 101 (1992).  The proposed rule would all but eliminate this cooperative federalism 
framework in favor of a system where states are subordinate sovereigns in service of 
tribal reserved rights, even where those reserved rights are implied and have not been 
established by a formal treaty or other act of Congress.  This puts states in an untenable 
position that was not considered or envisioned by Congress when it enacted the CWA. 
  
 
33 Ibid.  p.74,369. 
34 Ibid.  p.74,375. 

Proposed Rule on WQS and Tribal Reserved Rights:  Comments by the J.R. Simplot Co. 
 
P a g e  24 | 30 
 
As described in other sections, the CWA directs EPA to oversee the various regulatory 
and nonregulatory programs, but states are intended to be the primary administrators of 
these programs. EPA is supposed to establish the floor—the federal minimum 
requirements that the CWA demands and states are obligated to comply with this federal 
minimum, but may choose to enact more stringent programs.  Tribes that obtain TAS 
status have the same CWA rights and responsibilities as states, including to establish 
and protect water quality standards.  Contrary to this long-established framework, the 
proposed rule would for the first time put states in a parens patraie position over tribal 
human health and welfare.  Not only is this unconventional and well outside the CWA 
framework, it would seem to elevate tribal interests over those of the state and even put 
states in the role of trustee over tribal resources, a role that is assigned to the Federal 
government.  If the rule is finalized as proposed, it would significantly disrupt the 
distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government. 
 
The proposal would also establish EPA as the arbiter of disagreements between states 
and tribes.  In other words, EPA will mediate and negotiate disputes between two 
sovereigns over major environmental policy and public health risk management 
decisions.  Not only is there no evidence that Congress envisioned the CWA to be 
implemented in this manner, but EPA is not equipped or authorized to adjudicate such 
disagreements.  We recognize the dispute resolution provision in 40 CFR §131.7, as 
authorized by CWA section 518(e). 33 U.S.C. §1377.  However, that provision only 
authorizes EPA to implement dispute resolution when a state and tribe have different 
water quality standards on a common body of water.  The stringency of a water quality 
standard is appropriately within EPA’s expertise and managing disputes on this topic has 
been authorized by Congress.  However, Congress did not, in section 518(e), authorize 
EPA to arbitrate disagreements among between sovereigns over the meaning of treaties 
and other instruments of federal law.  Finalizing the proposed rule would significantly 
change the relationship between the national government and the states and would 
exceed the authority granted in CWA section 518(e).  
 
Moreover, EPA has not considered the substantial and direct burdens this proposal would 
place squarely on states.  If finalized, the rule would require states to research and identify 
all tribal reserved rights that exist within or across a state’s boundaries, evaluate whether 
those rights are currently protected and to what degree, undertake significant 
engagement with tribes to understand everything from historic fish consumption rates to 
historic hunting and agricultural rates, and then translate those rates into some actionable 
water quality standard.  Information in EPA’s rulemaking docket demonstrates that EPA 
is not planning to do any of this legwork as part of this rulemaking process, leaving it to 
the states to undertake this significant new workload.35  The proposed rule would impose 
significant new burdens on states to investigate tribal reserved rights and develop tools 
to determine an appropriate level of protection for those rights, including implied rights.

EPA’s proposed determination that this rule would not have any federalism implications

VI. The proposal could unlawfully create an actionable trust obligation  
 
In enacting the CWA, Congress did not create a trust obligation or fiduciary duty for EPA 
to protect tribal water resources. El Paso Nat. Gas Co. v. United States, 750 F.3d 863, 
899 (D.C. Cir. 2014).  Because the CWA itself does not set forth such an obligation or 
duty, EPA has no authority to impose such duties on itself or any other sovereign through 
rulemaking.  Regardless of these constraints on its authority, EPA has proposed a rule 
that mandates all water quality standards established and approved by EPA or states 
“protect tribal reserved rights.”  The proposal could be interpreted to unlawfully create an 
actionable trust obligation where none has been established by Congress.  At a minimum, 
the proposed rule’s language would create an appearance of a trust obligation under the 
CWA, opening the federal government and delegated state authorities to potentially 
significant and prolonged litigation on a question that is easily answered under 
longstanding legal precedent.  It is irresponsible for EPA to propose a regulation that 
could be construed to create trust obligations where it is plain that none exist.  
   
 
a.  Congress has the exclusive authority to create trust obligations on behalf of the 
federal government, and did not do so in the CWA  
 
The Supreme Court has long recognized and repeatedly reaffirmed that “the organization 
and management of the trust is a sovereign function subject to the plenary authority of 
Congress.”  United States v. Jicarilla Apache Nation, 564 U.S. 162, 175-78, 131 S. Ct. 
2313, 2323–25, 180 L. Ed. 2d 187 (2011) (citations omitted).  This means that Congress 
structures the trust relationship with Indian tribes and has done so in statutes that have 
“defined and redefined the trust relationship,” sometimes doing so to serve a narrow 
policy purpose or its own policy goals. Id. (citations omitted).  When Congress establishes 
trust obligations, the applicable statute and implementing regulations “define the contours 
of the United States’ fiduciary responsibilities” and, to assert a violation of such 
obligations, a tribe must be able to identify a “specific, applicable, trust-creating statute or 
regulation that the Government violated.” Id.  As the Federal government has argued in 
the Navajo Nation case, a trust obligation cannot be created by implication. Id. See also 
fn. 2. 
  
Here, the applicable statute is the CWA, and there is no reasonable argument that 
Congress created a trust obligation or fiduciary duty in the CWA, and courts have already 

Proposed Rule on WQS and Tribal Reserved Rights:  Comments by the J.R. Simplot Co. 
 
P a g e  26 | 30 
 
ruled that it does not.  In support of its proposed rule, EPA quotes one single provision 
from the CWA concerning treaties: “This Act shall not be construed as… affecting or 
impairing the provisions of any treaty of the United States.”36  The plain language of this 
provision obligates the federal government not to affect and not to impair the provisions 
of any treaty.  This provision contains no affirmative responsibility for EPA or any other 
federal or state agency to manage water resources for the benefit, the best interest, or 
the needs of tribal communities, or any other party to a treaty with the United States.  To 
underscore the mismatch, Section 511 applies to all treaties and does not specifically 
reference tribal treaties or any other instrument of federal law related to tribal rights.  
 
If Congress intended to create a trust obligation or fiduciary duty through the CWA, it 
would certainly know how to do so. See, e.g. United States v. Mitchell, 463 U.S. 206 
(1983) (holding that various timber management statutes create a fiduciary relationship 
between tribes and the federal government, as evidenced by the obligations of the 
government in the management and operation of Indian lands and resources detailed in 
the statutes); see also United States v. Navajo Nation, 537 U.S. 488, 506 (2003) (“[A] 
tribe must identify a substantive source of law that established a specific fiduciary or other 
duties...Although the undisputed existence of a general trust relationship between the 
Unites States and the Indian people can “reinforce” the conclusion that the relevant 
statute or regulation imposes fiduciary duties, that relationship alone is insufficient. . .”); 
United States v. White Mt. Apache Tribe, 537. U.S. 465, 471 (2003) (holding that the 
General Allotment Act creates nothing more than a “bare trust” and thus there is “no 
predicate in the statutes or regulations identified by the Tribe for finding a fiduciary 
obligation...”).  In short, a statute must unambiguously create a fiduciary duty and 
Congress did not do so in the CWA.  
 
 
b.  The proposed rule would purport to create a new trust obligation where none 
exists 
 
EPA’s proposed rule contains the very type of language that the Supreme Court has 
concluded in other contexts creates specific and actionable trust obligations.  Specifically, 
proposed 40 CFR §131.9(a) states, “Water quality standards must protect tribal reserved 
rights applicable to waters subject to such standards.”37 (emphasis added).  The proposal 
preamble explains EPA’s view that, “[w]here tribes have reserved rights to aquatic and/or 
aquatic-dependent resources, protection of such rights falls within the ambit of [the 
CWA’s] broad statutory directives and objectives...”38 (emphasis added).  EPA argues 
that the discretion afforded it to implement the CWA allows EPA to create a mandatory 
obligation to protect “all applicable reserved rights.”  Under the proposal, a failure by either 
EPA or a state to protect all such applicable reserved rights would be judicially 
enforceable and akin to a trust obligation.  The proposed rule stands in contrast to a large 
body of constitutional case law that requires specific language from Congress to create 
 
36 33 U.S.C. 1371(a) 
37 Federal Register.  2022.  Vol 87 (232) p.74,378. 
38 Ibid.  p. 74,365. 

Proposed Rule on WQS and Tribal Reserved Rights:  Comments by the J.R. Simplot Co. 
 
P a g e  27 | 30 
 
obligations for states and the federal government to protect reserved tribal rights within 
the CWA framework.   
 
Even more concerning than EPA’s assertion that it has the discretion to establish 
enforceable obligations related to tribal rights is that the proposed rule does not attempt 
to define the universe of reserved rights that must be protected or describe the degree of 
protection required.  Nor does the proposal explain how a state could or should go about 
identifying the universe of reserved rights or a scientific method for understanding how 
such rights “must be” protected.  EPA has failed to consider major aspects of the problem 
and has failed to sufficiently explain the proposed rule or the agency’s rationale for 
changing the water quality standards program.   
 
 
VII.  The Proposed Rule Ignores Existing Court Decisions on Tribal Treaties, Fish 
and Water Quality. 
 
EPA’s proposed rulemaking predisposes (assumes) that tribal treaties39 provide these 
“tribal reserved rights” in relation to water quality and fish.  During a 2014-2016, water 
quality rulemaking in Idaho, there was an assertion by several stakeholders that tribes 
have a legally protected property interest associated with treaty right rights to take fish in 
usual and accustomed places, including the preservation of the physical condition of fish 
taken.  For example, in its January 16, 2015 letter to the Idaho Department of 
Environmental Quality (Idaho DEQ), the Columbia River Inter Tribal Fish Commission 
(CRITFC) stated, “Tribal rights to fish are guaranteed in treaties with the United States. 
CRITFC’s member tribes ceded roughly one-third of the Columbia Basin to the United 
States government, but forever retained the right to take fish from these waters.  Implicit 
in the treaty promises of 1855 was the understanding that the fish taken would be healthy 
and safe to eat”.  Additionally, the Nez Perce Tribe asserted that its treaty rights included 
“a legally protected property interest” covering both access to usual and customary places 
and the taking of fish destined for those places.  
 
These representations are not supported by federal law interpreting the Nez Perce Tribe’s 
1855 treaty rights concerning the right to fish (see Appendix C – which was prepared for 
the 2014-2016 rulemaking).  In Nez Perce Tribe v. Idaho Power Co., the court held that 
the Nez Perce Tribe “does not own the fish runs or the fish but rather, it owns a treaty 
right to take fish from its usual and customary places as specified in the 1855 treaty.”  
Moreover, the Court found that “Indian tribes do not have an absolute right to the 
preservation of the fish runs in their original 1855 condition, free from all environmental 
damage caused by the migration of increasing numbers of settlers and the resulting 
development of land.”  The court went on to state that “the Tribe’s right to fish pursuant 
to the 1855 Stevens treaty only guarantees access to certain off-reservation fishing 
grounds and the right to attempt to catch available fish.  The Stevens treaties require that 
any development authorized by the states which injures the fish runs be non-
 
39 EPA is taking a very, very broad interpretation of what is legally binding in regards to tribal treaties.  
See Federal Register. 2022, Vol. 87 (232) p.74,363.   

Proposed Rule on WQS and Tribal Reserved Rights:  Comments by the J.R. Simplot Co. 
 
P a g e  28 | 30 
 
discriminatory in nature, but does not however, guarantee that subsequent development 
will not diminish or eventually, and unfortunately, destroy the fish.”  The Court’s ruling is 
consistent with Blackfeet, etc. Nations or Tribes of Indians, in which the Court of Claims 
held that “the right to hunt the common grounds did not include ‘any terms guaranteeing 
to the Indians a maintenance of the status quo for almost a century.”  Therefore, 
representations that treaty rights implicitly include the right to take fish of a certain quantity 
or condition is not supported by court decisions examining this question.  
 
 
VIII.  EPA needs to follow the example the State of Idaho has set. 
 
As described in these comments, Simplot recommends that EPA not move forward with 
the proposed rule.  EPA has proposed the question of whether water quality standards 
need clarification to protect aquatic and aquatic dependent resources reserved to tribes 
through treaties, statutes, executive orders or other sources of Federal law.  However, it 
is not EPA’s role to step in as the interpreter of treaties to decide how the Clean Water 
Act may apply to numerous tribal treaties.  As described in Section VII of these comments, 
the courts have already addressed the “objectives” that EPA is now trying to achieve 
through this rulemaking.  The CWA does not provide the legal basis for this rulemaking 
and court decisions do not neither. 
 
Thus, our recommendation is that if EPA believes that further work is needed to assure 
water quality designated uses, especially for human health for certain populations, are 
being met, an appropriate action would be guidance to the Regions and delegated States 
and TAS Tribes.  Potential topics for such a memorandum is updating the status (data) 
of contaminants in water and fish, using valid scientific methods determining fish 
consumption rates (including sub-population groups such as tribes), understanding the 
basis of fish consumption advisories and taking a look at how any such advisories are 
related to activities regulated by the Clean Water Act 
 
The State of Idaho provides an example of doing this.  There were regulatory and 
designated use questions on the levels of certain metal and metalloid contaminants in 
fish and water that required study.  Furthermore, potential updates for human health water 
quality criteria needed examination.  To address these, the State of Idaho did the 
following: 
 
• Extensive studies were done looking at concentrations of mercury, arsenic, and 
selenium in fish tissue and water in Idaho’s major river systems.  Several different 
studies were done over a period of years to gather this data. 
• The data was carefully analyzed.  This analysis included understanding how these 
contaminants are mobilized in the aquatic environment and the source of these 
contaminants.  As discussed earlier, a primary water (and fish) contaminant of 
concern is mercury; the State of Idaho concluded that aerial deposition is the likely 
source of the contamination in Idaho’s waters and fish.  Thus, further regulation of 

Proposed Rule on WQS and Tribal Reserved Rights:  Comments by the J.R. Simplot Co. 
 
P a g e  29 | 30 
 
mercury via Clean Water Act requirements would not in any meaningful way 
change these concentrations in fish and water. 
• Finally, two scientific rigorous surveys were done of the Idaho population, including 
tribal members, to provide current, updated information on fish consumption rates.  
DEQ derived a FCR of 66.6 grams per day for use in calculating human health 
criteria.  The FCR represents the mean (equivalent to the 70th percentile) of the 
consumption by the Nex Perce Tribe.  [The Nez Perce Tribe is the highest 
consuming tribal subpopulation].  This FCR was determined using the National 
Cancer Institute methods based on species of CWA relevance (freshwater, near 
coastal and estuarine species) and represents approximately the 95th percentile of 
the Idaho general population and the 90th percentile of the angler population 
consumption rate of all fish. 
• Finally, the information gathered from the studies (contaminant concentrations in 
water and fish and the FCR) was then used to update the human health water 
quality criteria. 
 
This work performed by the State of Idaho over approximately a twelve (12) year 
period has provided the scientific data to understand the status of these contaminants 
in Idaho’s water and fish, determine what current fish consumption rates were, 
evaluate what potential CWA actions could address fish consumption advisories and 
finally update human health criteria.  This process provides scientifically robust criteria 
that is protective of all Idaho citizens, including tribes. 
 
 
IX.  Summary 
 
EPA states in the preamble that:40 
 
“These revisions to EPA’s existing WQS regulation are intended to provide 
clarity, predictability, and transparency in EPA’s review of state WQS and 
promulgation of Federal WQS in waters where reserved rights to aquatic 
and/or aquatic dependent resources apply.” 
 
This proposed rule does the exact opposite of its stated objective.  The proposal has 
significant legal, technical and implementation deficiencies. 
 
• The CWA never envisioned EPA have this expansive role of interpreting Tribal 
treaties and creating new obligations on behalf of the federal government and 
states. 
• The proposed rule is in direct opposition to the position taken by the United States 
in the State of Arizona, et al., v. Navajo Nation, et al.; Department of Interior et al. 
v. Navajo Nation, et al. 
 
40 Federal Register.  2022.  Vol. 87 (232) p.74,366.  

Proposed Rule on WQS and Tribal Reserved Rights:  Comments by the J.R. Simplot Co. 
 
P a g e  30 | 30 
 
• The objectives purported to be obtained through this rulemaking have already 
been addressed by the courts.  These court decisions have soundly rejected what 
EPA is attempting to do with this rulemaking:  creating obligations under the CWA 
for certain quantities of fish and trying to mandate water quality conditions that 
might have existed over 175 years ago. 
• Technical concepts embedded in this rulemaking such as tribal fish consumption 
rate being limited by “suppression” due to poor water quality or that HHWQC are 
set at a cancer risk factor that is not protective of sub-populations (such as tribes) 
are not supported by a rigorous scientific examination. 
• The proposed rule fails to describe the implications of adjusting WQS for 
“suppression”, setting cancer risk factors at 10-5 or 10-6 for sub-populations, and 
creating new designated uses for "aquatic-dependent resources” such as plants.  
The likely outcome of these changes will be new criteria values that are very 
stringent to the point where there will be analytical measurement difficulties and 
lack of technology to treat to these low concentrations.  The results will be 
significant additions to the ‘impaired waters list” (CWA Section 303(d) list) and 
millions upon millions spent by the regulated community to try to achieve a “paper 
value” WQC that may not be able to be measured accurately, has a minimal benefit 
to the environment and likely will not increase fish availability or consumption. 
• The economic costs of implementing this rule for both the delegated authorities 
and the regulated community have not been determined.  These costs though will 
be in the millions of dollars with little evidence of benefits to the nations’ water 
quality. 
• The proposed rule purports through changes to WQS and other measures (such 
as potentially regulating water flows)41 to increase fish consumption by tribes by 
increasing the availability of fish and reducing the contaminants in fish.  Setting 
aside the legal question of what authorities EPA has to do this, EPA has not shown 
or provided any examples that such measures are really achievable.   
• The proposed rule interferes with state authorities including the setting of 
designated uses and water allocation.  A major example is the requirement to 
create a new category of designated uses for “aquatic-dependent resources.” 
 
The extent and magnitude of these deficiencies is such that this rulemaking should be 
stopped.  Moving forward with finalizing this rule will result in significant regulatory 
confusion, create significant burdens on the states, TAS tribes and the regulated 
community and ultimately extensive litigation.  Simplot recommends that EPA use an 
approach of cooperation rather than control in regards to HHWQC and subpopulations 
(such as tribes).  The State of Idaho has done considerable work in this area and offers 
an example that can be used by EPA. 
 
41 EPA in the preamble (pages 74,368 and 74,369) discusses designating waters for wild rice production 
in the Great Lakes area, including designating waters that currently do not support wild rice production.  
EPA then invites what changes can be made to “restore” the hydrological regime to support wild rice 
production.  Though EPA does acknowledge that hydrological changes and legacy contamination have 
occurred, EPA is clearly (such as through a 303(d) listing process, looking for States to implement plans 
which include hydrological changes to try to remedy “suppression” and “availability” of aquatic and 
aquatic-dependent resources that EPA believes are tribal reserved rights.

Dear Administrator Regan, 
 
The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) recently issued a new proposed rule, Water Quality Standards 
Regulatory Revisions to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights. This proposed rule dramatically impinges on states' 
rights to develop water quality standards for state waters as specifically reserved to the states by Congress in 
the Clean Water Act.  
 
The proposed rule asserts that states must now take into consideration tribal treaty rights outside of designated 
reservations in setting state water quality standards, a substantial change to federal interpretation of the Clean 
Water Act not based on any revisions to the law. Rather it is based on EPA's attempt to mandate a result 
based on treaty right interpretation--an area where the agency has no jurisdiction or expertise.  The Clean 
Water Act does envision a role for Tribes to set water quality standards within reservation boundaries under 
the treatment of state provisions of the Clean Water Act, and many Tribes have taken advantage of these 
provisions. However, there is nothing in the Clean Water Act that mandates Tribes must be part of the state 
water quality standards-setting process outside treaty land. The EPA proposal clearly encroaches on state 
sovereignty under the Clean Water Act and the U.S. Constitution. 
 
Additionally, the mandate in the proposed rule as to how states must set water quality standards for state 
waters based on implied tribal treaty rights is equally problematic.  Rather than requiring states to analyze 
current conditions of state waters, the proposed rule mandates that when setting water quality standards, 
states must now consider, or speculate, what water quality and aquatic resource conditions were when Tribal 
treaties were executed in the middle of the 19th century. This unprecedented requirement directs states to 
essentially ignore development over the last 175 years and set water quality standards accordingly whether 
such requirements are attainable or not. Nothing in the Clean Water Act mandates such a result, clearly 
indicating this proposed rule to be a severe overstep by the EPA. If such a requirement becomes part of the 
state standard-setting process, the ability for Idaho industries, businesses, and municipalities to economically 
operate within the law will be substantially affected.    
 
The proposed rule will uniquely impact Idaho due to recent legal developments within the state. Between 2014 
and 2019, the state of Idaho undertook a lengthy and comprehensive water quality standard-setting process 
that included engaging a statewide fish consumption study to set water quality standards, with consideration 
for modern Tribal fish consumption rates. Although the EPA balked at approving these science-based 
standards for the same reasons articulated in the new proposed rule, the standards were ultimately approved. 
The proposed rule would clearly undermine Idaho's extensive and collaborative efforts.  
 
Additionally, the proposed rule, which is based on the premise that Tribal treaties imply reserved rights to water 
quality in state waters outside reservations, could have significant and concerning implications for water 
quantity by suggesting that treaties give Tribes an implied reservation to water rights outside the Reservation.  

Although such broad claims were raised in the Snake River Basin Adjudication by the United States, they were 
soundly rejected by Idaho courts. This proposed rule would now embolden similar claims to be raised again 
throughout the state of Idaho, putting vested water rights at major risk.   
 
The proposed rule is a substantial overreach by the EPA beyond anything Congress ever envisioned.  The 
proposed rule must not go forward. We look forward to your action and response.    
 
 
 
Sincerely,  
 
 
 
                      
 
                    JAMES E. RISCH

RE:  
EPA Proposed Rule on Water Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions to
