Water Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights 
 
Dear Ms. Brundage,  
 
 
 
 
 
 
       
 
INTRODUCTION 
 
I submit these comments to the Environmental Protection Agency (“EPA”) regarding EPA’s 
proposed Water Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights, 
Docket No. EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791. I am a third-year student in Harvard Law School’s 
Emmett Environmental Law and Policy Clinic. Previously, I worked in the House of Commons 
of the Parliament of Canada. There, I conducted research for meetings of the Standing 
Committee on Justice and Human Rights concerning human trafficking and its impact on 
indigenous communities.  
 
I appreciate the opportunity to submit comments on these proposed regulatory revisions 
concerning tribal rights. Although I support EPA’s proposal, I submit a variety of comments 
intended to highlight difficulties indigenous communities face in asserting their water rights. I 
thank EPA for its thoughtfulness in examining this matter and for working to protect the interests 
of all. 
 
SUBSTANTIVE COMMENTS 
 
Summary 
 
1. Proposed 40 CFR 131.9(b) should be revised to require documentation of all tribal 
consultations with rights holders. 
2. Existing 40 CFR 131.10(a) should be revised to require consideration of spiritual and 
cultural uses of water when determining the water uses to be achieved and protected. 
 
Background 
 
I support EPA’s proposed regulatory revisions to the Water Quality Standards (“WQS”) of the 
Federal Clean Water Act. They seek to make the WQS framework more predictable, clear, and 

 
 
transparent. Instead of addressing tribal reserved rights on a case-by-case basis as state WQS are 
submitted to EPA for review, EPA intends to apply a uniform approach to establishing WQS 
where tribal reserved rights apply and to reviewing such WQS. I write to recommend further 
regulatory revisions within this new uniform framework to address difficulties indigenous 
communities face in asserting their water rights. 
 
Documentation of Tribal Consultations 
 
Proposed 40 CFR 131.9(b) should be revised to require documentation of all tribal consultations 
with rights holders. One major difficulty indigenous communities face in asserting water rights is 
poor legal representation, and a documentation requirement would help identify which tribes 
currently lack effective legal representation.  
 
Poor legal representation has long complicated indigenous tribes’ assertion of water rights. 
Beyond the economic hardship of obtaining effective legal representation, indigenous tribes have 
faced collusion between energy companies and their counsel. For instance, legal counsel has 
historically failed the Hopi tribe.1 The lawyer John Sterling Boyden represented the Hopi in their 
1966 negotiations with Peabody Energy (then, Peabody Western Coal Company) over mining 
and groundwater pumping in Black Mesa.2 But Boyden was working for Peabody at that time⸺a 
blatant conflict of interest.3 The negotiations left the Hopi with only 3.3 percent of gross coal 
sales, approximately half of what the federal government received for coal leases on federal 
land.4 The lease also lacked a reopener clause, a standard clause that allows for renegotiation of 
provisions after a provided number of years.5 The Hopi are just one example of an indigenous 
community not only exploited but also left wary of legal counsel.6  
 
The proposed provision should be revised to require documentation of all tribal consultations 
because, as the Government Accountability Office has determined, EPA’s tracking system does 
not include documentation for every tribal consultation that has occurred.7 And that 
documentation could create a record of which tribes obtain legal counsel to assist with 
consultations and how the legal counsel assists them, thus potentially indicating which tribes 
suffer from poor legal representation in their consultations with EPA. Thus, I recommend the 
revised section 131.9(b) read as follows:

(2002).

In reviewing State water quality standards submissions under this section, EPA will  
initiate tribal consultation with the right holders, consistent with applicable EPA tribal  
consultation policies, in determining whether State water quality standards protect  
applicable tribal reserved rights in accordance with paragraph (a) of this section and  
shall document all such consultation. 
 
Although the issue of tribes’ poor legal representation extends beyond tribal consultations, 
revising this provision would be an important step toward ensuring zealous advocacy for all 
indigenous communities.  
 
Spiritual and Cultural Uses of Water 
 
Existing 40 CFR 131.10(a) should be revised to require the consideration of spiritual and cultural 
uses of water when determining the water uses to be achieved and protected. When asserting 
water rights, indigenous communities face a disregard for spiritual and cultural uses of water, but 
consideration of those uses may be necessary to prevent the erasure of a tribe’s culture.   
 
Indigenous tribes have long faced a disregard for spiritual and cultural uses of water when 
asserting water rights. Although tribes believe “[s]prings, wells, and rivers are the homes of 
deities, have divine healing powers, and enhance processes of spiritual transformation,”8 legal 
instruments related to sustainable water management often fail to recognize spiritual and cultural 
uses of water. But these uses typically have immense importance to tribes. For example, the 
Shoshone people have significant spiritual and cultural uses of water. Water has a central place 
in Shoshone cultural life, and the Shoshone people believe that Bah-o-hah, or “water spirits,” 
live in creeks and springs.9 They thus conduct medicinal ceremonies at water sources for healing 
and well-being and believe that if the springs dry up, they will face a “future of perpetual 
poverty, loss of their lands, harm to their culture, and ultimately a decline in their population,” 
tantamount to “‘cultural genocide.’”10 The consideration of spiritual and cultural uses of water 
can therefore be critical to the cultural survival of indigenous tribes.  
 
To preserve indigenous culture, section 131.10(a) should therefore be revised to require the 
consideration of spiritual and cultural uses of water when determining the water uses to be 
achieved and protected. In section III(B) of the Notice, EPA does note that it “recognizes that 
tribal reserved rights to use and access natural and cultural resources are an intrinsic part of tribal 
life and are of deep cultural, economic, and subsistence importance to tribes,” importantly 
legitimating the cultural concerns tribes have concerning water rights. And section VI(B) of the 
Notice similarly states that “the concept of addressing suppression, as described in section 
 
8 Erica L. Porta & Aaron T. Wolf, Intrinsic and Spiritual Dimensions of Water at the Local Scale, and the 
Disconnect with International Institutions, 13 SUSTAINABILITY 16 (2021). 
9 GLENNON, supra at 181. 
10 Id. 

 
 
IV.C.2.ii. of this preamble, takes on a unique approach where tribal members are concerned by 
examining not only the current context but may also look at historical and cultural practices to 
establish the appropriate baseline.” But the existing section 131.10(a) states in part, “The 
classification of the waters of the State must take into consideration the use and value of water 
for public water supplies, protection and propagation of fish, shellfish and wildlife, recreation in 
and on the water, agricultural, industrial, and other purposes including navigation,” failing to 
require the consideration of spiritual and cultural purposes. I therefore recommend that section 
131.10(a) be revised to state: 
 
Each State must specify appropriate water uses to be achieved and protected. The  
classification of the waters of the State must take into consideration the use and value of 
water for public water supplies, protection and propagation of fish, shellfish and wildlife,  
recreation in and on the water, agricultural, industrial, spiritual, cultural, and other  
purposes including navigation. If adopting new or revised designated uses other than the  
uses specified in section 101(a)(2) of the Act, or removing designated uses, States must  
submit documentation justifying how their consideration of the use and value of water for  
those uses listed in this paragraph appropriately supports the State’s action. A use  
attainability analysis may be used to satisfy this requirement. In no case shall a State  
adopt waste transport or waste assimilation as a designated use for any waters of the  
United States. 
 
Such a mandate would align with EPA’s recognition of the cultural importance of water to 
indigenous communities and would simply require the consideration of spiritual and cultural uses 
of water among numerous other uses. Thus the revised provision would provide a workable 
solution that better safeguards tribal reserved rights. 
 
CONCLUSION 
 
EPA’s proposed revisions to the WQS better protect tribal reserved rights by providing 
predictability, clarity, and transparency. They also provide for the tribes themselves to inform 
determinations of reserved rights, and EPA clearly appreciates the deep cultural significance of 
water to indigenous communities. But the regulations can go even further in protecting tribal 
reserved rights, by requiring documentation of tribal consultations to address ineffective legal 
representation, and by requiring State consideration of spiritual and cultural uses of water. These 
revisions would not only recognize more fully the historical exploitation of indigenous 
communities but would also express a respect for indigenous concerns and culture. 
 
Thank you for the opportunity to provide comments on this crucial issue. 
 
 

 
 
Respectfully submitted, 
 
 
 
 
Samantha Ilagan

Comments on EPA Proposed Clean Water Act Water Quality Standards Regulatory 
Revisions to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights, Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791 
Dear Administrator Regan: 
 
On behalf of the undersigned organizations and their supporters, please consider the 
following comments for your consideration regarding the Environmental Protection Agency’s 
(“EPA”) Clean Water Act Water Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions to Protect Tribal 
Reserved Rights (“Proposed Rule”).  87 Fed. Reg. 74361 (Dec. 5, 2022).  We strongly support 
EPA’s efforts to protect water quality as an essential avenue to protect tribal reserved rights and 
other Indigenous rights to water resources.  We urge the EPA to finalize this rule in a manner 
consistent with the EPA’s trust responsibility to tribes.  We also acknowledge that many tribal 
governments and leaders are also submitting comments on the proposed rule, and we are broadly 
supportive of tribal efforts to protect tribal reserved rights and resources via adequate water 
quality standards.   
 
This proposed rulemaking increases tribal involvement in state processes for setting or 
revising state water quality standards.  EPA must support tribes in these state processes 
including, but not limited to, supporting the development of tribally produced data, studies, and 
reports, supporting the use of that data in EPA and state decision-making, and supporting tribes 
in dispute resolution processes.  Ultimately, EPA should provide support to tribes to gather all 
the necessary data that they will need to participate in the process of setting protective water 
quality standards.  EPA must support tribes in these processes such that state water quality 
standards are actually protective of tribal rights and resources. 
We recognize that many tribes have been stewards of the land since time immemorial and 
have knowledge about their traditional areas’ waters, lands, and other resources that are 
encompassed in Indigenous Knowledge (“IK”) or Traditional Ecological Knowledge (“TEK”).  
EPA must provide mechanisms to protect tribal Indigenous Knowledge or Traditional Ecological 
Knowledge as part of the process of setting or revising state water quality standards to protect 
tribal resources.  To the extent that tribes have IK or TEK of an area and its resources, we ask 
that EPA consider that tribes be designated as co-managers of water resources in that area.  
Where feasible, tribal co-management could be a fruitful and efficient approach to protection and 

 
 
 
2 
 
 
restoration of waters and resources that have been damaged as a result of colonial development.  
Co-management has the potential to encourage efficiency and a common approach to protecting 
the health of entire watersheds. 
The final rule should require that, where tribal rights apply, states must adopt designated 
uses specifically for the protection and restoration of tribal rights and resources.  In establishing 
these designated uses and attendant numeric and narrative criteria, states should consider TEK or 
IK, and also should consider adopting or incorporating designated uses that tribes may have 
established as part of their own EPA approved water quality standards.  EPA should not allow 
states to rely solely on antidegradation policy options as a mechanism to protect tribal reserved 
rights. Adopting designated uses that focus specifically on tribal rights would help ensure that 
tribal resources are protected through state programs including antidegradation measures. 
EPA should also clarify how it will review state enforcement of water quality standards 
developed to protect tribal reserved rights.  Setting protective water quality standards is only 
effective if those standards are enforced.  States have used water quality standard variances, 40 
C.F.R. § 131.14, in the past to circumvent meeting water quality standards for certain 
waterbodies.  See Upper Missouri Waterkeeper v. EPA, 15 F4th 966, 975 (9th Cir. 2021) (finding 
that approved variances “replace[] the base water quality standard with the most rigorous 
standard that can feasibly be attained”).  EPA must ensure that these mechanisms are not abused 
such that water quality continues to deteriorate and erode tribal reserved rights. 
Protecting water resources is vital to protecting tribal reserved rights and benefits us all. 
Accordingly, the undersigned organizations are supportive of protecting tribal treaty rights, tribal 
reserved rights, and the water resources necessary to protect those rights.  Requiring states to set 
water quality standards that are actually protective of tribal reserved rights and resources also 
supports healthier ecosystems, and ultimately, cleaner waters for all. 
 
Sincerely,

Nez Perce Tribe's Comments on 
EPA's Proposed Water Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions to Protect Tribal Reserved

EPA's Legal Duties 
•
The Nez Perce Tribe ("Tribe") appreciates that the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency 
("EPA") is acknowledging, through this rulemaking, its treaty and trust responsibilities to 
uphold tribal rights by protecting the water resources that sustain the Tribe's and other 
tribes' rights. 
•
Respect for the hierarchy of laws is fundamental to the U.S. legal system. The U.S. 
Constitution is the supreme law and may not be contradicted by federal statutes or other 
lesser laws. Moreover, under the U.S. Constitution, "all Treaties made, or which shall be 
made, under the Authority of the United States, shall be the supreme Law of the Land."4 
•
Tribes signed treaties with the U.S. Government. EPA's obligation, as both a party to the 
Tribe's treaty and a trustee of the Tribe's treaty-reserved resources, is to ensure that the 
United States honors its commitments in those treaties in all aspects of its work, including 
the implementation of federal statutes such as the Clean Water Act ("CWA"). Moreover, 
the CWA itself states that it "shall not be construed as . . . affecting or impairing the 
provisions of any treaty of the United States."' 
•
Under its 1855 Treaty,6  the Tribe is legally entitled to take up to half the legally harvestable 
runs for subsistence consumption and other purposes that are destined to pass through its 
usual and accustomed fishing places.' These Treaty-reserved fishing rights include 
meaningful protections against state interference.8  Since there is no plausible legal theory 
under which the United States could guarantee to tribes the right to subsistence fish and 
then purposefully undermine the conditions that make treaty-reserved subsistence fishing 
possible,9  EPA and states must ensure that Water Quality Standards ("WQS") for waters 
subject to the Tribe's treaty-reserved right do not hinder the Tribe's right to safely 
consume, or use for other purposes, up to half of the legally harvestable runs that are 
destined to pass through its usual and accustomed places. 
•
EPA's duty as a treaty signatory and trustee extends to off-reservation waters. EPA must, 
therefore, limit state discretion under the CWA to promulgate WQS in off-reservation

General Comments 
•
EPA's rulemaking is a positive step toward the United States upholding treaty and trust 
responsibilities to ensure tribes' off-reservation rights and resources are not impaired and 
tribal members can safely consume fish and rice at unsuppressed levels. However, EPA's 
rule does not do enough to fully uphold tribal rights and tribes' ability to preserve their 
culture and identity. 
•
To ensure tribal rights and resources are protected in the future, EPA must give states clear 
requirements and stringent compliance timelines and distinctly articulate the range of 
actions permissible under the CWA to uphold treaty-reserved rights in off-reservation 
waters subject to tribal rights. Specifically, EPA's final rule should include minimum,

o In 2019, the state of Idaho recommended, and EPA approved, Human Health 
Criteria based on a Fish Consumption Rate of 66.5 grams per day at 10. As EPA 
is aware, this Fish Consumption Rate and associated Cancer Risk Level is the 
functional equivalent of just 6.65 grams per day at 10-6. 
EPA previously used a default Fish Consumption Rate of 6.5 grams per day in 
estimates of health risk. When discussing this previous default rate, EPA's National 
Environmental Justice Advisory Council stated: "[t]his is about one 8-ounce fish 
serving per month - an amount that is outdated and inaccurate even for the general 
population. And, this amount grossly underestimates the consumption rates for 
many communities of color, low-income communities, tribes, and other indigenous 
people."15 
Needless to say, Idaho's rate—the functional equivalent of 6.65 grams per day at 
10-6—is not protective of the Tribe's reserved rights and resources. As a result, 
Idaho's current rate does not uphold the Tribe's right to take up to half of the 
harvestable fish that are destined to pass through its usual and accustomed fishing 
places.16  EPA needs to give itself the tools to right this wrong.

•
EPA should develop in regulation or guidance objective criteria for determining the 
jurisdictional boundaries of tribal waters. 
o
EPA should consider all waters within a tribe's ceded territory, as reflected in 
treaties and/or adjudicated by the Indian Claims Commission, to be tribal waters. 
For waters outside a tribe's ceded territory, tribes should be required to demonstrate 
established, federally-recognized legal rights, through treaty or other legal vehicle, 
as well as compelling evidence of the nature and scope of such rights. 
o
EPA should offer to consult with any tribe in whose ceded territory another tribe 
asserts rights prior to issuing any jurisdictional determinations regarding the 
boundaries of tribal waters and should only make jurisdiction determinations with 
the consent of affected tribes. 
o
States should have no role in determining the boundaries of tribal waters. Tribal 
rights stem from tribes' inherent sovereignty and from federal agreements, 
determinations, and law. States had no role in creating tribal rights and should, 
therefore, have no role in interpreting them. EPA and relevant tribes should, based 
on federal law, determine the boundaries of tribal waters and inform the relevant 
states. 
•

environmental justice for such communities. In his Executive Order on Tackling the 
Climate Crisis at Home and Abroad, President Biden stated:

•
The Tribe takes issue with an assumption at the heart of this rulemaking. The Federal 
Register notice for this rulemaking states: 
where a tribe has the right to hunt an aquatic-dependent 
species, for example, the species may already be protected 
in accordance with this proposed rulemaking by a state's 
"wildlife" designated use and associated criteria, such that 
this rulemaking would not require any additional protection 
of that species beyond what is already required under the 
CWA and EPA's existing WQS regulation....24 
EPA does not anticipate that more stringent criteria to 
protect aquatic or aquatic-dependent resources themselves 
would be necessary in most cases to comply with this 
proposed rulemaking than already required by the existing 
Federal WQS regulations.25 
The Tribe is concerned by these statements because it does not believe that current aquatic 
life criteria in the state of Idaho are protecting tribal rights. Aquatic life criteria are not a 
functional substitute for human health criteria. Aquatic life criteria are based on how much 
of a pollutant can be present in surface water before it is likely to harm plant and animal 
life. This is not the same as human health criteria, which are risk based and developed 
based on the maximum concentration of a pollutant in a water body considered to be 
protective of human health. 
•
This rulemaking again highlights the need for the United States to remedy a longstanding 
wrong by developing a comprehensive, searchable database of its legal agreements with 
tribal nations. 
•
EPA needs to protect tribal rights through rulemaking, which is binding, not through 
guidance, which is not binding.

Specific Comments and Questions on Text of Proposed Regulations 
•
EPA's proposed 40 C.F.R. § 131.5(a)(9): 
o
How will EPA determine whether "[s]tate adopted water quality standards protect 
tribal reserved rights, where applicable, consistent with § 131.9"? 
•
EPA's proposed 40 C.F.R. § 131.5(b): 
o
If EPA determines that a state's WQS are inconsistent with the factors listed in 40 
C.F.R. § 131.5(a)(1) through (9) and decides it must promulgate new or revised 
standards for the state, what criteria will it use to determine the new or revised 
standards it promulgates? 
•
EPA's proposed 40 C.F.R. § 131.6(g): 
o
The Tribe opposes EPA's proposal to require that states include in any WQS they 
submit to EPA for review, "information which will aid the agency in evaluating 
whether the submission protects tribal reserved rights consistent with § 131.9, 
including: (1) Information about the scope, nature, and current and past use of the 
tribal reserved rights, as informed by the right holders; and (2) Data and methods 
used to develop the water quality standards." 
•
Tribal rights are federal law and should be determined by the United States 
in conjunction with tribes, prior to, or in conjunction with, a state's 
submittal of WQS to EPA for review. 
•
Tribal treaties are a contract between the United States and the 
signatory tribe or tribes, and a "fundamental precept of common law 
[is] that the intention of the parties to a contract control[s] its 
interpretation."26 
•
EPA has a trust responsibility to advocate on behalf of tribes 
(whether they have reserved rights via treaty with the United States 
or hold other tribal rights) with states. 
•
The United States and affected tribes should, therefore, consult to 
determine the WQS requirements imposed by relevant tribal treaty 
or other tribal rights. EPA and affected tribes should then provide 
their understanding of what the treaties to which they are party or 
other tribal rights require of states, not the other way around. It is 
incompatible with EPA's treaty and trust duties to tribes for EPA to 
simply referee disputes between states and tribes. 
26  Firestone Tire & Rubber Co. v. United States, 444 F.2d 547, 551 (Ct. Cl. 1971) (internal citations omitted). 
10 

•
States should not be given license, or be required, to interpret the 
substantive requirements of applicable tribal reserved rights when 
developing proposed WQS. Such a requirement is unacceptable under treaty 
and trust legal principles. 
•
Under 40 C.F.R. § 131.6(g), states should simply be required, when 
submitting WQS to EPA for review, to provide EPA with an explanation of 
how they have accommodated or incorporated the WQS requirements of 
applicable tribal rights, as transmitted to them by EPA and affected tribes. 
•

states like Idaho the designation of ORWs requires legislative action (and, although 
several waterbodies in Idaho have been considered for ORW designation, none 
have received legislative approval). Thus, it is unlikely some states will designate 
ORWs. Unless EPA can require ORWs in tribal waters without state legislative 
approval, EPA requiring states to amend their antidegradation policy (option 2) will 
provide better minimal protection for tribal waters. The Tribe supports EPA 
requiring binding provisions on states that will not fail to protect tribal waters.

water quality standards, not a state. Although there may be a great deal of similarity in the 
Federal and state determinations under the final rule, we believe the trust relationship between 
the Federal government and Native American tribes requires that EPA determine if tribal 
reserved rights apply in waters subject to state WQS and derive WQS to protect tribal reserved 
rights. 
This is especially true for our land and water. The Bad River Reservation is located in 
the Western Lake Superior Region. Forests enveloped most of these lands except for a fan-
shaped northern stretch of coastal wetlands on Lake Superior and some agriculture in the 
southwest corner of the Reservation. Known as the Kakagon and Bad River Sloughs, the coastal 
wetlands complex consists of twelve square miles of wild rice emergent marsh, one of the many 
wetland types making up the sloughs and providing habitat alive with fish, mammals, herptiles, 
and nesting migratory birds. Dense stands of sugar maple, elm, basswood, cedar, and ash cover 
the rich low-lying river floodplains of the Bad, Marengo, White, Tyler Forks, and Potato Rivers 
as well as their tributaries. Upstream of the red clay plain (where the rivers have slowed and 
meandered to create their wide, rich floodplains), is the transition zone of glacial till deposits and 
then the higher areas like the Penokee Hills. See the attached Map Titled The Bad River 
Reservation and Watershed with Mapped Watercourses on Page 7. These areas exist mainly 
outside of the Bad River Reservation but the headwater wetlands and streams in them provided 
the basis for flow for the aforementioned rivers and act as recharge for the groundwater aquifers 
that feed the streams that form in the glacial till transition zone as well as the aquifers that the 
Tribe and many private landowners rely on for drinking water. 
Where these waters are subject to state WQS, there is no comparable water or water-
dependent resources anywhere. They are unique and irreplaceable resources, finite in nature, and

2. Comments regarding situations where the Band's reserved rights and regulatory 
processes have a significant interaction with the Proposed Rule's methodology for

Since reserved rights are often those that rely on an entire ecosystem, rather than 
bounding designated uses or water quality criteria to a specific location, standards should be 
based on the characteristics of the ecosystem. Some examples where this approach is warranted 
include: stream sections important for fisheries spawning and feeding that are within waters 
subject to state WQS; functional integrity of forested wetlands; and biological corridors and 
wildlife habitat that connect homeland or ceded territory hunting, fishing, and gathering access 
within waters subject to the state WQS. 
Section 1 above briefly describes the interconnected waters that depend on clean water 
from headwaters sources. The following are comments written to help address the sustainable 
use of reserved rights in those waters: 
a. The proposed rule describes three options that states would have to revise their 
WQS to ensure the protection of tribal reserved rights: (a) adopting a designated 
use(s), (b) adopt criteria (numeric and/or narrative); or (c) adopting changes to the 
antidegradation policy. States would have the option of choose which approach 
makes the most sense. However, there are some circumstances that warrant two 
of the three options being implemented to ensure the protection of tribal reserved 
rights and some circumstances that warrant all three of these options being 
implemented to ensure the protection of tribal reserved rights. An example of this 
type of circumstance is related to manoomin (wild rice) waters. A state may need 
to adopt a manoomin designed use and adopt criteria, such as sulfate, to proteCt 
the manoomin designated use and then adopt changes to their antidegradation 
policy and procedures to protect high quality waters where the current 
background levels of sulfate is substantially below the threshold of a sulfate 
criterion to prevent the pollution of sulfate up to that threshold. Tribal input 
should be considered when deciding the changes to the state's WQS necessary to 
ensure the protection of tribal reserved rights. The final rule should reflect that the 
preferred avenue for states to protect tribal reserved rights is by adopting all 
necessary options--whether designated uses specific to tribal reserved rights, 
narrative or numeric criteria, or antidegradation policy changes—to be adequately 
and fully protective. An example of a similar approach is the Marengo River

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791-0282 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791 ---
1 
 
March 6, 2023 
 
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency 
EPA Docket Center 
Office of Water Docket 
Mail Code 28221T  
1200 Pennsylvania Avenue NW  
Washington, DC 20460 
Submitted via regulations.gov 
Re: Docket EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791, 87 Fed. Reg. 74,361 (Dec. 5, 2022) 
To Whom It May Concern: 
On behalf of the Ridges to Riffles Indigenous Conservation Group (R2R) and the Natural 
Resources Defense Council (NRDC), please accept the following comments on the 
Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) proposed rule titled, “Water Quality Standards 
Regulatory Revisions To Protect Tribal Reserved Rights.” We appreciate the opportunity to 
provide our perspective on the proposed rule and support EPA’s effort to ensure that it and states 
carry out their Clean Water Act (CWA) responsibilities concerning the establishment, review, 
and enforcement of water quality standards that, as required by well-established legal principles, 
protects tribal reserved rights. EPA has a trust obligation to protect tribal trust resources, an 
obligation not shared by the state, and through this rule, EPA should ensure it develops national 
standards that do not provide states space or authority to diminish the full scope of the Tribes’ 
reserved rights.  
R2R is a conservation organization that supports the natural and cultural resources Indigenous 
government and peoples rely on for their economic, spiritual, and cultural identities. R2R 
partners with Tribes on fisheries and water issues on the Klamath River and advocates for state 
and federal regulatory policies that protect Tribal trust resources, much like EPA’s proposed rule 
here does. Of critical importance to R2R are water policies and standards that allow fishery 
populations to recover after decades of harmful state and federal management practices. 
NRDC works to safeguard the earth—its people, its plants and animals, and the natural systems 
on which all life depends. NRDC has U.S. offices in Washington, D.C., New York City, San 
Francisco, Chicago, Santa Monica, and Bozeman and has more than three million members and 
online activists. 

 
 
2 
 
Generally, we believe the proposed rule properly implements how the water quality standards 
program in the CWA should interact with the reserved rights held by Tribes in waters for which 
states (and Tribes with “treatment as a state” status) are responsible for establishing standards. 
We urge the agency to finalize a rule that provides the strongest possible protections for reserved 
rights, recognizing that tribal reserved rights require additional safeguards beyond the baseline 
that states might otherwise establish under the Clean Water Act.  
Below, we respond to specific issues the EPA requests comment and share additional thoughts 
on the proposed rule. 
 
1. In addition to “the rights to fish; gather aquatic plants; and to hunt for aquatic-dependent 
animals,” are there other kinds of rights that water quality standards should account for? 
The rule and water quality standards should account for tribal water rights that include 
agricultural and domestic purposes. For some contaminants, it is likely that fish consumption or 
other uses will be the most sensitive and human health criteria in support of those uses will be 
the strictest. However, if tribal reserved rights encompass agricultural purposes, or, if particular 
contaminants threaten rights-holders' agricultural activities but not human health in a particular 
area, water quality standards should be established in a way that fully protects those rights as 
well. For example, the Navajo Nation’s experience in response to the Gold King Mine spill 
shows the importance of clean water for economic and domestic needs, where Navajo irrigators 
were unable to farm after polluted water contaminated their fields.  
Similarly, water quality standards must protect the exercise of reserved rights that include a 
waterbody’s use as a drinking water source or source for aquatic resources used in cultural or 
ceremonial practices. Thus, the scope of a reserved right must account for the Tribe’s use of 
water to support the full breadth of water needs to make the reservation a homeland. See In re 
Gen. Adjud. of All Rights to Use Water in Gila River Sys. & Source, 35 P.3d 68, 79-80 (Ariz. 
2001).  
2. Should water quality standards be established to protect the “unsuppressed” exercise of 
the right? 
EPA proposes that states and Tribes with “treatment as a state” status, when setting and 
implementing water quality standards, ensure that such standards protect the “unsuppressed” 
exercise of reserved tribal rights. The proposal likewise would apply to EPA’s role in reviewing 
and approving or disapproving standards. 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,378 (proposed 40 C.F.R. 
§131.9(a)(1)). The preamble to the rule explains that the reference to the “unsuppressed” 
exercise of the right “is intended to address situations where existing water quality is lower than 
necessary to allow for right holders to fully exercise their reserved rights.” 87 Fed. Reg. at 
74,368. We fully support this requirement as it upholds the EPA’s duty to protect tribal trust 
resources and reserved rights. 

 
 
3 
Neither the scope of a Tribe’s reserved rights nor the conditions supporting that right can be 
diminished by the past and present environmental failure to protect the right.  Even if current 
conditions prevent the full exercise of a Tribe’s reserved right, Tribes are entitled to the full 
enjoyment of the right and the rule must reflect the unsuppressed right. At a minimum, that 
means water quality standards must be established in a way that does not incorporate currently 
suppressed exercise of the right due to poor water quality. We also believe that those standards 
should be reflective of the full exercise of the right as it was established, and thus disagree with 
EPA’s suggestion in the preamble to the proposal that states and EPA can establish and approve 
standards that set as their endpoint something less than a Tribe’s full use of the right: 
EPA is not proposing to require WQS to be established for every waterbody subject to a 
reserved right to protect the waterbody condition that existed at the time a reserved right 
was established. *** [T]he regulation is intended to result in WQS that protect reasonably 
anticipated future uses, taking into account factors that may have substantially altered a 
waterbody. 
87 Fed. Reg. at 74,366-67.  
This caveated approach introduces significant uncertainty into the process of reflecting reserved 
rights into water quality standards and invites conflict between states, the EPA, and Tribes. We 
anticipate disagreements over what is a “reasonably anticipated future use,” whether a water 
body has been “substantially altered,” and whether or to what degree current conditions reflect 
suppression effects or a water body alteration (for instance, temperature changes in a river could 
be affected by both discharges and physical alterations, to the detriment of cold-water fish 
populations).  Further, we are concerned that states and EPA will use this language to allow a 
less-than-full exercise of the right to persist indefinitely and, indeed, be incorporated into law as 
the ultimate goal for the water body.  
To properly protect tribal reserved rights, water quality standards must be based on the full 
exercise of the relevant right, not diminished by present impediments to achieving it arising from 
alterations to the water body. Setting standards that reflect the fully unsuppressed exercise of the 
right would mean that long-term planning for the watershed (such as total maximum daily loads) 
and restoration efforts (such as those in nonpoint source management programs) would consider 
ways to potentially mitigate the current impairment of the right and achieve properly established 
water quality standards. The language of the proposed regulation, in contrast to the preamble 
discussion quoted above, is more consistent with this kind of approach. See 87 Fed. Reg. at 
74,378 (proposed 40 C.F.R. §131.9(a)(1)) (“water quality standards must, to the extent supported 
by available data and information, be established to protect … [t]he exercise of tribal reserved 
rights unsuppressed by water quality or availability of the aquatic or aquatic-dependent 
resource” (emphasis added)). 
3. Are there unique sources of information that states should consider in establishing the 
level of needed water quality? 
EPA seeks comment on whether water quality standards to vindicate tribal reserved rights should 
be based on information apart from sources that have historically been considered in the routine 

 
 
4 
process of state-developed standards, namely: “fish consumption rate surveys, studies or 
accounts of heritage fish consumption rates, peer-reviewed articles or reports on the types and 
levels of pollutants that can adversely affect the resource in question, and monitoring data 
reflecting historic and/or current water quality.” 84 Fed. Reg. at 74,368. EPA must also consider 
Indigenous Knowledge that rights-holding Tribes can offer that are relevant to the both the uses 
encompassed within the tribal reserved right and the level at which water quality criteria must be 
set in order to safeguard those uses. Because it can be resource intensive to collect some of the 
kinds of information EPA identifies and because Tribes uniquely possess information about their 
exercise of reserved rights, the agency must not require water quality standards to be based only 
on the ordinary sources of information usually considered or give such information greater 
weight in the establishment of water quality standards protecting reserved rights.  
As this administration has recognized, incorporating Indigenous Knowledge in federal decision-
making is essential: 
Indigenous Knowledge is a valid form of evidence for inclusion in Federal policy, 
research and decision making. Indigenous Knowledge and other forms of knowledge do 
not depend on each other for validation, and each system can support the insights of the 
other. 
Office of Science & Technology Policy & Council on Environmental Quality, “Guidance for 
Federal Departments and Agencies on Indigenous Knowledge,” at 4 (Nov. 30, 2022), 
https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2022/12/OSTP-CEQ-IK-Guidance.pdf. At the 
same time, federal agencies must recognize legitimate concerns that Tribes may have with 
sharing information with the federal government and states:  
Agencies should also understand that Tribes and Indigenous Peoples may carefully guard 
information about their homelands and cultural connections to them. Recognizing and 
respecting divergent processes and world views, and the sensitivity of Tribes about 
sharing certain information about them, is important for relationship building and 
understanding how to appropriately engage with Indigenous Knowledge. 
Id. at 11 (footnote omitted). To address these issues, this administration’s policy is that 
“Agencies should consider co-management, collaborative management, and co-stewardship of 
lands and waters as opportunities to include Tribal Nations, Indigenous Peoples, and Indigenous 
Knowledge in Federal actions.” Id. at 12. In the context of water quality standards-setting, that 
means EPA should seek to collaborate with Tribes in all aspects of the process, and particularly 
with respect to the information that will be used to develop, review, and approve or disapprove 
standards. 
4. Should states have the option to accommodate tribal reserved rights in their water quality 
standards in the manners EPA suggests? 
EPA proposes to allow states to choose between, or combine, different options for protecting 
tribal reserved rights within their water quality standards. Specifically, EPA’s proposal would 
allow states to address tribal reserved rights entirely through state antidegradation requirements, 

 
 
5 
or entirely through designated uses and water quality criteria, or by using both. 87 Fed. Reg. at 
74,371-72 & 74,378 (proposed 40 C.F.R. §131.9(c)). EPA should require states to use both 
methods and should require that designated uses specific to reserved rights be identified, along 
with criteria set at a level to protect those uses.  
Having designated uses and related water quality criteria specifically tied to tribal reserved rights 
is preferable because it enables Tribes to focus on aspects of the water quality standards 
establishment, review, and approval/disapproval process that directly impact their rights.  
Additionally, antidegradation requirements must apply to all waters of the United States within 
the state, including those subject to tribal reserved rights. In that connection, however, we are 
concerned that reserved rights may not be adequately protected by one of the options EPA 
proposes, which would allow the degradation of high quality waters upon a finding “that such a 
lowering is necessary to accommodate important economic or social development in the area in 
which the waters are located.” 40 C.F.R. §131.12(a)(2)(ii). This approach should be allowed only 
if Tribes expressly agree that waters in which they have reserved rights will be adequately 
protected by this degree of antidegradation protection. 
5. Should water quality standards be set at levels designed to ensure that rights-holders do 
not experience risks greater than that of the general public? 
EPA proposes requiring standards be set in a way that ensures reserved rights holders do not face 
greater risks than others in the state. We support this proposal. For instance, as EPA 
acknowledges, in the case of carcinogenic contaminants in fish, water quality standards would 
need to account for increased fish consumption rates of rights-holders to calculate lifetime cancer 
risk and establish criteria for waters in which reserved rights are held such that rights-holders’ 
cancer risk doesn’t exceed whatever level (e.g., a 1-in-a-million risk) people in the general 
population of the state – with lower exposure rates – experience.  
EPA also seeks comment on whether there might be other situations where this provision could 
apply. To the extent EPA is asking whether it should apply more broadly than cancer risk from 
fish consumption, it obviously should, and we believe the proposed regulatory language is 
inclusive of more than that specific situation. See 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,378 (proposed 40 C.F.R. 
§131.9(a)(2)) (“water quality standards must... be established to protect … [t]he health of the 
right holders to at least the same risk level as provided to the general population of the State.”). 
In keeping with this provision, standards must protect against all other health harms associated 
with rights-holders exercise of reserved rights, such as acute and chronic non-cancer harms from 
fish consumption or other exposures (if, for example, rights holders have additional physical 
contact with the water than the general population and are at greater risk of exposure to 
pathogens). 
6. How should EPA deal with information gaps or conflicting information?  
In circumstances where there is uncertainty or disagreement about the necessary water quality to 
support tribal reserved rights, EPA proposes to use its usual approach of assessing what the “best 

 
 
6 
available information” indicates. EPA requests comment on whether to use a different approach 
in the case of water quality standards to protect reserved rights. 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,371.  
This is an area in which EPA’s leadership is critical – the agency must consult with Tribes and 
obtain tribal agreement on the level of protection necessary to fully secure their rights. As 
discussed above, in cases where Indigenous Knowledge may bear on the scope of the right or the 
stringency of standards needed to secure that right, EPA must collaborate with Tribes in carrying 
out its CWA duties. Additionally, as EPA observes, the federal government’s trust responsibility 
to Tribes requires that laws be construed in their favor; we believe that means that gaps or 
conflicts in information about the scope or stringency of rights-based standards should be 
resolved by deferring to Tribes’ understanding, or, in the absence of information, by acting 
cautiously to avoid allowing pollution or other degradation that would impair the full exercise of 
the reserved right. 
7. Should and, if so, how should states be allowed to employ a use attainability analysis to 
revise designated uses that protect reserved rights? 
EPA seeks comments on whether to authorize states to revised designated uses, following a use 
attainability analysis that finds it is not currently “feasible” to attain the use due to one of six 
different regulatory criteria. 87 Fed. Reg at 74,372 (citing 40 C.F.R. §131.10). In a word, no. 
In the case of water quality standards to protect tribal reserved rights, designated uses and the 
water quality criteria established to protect such uses are a manifestation of that underlying right, 
and they cannot be revised unilaterally by states, especially based on some of the criteria that the 
existing regulations permit to be used. See, e.g., 40 C.F.R. §131.10(g)(6) (authorizing removal of 
use if “[c]ontrols more stringent than those required by sections 301(b) and 306 of the Act would 
result in substantial and widespread economic and social impact”); id. § 131.10(k)(3) 
(authorizing removal of use without use attainability analysis if it is “a non-101(a)(2) use”).  
Should a Tribe with reserved rights expressly agree that a particular designated use is not 
necessary to effectuate the right, however, we believe that it would be appropriate to allow such 
a revision.  
8. Should general regulatory requirements concerning water quality standards, including 
variances and permit compliance schedules apply to standards protecting reserved rights? 
EPA should not permit states to deviate from the water quality standards requirements that 
protect reserved rights absent tribal agreement with any change. However, we do not object to 
including a provision in these regulations that allows the use of general state policies – e.g., 
mixing zones, see 40 C.F.R. § 131.13, variances for permittees or particular waters, see id. 
§131.14, and compliance schedules for water quality-based effluent limits in National Pollutant 
Discharge Elimination System permits, see id. §131.15 – under strict conditions, namely, only 
when the state has consulted with Tribes whose rights will be impacted, obtained written consent 
from such Tribes, and has implemented reasonable conditions as requested by the tribal rights 
holder.   
 

 
 
7 
Again, thank you for considering these comments in your process to develop a final rule. As 
tribal advocates, we support EPA’s work on this proposed rule and urge EPA to ensure the full 
scope of a Tribe’s reserved rights are protected through existing and future water quality 
standards.

Dear Ms. Brundage: 
On behalf of the Tribal Council of the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes of the 
Flathead Reservation (CSKT or Tribes), please accept these comments in support of the 
Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) proposed revisions to the Federal Clean Water Act 
water quality standards (WQS) regulation.  The Tribes strongly support the EPA’s proposal to 
clarify and prescribe how WQS must protect aquatic and aquatic-dependent Tribal trust and 
treaty resources. See 87 Fed. Reg. 74361 (Dec. 5, 2022). 
Our people have recognized the importance of protecting water and water-related 
resources for millennia.  As such we are uniquely qualified to provide these comments. Indeed, 
no natural resource is more vital to our people than water.  It is woven into all aspects of our 
lives. For thousands of years, the Bitterroot Salish, Kootenai, and Upper Pend d’Oreille, thrived 
in our aboriginal homeland situated in what is now Montana, Idaho, Washington, Wyoming and 
British Columbia, subsisting off of healthy native fisheries, plants, and wildlife.  
Under the 1855 Treaty with the Flathead, Etc. (Hellgate Treaty) 12 Stat. 975, the Tribes 
ceded over 20 million acres of our aboriginal territory and reserved a permanent homeland on the 
1.3 million-acre Flathead Reservation in western Montana.  The southern half of Flathead Lake 

2 
 
is included within the Flathead Reservation and is the largest natural freshwater lake west of the 
Great Lakes. The Tribes’ ownership of the bed and banks of Flathead Lake was upheld in 
Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes of the Flathead Reservation v. Namen, 665 F.2d 951 
(9th Cir. 1982), cert. denied, 459 U.S. 977 (1982).  Under the Hellgate Treaty, the United States 
guaranteed the Tribes that the Flathead Reservation would be set aside for our “exclusive use and 
benefit.”  “[T]he Reservation was a natural paradise for hunting and fishing.” Conf. Salish and 
Kootenai Tribes v. United States, 437 F.2d 458, 478 (Ct. Cl. 1971). 
Through Article 3 of the Hellgate Treaty, the Tribes also reserved “the exclusive right of 
taking fish in all the streams running through or bordering said reservation,” and “the right of 
taking fish at all usual and accustomed places . . . .”  State and federal courts have confirmed the 
right of CSKT members to exercise their treaty-reserved rights to hunt, fish, and gather in usual 
and accustomed places throughout the Tribes’ aboriginal territory. 
Despite the promises made, the United States has often failed to live up to the terms of 
the Hellgate Treaty including diminishing the Tribal land base by opening the Flathead 
Reservation to non-Indian homesteading and allotment of Tribal lands, constructing massive 
irrigation systems on Reservation lands that contaminate and dewater our streams and native 
fisheries and fish habitat, and sanctioning unmeasurable damages to water and water-related 
resources throughout our aboriginal territory.  
For thousands of years our people relied on the fish native to our homelands for 
nutritional and cultural sustenance.  Today, a history of federal actions (or inactions) have led 
once abundant and reliable runs of native fish to be listed under the Endangered Species Act 
(bull trout) or considered for listing (westslope cutthroat trout).  In response, our Tribes have 
undertaken significant and costly efforts to protect the remaining fisheries, restore fish and 

3 
 
wildlife habitat, protect water rights, and improve water quality.  Thus, specific consideration of 
treaty reserved rights in aquatic and aquatic-dependent resources when establishing State (and 
Tribal) Water Quality Standards (WQS) is critical to ensure that the benefit of the bargain our 
ancestors struck with the United States remains intact for future generations. 
Treaty rights are inseparable from the natural environment that Indian tribes rely upon for 
our wellbeing.  As EPA reviews and approves State WQSs, we submit that the law requires that 
the EPA consider the question: “What impacts will these standards have on tribes and on their 
specific treaty rights?”  Such an examination should begin with the fundamental principle that 
Indian tribes’ federally-protected rights to their homelands and to hunt, fish, gather, and pray can 
only be guaranteed when the natural world is healthy and safe enough to sustain those activities. 
Thus, we strongly support the EPA’s effort to amend the WQS regulation to explicitly address 
how WQS must protect tribal reserved rights to aquatic and aquatic-dependent resources.  This 
will ensure a WQS process that is transparent and consistent for all stakeholders. 
Determining if Tribal Reserved Rights Apply 
The EPA requested comments on whether there are additional types of tribal reserved rights 
that should be considered in addition to the right to fish, gather aquatic plants, and hunt for aquatic-
dependent animals.  87 Fed. Reg. 74367 (December 5, 2022).  From our perspective, all the species 
that we fish, hunt, and gather are aquatic-dependent resources.  Thus, in examining WQS standards 
we must consider not only fisheries, but waterfowl and terrestrial species (including plant species) 
that rely on our rivers and waterbodies to survive.    
In addition, we strongly suggest that the right to pray be included as a critical right and 
activity. The exercise of our hunting, fishing, and gathering is inseparable from our rights to 
practice our spiritual beliefs.  See Thompson Smith, Aáy u Sqélix ʷ: A History of Bull Trout and the 

4 
 
Salish and Pend d'Oreille People, EXPLORE THE RIVER: BULL TROUT, TRIBAL PEOPLE, AND THE 
JOCKO 
RIVER, 
Confederated 
Salish 
and 
Kootenai 
Tribes, 
http://fwrconline.csktnrd.org/Explore/ExploreTheRiver/CultureHistory/History/ (accessed March 
2, 2023).  See also City of Albuquerque v. Browner, 97 F.3d 415 (10th Cir. 1996).  We have prayed 
and used our waters for religious purposes since the beginning of time, and it is important that this 
right be recognized as a use of these waters in setting WQS.  These waters are our churches and 
baptistries and should be acknowledged as such.  
EPA should not require tribes to demonstrate where and how the treaty-reserved right is 
exercised by the right holders.  87 Fed. Reg. at 74367.  EPA should only require tribes to 
demonstrate the nature of the right, in broad geographic terms or in usual and accustomed places 
protected by Treaty.  We do not think it is necessary to ask how the right is exercised as we see no 
relevancy of this question to establishing WQS.  Treaty rights are rights that may be exercised at 
any moment in time by the rights holders; the rights are not dependent on active or continual use, 
and do not disappear or diminish when unexercised.    
However, if the EPA is going to insist on this as a prong of the inquiry, we would reframe 
the question as: “Why is the right being exercised?”  For CSKT and other tribes in the Northwest, 
we have a Treaty right to 50% of the harvestable fisheries species in our usual and accustomed 
places, and we exercise this right both for commercial and subsistence purposes.   We also gather 
other aquatic-dependent resources for subsistence and cultural purposes.  Thus, the inquiry should 
focus on whether the right is used for subsistence, treaty commercial, and/or cultural purposes, and 
not how the right is exercised.  Again, we rely on the waters of our territories for all of these 
purposes and believe that the WQS should be based on an understanding that these activities and 
uses coexist with one another.  

5 
 
Protecting Applicable Reserved Rights 
Determining the Level of Water Quality Necessary to Protect the Right  
We agree with the Preamble’s direction that States and Tribal right holders should establish 
lines of communications to develop WQS that are necessary to protect any aquatic or aquatic-
dependent resources.  Id. at 74368.  This includes working with tribal communities to gather 
accurate data on fish consumption rates, and utilization of aquatic-dependent resources (which 
again includes terrestrial resources and waterfowl), as well as the water itself (this includes not 
only for cultural/religious activities but also uses for activities like tribal fish hatcheries). The 
collaboration between CSKT, the Kootenai Tribe of Idaho (KTOI), Montana, Idaho, and the EPA 
to set the site-specific selenium standards for Lake Koocanusa and the Kootenai River, discussed 
in further detail below, provides a model for how tribes, states, and EPA can work together with 
open communication to develop WQS that will protect tribal reserved rights.  
Accounting for Suppression Effects 
We agree with the change to §131.9(a)(1) that WQS must be established to “protect the 
‘exercise of the tribal reserved rights unsuppressed by water quality or availability of the aquatic 
or aquatic-depended resource.’”  We also endorse the Preamble’s direction that States work with 
right holders to gather information about unsuppressed uses.  Id. at 74369.  This is consistent with 
the federal government’s elevation of Traditional Ecological Knowledge in its decision making.   
The Clark Fork River provides an example where WQS should not be suppressed by poor water 
quality.  As noted in our comments during consultation at the initiation of this rulemaking, the 
Clark Fork River just south of the Flathead Reservation near Missoula is within the Tribes' 
ancestral territory and is one of the usual and accustomed places where tribal members have a right 
to take fish. Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes, Consultation Comments, Sept. 9, 2022, 

6 
 
https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2022-09/Confederated-Salish-Kootenai-Tribes-
comments.pdf.  However, due to poor water quality and the presence of dioxins, furans, and PCBs, 
there is a fish consumption advisory for all fish species for a 148-mile stretch on the Clark Fork 
River.  Id.  Obviously, the right to take fish necessarily implies the right to eat that fish.  When 
tribal members cannot eat fish that they catch from the usual and accustomed places, the Tribes’ 
reserved treaty right to do so is clearly diminished.  Water quality on the Clark Fork must be 
improved so that our tribal members can exercise their treaty rights to take fish.  This will 
inevitably require more stringent WQS to clean up the river, and we urge the EPA to set WQS in 
the Clark Fork and other waters where tribes have treaty reserved rights that fully recognize and 
protect these rights.  
The Montana and Idaho selenium standard for Lake Koocanusa and the Kootenai River 
provides an example of a WQS that was not suppressed by poor water quality and will protect 
tribal reserved rights if enforced.  The transboundary waters of the Kootenai and Elk River 
systems, including Lake Koocanusa, have sustained our people since long before the imposition 
of international borders and have not only provided drinking water and critical foods, but also are 
critical to our cultural and traditional practices, community, transportation, and economic 
livelihood.  Selenium and nitrate contamination from over a century of open-pit coal mining in 
British Columbia has already damaged the integrity of these transboundary and traditional waters 
and threatens to cause irreparable harm.  Fish from the Elk River, Lake Koocanusa, and the 
Kootenai River exceed selenium toxicity thresholds for fish health, and data from KTOI and 
CSKT demonstrate that selenium has caused reproductive deformities in aquatic species in these 
waterbodies, leading to significant population decline over time. Working together with CSKT 
and KTOI, Montana and Idaho set—and EPA approved—the standard for dissolved selenium 

7 
 
concentration of 0.8 ug/L for Lake Koocanusa.  This standard is far more stringent than the 
national standard of 1.5 ug/L, and represents a situation where states and the EPA worked with 
CSKT and KTOI to ensure a standard that would protect tribal treaty resources.  This process, 
though undertaken prior to EPA’s proposal of this current rule, should be seen as a model for 
working with tribes to enact WQS that will protect tribal treaty and trust resources.  Any future 
reconsiderations of the selenium standard for Lake Koocanusa and the Kootenai River must 
follow a similar process and include meaningful and continuous consultation and cooperation 
with CSKT and KTOI.  Furthermore, the Tribes support any and all efforts by the federal 
government to improve water quality in the Clark Fork, Lake Koocanusa, the Kootenai River, 
and anywhere within our ancestral territory, in recognition of the federal government’s trust 
responsibility and Treaty obligations to CSKT.   
Protecting Right Holders to the Same Risk Level as the General Population 
We also endorse the proposed rule treating tribal members’ exercise of reserved rights as 
a distinct, identifiable class of individuals holding legal rights to resources, whose reserved rights 
are unique to them and have a defined geographic scope.  Id. at 74370.  This is critically important 
for deriving the human health water quality criteria and other purposes.  With regard to the human 
health criteria, the reservation of usual and accustomed fishing under our Treaty evidences the 
critical importance of fish in our diets and should be accounted for in the criteria.  Furthermore, 
tribal fishers/members often consume more and different fish (such as various species of bottom-
feeding suckers), consume different parts of the fish, and prepare and cook fish in different ways, 
all of which likely expose tribal fishers/members to higher levels of toxins in fish and thus 
necessitate more stringent criteria than for other fishers to assure fish are safe for tribal members 
to consume.  In addition, the criteria should account for other risk factors that put tribal members, 

8 
 
as an identifiable class, at a higher risk for diabetes, cancer, and other health conditions.  Thus, the 
change to §131.9(a)(2) is vital to ensuring that WQS are based on actual data regarding the use of 
the water and aquatic and aquatic-dependent resources by tribal right holders, as well as the 
recognized health risk factors that exist in tribal communities. 
Implementation of These Proposed Requirements. 
In the Preamble, the EPA requests comment on whether there are instances beyond fish 
consumption and protection of wild rice where “WQS may need to be adjusted to protect tribal 
reserved rights consistent with this proposed rulemaking.”  Id. at 74371.  As noted above, there 
are instances beyond fish consumption that necessitate more stringent criteria, in particular the 
commercial harvest and international trade of the resources.  In addition, the consumption and use 
of aquatic-dependent resources, including terrestrial wildlife and aquatic-dependent vegetation, 
which we not only consume, but also use for different cultural activities, can lead to exposure to 
higher levels of toxins through skin absorption of tribal members, and should thus require a more 
stringent criterion.  Finally, we have prayed, exercised our spiritual beliefs, and used the waters in 
our territory for religious purposes since the beginning of time, and we need these waters to be 
available to use for these purposes, as it is vital to our tribal way of life.  This use alone requires 
the most stringent WQS possible.    
EPA requested comment on whether in instances when there is conflicting information, 
gaps in information, or there is a difference of opinion between a state and tribe, if there are other 
factors beyond the best available information to determine that a criterion is “scientifically 
defensible, that EPA should consider in resolving the conflict or disagreement.”  Id. at 74371.  The 
scope of the best available information is critical, therefore state and tribal right holders must have 
a free and frank exchange of information.  In addition, the best available information must include 

9 
 
the Traditional Ecological Knowledge of the tribal people who have used and relied on the 
resources and waters for generations.  This information must be accepted as real data and not be 
viewed as anecdotal unreliable information.  
Options for Establishing WQS to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights  
We agree with the proposed rule designating tribal reserved rights as an explicit designated 
use.  Further, where a use is designated (e.g., fishing), WQS should be established that allow tribal 
people to employ traditional methods in the harvest, preparation, and consumption of those fish. 
For waters where a particular use is not designated, it is important that all tribal reserved rights be 
so designated, for example gathering aquatic or other vegetation, in addition to fishing, and that 
the criteria be adjusted accordingly.  And where a use such as fishing is designated, the criteria 
must be adjusted to ensure tribal member health is protected.  
Regarding the reliance on antidegradation, we agree that it is reasonable that WQS should, 
at a minimum, be established to ensure that the resources are maintained and not further degraded. 
But this must be the floor in setting WQS and not be the ceiling.  Thus, this option cannot exclude 
the other two options, but should be the baseline by which the other two options are implemented. 
We are also concerned with how this option will be implemented in concert with the §131.9(a)(1) 
requirement that WQS be established to protect the exercise of the tribal reserved rights 
unsuppressed by water quality or availability of the aquatic or aquatic-dependent resource.  Id. at 
74368.  Certainly, preventing further damage is critical, but that alone will not be sufficient for 
preserving and restoring tribal reserved rights into the future.  In places where water quality is not 
adequate to protect tribal reserved rights, preventing water quality from deteriorating is not 
enough; efforts must be made to improve water quality such that tribes can safely exercise their 
treaty rights. 

10 
 
We think the proposed rule must be clear that the States will likely need to combine these 
methods to protect tribal reserved rights.  Thus, designating a water body as an outstanding national 
resource waters (ONRW) to prevent further degradation alone is not likely to protect tribal reserved 
rights, and additional designated uses and corresponding criteria will likely be necessary.  
Use Attainability 
The Preamble to the proposed rule requests comment on how States can revise their 
designated uses to ensure compliance with the revised §131.9.  We agree that EPA should not 
modify §131.10 (designated uses), but rather include in §131.9 provisions that specify whether or 
how a State could revise designated uses to protect tribal reserved rights.  
We appreciate the opportunity to provide these comments and support EPA’s efforts to better 
protect the Tribes’ legally protected rights and resources, and thereby uphold the United States’ 
responsibility under treaties, statutes, and Executive Orders to tribes throughout the country.    
 
Sincerely, 
CONFEDERATED SALISH & KOOTENAI TRIBES 
 
 
__________________ 
Tom McDonald 
Chairman

Ms. Brundage, 
Miigwech for the opportunity to comment on the proposed revisions to the water quality standards regulation at 
40 CFR part 131. The White Earth Band of the Minnesota Chippewa Tribe agrees with the Environmental 
Protection Agency ("EPA") that these changes are necessary to ensure that the Clean Water Act will not "be 
construed as ... affecting or impairing the provisions of any treaty of the United States." CWA Section 511(a)(3). 
Water is life, for the Ojibwe people. It is the foundation of the Ojibwe origin and migration story, which 
instructed the Ojibwe people to travel westward to the place where wild rice grows upon the water. Clean and 
abundant freshwater supports the health of current and future generations, and healthy water resources, as 
identified in the proposed rule changes, are critical to sustaining in perpetuity an abundance of aquatic relatives 
that the Ojibwe people have a sacred duty to protect and restore. 
The White Earth Band, along with its sister Ojibwe bands located throughout the Great Lakes Region of the 
United States and Canada, reserved through treaties and equivalent mechanisms rights to hunt, fish and gather on 
tens of millions of acres of ceded territories. See, e.g., below map of ceded territories in Minnesota. However, as 
contemplated in the proposed rulemaking, the White Earth Band's reserved rights have been, in some instances, 
"impaired by water quality levels that limit right holders' ability to utilize their rights." 87 Fed.Reg. 74364. 
Accordingly, the Band applauds the EPA for taking this step to codify the principle long recognized by federal 
courts and the Department of Interior that "to be rendered meaningful, [tribal reserved] rights by necessity [must] 
include some subsidiary rights to water quality." 87 Fed.R.eg. 74364. Both the substantive and procedural changes 
that the agency proposes create a significant opportunity to improve protection for the Band's and other Tribes' 
federally protected property rights.

Below, the Band responds to EPA's specific requests for comments within the proposed rulemaking and also 
identifies significant concerns i.e., substantive and procedural aspects of the proposed rulemaking that create a 
substantial risk for undermining the purpose and goals of the proposed rulemaking. 
Specific comments and concerns: 
States should be required to amend all three aspects of their water quality standards (designated uses, 
criteria and antidegradation standards) to provide the most complete protections for Tribes' reserved 
rights. 

In cases where States feel that they have insufficient information to immediately provide for numeric 
criteria to protect reserved rights designated uses, narrative criteria should be immediately implemented. 
-
EPA must ensure that traditional ecological knowledge (TEK) and Indigenous wisdom receive equal 
treatment in determining water quality necessary to protect reserved rights. 
-
EPA's reference to "best available information" creates a risk that states may sideline TEK and 
Indigenous wisdom in determining water quality levels necessary to protect reserved rights. 87 Fed.Reg. 
74371. 
Tribes must be the primary determiners of the necessary balance to be struck in protecting their reserved 
rights. Tribes are, in fact, entitled to seek protection of"the waterbody condition that existed at the time a 
reserved right was established." 87 Fed. Reg. 74366, 74367. However, the Band understands that in some 
cases, this may no longer be achievable. 
The Band agrees that there is a significant risk that insufficient water quality standards may "merely 
reinforce an existing suppressed use that may already limit right holders' ability to exercise their reserved 
rights, or worse, set in motion a "downward spiral" of further reduction/ suppression." 87 Fed.Reg. 
74369. 
The best way to avoid a downward spiral of reserved rights protections is to defer, to the greatest extent 
possible, to Tribes' TEK and Indigenous wisdom regarding conditions necessary to protect reserved 
rights. 
Consultation required to accomplish the goals of the proposed rule revision will likely be extensive and, 
to be sufficient, may require significant delay in states' upcoming triennial reviews. EPA and states 
should prepare for necessary delays required to give force to the proposed rule revisions and not, in the 
name of expediency, delay additional protections for Tribes. 
In many cases, Tribes have not had the capacity or resources to judicially confirm reserved rights in ceded 
territories. In instances where rights in ceded territories have not been judicially confirmed, EPA should 
be prepared to immediately help states and Tribes reach negotiated agreements regarding the existence of 
reserved rights, so that the proposed consultations regarding necessary amendments to water quality 
standards can proceed without delay. 
The White Earth Band of the Minnesota Chippewa Tribe would again like to thank the EPA for taking a critical 
step to address deficiencies in the water quality standaids provision of the Clean Water Act regulations. These 
changes are, indeed, necessary to ensure that treaties are respected as the supreme law of the land, as required by 
Article VI of the United States Constitution. While the proposed draft rule is a laudable first step, meaningful 
implementation will be the true test of whether the proposed rule bears fruit. The Band looks forward to 
forthcoming consultations with EPA and the State of Minnesota and jointly working to ensure the greatest 
possible protection and restoration of water quality and aquatic relatives in ceded territories wherein the Band 
maintains federally protected hunting, fishing and gathering rights. 
Thank you again, Miigwech,
