of a water body, the Rule requires balancing of “heritage use of a resource with what is currently 
reasonably achievable for a particular waterbody.”64 EPA has requested comment on “whether 
additional language should be included in the final rule specifying the considerations for determining 
unsuppressed WQS.”65 In determining what is reasonable to achieve for the waterbody, EPA should 
specify that compliance with other federal statutes, including the Endangered Species Act (ESA), is 
an important component of “reasonableness.” This may come into play when the ESA requires 
designation of part of a water body as critical habitat for an endangered or threatened species, thus 
restricting activities on the water body.66 Any cooperative agreements between Federal and State 
agencies that establish a program for the conservation of endangered and threatened species should 
also provide the state with valuable information regarding what is “reasonable to achieve” for a body 
of water.67  
 
For example, the District Court for the Northern District of California ruled on February 6th 
of this year that an order by the Oregon Water Resources Department blocking water releases from 
the Upper Klamath Lake impermissibly threatened downstream Coho Salmon and Southern Resident 
killer whale populations under the ESA.68  In determining unsuppressed use of any aquatic or aquatic-
dependent resources on the Klamath River to which tribal reserved rights apply, what is “reasonable 
to achieve” must include the planned water releases as well as any other future obligations imposed 
by the ESA to protect endangered or threatened species in the river. If the ESA compels a certain 
action to be taken on a water body, this action, and its attendant effects on water quality, should be 
considered per se reasonable to achieve for that body of water. 
 
B. Additional Guidance Should be Provided on Evaluating Evidence in Determining 
Unsuppressed Levels of the Exercise of Tribal Reserved Rights 
 
EPA lists several types of evidence when considering water quality necessary to protect 
aquatic or aquatic-dependent resources or users of the resources, including consideration of “fish 
consumption rate surveys, studies or accounts of heritage fish consumption rates, peer-reviewed 
articles or reports on the types and levels of pollutants that can adversely affect the resource in 
question, and monitoring data reflecting historic and/or current water quality.”69 The Yurok Tribe 
generally supports using available data and information as outlined in the proposed regulations to 
consider the water quality necessary to support meaningful exercise of tribal reserved rights, subject 
to the amendments outlined above. However, another important consideration to emphasize is the 
need to consider indigenous knowledge and tribal input at every stage in the process; not only 
should states consult with tribes when compiling data on the nature and scope of the impacted 
rights, but also when that data is being assessed, evaluated, and used to set protective WQS. Thus, in 
addition to amending proposed provision 40 C.F.R. § 131.6 (g) to require consideration of TEK 
when made available by tribes as outlined above, EPA should consider releasing robust guidance on 
what data sources are relevant to this inquiry and how these sources of information should be 
balanced and weighed to determine the appropriate action to take.

In declining to set a national applicable threshold for unsuppressed levels or use of a 
resource, EPA cites to the National Environmental Justice Advisory Committee (NEJAC)'s 2002 
report, which notes that suppression effects may occur in two circumstances: (1) when a waterbody 
and the resources it supports become contaminated such that individuals refrain from consuming 
fish caught from the body of water, and (2) when fish populations are depleted from their historic 
quantities and species varieties such that individuals cannot catch or consume as many fish as “they 
had or would.”70 However, the NEJAC report also notes the “downward spiral” that may ensue if 
environmental standards permit further and further contamination or depletion of fish.71 For 
example, if WQS are set based “on a picture of exposure” that assumes current fish consumption 
rates of an impacted community will remain stable, when that rate includes suppression resulting 
from water quality or resource availability, agencies will “permit relatively greater quantities of 
pollutants to remain in or be discharged to the waters and sediments.”72 Thus, NEJAC recommends 
that EPA identify appropriate “baselines” reflecting higher levels of consumption to be employed 
when setting and approving WQS, taking into account historic, cultural, and aspirational interests of 
the impacted communities.73 
 
Given these concerns, the Yurok Tribe supports proposed 40 C.F.R. 131.9(a)(1), which 
requires that state and federal WQS protect tribal reserved rights at an unsuppressed level. As EPA 
aptly raises,74 for many, including the Yurok Tribe, in determining unsuppressed levels, what is 
reasonably achievable will not be the current fish consumption rate. Because “the snapshot of 
contemporary consumption practices provided by recent surveys arguably represents a nadir—a low 
point from which tribes are working to recover as environments are restored and traditional 
practices reinvigorated.”75 As such the Tribe emphasizes the point that EPA raises—that it is 
imperative that when states and EPA are determining an unsuppressed level, that they not only 
consider the legally protected nature of the tribal reserved right, but also past and future uses of the 
rights, including restoration efforts that are underway such as habitat restoration and mitigation 
efforts.  
 
While the Tribe supports the inclusion of historic data, of equal or even greater importance 
in some aquatic ecosystems are models of future projected water quality and ecosystem functioning 
following restoration efforts. For example, with the impending removal of dams on the Klamath 
River, historic habitat areas for salmon and other aquatic species for which historic data may not 
exist will become available for repopulation. For such areas, the only potentially relevant data may be 
from models projecting how dam removal will affect their hydrology and ecology. Thus, it is 
imperative that states and EPA utilize such data in determining whether water quality standards set

for these areas will be sufficient. This is vastly preferable to utilizing only historic data, or worse, 
where no historic data exists, no data to determine the necessary water quality standards in these 
areas. Not using model outputs risks setting inadequate water quality standards that fail to protect 
reserved rights once restoration efforts are underway and such habitat areas are modified. Further, 
to the extent that certain data is unavailable, it is all the more important for EPA to provide funding 
and technical assistance to tribes to commission studies, modeling, and data analysis relevant to 
determining unsuppressed levels. It is imperative that both state and federal agencies establish a 
framework enabling direct payment to tribes for services rendered. Presently, there has been

services that benefit the general public. It is crucial that a mechanism be established to facilitate this

When unsuppressed levels are determined, Yurok encourages EPA to ensure more 
protective WQS are established, taking into account historic, cultural, and aspirational interests of 
the tribes to avoid further depletion and contamination of tribal resources. Yurok hopes close 
consultation between tribes, EPA, and states as this regulatory framework is implemented and as 
states begin the process of reviewing their WQS for compliance with the proposed regulation will 
help achieve this outcome. Consultation is key to ensure the rights of tribal communities are 
protected.  
 
C. In Furtherance of Protecting Tribal Subsistence Fishing, EPA Should Set a Mandatory 
Risk of Cancer Rate of at least 10-6 
Proposed 40 CFR 131.9(a)(2), requires that the “health of the right holders to at least the 
same risk level as provided to the general population of the State.”76 EPA explains that it anticipates 
this provision would mean that the appropriate cancer risk level for the general population, of “at 
least 10−5 along with a fish consumption rate that reflects the reserved right,” would apply when 
determining human health criteria.77 The Yurok Tribe respectfully suggests that such a proposed 
acceptable risk level is not sufficiently stringent.  The Tribe agrees with EPA’s determination that 
tribes exercising their rights should not be considered “highly exposed” subgroups based on their 
increased rates of fish consumption, which would mean a higher acceptable risk of cancer level of 
10-4  under EPA’s 2000 methodology.78 However, as proposed by EPA, states are left with the option 
of setting an acceptable risk of cancer level of either 10-5 (or one in 100,000) or 10-6 (one in one 
million) for tribes exercising their rights. EPA should instead mandate a higher protection for tribal 
populations by requiring that states use at least a 10-6 risk level when setting WQS in bodies of water 
that impact tribal reserved rights, either directly or because the tribal reserved rights are located 
downstream.  
 
EPA calculates ambient water quality criteria at a 10-6 (one in one million) cancer risk level 
for the general population, which the agency views as “appropriate for the general population.”79 
And while EPA may accept higher levels of risk (10-5), EPA should impose standards that would 
 
76 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,378.   
77 Id. at 74,369.  
78 EPA, Methodology for Deriving Ambient Water Quality Criteria for the Protection of Human Health 2-6 (2000) 
https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2018-10/documents/methodology-wqc-protection-hh-2000.pdf.

protect tribal members who exercise tribal reserved rights, and in particular those who exercise 
subsistence living, to the highest extent possible.  This would be in line with EPA’s long held view 
that fish consumers at higher risk of exposure to certain carcinogens may warrant increased 
protection.80 As such, the Tribe suggests adding the following language to 40 C.F.R. § 131.9(a)(2): 
§ 131.9 Protection of tribal reserved rights.
(a) Water quality standards must protect tribal reserved rights applicable to waters
subject to such standards. To protect tribal reserved rights, water quality standards
must, to the extent supported by available data and information, be established to
protect:
…
(2) The health of the right holders to at least the same risk level as provided to the
general population of the State, provided that the cancer risk level used in deriving
human health water quality criteria for carcinogens where there are applicable
tribal reserved rights is not greater than 10-6 (one in one million).
*** 
The Yurok Tribe appreciates the opportunity to comment on the proposed rule to review 
WQS regulations at 40 C.F.R Part 131, to require state and federal WQS to protect tribal reserved 
rights to aquatic and aquatic-dependent resources. With the recommendations included above, this 
proposal is consistent with the Biden-Harris Administration's commitment to tribal communities in 
addressing continuing threats to human health and the environment. We look forward to engaging 
with the EPA for further consultation. Please contact Melodie Meyer (mmeyer@yuroktribe.nsn.us) 
and Alexander Mesher (amesher@yuroktribe.nsn.us) with any questions about the points raised in 
this letter.

Regulatory Revisions to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights  
 
To the EPA: 
 
I serve as Chairwoman of the Standing Rock Sioux Tribe.  We are concerned with the potential consequences of 
the Proposed Rule on Water Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions to Protect Tribal Reserved rights. (87 Fed. 
Reg. 74361, December 5, 2022).  This letter represents our comments on the proposed rule. 
 
Our Tribe possesses reserved rights to all waters of the Standing Rock Reservation.  Some of our water basins, 
such as the Oak Creek and Porcupine Creek, are wholly within the Standing Rock Reservation boundaries and 
are not subject to state water quality standards in any segment of the river systems.  Many of our waters are 
boundary waters or flow through the Reservation, such as the Missouri River, Cannon Ball River and Grand 
River, and they are impacted by state standards.  Consequently, the proposed rule affects Standing Rock. 
 
Standing Rock has long fought to defend the rights reserved under our Treaties.  With respect to the proposed 
rule, the reserved rights that are impacted include reserved water rights, reserved gathering rights for traditional 
foods and medicine plants, and reserved subsistence hunting and fishing rights.  These are important rights that 
we continue to exercise today, as part of our culture.   
 
I do not support authorizing the states to identify or evaluate Tribal reserved rights as part of the tri-annual review 
of state water quality standards.  The states have no authority or expertise in this area.    Standing Rock’s

permit into the Oak Creek for a regulated entity on our Reservation.  We requested inclusion of a permit term for 
compliance with the Standing Rock Water Code.  EPA initially agreed, but the regulated entity filed an appeal 
with the Environmental Appeals Board.  Upon receiving the appeal, EPA reversed course, and deleted the term, 
thereby undermining Tribal sovereignty and allowing a regulated entity to impact the waters of the Reservation 
in violation of Tribal law.  Significantly, the habitat for traditional foods is impacted, yet EPA opposed our 
reserved right to gather these fruits.   
 
Thus, the EPA ignored our Tribal ecological knowledge and practices along the Oak Creek, which is wholly 
within Reservation boundaries.  We cannot trust EPA to support our sovereignty and traditional practices on 
border waters and river systems that cross Reservation boundaries,  when it refuses to do so for waters wholly 
within our Reservation and our jurisdiction.   
 
EPA should enhance its consultation protocols with Tribes, rather than promulgate a regulation that will codify a 
state role in identifying and evaluating Tribal reserved rights in water basins subject to state water quality 
standards.  This would enable EPA to learn more about our Treaty-protected reserved rights, and to protect them 
at the federal level in the approval process for state standards.  The states should not be provided authority to 
identify or evaluate our rights in the water quality standards process.  
 
For these reasons, I oppose the proposed rule, and request that EPA take no further action.  Thank you for 
consideration of these comments. 
 
 
 
Sincerely, 
 
 
 
Janet Alike, Chairwoman 
Standing Rock Sioux Tribe

water to thrive.  The federal government’s obligations as a treaty signatory, therefore, require it to 
provide water resources with the greatest protection possible.  To do less would undermine the

GLIFWC’s member tribes understand that clean water is fundamental to life.  They regard it as “the 
first medicine,” and as the blood of their mother, the earth.  With this perspective in mind, it would be 
difficult to overstate the importance of water to the spiritual, cultural, medicinal, and subsistence 
practices that underlie the tribal lifeway.  GLIFWC’s member tribes also believe that actions affecting 
natural resources must be judged on how they will impact the health and sustainability of those 
resources seven generations hence.  They seek to ensure that principles of ecosystem management and 
biological diversity recognize and protect the fundamental interdependence of all parts of the 
environment. 
 
Because of the deep importance of water and its vital role in supporting resources located within 
the treaty ceded territories, the Voigt Intertribal Task Force welcomes actions by the EPA to require that 
water quality standards consider the health of treaty resources and the health of rights holders.  The 
Task Force supports the concepts and ideas outlined in the Proposed Rule, but believes the Proposed 
Rule could be strengthened to more completely fulfill the responsibilities of the federal government 
towards tribes and their reserved treaty rights. 
 
I. 
Water as a Sacred Being 
 
Indigenous peoples are the original caretakers of their lands and waters, and Indigenous worldviews 
on the sacredness of water are shared across many, if not all, Indigenous communities.  While specific 
goals and challenges within individual tribal nations can vary, Indigenous communities generally are 
committed to the stewardship and protection of the quality and health of waters, ecosystems, and the 
non-human beings within them.  Traditional worldviews understand that Earth is an interconnected 
system in which the health of any part affects the health and well-being of the whole.  The Tribal and 
First Nations Great Lakes Water Accord, signed on November 23, 2004, illustrates this well.  In part, the 
Tribal and First Nations Great Lakes Water Accord states that “[t]raditional teachings and modern 
science combine to strengthen our historical understanding that Water is the life-blood of our Mother 
Earth. […] We understand that the whole earth is an interconnected ecosystem.  The health of any one 
part affects the health and well-being of the whole.  It is our spiritual and cultural responsibility to 
protect our local lands and Waters in order to help protect the whole of Mother Earth.”5 
 
Ojibwe-Anishinaabe teachings provide a good framework to demonstrate how adverse impacts on 
water can impact the cultural, ceremonial, and overall well-being of plants, wildlife, and people.  In 
Ojibwe-Anishinaabe teachings, there are four orders of creation.  They are the order in which the beings 
on Mother Earth were created: (1) elements, including fire, water, earth, and air; (2) plants; (3) non-
human animals; and (4) people. According to traditional teachings, each of the orders can exist and 
survive without those that come after it, but cannot exist without those that come before it.  In this way, 
water is an elder sibling and teacher to people.  People depend on water both directly and indirectly, 
 
5 https://www.nofnec.ca/PDF/2012/Tribal-and-First-Nations-Great-Lakes-Water-Accord.pdf. 

Comments from the Great Lakes Indian Fish and Wildlife Commission 
Water Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights 
Docket ID:  EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791 
March 6, 2023 
Page 4 
 
and plants and non-human animals rely on it as well.  As a creation of the first order, water is a relative 
that has generations of memory and knowledge to teach.  Water is a sacred element, and water-
dwelling and water dependent plants and animals are particularly sacred and greatly influenced 
historical lifeways, tying many tribal communities to their historic homelands. 
 
While the teachings of each tribe and tribal community are unique, most teach that the relationship 
between the orders of creation requires reciprocity and respect.  The relationship, and respectful 
reciprocity, between humans and their non-human teachers ensures an equitable, long-term, 
sustainable, and generational existence for human and non-human communities.  These relationships 
have passed down knowledge of place through thousands of years, and provide a framework and 
roadmap to a sustainable way of life, with respect and understanding for all aspects of creation.  Plants, 
animals, and other spirits are relatives and original teachers – humans have always been the younger 
siblings and students.  For these teachers to continue teaching, humans must continue to acknowledge 
and value their wisdom.  “When their wisdom is not valued, our teachers and relatives quickly become 
‘resources’ that are stripped of their true identities and sold on the open market to the highest bidder.”6 
 
These teachings must be taken seriously in the development of a final framework for drafting new or 
revising existing WQS.  For example, many tribes will not want to quantify their tribal-reserved resources 
and, as such, EPA must make it clear that it recognizes the integrated and interdependent nature of the 
ecosystems on which tribal reserved rights rely, as well as how the health of those ecosystems are 
intricately interwoven with the health and sustainability of traditional tribal lifeways.  EPA must work to 
fulfill its trust responsibility by supporting the health of ecosystems within this final rule. 
 
II. 
Background Considerations 
 
As the EPA is aware, the federal government holds a unique, government-to-government 
relationship with federally recognized tribes. In addition, and with respect to GLIFWC’s member tribes, it 
also assumed particular treaty obligations when it signed the treaties through which GLIFWC’s tribes 
reserved the right to continue their lifeway. Thus, the federal relationship includes both particular treaty 
obligations and the federal trust responsibility – a legal obligation towards tribes that has been 
recognized since Cherokee v. Georgia in 1831.7  The legal obligations are especially potent in cases 
where rights have been explicitly reserved by treaties with Indian tribes – as is they are in the treaties 
through which GLIFWC member tribes ceded land to the federal government, and in which they 
reserved their rights to hunt, fish, and gather on those lands.8  The U.S. Supreme Court has defined 
 
6 Tribal Adaptation Menu Team.  2019 Dibaginjigaadeg Anishinaabe Ezhitwaad: A Tribal Climate 
Adaptation Menu, at 9.   
7 30 U.S. 1 (1831). 
8 Specifically, the Treaty of 1836, 7 Stat. 491; Treaty of 1837, 7 Stat. 536; Treaty of 1842, 7 Stat. 591; 
and Treaty of 1854, 10 Stat. 1109.  The rights guaranteed by these treaties have been affirmed by 
various court decisions, including a 1999 US Supreme Court case. 

Comments from the Great Lakes Indian Fish and Wildlife Commission 
Water Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights 
Docket ID:  EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791 
March 6, 2023 
Page 5 
 
treaties as “the supreme law of the land,”9 which only adds weight to the federal government’s 
responsibility towards tribes and their treaty resources. 
 
The Proposed Rule properly recognizes the strength of federal treaties, and also properly recognizes 
that the health and sustainability of treaty resources are susceptible to impaired water quality, including 
in water bodies outside reservation boundaries.  Impaired water quality would negatively impact, or 
suppress, the ability of rights holders from exercising their tribal reserved rights, rendering them 
effectively nonexistent.10   
 
However, with this recognition, the EPA must recognize that the federal government’s treaty 
obligations and trust responsibility cannot be delegated to any other entity, including states – even 
when states assume responsibilities under a federal program.  The Proposed Rule, as written, implies 
that states will make several determinations regarding tribal reserved rights.  These include making 
determinations about whether rights exist, and the geographic extent of those rights.  This is an 
especially egregious and impermissible delegation of federal responsibility because a substantial 
amount of information regarding treaty rights could come from Indigenous Knowledge (otherwise, 
“Traditional Ecological Knowledge” or “TEK”), and the Proposed Rule is silent regarding the weight that 
should be given to Indigenous Knowledge.  In other words, it is possible that states would determine 
that information provided through Indigenous Knowledge, usually in the form of stories, would be of 
less value than that provided through western scientific data – a medium most are more familiar and 
therefore comfortable with.  The inherent risk is that states will make determinations regarding tribal 
reserved rights that exceed their authority, potentially making legal determinations that will curtail 
tribal rights into the future.  The EPA must ensure that this Rule does not delegate final decision-making 
authority regarding the existence and extent of tribal reserved rights – an especially fraught possibility in 
cases in which treaty rights have not been adjudicated. 
   
III. 
 Procedural Concerns  
  
A. The Proposed Rule Codifies an Overly Deferential State Led Process 
 
As discussed above, the Voigt Task Force is appreciative of the Proposed Rule’s stated purpose to 
establish new requirements that build on existing regulations to provide a framework to “ensure that 
WQS protect applicable reserved rights.  These revisions to EPA’s existing WQS regulation are intended

thereby, anything in the constitution or laws of any State to the contrary notwithstanding.’’) 
10 The Proposed Rule recognizes that “Courts also have held that tribal reserved rights encompass

to provide clarity, predictability, and transparency in EPA’s review of state WQS and promulgation of 
Federal WQS in waters where reserved rights to aquatic an/or aquatic-dependent resources apply.”  87 
Fed. Reg. at 74366.  However, the processes outlined in the Proposed Rule leave tribes in a position of 
relying on states to accurately collect and interpret information from tribes.  This is especially 
troublesome in the many parts of the Proposed Rule where the EPA merely states that the states should 
communicate with tribes and should balance competing lines of inquiry.   
 
This process does not differ substantially from the current rule or processes undertaken by states, 
and does not go far enough to ensure that tribal reserved rights are adequately considered in the 
development of new WQS.  EPA must acknowledge that the nature and scope of many treaty rights have 
been the subject of sometimes decades-long court battles, and the determination of the scope, location, 
and manner of the exercise of the rights may be controversial and be met with resistance by states.  The 
Voigt Task Force recommends: 
 
• 
The final rule should ensure that there is a system by which a minimum threshold for 
state engagement with rights holders is developed, and by which a uniform process for 
consideration of tribal reserved rights is developed.   
• 
The final rule should also create a system by which there is a minimum threshold of 
engagement between EPA and tribes to ensure the EPA retains its federal trust 
responsibility and does not improperly rely on the states. 
• 
EPA must require states to communicate early and often with tribes throughout their 
WQS processes. 
• 
The EPA must make clear that competing lines of inquiry must be balanced between the 
states and tribes. 
 
B. Additional Burden on Tribes 
 
The Proposed Rule offers three options for establishing WQS to protect tribal reserved rights – the 
state could adopt designated uses that explicitly recognize and identify tribal reserved rights to aquatic 
and/or aquatic-dependent resources and water quality criteria to protect those uses; the state could 
adopt criteria protective of tribal reserved rights and associate those criteria with a current designated 
use that already encompasses the tribal reserved rights; or the state could use its antidegradation policy 
to protect tribal reserved rights.  The amount of resources that would be required for tribes, especially 
tribes that have tribal reserved rights in multiple states, to adequately participate in these processes 
would be immense.  The triennial review process is used below to illustrate the potential burden and 
complexity of these processes. 
 
States are required to review their water quality standards every three years (“triennial review”), 
and, if appropriate, to revise or adopt new standards (CWA section 303(c)(1)) and any revised or new 
standards must be submitted to the EPA for review.  In this Proposed Rule, the EPA is proposing to 
modify the procedures for state review and revision of its water quality standards to require that the 
triennial review process include an evaluation of whether there are tribal reserved rights applicable to 
waters subject to the state’s WQS and whether WQS need to be revised to protect those rights. 
 

Comments from the Great Lakes Indian Fish and Wildlife Commission 
Water Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights 
Docket ID:  EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791 
March 6, 2023 
Page 7 
 
The proposed rule, at 40 CFR 131.20(a), provides a mechanism for starting the process of 
engagement with tribes -- it would require states to evaluate whether there are applicable tribal 
reserved rights relevant to waters subject to the state’s WQS during the public triennial review process. 
To help satisfy this requirement, the Proposed Rule says that states “should” explicitly request 
information regarding the nature and scope of tribal reserved rights in each triennial review.  This would 
provide an opportunity for the right holders to engage and provide information the state can use in its 
evaluation. 
 
Incorporating the evaluation of tribal reserved rights into already-existing state triennial review 
processes is likely to create complicated and onerous processes.  The states have independent triennial 
review schedules, and the schedule for review is likely to be different for each of the three states in 
which the Ceded Territories lie.  One triennial review process is a long and complicated process.  
Navigating three will be an onerous process for GLIFWC and its member tribes to participate in.  In 
addition, as a regulatory action, the proposed rule does not contemplate EPA funding for tribes to 
participate in the triennial review process.  GLIFWC staff currently work in a patchwork of WQS review 
processes and recognizes the amount of work it will take to participate effectively.  Therefore, based on 
the experience of GLIFWC staff, the Voigt Task Force recommends: 
 
• 
that EPA implement, in this rule, a process that coordinates the review between states that 
share ceded territories or usual and accustomed places;  
• 
that EPA ensure there are resources to support full time staff to effectively participate, and 
that the EPA has the resources to provide effective technical assistance; 
• 
that where tribal reserved rights have been adjudicated, there are no lines of inquiry to be 
made into the existence or scope of those rights; and 
• 
that the final rule prioritize adopting designated uses specific to tribal reserved rights. This 
way, it will be more difficult for tribal uses to be subsumed within other considerations. It 
may also be necessary to adopt specific criteria to protect tribal reserved rights as well as 
implement antidegradation measures. 
 
In addition to the additional burden to tribes with treaty rights in numerous states to participate in 
the triennial review processes of each state, multiple designated use processes would add complexity 
and burdens to GLIFWC staff and the staff of GLIFWC member tribes.  In this Proposed Rule, the EPA 
anticipates one area in which WQS may need to be adjusted to protect tribal reserved rights will be 
where a reserved right is not already accounted for as a designated or presently attained use for a 
waterbody, but that waterbody could be reasonably expected to support that right in the future.  In 
these cases, after determining whether tribal reserved rights apply and the level of water quality 
necessary to protect those rights, states would be required to revise their WQS to ensure the protection 
of those rights using designated uses, criteria, and/or antidegradation.  GLIFWC will likely be in a 
situation where the states of Minnesota, Wisconsin, and Michigan will set different designated uses and 
WQS in portions of the ceded territories that fall inside their respective state boundaries.  This will be a 
complicated patchwork of standards to navigate. 
 
The Voigt Task Force has the following recommendations to help alleviate the additional burden 
placed on tribes through this Proposed Rule: 

Comments from the Great Lakes Indian Fish and Wildlife Commission 
Water Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights

March 6, 2023 
Page 8 
 
 
• 
As with the triennial review process, EPA should require states to work together in a 
ceded-territory wide review and designation process.   
• 
Emphasize protecting suitable habitats as protective of key resources.   
• 
The EPA must make it explicit that a tribe is not precluded from participating in any 
process for state revisions to existing or drafting new WQS if it does not participate in 
the initial process. 
• 
States must not be given the authority to make final determinations about the 
existence, nature, or scope of any tribal reserved right.  
• 
EPA should consider developing and hosting trainings for tribes regarding how the 
CWA can assist tribes in the protection of tribal reserved rights. Similarly, the EPA 
should consider hosting trainings (with tribes as co-hosts perhaps) for states regarding 
implementation of this rule change. 
• 
Tribes should be able to define their own designated uses in areas where they hold 
reserved rights; and states should not be able to veto these designations once tribes 
have made them. 
 
C. Process to Resolve Disagreements 
 
As discussed above, implementation of the Proposed Rule may result in situations in which a tribe 
and a state disagree.  As stated in the Federal Register notice, whether and where reserved rights exist 
would be “informed by several factors, including input from the right holders, other sources of 
information regarding relevant tribal reserved rights (including information about the geographic scope 
of those rights), and the available data to inform the level of water quality needed to protect the 
reserved rights.”  87 Fed. Reg. 74367.  The Federal Register notice goes on to say, “[f]or purposes of 
implementation of this proposed rulemaking, the critical information needed to determine if a reserved 
right applies to a state’s waters includes, but may not be limited to: (1) the nature of the right (i.e., a 
fishing right, a hunting right, a resource gathering right); (2) where the right applies (i.e., to a specific set 
of waterbodies or to waters generally within a broad geographic area); and (3) how the right is exercised 
by the right holders (e.g., for subsistence purposes).”  As discussed above, this inquiry should not be 
controversial in the case of GLIFWC’s member tribes. However, as will be discussed later, providing 
these types of evidence might be a sensitive request for several reasons, and the type of data used 
might cause states to argue their validity.   
 
The Federal Register notice goes on to lay out that “[t]hese proposed provisions would provide a 
role for the right holders in informing both the initial inquiry of whether tribal reserved rights apply and, 
where reserved rights are applicable, how those reserved rights could be protected through 
implementation of the requirements of the proposed rulemaking. Specifically, determinations regarding 
protection of tribal reserved rights should be made through a process of mutual consideration and 
discussion between right holders, states, and the Federal government.”  Id. at 74367 – 74368.  
 
After determining that treaty rights exist within a subject body of water, the proposed rule would 
require the state to derive WQS to protect any of those tribal reserved rights that were determined to 
be applicable. This would require determining the level of water quality necessary to protect users of 

Comments from the Great Lakes Indian Fish and Wildlife Commission 
Water Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights 
Docket ID:  EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791 
March 6, 2023 
Page 9 
 
the resource and/or the aquatic or aquatic-dependent resource itself, based on available data. This, 
again, brings up the issue of types of data that will be discussed below.  For the purposes of this 
discussion, this is a point at which it is possible, if not likely, that the state(s) and tribe(s) can disagree as 
to the level of protection necessary.   
 
Another point of contention is in the determination of level of suppression. “Proposed 40 CFR 
131.9(a)(1) would require that WQS, to the extent supported by available data and information, be 
established to protect ‘the exercise of the tribal reserved rights unsuppressed by water quality or 
availability of the aquatic or aquatic-dependent resource.’’’  Id.  Because the Proposed Rule does not 
“establish any nationally applicable thresholds for unsuppressed levels or use of a resource,” this 
determination will be made on a case-by-case basis.  The supplementary information lays out a 
balancing test for making this determination:  “The unsuppressed level should balance heritage use of a 
resource with what is currently reasonably achievable for a particular waterbody. For example, in 
determining the unsuppressed level of a resource for the purpose of establishing WQS, it may be 
appropriate to take into consideration both heritage rates of use of that resource and factors that have 
substantially altered the pollutant burden, hydrology, or availability of the resource, such that use of the 
resource at heritage rates is not feasible.” 87 Fed. Reg. at 74369 (italics added).  This language does not 
require or provide weight for such a balancing test, and does not explain what, exactly, should be taken 
into consideration.   
 
In all these circumstances, the Federal Register notice is silent on what occurs when states and 
tribes disagree.  The Proposed Rule lacks any clear teeth to ensure that the states are giving the 
appropriate weight to the points of view of tribes or rights holders.  While, ultimately, the EPA must 
approve state WQS, and these regulations would require tribal reserved rights are considered in the 
process before new or updated WQS are approved, that is not enough.  At the least, the final rule should 
explicitly require states to show how the information and data provided by tribes were considered in the 
various processes outlined in this Proposed Rule.  Additionally, the final rule should make clear that the 
information provided by tribes and rights holders, specifically including information that was provided 
through Indigenous Knowledge, or TEK, processes, must be weighted equally to the information 
provided by states and through western scientific processes.   
 
On November 15, 2021, the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (“OSTP”) and the 
White House Council on Environmental Quality (“CEQ”) jointly released a memorandum that commits to 
elevating TEK in federal scientific policy processes.11  This memo defines “TEK [as] a body of 
observations, oral and written knowledge, practices, and beliefs that promote environmental 
sustainability stewardship of natural resources through relationships between humans and 
environmental systems.”12  This memorandum also formally recognizes TEK as one of many bodies of 
knowledge that are valuable to improving policy making, and that its inclusion in federal policy making is 
consistent with the Administrations commitment to “scientific integrity and knowledge-and evidence-
 
11 Office of Science and Technology Policy, Council on Environmental Quality.  Indigenous Traditional 
Ecological Knowledge and Federal Decision Making [Memorandum].  (November 15, 2021).   
12 Id at 2. 

Comments from the Great Lakes Indian Fish and Wildlife Commission 
Water Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights 
Docket ID:  EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791 
March 6, 2023 
Page 10 
 
based policymaking.”13  While it is up to Indigenous communities to define TEK, this memo makes clear 
that knowledge based on traditional teachings and life experience, and shared through stories has at 
least as much weight as other forms of knowledge – including data and information shared through 
western scientific methods – when it comes to influencing federal decision making.  The EPA must make 
clear that the states must evaluate such information received from rights holders, and must show the 
EPA how that information was integrated into their WQS or anti-degradation processes. 
 
Historically, tribes and states have ideologically differed on approaching water quality management, 
from how climate change will impact water resources, to cumulative impacts.  The often-differing 
approaches have the potential to lead to conflicting data and priorities, as well as different standards for 
designated uses.  As part of its federal treaty obligations and trust responsibility, the EPA must ensure 
that states do not run roughshod over any conflicting data or competing ideologies that come from 
tribes with tribal reserved rights.  This Proposed Rule must make clear how such differences will be 
addressed and resolved.   
 
IV. 
  Data Concerns 
 
A.  Potentially Sensitive Information 
 
As discussed above, the EPA acknowledges that it may be a complex inquiry to determine if tribal 
reserved rights apply in waters subject to state WQS and, if so, understand the nature of those rights 
and where they apply.  The EPA views the critical information for this determination to be the nature of 
the right (i.e., a fishing right, hunting right, a resource gathering right); where the right applies (i.e., to a 
specific set of waterbodies or to waters generally within a broad geographic area); and how the right is 
exercised by the right holders (e.g., for subsistence purposes).  This line of inquiry runs several risks. One 
of the risks is that the inquiry requires the provision of information that could be deemed sensitive. 
There are several very good reasons to protect sensitive information.  Certain waterbodies or aquatic-
dependent resources may be used for cultural or religious uses.  Locations of certain resources may be 
guarded to protect against their harvesting by non-rights holders. 
 
 As an example, in the relationship between GLIFWC member tribes and the United States Forest 
Service, it is understood that tribes may not wish to disclose particular medicinal plants that they 
harvest, nor the locations of those activities. For example, the Memorandum of Understanding that 
implements treaty reserved gathering rights on Forest Service lands commits the parties to protect and 
restore native communities and species diversity; general language that recognizes that a diversity of 
healthy ecosystems is necessary for tribal traditional practices.   
 
Accepting such generalized information may be a hard pill for some states to swallow.  Because the 
Proposed Rule currently leaves it up to the states to determine whether and to what extent a tribal right 
exists in discrete cases14, it is potentially less likely that a state will accept the existence of a tribal 
 
13 Id at 1. 
14 Again, the Voigt Task Force reiterates that the final rule must make clear that any adjudicated tribal 
reserved rights are not subject to such inquiry. 

Comments from the Great Lakes Indian Fish and Wildlife Commission 
Water Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights 
Docket ID:  EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791 
March 6, 2023 
Page 11 
 
reserved right in an area without more specific data than the rights holders may be willing to provide.  
The Voigt Task Force recommends: 
 
• 
Any final rule should recognize the sensitivity of some of this information, especially in light 
of the sometimes-fraught relationships between tribes and states, and require states to 
respect tribal boundaries for sharing sensitive information. 
• 
Any final rule should create a standard practice for how sensitive information will be dealt 
with in the WQS processes. 
• 
Any sensitive information should explicitly be protected from Freedom of Information Act 
requests. 
 
B.  Role of Indigenous Knowledge 
 
Another issue is the type of data that may exist around Indigenous Knowledge, or TEK.  In a 
footnote, the EPA recognizes the importance of encouraging the use of TEK in making the determination 
of whether tribal reserved rights apply, and recognizes that the EPA and right holders should determine 
in those instances the rules of information gathered through TEK.  However, there is nothing in the body 
of language accompanying the Proposed Rule that makes it clear that TEK is not only acceptable, but 
that information gathered through Indigenous Knowledge should have the same weight as the 
information that is provided through western science.  Additionally, the Proposed Rule repeatedly states 
a preference for and reliance on peer-reviewed studies.  As discussed in subsection III(C) above, this 
goes against the express policy of the Administration.  The Voigt Task Force recommends: 
 
• 
A final rule must make it clear within the rule itself the importance of TEK in the WQS 
processes.   
• 
States must show how information from tribes, including TEK, was incorporated into 
their decision-making. 
• 
When facing conflicting information from TEK and western scientific data, EPA must err 
on the side of protecting and restoring resources, as contemplated in the CWA itself. 
 
V. 
 Lack of Clear Criteria 
 
The Proposed Rule clarifies that rights holders cannot be impacted by water quality to a greater 
degree than non-tribal populations. However, the rule should also make clear that the EPA would not 
accept WQS that would decrease protection to equalize the impacts across populations.  
 
When making a determination about suppression levels, the EPA suggests that the unsuppressed 
level should balance heritage use of a resource with what is currently reasonably achievable for a 
particular waterbody.  There should be clear criteria for this balancing act, so that states cannot rely on 
an argument that heritage usage is unachievable.  With regard to suppression levels, the Voigt Task 
Force recommends: 
 

Comments from the Great Lakes Indian Fish and Wildlife Commission 
Water Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights 
Docket ID:  EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791 
March 6, 2023 
Page 12 
 
• 
States should be required to incorporate available data and information that includes 
tribally produced historical data about resource abundance and location, as well as historical 
and current tribal uses of resources. 
• 
When analyzing data and making decisions, the extent to which the tribal reserved rights 
have already been diminished, as well as the length of time rights holders were prevented 
from exercising their reserved rights, should be taken into consideration. 
• 
Suppression must include both a consumption component and a location component. For 
example, there are lakes in the ceded territory that cannot be accessed due to land 
ownership patterns. Unsuppressed use would imply that theses lake should be protected 
just as lakes with current tribal use. 
• 
Antidegradation provisions must apply broadly to habitat types within the areas in which 
tribal reserved rights exist, as well as specific geographic locations (i.e., lakes or streams) as 
defined by the rights holders. 
 
VI. 
Enforcement 
 
The EPA should be explicit in this rule that states must not only set standards that protect tribal 
reserved rights, but that they must enforce those standards. Unfortunately, the State of Minnesota’s 
sulfate standard (set explicitly to protect wild rice) provides an excellent example of a state’s failure to 
implement and enforce an existing, approved standard. The EPA should consider authorizing tribes (or 
properly delegated intertribal agencies) to confirm that states are respecting standards set to protect 
tribal uses, perhaps by implementing a procedure similar to the 401 certification that is currently used 
by tribes for on-reservation water quality standards compliance. 
 
VII. 
Specific requests for information 
 
 The EPA makes several specific requests for information throughout the Proposed Rule.  The Voigt 
Task Force has attempted to provide answers to as many as possible below. 
 
A.  Tribal Reserved Rights. 
 
The Proposed Rule adds a new definition to 40 CFR 131.3 defining “tribal reserved rights” as “any 
rights to aquatic and/or aquatic-dependent resources reserved or held by tribes, either expressly or 
implicitly, through treaties, statutes, executive orders, or other sources of federal law.” The EPA 
requests comment on whether there are additional types of tribal reserved rights that it should 
consider.   
 
The definition should make clear that tribal reserved rights can include not only hunting, fishing, and 
gathering rights, but cultural, subsistence, ceremonial, religious, and economic uses.  The definition 
should also make clear that “aquatic and/or aquatic dependent resources” includes, but is not limited 
to, aquatic and wetland plants, aquatic and amphibious animals, and waterfowl, including migratory 
birds. 
 
B.  Types of Historic Information to be Considered. 

Comments from the Great Lakes Indian Fish and Wildlife Commission 
Water Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights 
Docket ID:  EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791 
March 6, 2023 
Page 13 
 
 
The Proposed Rule states that evidence to be used when determining the level of water quality 
necessary to protect a right include fish consumption rate surveys, studies or accounts of heritage fish 
consumption rates, peer-reviewed articles or reports on the types and levels of pollutants that can 
adversely affect the resource in question, and monitoring data reflecting historical and/or current water 
quality.  The EPA requests comment on the types of historic information that states and the EPA should 
consider. 
 
This is a good place for the Proposed Rule to make clear that Indigenous Knowledge is vital to the 
inquiry.  Indigenous Knowledge often entails the use of stories to demonstrate the interconnectedness 
of an ecosystem, information that cannot be easily captured in a data sets.  In this way, Indigenous 
Knowledge could reveal the water quality necessary to protect a set of interconnected resources. 
 
C.  Unsuppressed Tribal Reserved Rights. 
 
The EPA requests comments on whether additional language should be included in the final rule 
specifying the considerations for determining unsuppressed WQS. 
 
This is another place where it would be important to include language specific to TEK.  Specifically, 
the language could read: 
 
(a)  Water quality standards must protect tribal reserved rights applicable to waters 
subject to such standards.  To protect tribal reserved rights, water quality 
standards must, to the extent supported by available data and information, 
including Traditional Ecological Knowledge and tribal historical data, be 
established to protect:  …. 
 
The EPA limits its proposed interpretation regarding suppression to protecting “reasonably 
anticipated future uses, taking into account factors that may have substantially altered a waterbody.” 
Fed. Reg. at 74366-67. This interpretation is too limited. Restoration efforts are planned or underway  
for a number of resources where substantial alterations have occurred but can be reversed or corrected. 
Protecting the habitat conditions that can allow for a reasonably anticipated future use should be 
considered a part of achieving an unsuppressed use. 
 
D.  Conflicting Information, Gaps in Information, Differences of Opinion. 
 
Where information is conflicting, there are gaps in information, and/or a difference of opinion exists 
between the state and one or more tribes about the level of water quality necessary to protect a 
reserved right, the EPA requests comment on factors it should consider when making decisions. 
 
The EPA should consider the overall purpose and intent of the Clean Water Act itself when making 
decisions.  The intent of the CWA is to “restore and maintain the chemical, physical, and biological 
integrity of the Nation’s waters,” as it states in section 101(a).  Any consideration of conflicting or 

Comments from the Great Lakes Indian Fish and Wildlife Commission 
Water Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights 
Docket ID:  EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791 
March 6, 2023 
Page 14 
 
missing information and differences of opinions should always err on the side of protection and 
restoration, thus fulfilling this intent.   
 
E.  How States Can Revise Designated Uses. 
 
The EPA requests comment on whether and how states can revise designated uses, as provided for 
by 40 CFR 131.10, while also ensuring the protection of tribal reserved rights.  Specifically, EPA 
requested comment on whether any discrete additions to the current regulatory framework may be 
necessary to protect tribal reserved rights. The final rule must include language that prevents a change 
in a designated use, and/or prevents the issuance of a variance on a waterbody that would impact tribal 
reserved rights, without consultation with and agreement of the impacted tribe(s). 
 
The EPA must make an addition to the regulatory framework that requires both existing and 
revisions to designated uses encompass protection of tribal reserved rights at their unsuppressed level. 
 
The Voigt Task Force appreciates the EPA’s willingness to exercise its treaty obligations and trust 
responsibility in a manner that promotes the protection of tribal reserved rights under the auspices of 
the Clean Water Act. It hopes these comments will further strengthen the final rule.

Dear Administrator Regan: 
On behalf of a coalition of Maine municipalities and quasi-municipal entities,1 we are offering 
these comments on the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA’s) proposed rule “Water 
Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights” (the “Proposed 
Rule”) under the Clean Water Act, 33 U.S.C. §§ 1251, et seq. (“CWA”), 87 Fed. Reg. 74361 
(December 5, 2022). 
The coalition requests that EPA expressly recognize that the Proposed Rule, if adopted, 
would not apply in Maine.  It would not apply in Maine because (1) it would affect the 
regulatory jurisdiction of the State of Maine, and the Maine Indian Claims Settlement Act 
(“MICSA”), 25 U.S.C. §§ 1721-1735, provides that no federal law which accords a special 
status or right to Indians shall apply in Maine if it affects the jurisdiction of the State of 
Maine, and (2) the Maine tribes’ sustenance fishing right is derived from Maine state law – 
the Maine Implementing Act (the “MIA”), 30 M.R.S. §§ 6201-6214 – not from federal law.  
Further, the Maine tribes’ right to sustenance fishing does not guarantee a special quality 
and quantity of fish.  And, in any case, Maine has adopted human health criteria that are 
sufficiently protective of sustenance fishing by Maine tribal members, so there is no need for 
EPA to seek any more restrictive standards to protect tribal members in Maine.  
I.
The Settlement Acts
In 1980 the United States, the State of Maine, and the Penobscot Nation and 
Passamaquoddy Tribe entered into a settlement agreement that is embodied in MICSA and 
its state law counterpart, the MIA (collectively known as the Settlement Acts).  Attached as

Exhibit A is an article I co-authored in 2016 that summarizes the background of the 
Settlement Acts.  Relations between Maine tribes, the State of Maine, and the federal 
government are now controlled by the Settlement Acts.  Under the Settlement Acts, Maine 
and Maine tribes have a relationship unlike any other tribal-state relationship in the United 
States in which Maine tribes are subject to all laws of the State of Maine, including 
environmental laws.2  
II.
The EPA’s proposed amendments cannot be applied in Maine under 25
U.S.C. § 1725(h).
MICSA provides, in 25 U.S.C. § 1725(h), that no federal law or regulation shall apply within 
Maine if it (1) accords or relates to a special status or right of or to any Indians or Indian 
lands, and (2) affects or preempts the jurisdiction of the State of Maine, expressly including 
laws of the State relating to land use or environmental matters.  Because the Proposed Rule 
would accord a special status or right to Indians, and because it would affect the jurisdiction 
of the State of Maine with respect to Maine’s environmental laws, it cannot apply in Maine.3  
III.
Maine tribes’ sustenance fishing right is a product of Maine State law,
not federal law.
As the Supplementary Information accompanying the Proposed Rule recognizes, “tribes in 
Maine have statutorily-reserved rights to practice traditional sustenance lifeways such as 
fishing in certain waters,” citing to the MIA, 30 M.R.S. § 6207(4).4  Those “certain” waters 
are limited to waters within the boundaries of the Penobscot and Passamaquoddy Indian 
reservations.5 Although the MICSA “approved, ratified, and confirmed” the MIA in Section 
1725(b)(1), MICSA did not adopt or enact MIA as federal law.  Thus, the Maine tribes’ 
sustenance fishing right does not meet the Proposed Rule’s definition of a “Tribal reserved 
right,” which is “any rights to aquatic and/or aquatic-dependent resources reserved or held 
by tribes, either expressly or implicitly, through treaties, statutes, executive orders, or other 
sources of Federal law” (emphasis added).6  The source of the Maine tribes’ sustenance 
fishing right, the MIA, is Maine law, not federal law.

IV.
The Maine tribes’ right to sustenance fishing does not guarantee a
special quality and quantity of fish.
Additionally, even if the source of the Maine tribes’ sustenance fishing right were in federal 
law, that right does not provide a right to any special quality and quantity of fish.  There is 
nothing in the Settlement Acts that suggests that MIA was intended to provide Maine tribes 
a right to a higher quality of fish than that to which other Maine citizens are entitled.  In 
fact, at the time of the Settlement Acts in 1980 Maine fish were fewer and more 
contaminated with pollutants than they are today, and it could not have been the case that 
MIA was intended to ensure that the tribes had a right to consume fish of a different, better 
quality than the fish that swam in Maine waters at that time.  Please see Exhibit B, a June 3, 
1997, letter to EPA from Maine’s Attorney General, at pages 4-6, for further discussion of 
this point.   
EPA’s current position is contrary to its prior stated position, which was that MIA’s tribal 
right to sustenance fishing does not equate to a separate water quality standard.  In 2020, 
when EPA approved Maine’s WQS, it noted that “the Settlement Acts themselves do not 
address or reference designated uses, water quality criteria, or the desired condition or use 
goal of the waters covered by the sustenance fishing provisions.  Rather, MIA refers to a 
type of fishing/consumption that can occur in certain waters, and that consumption can be 
protected under the State’s fishing designated use,” rather than reinterpreting that 
designated use to include a subcategory of sustenance fishing.  Further, MIA’s provision of 
certain sustenance fishing rights “does not constitute the establishment of a new or different 
water quality goal use that EPA must review under the CWA.”7  Therefore, EPA’s position 
now, that MIA’s right to sustenance fishing guarantees Maine tribes a special quality and 
quantity of fish, contradicts EPA’s prior position that the sustenance fishing right is not a 
water quality standard, but simply “a clear recognition of where sustenance fishing can 
occur.”   
V.
Maine has already incorporated sustenance fishing into its WQS.
In any case, there is no cause for EPA to be concerned about the quality of fish being 
consumed by Maine tribal members, because Maine has already accounted for sustenance 
fishing in its WQS.  As EPA notes in its Supplementary Information, at note 34, “After 
subsequent collaboration among the State, EPA, and the tribes, in 2019 the State of Maine 
adopted a new sustenance fishing designated use subcategory which addresses tribal 
sustenance fishing.” 
For waters subject to the sustenance fishing designated use the assumed fish consumption 
rate is 200 grams per day (g/day),8 which is higher than the observed unsuppressed fish 
consumption rate for Maine tribes.9  Maine also implemented a cancer risk level of 10-6 in 
7 U.S. EPA, Withdrawal of Certain of EPA’s February 2, 2015, Decisions Concerning Water Quality 
Standards for Waters in Indian Lands (2020), p. 20. 
8 38 M.R.S. § 466-A(1).  
9 Ebert et al., Estimating Consumption of Freshwater Fish among Maine Anglers (1993).

waters subject to sustenance fishing, which is the risk level that EPA recommends in its 
proposed WQS amendments.  Thus, because Maine’s WQS already account for tribal 
sustenance fishing, there is no cause for concern.  
VI.
The Proposed Rule misstates the scope of the Maine Tribes’ sustenance
fishing right.
The Proposed Rule misstates the Maine tribes’ right to sustenance fishing to make it broader 
than provided by MIA.  As noted above, EPA claims that Maine tribes have a right to practice 
“traditional sustenance lifeways such as fishing,” suggesting that that right extends to some 
unnamed “lifeways” beyond merely fishing.  That suggestion is false.  Under 30 M.R.S. § 
6207(4), the members of the Penobscot Nation and the Passamaquoddy Tribe have a 
statutorily reserved right only to “take fish.”  EPA’s attempt to expand the Maine tribal 
members’ reserved sustenance fishing right in this manner is entirely unsupported.  The 
Proposed Rule is, in short, an overreach that would violate the Settlement Acts. 
VII.
The Proposed Rule would create unnecessary regulatory uncertainty.
Finally, the Proposed Rule would create an enormous amount of regulatory uncertainty.  The 
rule would require states to establish WQS that protect “the exercise of tribal reserved 
rights unsuppressed by water quality or availability of the aquatic or aquatic-dependent 
resource.”  This standard is not a standard at all, but a broad and subjective requirement to 
protect all possible tribal consumption in a hypothetical pristine environment, regardless of 
the presence of fish, in any amount.  This is not a standard at all, but a dictate of pristine 
water quality, and one that would make it impossible for a permittee, or an entity 
considering applying for a permit, to predict whether they could comply with the new limits 
that this rule would require.  It would create enormous regulatory uncertainty, and is an 
overreach of EPA’s regulatory authority.

Exhibit A 
 
 
 

Water, Tribal Claitns, and Maine's 
Not-So-Settled Settletnent Acts 
Matthew D. Manahan and Catherine R. Connors 
I 
n most regions of the United States, control over natural 
resources vis-a-vis American Indian (hereinafter Indian) 
tribes is addressed at the federal level. Maine, however, 
is not like other states. The history of federal-state-tribal 
control over Maine waters tells a unique and at times tortured 
tale still being written in the courts. The moral of the story so 
far is that, with sufficient financing and fading memories, even 
the clearest settlement language will be challenged, over and 
over and over again. 
In examining the period when colonists from England, and 
later Massachusetts, settled throughout the area that eventu-
ally became Maine, historians differ as to how many Indians 
lived in the area, whether they were nomadic or riverine, orga-
nized or conquered, where they could be found, and when. As 
of 1820, however, when Maine became a state, it was clear 
that few Indians remained, and they were regulated by state, 
not federal, authorities. As Congress stated, since 1820, the 
state of Maine "provided special services to the Indians resid-
ing within its borders," while the United States "provided few 
special services to the ... [tribes] ... and repeatedly denied 
that it had jurisdiction over or responsibility" for them." 25 
U.S.C. § 172l(a)(7). 
After 150 years of such state oversight, however, Maine was 
hit with a legal lightning bolt. In 1972, the Passamaquoddy 
Tribe and the Penobscot Nation filed suit in federal court in 
Maine, asking the court to require the U.S. Department of the 
Interior (DOI) to file suit against the state for the return of the 
tribes' aboriginal lands. The tribes argued that certain treaties 
between the tribes and Maine and Massachusetts were invalid 
because they were not approved by Congress, as required by 
the Indian Nonintercourse Act of 1790, 25 U.S.C. § 177. 
This theory about the Nonintercourse Act, combined with 
a U.S. Supreme Court ruling in 1974 finding federal subject 
matter jurisdiction for tribal land claims, led to a cascade of 
similar lawsuits by other tribes in other states. 
In the Maine litigation, the trial court agreed with the 
theory, and the First Circuit Court of Appeals upheld that 
decision. See Passamaquoddy Tribe v. Morton, 528 F2d 370 (1st 
Cir. 1975). After Morton gave the Indians' position traction, 
the first settlement of a tribal land claim in this wave of liti-
gation came in 1978. Congress, which must approve all such 
settlements, agreed to a settlement in Rhode Island with the 
Narragansett Tribe, which had claimed a few thousand acres of 
land. 
Mr. Manahan and Ms. Connors represent the coalition of municipalities 
and businesses supporting the position of the state of Maine in Penobscot 
Nation v. Mills. Mr. Manahan may be reached at mmanahan@ 
pierceatwood. com, and Ms. Connors may be reached at cconnors@ 
pierceatwood. com. 
24 
In Maine, however, the stakes were far higher-the tribes 
were claiming two-thirds of the land mass of the state. As 
Congress put it: "Substantial economic and social hardship to 
a large number of landowners, citizens, and communities in 
the State of Maine, and therefore to the economy of the State 
of Maine as a whole, will result if the aforementioned claims 
are not resolved promptly." 25 U.S.C. § 1721(a)(6). The law 
firm of Ropes & Gray issued an opinion that a state munici-
pal bond issue could not go forward using property within the 
claimed territory as collateral. Title companies refused to write 
title insurance for any land claimed by the tribes in Maine, 
causing residential and commercial transactions in these areas 
to come to a halt. 
Much negotiation ensued. At one point, Archibald Cox 
of Watergate fame was on the tribes' side, with famed defense 
attorney Edward Bennett Williams representing the state. 
There were multiple task forces appointed by President Carter; 
the tribes' main ally in Congress was defeated in his Senate 
re-election bid; and Senators Edmund Muskie and George 
Mitchell, among others, played roles. Eventually a final deal 
was struck in 1980, when the possibility of Ronald Reagan's 
election as the next president raised the specter that he might 
veto a settlement favorable to the tribes were he elected. 
The resulting, comprehensive settlement, agreed upon by 
the United States, the state of Maine, the Penobscot Nation, 
and the Passamaquoddy Tribe, is embodied in the federal 
Maine Indian Land Claims Settlement Act and its state law 
counterpart, the Maine Implementing Act (collectively, the 
Settlement Acts). Under the terms of the Settlement Acts, 
the Maine tribes agreed to extinguishment of their claims in 
exchange for the establishment of Indian Reservation and Ter-
ritory lands, and to payment to the tribes of over $81 million 
(about $230 million in 2016 dollars). As the Settlement Acts 
recite, the purpose of the settlement was to remove the cloud 
on titles, settle all the tribes' claims, and clarify the status of 
the other land and natural resources in the state. 25 U.S.C. 
§ 1721(b). 
The Settlement Acts were unique in establishing a new 
type of relationship between the federal, state, and tribal gov-
ernments unlike the relationship of any tribes to any other 
state, with the Indians "subject to all laws of the State of 
Maine." Id. § 1721 (b)(4 ). The Settlement Acts gave the state 
of Maine civil and criminal-including environmental-juris-
diction over Maine Indian lands: 
Except as otherwise provided in this Act, all Indians, 
Indian nations, and tribes and bands of Indians in the 
State and any lands or other natural resources owned by 
them, held in trust for them by the United States or by 
NR&E Fall 2016 

any other person or entity shall be subject to the laws of 
the State and to the civil and criminal jurisdiction of the 
courts of the State to the same extent as any other per-
son or lands or other natural resources therein. 
30 M.R.S. § 6204. 
Thus, this settlement among the federal, state, and tribal 
governments created a jurisdictional arrangement unlike what 
exists in western states, where state laws are generally not 
applicable to tribes or tribal lands. Except as to "internal tribal 
matters," under the Settlement Acts, Maine tribes are subject 
to Maine law, and have the same governmental authority as a 
Maine municipality. Tribal members may catch fish for their 
individual sustenance and not be subjected to state fishing 
license requirements and bag limits, but with limits to prevent 
overfishing. The Settlement Acts explicitly provide that no fed-
eral laws or regulations intended to accord any special right or 
status to any Indians or Indian lands and affect or preempt the 
regulatory jurisdiction of the state of Maine-including envi-
ronmental regulatory jurisdiction-apply to the Maine tribes. 
In sum, the Settlement Acts were designed to be just that: 
a comprehensive and global settlement of all tribal claims in 
Maine. The legal framework adopted was clear, incorporat-
ing a unique state-tribal relationship, in which there was no 
interference with the tribes' self-governance, but regulatory 
authority remained with the state. 
End of story? Oh no. This was just the beginning. 
Tribal Opposition to Maine NPDES 
Delegation 
Time passed, and the Maine tribes no longer wanted to be 
unique. They are federally recognized, and would like the same 
federal sovereign-to-sovereign relationship as their western 
counterparts. Federal administrative bodies, comfortable with 
the general federal-tribal regulatory template, have no stake 
in maintaining the state of Maine's interests. Hence, after a 
short lull to let memories fade, the tribes' pushback began in 
the early 1990s. As a part of this federal-tribal cooperative 
effort, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) even 
entered into "Tribal Environmental Agreements," requiring 
EPA to do everything in its power to prevent disclosure under 
the Freedom of Information Act of its communications with 
the Maine tribes, leaving the state of Maine in the dark about 
their discussions. 
The first avenue pressed to expand tribal regulatory 
authority focused on "internal tribal matters"-the area of self-
control not subject to state regulation under the terms of the 
Settlement Acts. The argument was launched that this self-
governance exemption was far broader than it appears on its 
face, embracing water quality and its regulation. 
The Clean Water Act (CWA) National Pollutant Dis-
charge Elimination System (NPDES) program requires a 
permit for the discharge of any pollutant into navigable waters. 
33 U.S.C. § 1342(a). The CWA assigns permitting responsi-
bilities first to EPA, but a state may apply to EPA to administer 
the NPDES program for discharges into navigable waters 
within its jurisdiction. 33 U.S.C. § 1342(b). The EPA admin-
istrator "shall approve each submitted program unless he 
determines that adequate authority does not exist." Id. 
NR&E Fall 2016 
In November 1999, the state of Maine submitted an appli-
cation to EPA seeking NPDES delegation for the entire state, 
including areas that may fall within or near "Indian Territory," 
for authority to issue wastewater discharge permits under 
the CWA. (Indiari Territory is a defined term under the Set-
tlement Acts, including reservations and some additional 
property acquired by DOI for the tribes.) 
The legal framework adopted 
for the Settlement Acts was 
clear, incorporating a unique 
state-tribal relationship, 
in which there was no 
interference with the tribes' 
self-governance, but regulatory 
authority remained 
with the state. 
The tribes in Maine objected, saying they thought the fed-
eral government should retain oversight in tribal territories 
because, they alleged, the state does not have authority over 
tribal waters. In January 2001, EPA approved Maine's applica-
tion to implement the NPDES program, but only in areas of 
the state "outside Indian Country." That partial approval took 
no action on the state's program obligation as it applied to the 
territories and lands of the four federally recognized Indian 
tribes in Maine. EPA said it needed to study further what to do 
in Indian Territory. 
On October 31, 2003, EPA authorized the state to imple-
ment the NPDES program as it applies to the territories of the 
Penobscots and the Passamaquoddies. EPA did not, however, 
delegate permitting authority for "disputed" Indian Territory, 
including tribal facilities located on tribal reservations that 
discharge into Maine's navigable waters, characterizing such 
discharges as "internal tribal matters." EPA said it would apply 
a balancing test to determine whether the state or the tribes 
have jurisdiction over specific discharges, and expressed its 
intent to protect fish that the tribes may catch for sustenance 
purposes by imposing conditions in Maine-issued NPDES per-
mits to non-Indian dischargers not in Indian Territory and by 
taking over Maine's water quality standards. 
The state of Maine appealed EPA's decision to the First Cir-
cuit Court of Appeals. The court agreed with the state and 
rejected EPA's and the tribes' position. In so ruling, the court 
noted that it had no need to wade into any dispute about 
Indian Territory, because Maine has jurisdiction over all dis-
charges in the state, including those within Indian Territory 
and over tribal discharges themselves. See Maine v. Johnson, 
498 F.3d 37 (1st Cir. 2007). 
Did that end the discussion? Guess again.
