Dear Administrator Regan: 
 
SUBJECT:  Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791 
USEPA’s Proposed Tribal Reserved Rights Rule 
 
The Water Resources Division of Michigan’s Department of Environment, Great Lakes, 
and Energy (EGLE), submits this comment letter concerning the United States 
Environmental Protection Agency’s (USEPA’s) proposed Tribal Reserved Rights Rule 
concerning section 303(c) of the federal Water Pollution Control Act, known as the 
Federal Clean Water Act, 33 U.S.C. 1313(c). The rule, if promulgated as currently 
drafted, would revise 40 C.F.R. § 131 to require states to adopt water quality standards 
that protect tribal rights reserved under treaties, statutes, executive orders, and other 
unnamed federal authority.  
EGLE recognizes USEPA’s trust relationship with the 574 federally recognized Indian 
tribes in the United States, as well as the pressing water quality issues tribal 
communities face. Likewise, EGLE understands that federal law both recognizes tribal 
reserved rights and the rights the federal government has granted to federally 
recognized Indian tribes, which are enforceable under the United States Constitution 
against states and other parties. EGLE does not dispute its obligation to follow federal 
law concerning both types of tribal rights. It confirms its commitment to working with its 
tribal partners in Michigan to address water quality issues. 
However, EGLE has substantial concerns about the proposed rule’s legal basis, 
vagueness, ability to be implemented, burdens on states, and rushed timeline. EGLE 
finds it highly problematic that USEPA appears to be pursuing a theory that all treaties 
and other authorities that reserve rights to tribes have an implied environmental 
servitude, an argument that is not on firm legal ground. Most of all, EGLE is troubled 
about the way the proposed rule would pit states and tribes against one another rather 
than providing opportunities for them to work with each other. That outcome is wholly 
unnecessary and detrimental to the working relationship between federal, state, and 
tribal governments, while doing nothing to enhance water quality beyond what the 
current regulations require. For all these reasons, EGLE urges USEPA to stop pursuing 

SUBJECT:  Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791 
USEPA’s Proposed Tribal Reserved Rights Rule 
Page 2 
March 6, 2023 
 
 
this nationwide rule to protect tribal reserved rights because it is at odds with the 
individual nature of reserved rights. Instead, USEPA should take three steps. 
First, USEPA should actively work with states and tribes to understand the threats to 
aquatic resources on which tribal communities rely that can be mitigated under existing 
federal Clean Water Act authority concerning water quality standards, including state 
regulations that satisfy the federal Clean Water Act. Second, USEPA should seek 
amendments to the federal Clean Water Act to obtain the authority to address modern 
and emerging threats to tribal communities that the federal Clean Water Act does not 
currently provide, rather than attempt to rework treaties, statutes, executive orders, and 
other federal authority to provide remedies for problems that were never contemplated 
at the time they became law. Finally, USEPA should develop a far narrower rule or 
guidance that provides a framework for assessing and responding to evidence that 
water quality standards in a particular state violate tribal reserved rights to avoid any 
conflict between the federal Clean Water Act and a treaty or other binding law. 
 
USEPA has not articulated a legal basis for the proposed rule. 
The federal Clean Water Act does not have a single provision that allows or directs 
USEPA to determine whether a federally recognized Indian tribe (tribe) has explicit or 
implied “reserved rights” under a treaty, statute, executive order, or other unnamed 
federal authority. Nor does the federal Clean Water Act require states to search for such 
reserved rights and propose water quality standards to protect them, much less that 
they should do so every three years. If any authority existed in the federal Clean Water 
Act to pursue reserved rights in this way, USEPA would have cited it in its public notice.   
Instead, USEPA’s public notice cites § 511(a)(3) of the federal Clean Water Act, 
33 U.S.C. § 1371(a)(3), and the agency’s “discretion” under the federal Clean Water Act 
to require states to adopt water quality standards as the legal basis for the proposed 
rule. That claim does not withstand scrutiny. 
 
Section 511(a)(3) is a statement by Congress concerning how to 
interpret the Clean Water Act, not a source of authority on which 
USEPA can rely to expand its powers. 
Section 511(a) of the federal Clean Water Act, 33 U.S.C. § 1371(a)(3), provides, “This 
chapter shall not be construed as … (3) affecting or impairing the provisions of any 
treaty of the United States.” The statutory language explains that the provisions within 
the “chapter,” i.e., Chapter 26 of the federal Clean Water Act, 33 U.S.C. §§ 1251–1389, 
cannot be understood to affect or impair a United States treaty, regardless of the type of 
treaty at issue.  
The type of conflict that Congress prohibited in § 511(a)(3) is one that would change or 
make worse the terms of any treaty, regardless of whether the treaty is with an Indian 
tribe or other country. See Merriam-Webster.com, 

SUBJECT:  Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791 
USEPA’s Proposed Tribal Reserved Rights Rule 
Page 3 
March 6, 2023 
 
 
Merriam-Webster.com/Dictionary/Affect (last visited January 27, 2023) (to “affect” 
means to “act on and cause a change in” a thing); Merriam-Webster.com, Merriam-
Webster.com/Dictionary/Impair, (last visited January 27, 2023) (to impair means “to 
diminish in function, ability, or quality” or “to weaken or make worse”). Nothing in this 
statutory language delegates authority or discretion to USEPA. In fact, the statutory 
language does not refer to USEPA at all, much less empower it to take any actions 
regarding treaties or treaty rights, federally recognized Indian tribes, or any other related 
matter. Nor does it refer to states or impose any obligations on states concerning treaty 
rights, federally recognized Indian tribes, or any other matter. 
If anything, § 511(a)(3) carefully guards against Executive branch agencies like USEPA 
usurping the Senate’s power to have the final say on a treaty’s terms by claiming to give 
effect to treaty rights. See U.S. Const, Art. 2, §2, cl. 2 (treaty clause requires the “Advice 
and Consent of the Senate” to ratify treaties). As former USEPA Administrator Gina 
McCarthy recognized, “[T]reaties do not expand the EPA’s authority….” See McCarthy, 
USEPA, Memorandum, Commemorating the 30th Anniversary of the EPA's Indian 
Policy (December 1, 2014), p. 1. Rather, USEPA’s role is simply to “ensure its actions 
do not conflict with tribal treaty rights.” McCarthy Memorandum, p 1 (emphasis added). 
But USEPA far exceeds its obligation not to take actions that conflict with treaty rights in 
the proposed tribal reserved rights rule. USEPA is attempting to create a new, 
affirmative obligation for states to search for reserved rights in 370 Senate-ratified 
treaties, something not contemplated in § 511(a)(3), and to somehow return water 
quality and resource availability to what it was at a point in the distant historical past. 
USEPA only cements the conclusion that it has far exceeded its statutory authority by 
proposing to require states to shoulder this research burden for an unknown number of 
statutes, executive orders, and other federal authority it does not (or cannot) identify, 
none of which are mentioned in § 511(a)(3). Section 511(a)(3) unmistakably fails to give 
USEPA’s authority to promulgate the proposed rule. 
 
Promulgating the proposed rule would put the Administrator at risk 
of repeatedly causing conflict with treaties, which Congress did not 
intend when it enacted § 511(a)(3). 
Adopting the proposed rule would put the Administrator in the position of running afoul 
of § 511(a)(3) repeatedly by altering the meaning of treaties because USEPA’s 
proposed process for determining reserved rights appears not to be calculated to 
provide the serious, individualized analysis the Indian canons of construction require. 
According to USEPA, under the proposed rule states must go to rights holders to start 
an engagement process that will result in the rights holders sharing information that the 
state can “use in its evaluation” of reserved rights. 87 Fed. Reg. 74,367 (December 5, 
2022). USEPA envisions that it could then participate in discussions with the state and 
rights holders that will result in the rights holders influencing the decisions concerning 
“whether tribal reserved rights apply and, where reserved rights are applicable, how 

SUBJECT:  Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791 
USEPA’s Proposed Tribal Reserved Rights Rule 
Page 4 
March 6, 2023 
 
 
those reserved rights could be protected through implementation of the requirements of 
the proposed rulemaking.” 87 Fed. Reg. 74,367. USEPA adds that it will also “consider 
other sources of information regarding applicable tribal reserved rights including the 
language of the treaties, statutes, or Executive orders and relevant judicial precedent.” 
Id. 
USEPA misses the mark with the process, which is designed to obtain concurrence 
from rights holders, but not designed to determine the historical Indian understanding of 
a treaty, statute, etc. See Tulee v. State of Washington, 315 U.S. 681, 684 (1942) 
(Indian canons require treaty to be understood “by the tribal representatives at the 
council” where the treaty was negotiated). USEPA also assumes that rights holders 
have information that sheds light on how the individual tribal leaders who negotiated 
with the United States understood the document being negotiated at the time it was 
negotiated and that they will share it with states and the federal government.  
In reality, some rights holders may have very little information or no information that is 
germane to a historical Indian understanding analysis. Nor are they guaranteed to have 
the evidence relevant to determining whether:   
• A subsequent treaty or act of Congress abrogated the rights, see United States 
v. Dion, 476 U.S. 734, 738–39 (1986); 
• The treaty tribes gave up their rights by abandoning the place where the rights 
could be exercised, Williams v. City of Chicago, 242 U.S. 434, 437 (1917); or 
• The treaty rights terminated pursuant to the treaty’s terms, such as when treaty 
rights are temporary and time passes, Lac Courte Oreilles Band of Lake Superior 
Chippewa Indians v. Voigt, 700 F.2d 341, 358 (7th Cir. 1983), or when a 
designated extinguishing event occurs, Minnesota v. Mille Lacs Band of 
Chippewa Indians, 526 U.S. 172, 207 (1999). 
And even if the rights holder had the best document collections, nothing in the federal 
Clean Water Act or the proposed rule compels rights holders to share those documents 
with states. As a result, this engagement process may not offer states any materials to 
analyze, or the information states obtain may be inadequate for developing water quality 
standards. 
USEPA’s statement that it will consider the plain language of treaties, statutes, and 
executive orders as well as judicial decisions offers little comfort to a state like Michigan. 
Between the Treaty of Fort M’Intosh, 7 Stat. 16 (January 21, 1785) and the Treaty with 
the Chippewa of Saginaw, Black River, and Swan Creek, 14 Stat. 657 (October 18, 
1864), the United States executed more than twenty-five treaties (including 
supplementary articles) with indigenous people living in what is now Michigan. But so 
far, the courts have adjudicated tribal usufructuary rights claims under only two treaties:  
the Treaty of Washington, 7 Stat. 491 (March 28, 1836) and the Treaty of LaPointe, 7 

SUBJECT:  Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791 
USEPA’s Proposed Tribal Reserved Rights Rule 
Page 5 
March 6, 2023 
 
 
Stat. 591 (October 4, 1842). See People v. LeBlanc, 248 N.W.2d 199 (1976); People v. 
Jondreau, 185 N.W.2d 375 (1971). 
The limited case law concerning usufructuary rights in Michigan leaves a vast gap 
between the settled judicial understanding of tribal reserved rights in Michigan and the 
entirety of the rights USEPA seeks to establish. For example, the proposed rule does 
not explain how USEPA intends for states and its own staff to proceed if: 
• The language of the treaty, statute, executive order, or other federal authority is 
not clear about reserved rights; 
• There is no judicial precedent, or the precedent does not resolve the specific 
right claimed to be reserved; 
• The rights holders do not have relevant information or are unwilling to share the 
information they do have; 
• There is a conflict among the rights holders about the rights reserved or the 
water quality standards required to protect them; 
• There is no clear connection between water quality standards that a state can 
implement and the conditions threatening water quality or aquatic resources; or 
• Other federal agencies disagree about the existence or nature of the tribal 
reserved rights in a particular instance. 
Nor does USEPA explain why states should be required to determine reserved rights 
under all treaties, statutes, executive order, and other authority that might exist if they 
set statewide water-quality standards, particularly if those standards already protect 
reserved rights. And these are just a sampling of the issues that may arise when 
attempting to determine whether reserved rights exist. 
This gray area about reserved rights is exactly what places the Administrator at risk of 
violating § 511(a)(3) if USEPA promulgates this proposed rule. If USEPA acts with too 
little information about tribal reserved rights, it stands a significant chance of 
inadvertently (but avoidably) altering a treaty’s terms and therefore causing an 
impermissible conflict by its action on the state’s water quality standards. The fact that 
USEPA’s action may benefit rights holders and have their support is immaterial because 
it has no authority over treaty terms, which are entrusted to the President to negotiate 
and the United States Senate to ratify. 
If USEPA expects states to take on the time-consuming and expensive historical and 
anthropological research and analysis required to determine Indian understanding of 
historical treaties, statutes, and executive orders, it is entirely unclear whether those 
steps will serve any purpose. Three years is often not enough time to conduct the 

SUBJECT:  Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791 
USEPA’s Proposed Tribal Reserved Rights Rule 
Page 6 
March 6, 2023 
 
 
research and analysis necessary to resolve the status or contours of tribal reserved 
rights. Indeed, during the COVID-19 pandemic, many of the key institutions that hold 
historical documents, such as the National Archives and state archives, were closed to 
researchers for an extended period. Even if states do obtain the needed information, it 
is not at all clear how to translate the observations in historical records into modern 
water quality standards. And it is also unclear how tying updated water quality 
standards to historical research may limit a state’s ability to respond in a timely way to 
emerging pollutants and other critical water quality issues. 
In any case, USEPA has not committed to reviewing the historical documents states 
collect. And if the agency were to review those historical documents, its ability to 
interpret them and properly understand them in context is doubtful. Congress certainly 
did not intend § 511(a)(3) to give USEPA the authority to take on a task so distant from 
its scientific expertise and with such potentially significant consequences for treaty 
terms over which it exercises no control. 
 
USEPA’s general authority to require states to adopt water quality 
standards does not include the discretion to determine the 
existence, nature, and scope of reserved rights.  
USEPA also claims that the “structure and objectives for the establishment and 
oversight of” water quality standards give it the “discretion” to adopt the proposed rule. 
But that is not the case. See generally City of Albuquerque v. Browner, 97 F.3d 415, 
424–25 (10th Cir. 1996) (Congress intended USEPA “to have a very limited role” in 
reviewing water quality standards proposed by states or tribes). 
Section 501 of the federal Clean Water Act, 33 U.S.C. § 1361(a), grants the USEPA 
Administrator authority to “prescribe such regulations as are necessary to carry out his 
functions under this chapter.” (Emphasis added). But nothing in Chapter 26 of the 
federal Clean Water Act makes it the Administrator’s function to determine the 
existence, nature, and scope of tribal rights reserved in treaties, statutes, executive 
orders, or other sources of federal authority. Congress had no reason to give the 
Administrator any of those duties. 
The Administrator’s staff at USEPA—like EGLE’s own staff—is comprised of scientists 
and engineers. Even USEPA’s lawyers are not historians, ethnohistorians, linguists, 
geographers, and the other professionals who have the education, skill, and experience 
to research and interpret treaties, statutes, executive orders, and other federal 
authorities in historical context. Without a statutory function that coincides with this sort 
of broad authority over Indian affairs, the rule cannot be considered necessary within 
the meaning of § 501. 
If Congress wanted USEPA to be able to determine whether tribal reserved rights exist 
and how to address them when administering the triennial review process under 
§ 303(c) of the federal Clean Water Act, it would have said so explicitly. Six different 

SUBJECT:  Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791 
USEPA’s Proposed Tribal Reserved Rights Rule 
Page 7 
March 6, 2023 
 
 
provisions in Chapter 26 of the federal Clean Water Act expressly refer to treaties. See 
33 U.S.C. §§ 1253, 1268, 1271, 1320, 1321b, 1371. Fifteen provisions in Chapter 26 
use the term “Indian,” “tribe,” or “tribal.” See 33 U.S.C. §§ 1254, 1268, 1275, 1276, 
1302f, 1314, 1321, 1321a, 1321b, 1330, 1346, 1362, 1377, 1377a, 1383. But none of 
those terms appear in § 303(c), 33 U.S.C. § 1313(c), much less language that requires 
states to seek out tribal reserved rights and tailor their water quality standards to those 
protect the “unsuppressed” use of those rights. Congress would not have left USEPA 
searching the structure and objectives of the federal Clean Water Act for a hint about its 
authority concerning tribal reserved rights if authority existed. See generally Food & 
Drug Admin. v. Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp., 529 U.S. 120, 160 (2000) 
(expressing doubt that Congress would have conferred important regulatory powers in a 
“cryptic … fashion”). 
 
The proposed rule cannot be adopted because it is vague. 
The federal Clean Water Act is a national act and USEPA proposes to adopt a 
nationwide rule concerning tribal reserved rights. But treaties, statutes, or executive 
orders involving Indian tribes do not reflect nationally uniform terms and rights. And how 
could they? Tribal reserved rights arise in highly distinctive contexts with certain people, 
particular places, and a specific historical backdrop, all of which was understood 
through the different languages and cultural perspectives of distinct indigenous people. 
Looking for those nuances is exactly what the Indian canons of construction require. 
See Mille Lacs, 526 U.S. at 202 (“the history and the negotiations of the agreements is 
central to the interpretation of treaties”). That makes for a very bad fit between the 
sources of federal law that have recognized tribal reserved rights and this type of 
nationwide rule USEPA is proposing. 
That misfit is apparent from the fact that USEPA has had to omit all meaningful details 
from the rule to try to make it apply nationwide. The result is that the proposed rule, if 
adopted, would be fundamentally flawed because it is vague. See generally New York 
State Comm'n on Cable Television v. F.C.C., 669 F.2d 58, 66 (2d Cir. 1982) 
(considering whether federal agency’s order was “based upon adequately articulated 
factual and legal premises” or was vague). The weaknesses in the proposed rule are 
apparent from the fact that USEPA could easily make it more specific or tailored, but the 
agency has chosen not to make it so. See New Mexico v. EPA, 114 F.3d 290, 294 (D.C. 
Cir. 1997) (“Everything else being equal, the better a petitioner can demonstrate the 
feasibility of greater specificity the more convincing its attack on agency vagueness.”). 
 
The proposed rule fails to identify the type of reserved rights that 
states must address through their water quality standards. 
The most glaring omission in the proposed tribal reserved rights rule is its failure to 
identify the type of reserved rights that would be subject to the rule. According to 
USEPA’s public notice, “‘tribal reserved rights’ means any rights to aquatic and/or 
aquatic-dependent resources reserved or held by tribes, either expressly or implicitly, 

SUBJECT:  Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791 
USEPA’s Proposed Tribal Reserved Rights Rule 
Page 8 
March 6, 2023 
 
 
through treaties, statutes, executive orders, or other sources of Federal law.” 87 Fed. 
Reg. 74,363 (December 5, 2022) (emphasis added). 
Are the rights referenced in the proposed rule usufructuary rights? Property rights? 
Some other type of rights that may or may not be relevant in a riparian rights state? The 
proposed rule fails to make the type of right or rights clear. Indeed, the reference to 
“other sources of Federal law” that USEPA does not name suggests that this vagueness 
is intentional and intended to evade limits and predictable applications. That vagueness 
denies states the opportunity to use existing case law to clarify which rights fall within 
the scope of the proposed rule and, therefore, understand how to comply with it. 
Likewise, it is likely to lead to arbitrary and capricious decision by USEPA concerning 
which tribes have reserved rights and what those rights include. 
 
The proposed rule fails to identify rights holders states must consult. 
Michigan is currently home to twelve federally recognized Indian tribes, each of which is 
identified annually in a list published by the Bureau of Indian Affairs in the Federal 
Register. See Federally Recognized Indian Tribe List Act of 1994, Pub. L. 103–454; 108 
Stat. 4791 (November 2, 1994). Should the United States recognize additional tribes, 
EGLE need only consult that list and other formal notices by the Bureau of Indian Affairs 
to confirm the identity of the tribes. 
The State of Michigan maintains a government-to-government relationship with each 
federally recognized Indian tribe in the state. Every department of the Executive branch 
of Michigan’s government, including EGLE, has at least one staff member designated 
as a tribal liaison. See Executive Directive 2019-17 (February 21, 2020), available at 
Michigan.gov/Whitmer/News/State-Orders-and-Directives/2020/02/21/Executive-
Directive-2019-17. Both EGLE’s tribal liaisons and many of its program staff have 
experience consulting and working with the environmental staff for the Michigan tribes, 
with higher-level state and tribal officials maintaining more formal aspects of the 
relationship. USEPA would not have to include engagement as a part of the proposed 
rule for that to be part of EGLE’s approach to developing water quality standards that 
affect Michigan’s tribes. 
But USEPA has not limited the proposed rule to reserved rights issues involving 
federally recognized Indian tribes. The proposed rule leaves unanswered who USEPA 
thinks are the other rights holders who should be involved in this reserved rights 
process. USEPA does not explain how states should search for these individuals or 
groups, or how they should determine who has a legitimate claim to extant reserved 
rights. Nor does USEPA say how it expects states to resolve disputes among multiple 
individuals or groups claiming to hold reserved rights, or how it will harmonize its 
decisions about rights holders who have sought but been denied federal 
acknowledgment by Congress or the Bureau of Indian Affairs. Given the prominent roles 
that non-tribal rights holders play in the proposed rule, the vagueness is a critical flaw 
that cannot be overlooked.

The proposed rule fails to define or adequately explain key terms and 
concepts. 
The proposed rule is also vague because it fails to define key terms that provide the 
substance of what states would be required to do or protect if the rule is promulgated. 
For instance, “aquatic-dependent resource” is a core term in the proposed rule that is 
not defined. USEPA leaves unknown whether that term refers to wildlife that spends its 
life in water or if it is broad enough to encompass every bird and mammal that uses 
surface water at some point throughout its lifecycle, including for drinking. The notice of 
the proposed rule refers repeatedly to fish and wild rice, but that does not address what 
else falls under this rule and how far-reaching it could extend. 
Similarly, identifying the “unsuppressed level” of a heritage use leaves many 
ambiguities surrounding the process, including additional undefined terms that will only 
add to problems with interpretation and implementation. EGLE has concerns over terms 
like “currently reasonably achievable” and the notion of certain issues as not “feasible” 
to address, seeming to offer a potential off-ramp or redefining of unsuppressed levels. 
Hydrology changes and legacy contaminants are both examples of factors that may not 
be feasible to address through water quality standards. They also highlight additional 
concerns over the practical difficulties in implementation when both conditions are 
potentially highly relevant to the focus on fish consumption and wild rice rights noted 
throughout the preamble. 
USEPA should consider adding significantly clearer and more extensive language to 
expand the process for determining unsuppressed levels of rights. It is important to 
include clear distinctions between heritage use and unsuppressed level, and also to 
explain how far-reaching the agency’s intent is when using terms like achievability “in 
the future.” Further, USEPA should explain what conditions it considers to be not 
feasible and how those conditions are reflected under a proposed rule that water quality 
standards must be established to protect unsuppressed rights. 
Within the context of the proposed rule, providing definitions and the intent behind the 
terms “feasible” and “achievable” are particularly relevant when considering legacy 
contaminants and atmospheric deposition. Legacy contaminants and atmospheric 
deposition are largely the reason for broad fish-consumption-restriction 
recommendations in Michigan. But, because of the ambiguity in the terms USEPA uses 
in the proposed rule, it remains unclear whether these are conditions considered not 
“feasible” to address. The examples USEPA gives also leave the answer to this 
feasibility question unclear. 
A lack of feasible near-term options makes sense for these long-term legacy issues. But 
then it is difficult to understand where practical gains in fish consumption levels and 
rights advances in increased consumption of fish will be realized. While the theory of 
protecting greater consumption rates makes sense, the practical application of the 

SUBJECT:  Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791 
USEPA’s Proposed Tribal Reserved Rights Rule 
Page 10 
March 6, 2023 
 
 
proposed rule to water quality conditions that are arguably not “feasible” results in 
unlikely practical advances in realization of tribal reserved rights. Similarly, USEPA has 
provided no basis to understand how the unsuppressed use of natural resources it 
seeks to protect differs from the existing designated use to protect wildlife and fish in 
§ 303(2)(A) of the federal Clean Water Act, 33 U.S.C. § 1313(2)(A). 
 
The proposed rule fails to offer adequate examples for 
implementation. 
USEPA offers three options for protecting tribal reserved rights, including: 
• Adopting designated uses that recognize and identify tribal reserved right; 
• Adopting criteria protective of tribal reserved rights under existing designated 
uses; or 
• Utilizing anti-degradation policies (including designating waters as outstanding 
state resources) to comply with the proposed rule. 
While USEPA may believe it is offering states flexibility by offering  these options they 
remain vague, particularly in areas where state jurisdiction and tribal reserved rights 
overlap. These options are likely to create significant issues in the Great Lakes basin 
and increase regulatory uncertainty that states, tribes, the public and the regulated 
community face. 
Further, Michigan is a riparian rights state with abundant water and aquatic resources 
and water quality standards set according to guidance specific to the Great Lakes basin. 
In contrast, many states with tribal communities are located in the arid west and operate 
within a prior appropriation system of water rights. The issues involving water quality 
and aquatic resource availability in Michigan can be very different from other states. 
USEPA has provided no examples that illustrate how a state like Michigan could 
implement any of these options and achieve the sort of feasible improvement the 
proposed rule would require. 
 
The proposed rule appears to be poorly integrated with USEPA’s 
future rulemaking. 
USEPA has suggested for many years that it will be adopting baseline water quality 
standards for inside of Indian country. Presumably, USEPA will adopt standards it 
believes will protect tribal reserved rights inside of Indian country. But USEPA suggests 
that this proposed rule would apply both inside and outside of Indian country without 
explaining how it would work with future baseline water quality standards. For States 
like Michigan, which have more checkerboarded trust lands than consolidated Indian 
reservations with defined external boundaries, this is critical information that it should 
have in hand so it can give comprehensive comments on this proposed rule.

The proposed rule improperly attempts to impose a new nationwide 
environmental servitude on all Indian treaties, statutes, executive orders, 
and other federal authority without supporting legal authority. 
One of the central features of USEPA’s proposed rule is the requirement that water 
quality standards protect “unsuppressed” uses of aquatic and aquatic-dependent 
resources. In USEPA’s view, tribal rights reserved under Indian treaties, statutes, 
executive orders, and other federal authority require all states to maximize the amount 
of the natural resources available to those who exercise the tribal reserved rights. 
But there is no case law holding that states must adopt water quality standards to 
achieve that end, i.e., maximizing available resources for tribes to satisfy their reserved 
rights. Nor has USEPA identified any scientific data that demonstrates going through 
the process of identifying water quality at a particular period in history would be possible 
or that adopting water quality standards to reflect historical levels would lead to 
maximizing the available resources. Instead, to adopt unsuppressed uses as a goal, the 
agency relies on the Ninth Circuit’s decision in what is known as the Culverts Case, 
United States v. Washington, 853 F.3d 946 (9th Cir. 2017), aff’d by an equally divided 
court 138 S.Ct. 1832 (2018). Yet, there are many reasons why the Culverts Case does 
not support the proposed rule. 
 
The Culverts Case does not address water quality standards and 
does not endorse the concept of a general environmental duty or 
servitude. 
The Culverts Case does not substantively address water quality standards. Rather, it is 
one small part of more than fifty years of litigation concerning the fishing rights that 
tribes living in the Pacific northwest reserved to themselves in land cession treaties their 
ancestors signed in 1854 and 1855 (the Stevens Treaties). See Washington, 853 F.3d 
at 953–54, 958–60. In 2001, twenty-one tribes claimed that the State of Washington 
was violating the Stevens Treaties by building barrier culverts that harmed salmon in a 
variety of ways that decreased the tribal harvest. See id.at 954, 960. Nothing in the 
decisions by the courts in that case imposed on Washington any duty to improve water 
quality to maximize the availability of fish to catch, much less to return water quality 
standards to what they were in the 1850s when the tribes signed the Stevens Treaties. 
Further, the Culverts Case decision did not endorse a general environmental duty or 
environmental servitude to prevent pollution of water resources as a treaty obligation. 
The United States had sought to establish a generalized environmental duty in an 
earlier phase of litigation involving the Stevens Treaties, but the courts rejected its 
claim. Washington, 853 F.3d at 959. As the Ninth Circuit explained, the “environmental 
issue” was “too broad and varied to be resolved in a general and undifferentiated 
fashion, and that the issue of human-caused environmental degradation must be 
resolved in the context of particularized disputes.” Id. (emphasis added). The federal 
courts only waded into the barrier culverts issue years later because it was a narrower 

SUBJECT:  Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791 
USEPA’s Proposed Tribal Reserved Rights Rule 
Page 12 
March 6, 2023 
 
 
issue with particularized facts concerning a single state, single type of problem, and 
single type of natural resource (fish). See Id. at 961. 
But USEPA’s proposed rule attempts to establish a general environmental duty for fifty 
states plus additional territories, 574 tribes, 370 treaties, and countless statutes, 
executive orders, and other federal authority in a single rule concerning an unknown 
range of natural resources and without any specific facts to consider. The narrow 
reasoning the Ninth Circuit adopted to reach the barrier culverts issue does not support 
adopting this broad proposed rule. 
 
The Culverts Case involved a true Indian understanding analysis, 
which the proposed rule does not include. 
Nor can USEPA rely on the Culverts Case as authority for the process it prescribes for 
determining tribal reserved rights. From all appearances, USEPA intends for the 
proposed rule to fast-track or shorten the analysis that determines whether a treaty, 
statute, or executive order reserves rights because there is a very short statutory 
timeline for developing water quality standards. The review in § 303(c) occurs every 
three years. 33 U.S.C. § 1313(c)(1). USEPA has only sixty days to review a state’s 
proposed water quality standards, with an additional ninety days to specify the new 
water quality standards if the agency does not approve the state’s proposed standards. 
33 U.S.C. § 1313(c)(3). 
But the Ninth Circuit did not suggest that there is any shortcut around a traditional treaty 
analysis that considers historical and anthropological evidence to get at the Indian 
understanding of a treaty if its plain language is ambiguous. Instead, the courts in the 
Culverts Case conducted a traditional Indian understanding analysis. That analysis, 
which involved work by experts, considered aspects of the trade language the tribes 
spoke, statements made by the Indian delegates to the treaty council, and assurances 
made by federal representatives. Washington, 853 F.3d at 963–64. 
Perhaps Washington already had the materials and experts they needed for the treaty 
arguments regarding barrier culverts due to its decades of litigation. But other states, 
including Michigan, would have to start at the beginning when analyzing the treaties, 
statutes, and executive orders within the scope of the proposed rule, regardless of what 
conclusion it might reach on the existence of tribal reserved rights. There is very little 
likelihood that the type of research and analysis the Ninth Circuit relied on in the 
Culverts Case would fit within USEPA’s abbreviated timeline. And nothing in the 
Culverts Case or other case law would excuse USEPA and the states from doing that 
hard work.

USEPA’s Proposed Tribal Reserved Rights Rule

March 6, 2023 
 
 
 
The Culverts Case does not support the proposed rule because it is 
not precedent. 
Even if there were some persuasive reasoning in the Ninth Circuit’s decision in the 
Culverts Case supporting of the proposed rule, that decision is not precedent on which 
USEPA can rely. While the USEPA suggested that the United States Supreme Court 
had “aff’d” (meaning affirmed) the Ninth Circuit’s decision, that is not true. 87 Fed. Reg. 
74,363, n.13. The Supreme Court issued a per curiam opinion in which it stated that the 
“judgment is affirmed by an equally divided Court.” Washington, 138 S.Ct. at 1832. 
Affirming a lower court decision and affirming it by an equally divided court are two 
different judicial results. 
As the Supreme Court itself explained more than a century ago: 
Under the precedents of this court, and, as seems justified by reason as 
well as by authority, an affirmance by an equally divided court is, as 
between the parties, a conclusive determination and adjudication of the 
matter adjudged; but the principles of law involved not having been agreed 
upon by a majority of the court sitting prevents the case from becoming an 
authority for the determination of other cases, either in this or in inferior 
courts.” 
Hertz v. Woodman, 218 U.S. 205, 213–14, (1910) (emphasis added). In short, a 
majority of Supreme Court justices did not agree that the Ninth Circuit correctly 
decided the Culverts Case nor that it erred, which means it is not binding 
authority on anyone other than the parties. 
 
USEPA has not considered any of the authority adverse to the 
proposed rule. 
USEPA has also seemingly failed to consider any of the case law that is adverse to its 
proposition that treaties and all other sources of federal law that reserve rights to natural 
resources include an environmental servitude that extends to water quality standards. 
See, e.g., Menominee Indian Tribe of Wisconsin v. Thompson, 922 F. Supp. 184 (W.D. 
Wis. 1996), aff’d, 161 F.3d 449 (7th Cir. 1998). 
The problem that the tribe in Menominee, and now the USEPA, is attempting to fix is not 
one that case law in this context supports. As the district court in Menominee explained: 
The interference with plaintiff's [sturgeon] harvest comes not from other 
fishers but from the encroachment of industry, commerce and residential 
development that are the accompaniments of the westward expansion of 
European settlement and economic growth. In this respect, this case is 
like cases in which other tribes have sought to articulate a right to an 
environmental servitude that would require states to protect fishing 

SUBJECT:  Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791 
USEPA’s Proposed Tribal Reserved Rights Rule 
Page 14 
March 6, 2023 
 
 
habitats from environmental degradation. Although a number of 
commentators have advanced the idea that such a right should be 
recognized in order to protect treaty fishing rights, … the concept has not 
fared well in the courts. 
Menominee, 922 F. Supp. at 215–16 (emphasis added and internal citations omitted). 
The district court in Menominee went on to discuss the cases where the parties sought 
to counter the effects of environmental degradation on the availability of fish. 
Menominee, 922 F. Supp. at 216. It concluded that the cases did not require ensuring 
that more resources were available to tribes so that they could increase their catch; the 
cases merely required reallocating the share of the existing catch so that the treaty 
fishers could obtain their fair share of the harvest. Id. Suffice it to say, an administrative 
rule that governs water quality is completely unrelated to reallocating the shares of a 
harvest and outside the scope of USEPA’s authority under the federal Clean Water Act. 
The district court in Menominee also concluded that there are only two potential 
remedies if a tribe loses a “guaranteed usufructuary right.” Menominee, 922 F. Supp. at 
216. The tribe could seek “monetary compensation for the lost opportunity from 
Congress, the Court of Claims, or the now-defunct Indian Claims Commission[.]” Id. 
That remedy holds the United States responsible for the promises it made in a treaty, 
statute, executive order, or other federal authority. Alternatively, the tribe could “sue for 
an injunction preventing the construction of a dam or other obstruction or requiring that 
it be removed.” Id. That remedy guarantees the rights holder physical access to the 
resource. See, e.g., United States v. Winans, 198 U.S. 371, 381–82 (1905) (Yakima 
Indians were entitled to cross private lands to enjoy their treaty-reserved right to fish, 
which had been contemplated when the treaty was negotiated); Winters v. United 
States, 207 U.S. 564, 565 (1908) (non-Indians upstream of the Fort Belknap 
Reservation were barred from diverting water flowage in the Milk River because it 
denied the tribes residing on the reservation access to the irrigation water they needed 
and subverted the purposes of the treaty that reserved the Indian reservation). 
But USEPA’s proposed regulation does not fit in either category of remedy or 
meet the aims of either remedy. USEPA is not authorizing claims against the 
United States, which it could not do. Nor is it granting injunctive relief in a specific 
set of facts where access to a natural resource has been blocked. Further, for 
states in the Great Lakes region with separate water quality standards guidance 
from the rest of the country, it is questionable whether stricter and less obtainable 
water quality standards (e.g., for a widespread contaminant like mercury) will 
make a positive difference for tribal reserved rights at all. 
Finally, USEPA has failed to consider one of the bedrock principles of the Indian 
canons of construction that is adverse to what it seeks to accomplish with the 
proposed rule:  modern decisionmakers cannot change the historical bargains 
struck between the United States and Indian tribes, even to achieve laudable 

SUBJECT:  Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791 
USEPA’s Proposed Tribal Reserved Rights Rule 
Page 15 
March 6, 2023 
 
 
goals. As the Supreme Court has said, “[C]ourts cannot ignore plain language 
that, viewed in historical context and given a fair appraisal, clearly runs counter to 
a tribe's later claims.” Oregon Dep’t of Fish & Wildlife v. Klamath Indian Tribe, 
473 U.S. 753, 774 (1985) (internal quotation marks and citation omitted). That 
principle builds on earlier precedent, including Choctaw Nation of Indians v. 
United States, 318 U.S. 423, 432 (1943), in which the Supreme Court explained, 
“Indian treaties cannot be re-written or expanded beyond their clear terms to 
remedy a claimed injustice or to achieve the asserted understanding of the 
parties.” See also Confederated Bands of Ute Indians v. United States, 330 U.S. 
169, 179 (1947) (“[W]e cannot, under the guise of interpretation, create 
Presidential authority where there was none, nor rewrite congressional acts so as 
to make them mean something they obviously were not intended to mean.”). In 
short, “Times change and people change, but treaties do not.” Menominee, 
161 F.3d at 462–63 (Wood, J., concurring). 
Clearly, USEPA is attempting to address modern problems facing Indian tribes 
and other indigenous people, like climate change. See 87 Fed. Reg. 74,366. But 
it cannot provide that help by ignoring the unique Indian understanding of 
individual treaties, statutes, and executive orders to establish a broad, nationally 
uniform right to certain actions involving water quality standards. Many of today’s 
pressing issues would have been entirely foreign both to the federal and 
indigenous negotiators of the treaties, statutes, and executive orders that 
reserved rights to aquatic resources in the eighteenth, nineteenth, and first part 
of the twentieth century. 
It is tempting to think that stretching those authorities to address water quality is 
permissible because it may benefit tribal and indigenous communities. But that is 
not a permissible way to interpret treaties, statutes, and executive orders 
reserving rights and certainly not something that Congress endorsed when it 
enacted § 511(a)(3). 
 
The details of the proposed rule are unworkable. 
The general vagueness and lack of detail in the proposed rule leaves EGLE with great 
concern for how USEPA will implement the rule if it is promulgated. There are significant 
concerns over USEPA’s undefined expectations (e.g., does the reserved rights analysis 
occur once or in every triennial review?) and timeframe necessary to adequately 
incorporate this rule into the triennial review process given the level of effort this will 
require. 
Scientists and program experts who work in federal Clean Water Act programs lack the 
expertise, understanding, and historical context on tribal rights to carry out the 
obligations in this proposed rule. They have every reason to be concerned about the 
distinction between identifying safe levels of pollutants to protect uses, which is within 
the scope of what they do, and guaranteeing the availability of those resources, which is 

SUBJECT:  Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791 
USEPA’s Proposed Tribal Reserved Rights Rule 
Page 16 
March 6, 2023 
 
 
not part of their responsibilities. The definitions critical to understanding the proposed 
rule and its implementation are highly subjective and ultimately lacking. 
 
USEPA would better protect tribal reserved rights if it focused on 
states’ existing water quality authorities, such as site-specific 
standards.  
USEPA would lend more assistance to tribes and other rights holders seeking to protect 
their reserved rights if the agency focused on authorities that currently exist rather than 
promulgating the proposed rule requiring state staff trained in water quality and 
environmental protection to interpret treaties, statutes, executive orders, or other 
unnamed federal authority. For example, in keeping with 40 C.F.R. Part 132, Michigan’s 
Part 4 Water Quality Standards, Mich. Admin. Code R. (“Rule”) 323.1041 et seq., allow 
site-specific water quality values to be derived for toxic substances under Rule 
323.1057. The rule allows the site-specific standard to reflect localized environmental 
conditions that might affect aquatic life or wildlife values. See Rule 323.1057(2)(r) and 
Rule 323.1057(3)(n). It also allows the standard to reflect localized environmental 
conditions or human exposure in developing human health values. See Rule 
323.1057(4)(h). These authorities, which are aimed at protecting both natural resources 
and the humans who use them or are exposed to them, already exist in Michigan 
without any further action by USEPA. 
USEPA should review state rules to determine which states have this legal authority to 
adopt site-specific standards. If that authority does not exist in some states, it may 
consider recommending rule updates that would allow states to develop site-specific 
criteria to address the tribal communities and the resources that USEPA seeks to 
protect with this proposed rule. The agency can also provide guidance to states on how 
to solicit and navigate tribal requests for site-specific standards, as well as supply 
additional funding and guidance to tribes so that they can effectively participate in these 
existing frameworks for addressing their individual problems or needs. 
To date, EGLE has not received any formal submittal from a tribe to develop site-
specific criteria. This is likely an issue related to a lack of awareness of site-specific 
water quality standards as an available option, as well as the limited staff capacity that 
tribes have to utilize this opportunity. Unfortunately, the proposed rule overlooks site-
specific standards while also failing to raise tribal awareness of site-specific standards 
or to enhance the tribal staff capacity to advocate for their needs with state regulators. 
This is truly a missed opportunity. 
 
There may be no relationship between water quality standards and 
the availability of resources. 
The proposed rule conflates the notion of identifying water quality standards that are 
protective of tribal reserved rights with that of ‘availability’ of aquatic and aquatic-
dependent resources. This pushes the proposed rule outside the bounds of the federal 

SUBJECT:  Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791 
USEPA’s Proposed Tribal Reserved Rights Rule 
Page 17 
March 6, 2023 
 
 
Clean Water Act and the state regulators who implement it into the roles and 
responsibilities of other state agencies, at best. While work developing appropriate 
water quality standards to provide supportive conditions for various uses is expected 
under the federal Clean Water Act, the ‘availability’ of those aquatic and aquatic-
dependent resources is often dictated by issues beyond water quality. 
For example, the Great Lakes basin has experienced significant shifts in the availability 
of historic resources due to the irreversible changes that come with millions of additional 
people living on the landscape and the results of their impacts and decisions, including:   
• Widespread land use changes through forestry; 
• Agricultural, residential, commercial, and industrial development practices; 
• Invasive species;  
• Species loss and exotic replacement, e.g., extensive long-term stocking of pacific 
and European salmonids; 
• Stock management decisions by fish and game agencies; and 
• Broad fish and wildlife consumption restrictions based on historic and/or 
atmospheric deposition of bioaccumulative chemicals that come from within and 
outside the region. 
Tying protective water quality standards to the availability of a resource inappropriately 
links the federal Clean Water Act’s tools to practical realities that are beyond its scope. 
 
USEPA does not use sound scientific principles when it merely 
assumes that waterbodies historically had better quality and that 
those conditions are still achievable in all cases. 
USEPA’s proposed rule idealizes the historical quality of waters of the United States, 
even during eras when human uses were unregulated, and no treatment was available. 
It has not cited a single scientific study that suggests that water quality in the 
eighteenth, nineteenth, and early twentieth century was uniformly pristine across the 
country. It has not considered the types and locations of historical industry and other 
impacts to resources. It has not attempted to identify the historical events involving the 
negative impacts to the availability of natural resources that forced some indigenous 
people to enter into treaties or other agreements. Nor has it pointed to a study that 
demonstrates a correlation between the time a treaty, statute, or executive order 
becomes effective and the maximum availability of an aquatic or aquatic-dependent 
resource. In short, there may have been better times in history for the availability of 
aquatic and aquatic-dependent resources for tribes with reserved rights, but the 
proposed rule has not found a scientific way to locate that time or pinpoint those places. 

SUBJECT:  Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791 
USEPA’s Proposed Tribal Reserved Rights Rule 
Page 18 
March 6, 2023 
 
 
Even more importantly, it is highly questionable that adopting any particular water 
quality standards would achieve historical conditions for many aquatic and aquatic-
dependent resources, at least within any reasonable timeframe. The changes that have 
occurred over time that affect water quality are, to a significant extent, beyond USEPA’s 
ability to fix with this proposed rule. Species loss, exotic species replacement, invasive 
species, permanently altered hydrology and connectivity such as land use changes, 
dams, climate change related precipitation changes, and legacy and atmospheric 
contamination all have significant implications for meeting historical targets that may no 
longer be possible, even with appropriate water quality standards. The proposed rule 
does little to acknowledge the practical application of a changed environment when 
aspiring to regain historical conditions. 
 
The proposed rule would impose substantial and unwarranted 
burdens on states. 
EGLE expects the proposed rule’s broad application could be particularly burdensome 
on states and their program staff who develop water quality standards. A wide range of 
issues make this proposed rule more burdensome than other regulations, including: 
• Program staff’s lack of expertise in tribal treaty rights and historical matters, 
particularly within a water quality standards program context; 
• The difficulty vetting and understanding potential reserved rights and their 
historical context; 
• The challenge of translating historical observations about aquatic and aquatic-
dependent resources into actionable data; 
• The effort to clarify meaningful water quality conditions that may be impactful; 
• The complexity of identifying the gap in water quality standards needed to 
support aspirational targets; and  
• The procedures states must follow to propose water quality standard changes. 
The impact this proposed rule will have on states will extend beyond a rule-making 
process. States like Michigan with multiple tribes, many different treaties, 
unconsolidated Indian country, jurisdictional overlap with tribes and other states, and 
the myriad of unknowns discussed earlier in this letter make moving forward in a 
meaningful way under the proposed rule extremely difficult. 
Additionally, the USEPA’s Economic Analysis is inadequate in its potential reflection of 
the coordination efforts between states and tribes if the intent is to have a thorough, 
meaningful, respectful, accurate process that results in change. Similarly, although the 

SUBJECT:  Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791 
USEPA’s Proposed Tribal Reserved Rights Rule 
Page 19 
March 6, 2023 
 
 
impacts of the proposed rulemaking are uncertain on regulated entities, it is critical to 
acknowledge that there will be an impact and it may be significant. 
 
The proposed rule will lead to unnecessary litigation or conflict between 
tribes and states. 
EGLE finds itself in a very difficult position with this proposed rule. On the one hand, 
Michigan is working toward a better relationship with Indian tribes concerning water and 
aquatic resources. Michigan also has a markedly different approach to reserved rights 
than it had in the past. For instance, in December 2022, Michigan joined the United 
States and four out of five tribes with treaty-reserved usufructuary rights under the 1836 
Treaty of Washington to propose a new consent decree concerning fishing in the Great 
Lakes, which would have been unthinkable just a few decades ago. 
On the other hand, the triennial review process leaves such little time to address 
reserved rights that it seems inevitable that at least some states will be forced to 
challenge aspects of the proposed rule simply to be able to resolve the reserved rights 
issues consistently with controlling authority. Alternatively, states may be forced to 
consider challenges to the rule to be able to abide by legally binding agreements, 
including ones under state law, that control tribal—state relations regarding reserved 
rights to natural resources. 
The prospect of litigation is counterproductive; it simply diverts tribal, state, and federal 
resources from protecting water and aquatic resources and forces these governments 
to battle with each other. EGLE has searched the proposed rule to find some alternative 
that would allow federal, tribal, and state sovereigns to find common ground with 
respect to how water quality standards can and should be used to protect tribal 
communities and indigenous people generally, even where they disagree on the 
question of reserved rights. For instance, an option for developing a reasonable plan to 
identify reserved rights, flexibility in setting standards, or the ability to take interim or 
transitional steps. But no such provisions exist in the rule, which suggests that this 
proposed rule may seek to protect reserved rights, but it may ultimately fail to protect 
people and aquatic resources, or at least unnecessarily delay what is possible to 
implement in return for resolving historical questions. And in the process, states may not 
only challenge USEPA, but tribes will be forced to intervene to be able to defend what 
they believe are their reserved rights. This lack of any viable alternatives to litigation to 
resolve disputes is a critical deficiency in the proposed rule and one that must be 
corrected. 
And to be clear, it is not legally adequate for USEPA to become the final arbiter of the 
reserved rights issue. Due to its federal trust responsibilities, USEPA is not qualified to 
act as a neutral decision maker, particularly in an area in which it has no expertise. 
Moreover, USEPA must be aware that the details of this proposed rule have not gone 
through the discussion and vetting with states that it deserves so that it remains within 

SUBJECT:  Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791 
USEPA’s Proposed Tribal Reserved Rights Rule 
Page 20 
March 6, 2023 
 
 
the scope of the agency’s statutory authority and has had some of its least workable 
features fixed. Notably, when EGLE staff have talked to USEPA staff about the 
proposed rule, they have had no answers to key questions. Even USEPA knows it is 
missing key pieces of information, which is why it solicits more information on several 
topics in the public notice. These and other problems are only compounded by the fact 
that USEPA rushed to publish its public notice, allowing only ninety days for public 
comment even though the first thirty days of the comment period were at the end of the 
year, when many state and tribal employees are away from the office. Had USEPA 
engaged with the states on the details of the rule it was contemplating or allowed more 
time for comment, EGLE may have been able to provide more targeted comments that 
could have helped avoid the many problems in the proposed rule. 
 
Conclusion 
At the beginning of this letter, EGLE suggested that USEPA not pursue this rule and 
should, instead, take three steps. Those steps are better calculated to improving the 
challenging water quality issues that tribes face within the scope of authority that the 
federal Clean Water Act provides USEPA. 
First, EGLE would look forward to partnering with USEPA Region 5 and Michigan tribes 
to identify the water quality issues that tribal communities face in the state and that can 
be addressed under existing authority, such as site-specific standards. There are likely 
other opportunities for EGLE and Michigan tribes to partner with other Great Lakes 
states and tribes to capitalize on each other’s experiences and ideas to find solutions to 
pressing problems without delay. 
Second, USEPA should seek amendments to the federal Clean Water Act to obtain the 
authority to address modern and emerging threats to tribal communities. If USEPA 
works closely with both tribes and states, USEPA will stand the best chance of 
determining what is truly lawful, workable, and helpful for the long-term protection of 
tribal communities and their water quality needs. 
Finally, USEPA should develop a far narrower rule or guidance that provides a 
framework for USEPA’s staff to assess and respond to evidence in the 60/90-day 
process that water quality standards in a particular state violate specific tribal reserved 
rights to avoid any conflict between the federal Clean Water Act and a treaty or other 
binding federal law. Because the other steps that EGLE proposes deal with both 
immediate and long-term goals for protecting water quality, aquatic resources, and tribal 
communities, this narrower rule can be faithful to the Indian canons of construction and 
the prohibition against altering treaties without risking that tribal water quality issues will 
remain unremedied.

RE:  Water Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights 
(Docket#: EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791)  
 
Please accept the following comments from the Center for Biological Diversity (“Center”) on the 
Environmental Protection Agency’s (“EPA”) revisions to Water Quality Standards (“WQS”) to 
protect tribal reserved rights. These long overdue revisions affirm that the EPA has a broader 
authority to set WQS than previously acknowledged, and the agency must leverage this authority 
to protect culturally important and imperiled aquatic animal and plant species, such as salmon, 
the Clear Lake hitch, and the tule plant. 
 
We generally support the EPA’s revisions to protect tribal reserved rights as well as its 
acknowledgement that tribes hold many such rights “within and outside their reservation 
boundaries.” By proposing these regulations, the EPA seems to acknowledge its broad authority 
to set WQS in a way that pushes the envelope, and we encourage it to continue down this path 
and make sure the revisions are appropriately implemented to protect species nationwide. If 
anything, these revisions mean that the EPA must be more protective of endangered, imperiled, 
and culturally significant aquatic species throughout their range.  
 
Water quality issues are suppressing water-dependent species that indigenous peoples rely upon 
for cultural, spiritual, and economic purposes. For example, salmon are a culturally significant 
species for many Pacific Northwest Tribes, who are, by treaty, entitled to collect a moderate 
amount of coho and Chinook salmon in “usual and accustomed areas,” but range wide, degraded 
and impaired water quality threatens both the existence of the salmon and the way of life of the 
Tribes.1 In another example, the Clear Lake hitch is a culturally significant species for various 
Pomo Tribes surrounding Clear Lake, California, who have depended on the Clear Lake hitch for 
sustenance for generations, but now, the effects of water pollution in the watershed and toxic 
algal blooms in the lake have pushed the sacred minnow to the edge of extinction.2 As a third 
example, the Pomo Tribes around Clear Lake also rely on the tule plant as a material to make 
clothes, shelter, baskets, and boats, but high levels of mercury in Clear Lake put tribal members 
at higher risk of mouth cancer and dental issues—the cultural practice of basketry involves 
placing the tule reed into the mouth.3 This is why EPA must set water quality standards as

protective as possible of water quality to support tribal reserved water rights as well as the 
culturally and biologically important aquatic species that are at risk by rampant water pollution. 
 
I. 
The WQS Provide the EPA with Broader Authority Than Previously Recognized to 
Protect Water Quality 
 
We generally support the EPA’s assertion that Section 303(c) of the Clean Water Act (“CWA”) 
must be broadly read, necessitating the protection of tribal reserved rights unsuppressed by water 
quality or water availability. We also support the EPA’s inclusion of additional definitions and 
clarification in the regulations to define tribal reserved rights and ensure that tribes are protected 
to the same risk level as the general population. Given that the EPA has previously asserted that 
it was “unnecessary” to protect tribal reserved rights and that states could already protect tribal 
reserved rights under existing regulations, the EPA is right to explicitly acknowledge that the 
WQS can be used to protect tribal reserved rights.  
 
As the EPA notes, “protection of such rights falls within the ambit of these broad statutory 
directions and objectives” of the CWA.4 The CWA’s structure, objectives, and discretion 
afforded to the EPA provide ample room to consider and give effect to all applicable reserved 
rights. While protecting tribal reserved rights is a critical step to “restore and maintain the 
chemical, physical, and biological integrity of the Nation’s waters,” the proposed revisions 
clearly indicate that the EPA has a broader authority to set water quality standards than 
previously acknowledged or exerted.  
 
There are other situations where the EPA has implied that existing regulations are adequate to 
protect an interest where an explicit clarification is warranted. Despite regulations requiring that 
the EPA ensure WQS are protective of endangered and threatened species, the EPA has a history 
of failing to consult with expert wildlife agencies to ensure that any changes do not jeopardize 
the species.5 Many pollutants with identified impacts to endangered species have been revised 
without consultation.6 The WQS program is one of the only ways to avoid piecemeal destruction 
of species and habitat, and the EPA should endeavor to use this program to proactively conserve 
species.  
 
II. 
The Proposed Rule Necessitates Revising Water Quality Criteria to Protect Listed 
Salmon Throughout their Range. 
 
In the Pacific Northwest, treaties explicitly reserved for many tribes the right to fish in their 
“usual and accustomed” fishing grounds and stations both within and outside their reservation 
boundaries.7 Salmon have sustained indigenous peoples for thousands of years, and many tribes

(Nov. 28, 2022). 
5 EPA Weakens Water Quality Standards for Harmful Selenium (July 12, 2016)

6 Legal Action Launched to Strengthen Water Quality in Vermont, New Hampshire, Maine, Connecticut (Oct. 26,

7 U.S. DOI, Fishing Rights of the Yurok and Hoopa Valley Tribes at 23. 

3 
 
depend on salmon spiritually, culturally, and economically.8 Salmon are also a dietary staple, 
putting tribal members at greater risk of harm when eating fish laden with toxic chemicals that 
bioaccumulate in salmon.9 While many populations of salmon like coho and Chinook salmon 
that Northwest tribes traditionally relied upon are now listed as threatened, authorized tribes in 
certain situations can continue to collect listed salmon without violating take prohibitions 
adopted under section 9 of the Endangered Species Act (“ESA”).10 Listed Chinook salmon “are 
harvested intentionally and incidentally” under harvest management plans that significantly 
restrict time and place of operation while putting a premium on recovering the species.11 
 
The EPA envisions two situations where WQS may need to be adjusted – human health criteria 
in recognition of fish consumption and where a reserved right is not accounted for, but could 
appear in the future as a result of restoration efforts. After 25 years, the EPA finally restored 
quintessential human health criteria that accounted for indigenous communities’ increased fish 
consumption. However, the aquatic life criteria – a critical metric necessary to protect the 
abundance of salmon – has not been updated since 1986. Since the purpose of these revisions is 
to ensure “the exercise of the tribal reserved rights unsuppressed by water quality or availability 
of the aquatic or aquatic-dependent resource,” it makes sense to consider situations where 
aquatic life criteria must be adjusted to protect culturally important resources like salmon. 
Availability of fish is also something the EPA specifically notes that it will consider in 
determining whether a right is suppressed. 
 
Protecting the right to fish in the “usual and accustomed areas” also implicates updated 
protections that consider the entire range of the salmon. Most Pacific salmonids are anadromous, 
migrating from the ocean upstream to the freshwater streams of their birth, growing through six 
basic life history stages, each with a different chemical sensitivity. Therefore, an aquatic life 
criteria that just focuses on adult salmon in the ocean would fail to consider stream-bound fry or 
eggs in gravel beds. Criteria that consider range-wide pollutants and the life-history of the 
salmon are critical to ensuring the recovery of these species as well as the unsuppressed right to 
fish at usual and accustomed areas both on and off reservation. Through consultation with the 
National Marine Fisheries Service, the EPA could realize these protections. 
 
The Northwest tribes have always been strong advocates of fish and wildlife, having repeatedly 
restrained harvest while maintaining and monitoring fisheries in the interest of conservation. 
These efforts will be negated, and tribal reserved rights suppressed, if the EPA does not improve 
the aquatic life criteria.

III. 
WQS Must Ensure the Health of the Clear Lake Hitch.  
 
The Clear Lake hitch is a large minnow found only in Clear Lake and its tributaries. The hitch 
has strong cultural significance for several indigenous Pomo tribes of the Clear Lake region that 
rely on the hitch (or “chi”) for spiritual purposes, traditions, and as a primary food source.12 
Historically, the hitch likely numbered in the millions, but the species has plummeted so far in 
recent years that extinction is a distinct possibility if swift action is not taken.  
 
Clear Lake is the largest freshwater lake named to the California list of impaired water bodies. 
The water has been polluted historically and contains remnant toxic pesticides and mercury from 
a nearby superfund site, while unfettered agricultural runoff causes harmful algal blooms that 
suffocate the lake and shut down recreation and cultural practices.13 The tribes have led the way 
on water quality monitoring around the lake to track ecotoxicology, but they expect and rely on 
the federal government to carry out its responsibilities in managing the land, water, and 
wildlife.14 Four species of culturally significant fish – fish found nowhere else in the world – 
have already been pushed to extinction in the area. The Clear Lake hitch is fifth on the chopping 
block, and while the state of California listed the minnow as threatened in 2014, the hitch is on 
such a steep decline that tribes have requested emergency protections under the federal 
Endangered Species Act. 
 
President Biden has acknowledged that Indigenous Knowledge is to be considered in policy and 
agency decision making, and the EPA encourages the consideration and incorporation of any 
Indigenous Knowledge that is freely provided by the tribes.15 While EPA’s proposed WQS 
rulemaking purports to benefit tribes by improving the ability to maintain traditions and reduce 
health risks, the agency cannot do so unless it actually incorporate such knowledge in its water 
quality standards. Many tribes in the area are federally recognized tribes experienced with 
federally reserved water rights, and the EPA cannot ignore the history and connection to the 
hitch when it is given a chance to in this rulemaking.  
 
Jesse Gonzalez, vice chair of Scotts Valley Band of Pomo Indians recalls catching chi as a young 
boy, but fears that “future generations will never have that opportunity.”16 The Pomo tribes of 
the Clear Lake have a right to collect and consumer this fish unsuppressed by water quality, and 
the EPA should make every effort to protect this right. 
 
IV. 
WQS Must Account for Traditional Uses of the Tule Plant to Protect Indigenous 
Health.

Tules are reed-like aquatic plants that have been a major component of the wetlands that 
surrounded Clear Lake for hundreds of thousands of years.17 Intact tule wetlands provide 
important habitat for juvenile Clear Lake hitch, though 85 percent of wetland nursery habitat has 
been removed post-colonization. The tule plant has long played an important role for indigenous 
communities in Lake County, with the Pomo tribes in the area using tule to make clothes, 
shelters, boats, and baskets. 18 Tules were also used for food and medicine.  
 
The Pomo tradition of using the tule for basketry is a clear example of a differential health risk 
for tribes that must be considered by the EPA when setting WQS. Clear Lake suffers from 
elevated mercury levels due to a nearby superfund site. According to Meyo Marryfo of the 
Eastern Pomo from the Clear Lake Basin: 
 
You put poison into a land you are harming the whole lake ecology. So Pomos are 
a basketry people, which means our plants go in our mouths when we process our 
basketry. So, as we are doing this, we are putting possibly contaminated things 
into our mouths. So, you’re then seeing mouth cancers, you’re seeing things that 
are happening with your teeth.19 
 
While declining abundance of the tule is also an issue, the processing of tule reeds to make 
basketry presents a unique differential health risk that the EPA must consider. It is also a 
situation where Indigenous Knowledge is critical to making sure WQS are sufficiently 
protective. Given the proposed revisions and the Biden administration’s commitment the 
valuable contributions of the Indigenous Knowledge that tribal nations and indigenous peoples 
have gained and passed down for generations, the EPA should ensure these health risks are 
considered in revising WQS.  
 
V. 
The EPA Must Expeditiously Update its 1985 Guidelines. 
 
We remain concerned that the EPA continues to rely and build upon the 1985 Guidelines for 
Deriving Numerical National Water Quality Criteria for the Protection of Aquatic Organisms 
and Their Uses (“1985 Guidelines”), an out-of-date methodology that has allowed the agency to 
justify a higher threshold that has been excoriated by the scientific community.20 The EPA has 
indicated in previous rulemakings that it intends to update its 1985 Guidelines, but since these 
guidelines are still used and cited to in the interim to rationalize maximum concentrations, we 
urge the EPA to update these guidelines as expeditiously as possible. 
 
VI. 
Conclusions 
 
As the EPA recognizes, “tribal reserved rights to use and access natural and cultural resources 
are an intrinsic part of tribal life and are of deep cultural, economic, and subsistence importance

While the proposed revisions should be leveraged to protect listed salmon, the Clear Lake hitch,

I write on behalf of the Tribal Council of The Confederated Tribes of the Warm Springs 
Reservation of Oregon (“CTWS” or “Tribe”) to provide comments on the Environmental 
Protection Agency’s (“EPA”) proposed rule to revise Clean Water Act (“CWA”) regulations on 
water quality standards to protect tribal reserved rights (“Proposed Rule”). The Tribe appreciates 
the EPA’s efforts to ensure that the CWA regulations are consistent with established principles 
concerning the supremacy of tribal reserved rights under federal law. CTWS offers these 
comments to assist the EPA in understanding how the Proposed Rule affects the Tribe’s sovereign 
interests and provides some recommendations for improving the Proposed Rule so that it is more 
protective of those interests.  
I. 
CTWS Interest in the Proposed Rule. 
CTWS is a sovereign and federally recognized Indian tribe. The Tribe is organized under 
a Constitution and Bylaws ratified by its members on December 18, 1937, and approved by the 
United States Department of the Interior on February 14, 1938, pursuant to Section 16 of the Act 
of June 18, 1934 (48 Stat. 984), as amended by the Act of June 15, 1935 (49 Stat. 378). The Tribe 
is also the legal successor-in-interest to the Indian signatories of the of the Treaty With The Tribes 
of Middle Oregon, which was executed on June 25, 1855 and ratified by Congress on March 8, 
1859 (12 Stat. 963) (“1855 Treaty” or “Treaty”).  
Pursuant to the Treaty, the Tribe ceded certain rights to approximately 10 million acres of 
land to the United States and reserved approximately 640,000 acres for the exclusive use and 
occupation of the Tribe and its members as a permanent homeland (“Warm Springs Reservation”). 
The southern boundary of the Tribe’s ceded lands is the 44th parallel, the northern boundary is the 
Columbia River, and the western boundary is the crest of the Cascade Mountain Range. The middle 
of the channel of the Deschutes River forms the eastern boundary of the Warm Springs 
Reservation, and one of the Deschutes River’s major tributaries, the Metolius River, forms a 
significant portion of the southern boundary of the Reservation.

The 1855 Treaty recognizes the Tribe as a sovereign, possessing inherent rights to provide 
for the general welfare of its people, including the right to manage its natural resources for their 
benefit. The Treaty expressly reserves rights to the Tribe for its members to go outside (or “off”) 
the Warm Springs Reservation to all of the lands and waters that it had used prior to the Treaty to 
hunt, fish, gather roots and berries, and to pasture livestock. Those rights have been defined and 
upheld, by federal courts, since the early 1900’s, meaning that the Tribe has legally enforceable 
Treaty protected rights throughout its ceded lands and those areas beyond its ceded lands that were 
customarily used from time to time by the Tribe’s members and their ancestors.1  
The Tribe’s treaty-reserved rights are the cornerstone of the legal protections for its culture. 
Simply put, we are a salmon people whose treaty-reserved rights to fish are “not much less 
necessary” to our existence than the “atmosphere” we breathe.2 Our treaty-reserved rights fall 
squarely within the Proposed Rule’s definition of “tribal reserved rights.”3 CTWS is a “right 
holder” for purposes of the Proposed Rule and has a significant interest in the EPA’s development 
of these regulations.4

A. 
The EPA should clarify that water quality standard submissions and decisions 
cannot affect the location, existence, or scope of tribal reserved rights. 
Federal statutes do not abrogate tribal treaty rights unless the language of the statute 
“clearly express[es] its intent to do so.”8 Federal courts interpret statutes to adjudicate and resolve 
disputes concerning the scope of tribal treaty and other reserved rights.9 Neither state governments 
nor the EPA, however, have any authority to abrogate, modify, or adjudicate tribal reserved 
rights.10  
The lack of state authority over tribal reserved rights means that a description, or omission 
of a description, of tribal reserved rights in a state water quality standard submission has no legal 
bearing on the existence, location, scope, or nature of those rights. Likewise, because the EPA has 
no authority over tribal reserved rights, EPA decisions regarding state consideration of tribal 
reserved rights in water quality standard submissions do not affect the existence, location, scope, 
or nature of those rights.11
