Dear Administrator Regan, 
The Mille Lacs Band of Ojibwe submits these comments regarding protecting Tribal 
reserved rights in Water Quality Standards (WQS). We respectfully request that these comments 
be included in the official comment record to Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791: Water 
Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights. 
The Mille Lacs Band of Ojibwe (Band) is a federally-recognized American Indian Tribe 
located in east-central Minnesota, with adjudicated reserved rights by retaining “[t]he privilege 
of hunting, fishing, and gathering the wild rice [manoomin; Zizania palustris], upon the lands, 
the rivers and the lakes included in the territory ceded” in the 1837 Treaty of St. Peters (7 Stat. 
536) and in the 1842 Treaty of La Pointe (7 Stat. 591), of what today are Minnesota, Wisconsin, 
and Michigan, so that we could continue our  bimaadiziwin or traditional lifeways in a manner 
that meets our subsistence, economic, cultural, medicinal, and spiritual needs.  The full exercise 
of these lifeways require access to clean, healthy, and abundant natural resources, which in turn 
requires clean water to thrive.  As a member of the Great Lakes Indian Fish and Wildlife 
Commission (GLIFWC), we coordinate with other member Tribes and with the States in co-
managing treaty-protected resources.  Additionally, our Tribal band members who possess a 
valid Tribal identification card from a federally-recognized Tribe located in Minnesota, our 
citizens are deemed to have a license to harvest manoomin anywhere within the State of 
Minnesota, per Minnesota Wild Rice Regulations. With these comments, we will remind EPA 
that although Tribes and intertribal agencies representing Tribes may submit comments during 
this public comment period, we must not be treated as other stake-holders who act as public 
commenters, but as the sovereign governments that we are. We are pleased to submit our 

 
 
 
Comment Letter on  
Water Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights 
Mille Lacs Band of Ojibwe 
 
2 
 
comments to the United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) in your effort in 
enacting WQS regulatory revisions to protect Tribal reserved rights. 
As stated in our comment letter to you on this topic back on September 13, 2021, the 
Band is fully supportive of the EPA’s effort to bring about WQS that are protective of Tribal 
subsistence practices. The Band believes that this action by the EPA reflects the manner in which 
the Clean Water Act was intended to protect the health of people and the health of the 
environment, because clean water is fundamental to life and is the onji-mashkiki or the first 
medicine, the blood of our mother, Earth. 
First of our concerns is in regards to the State of Minnesota having EPA-approved WQS, 
but the State repeatedly failing to enforce the EPA-approved standards that are on their books.  
We have expressed this concern already in our 2021 letter, but we would like to express it once 
again, as it is of the utmost importance.  For many years, the Mille Lacs Band and other Tribes in 
Minnesota have asked the State of Minnesota to ensure protection of these waters in our treaty-
ceded territories through listing of impaired waters per the Clean Water Act Section 303(d) and 
to establish the appropriate Total Maximum Daily Loads (TMDLs) protective of those listed 
waters. We have further repeatedly requested that the State properly designate and enforce State 
Class 3 and 4 WQS and that the State enforce the municipal and industrial wastewater discharge 
limits set under the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) permit program. 
As you recall, the State had declined our request for approximately ten years. After EPA 
conducted consultation sessions with Tribal governments as part of its review of the State’s 
WQS review, EPA agreed with the Tribes’ position and has added certain bodies of water to the 
various waters lists.  Since that time, the State has moved to list these waters and additional 
waters.  However, the State is still reluctant in enforcing the EPA-approved WQS.  We thank the 
EPA for respecting the Tribes’ unique needs for enhanced water quality for subsistence living, 
and by having Tribes cooperatively working together with the State and EPA on a government-
to-government basis, we have inched the State to do what is right for the health of the people and 
for the environment.  But we must continue to encourage the State in the enforcement of those 
WQS so the full intent of the Clean Water Act can be realized.  Please also note that in order for 
Tribes to adequately participate, review, and make comments and request to the State in their 
triennial review process, it is a significant burden on Tribes, but we do this because it is of great 
importance to us to protect our reserved rights resources by ensuring that the States do their job 
in water quality protection. 
We have other concerns that we would like to share with you today that we did not 
express in our 2021 letter. In order to ensure water quality protection in our treaty-ceded 
territories, Tribes may need additional personnel to work closely with our State partners so that 
we can ensure our shared resources are cared for properly. Currently, there are monies made 
available through the Great Lakes Restoration Initiative (GLRI) for waters within the Great 
Lakes basin, but no such pots of monies are available for the Mississippi River basin. Minnesota 
Fourth Congressional District Representative Betty McCollum has introduced a bill for the 
Mississippi River Restoration and Resilience Initiative (MRRRI; H.R. 4202), which potentially 
can provide funds to States, Tribes, and Local governments—and even to non-governmental 
organizations—to allow the fund recipients to jointly perform water quality protection work in 
the Mississippi River basin similar to how GLRI does within the Great Lakes basin.  For Tribes, 
funding such as these are critical because without funding support, we cannot hire and retain 

 
 
 
Comment Letter on  
Water Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights 
Mille Lacs Band of Ojibwe 
 
3 
 
qualified individuals to perform this needed work in ensuring WQS that are protective of our 
treaty reserved rights in safeguarding our treaty protected resources. 
Additionally, without reliable and sustained funding, Tribes cannot hire the staff for their 
water programs that are needed to conduct our most basic analysis on water bodies with a nexus 
to the Reservation.  Having project funds made available for only 2- to 4-years may accomplish 
project goals, but projects alone do not sustain Tribal water programs.  Without funding for 
Tribal water programs to retain staff, Tribes are not able to go after project funding. This is an 
on-going issue, and adds to the burden of monitoring treaty-ceded territories where we exercise 
our reserved rights. 
Next, in addition to the rights to hunt, fish, and gather, Tribal reserved rights may include 
all sorts of other resource gathering methods such as trapping and agriculture, or ensuring our 
cultural landscapes and sacred sites are protected for ceremonial and cultural uses.  Our 
Anishinaabe gikinoo’amaadiwin or traditional teachings provide a good framework to 
demonstrate how adverse impacts on water can impact the cultural, ceremonial, and overall well-
being of plants, wildlife, and people.  Our teachings speak of four orders of creation.  They are 
the order in which the beings on Mother Earth were created were: (1) the elements, which 
includes air, energy, land, and water; (2) plants and other non-animal life; (3) non-human 
animals; and (4) us humans. According to our gikinoo’amaadiwin, each of the orders can exist 
and survive without those that come after it, but cannot exist without those that come before it.  
In this way, water is an elder sibling and teacher to us Anishinaabeg.  We humans depend on 
water both directly and indirectly, and plants and non-human animals rely on it as well.  As a 
creation of the first order, water is our relative that has generations of memory and knowledge to 
teach us.  Water is a sacred element, and water-dwelling and water dependent plants and animals 
are particularly sacred and greatly influenced our bimaadiziwin, tying many Tribal communities 
to each of our historic homelands. Consequently, we would like to point out to the EPA that all 
these constitute “beneficial use of water” for us.  In Peace and Friendship treaties, the phrase “As 
long as the Sun shines, the Rivers flow and the Grass grows, ...” is used, first appearing in the 
Tawagonshi Agreement of 1613 between the Five Iroquois Nations and the Republic of the 
Seven United Netherlands, and since then, the variations of that phrase were implemented by the 
governments of United Kingdom, United States, and Canada.  With this language, we and other 
Tribes believed at the time treaties were signed that the reserved resources would be usable—i.e., 
air would be clean to breathe, fish are safe to eat, water is safe to drink and bathe in, and plants 
are not genetically modified.  These ideas we like to note are canons of construction of Indian 
law, and it dictates that EPA must consider those Tribal needs based on the above understanding 
of reserved resource access. 
Next, EPA must recognize that the federal government’s treaty obligations and trust 
responsibility cannot be delegated to any other entity, including to the states – even when states 
assume responsibilities under a federal program.  The Proposed Rule, as written, implies that 
states will make several determinations regarding Tribal reserved rights.  These include making 
determinations about whether rights exist, and the geographic extent of those rights.  This is an 
especially egregious and impermissible delegation of federal responsibility because a substantial 
amount of information regarding treaty rights could come from Indigenous knowledge 
Traditional Ecological Knowledge (TEK), and the Proposed Rule is silent regarding the weight 
that should be given to TEK.  In other words, it is possible that states would determine that 

 
 
 
Comment Letter on  
Water Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights 
Mille Lacs Band of Ojibwe 
 
4 
 
information provided through TEK—usually in the form of our inaajimowin or stories—would 
be treated with less value than what is provided through western scientific data – a medium most 
are more familiar and therefore comfortable with.  The inherent risk is that states will make 
determinations regarding Tribal reserved rights that exceed their authority, potentially making 
legal determinations that will curtail Tribal rights into the future.  The EPA must ensure that this 
Rule does not delegate final decision-making authority regarding the existence and extent of 
Tribal reserved rights – an especially fraught possibility in cases in which treaty rights have not 
yet been adjudicated. Historically, Tribes and states have ideologically differed on approaching 
water quality management, from how climate change will impact water resources, to cumulative 
impacts.  The often-differing approaches have the potential to lead to conflicting data and 
priorities, as well as different standards for designated uses.  As part of its federal treaty 
obligations and trust responsibility, the EPA must ensure that states do not run roughshod over 
any conflicting data or competing ideologies that come from Tribes in regards to our Tribal 
reserved rights.  This Proposed Rule must make clear how such differences will be addressed and 
resolved.   
Next, we would also like to share with you that under the current EPA funding 
mechanism for Tribal water quality protection only allows for Tribes to do work only in Indian 
Country, limiting us to do water quality protection on our Indian Reservations and on our Indian 
Trust lands, cutting off the Tribes from ensuring States are actually doing the water protection 
Tribes need to protect our reserved rights on a daily basis.  Processes outlined in the Proposed 
Rule leave Tribes in a position of relying on states to accurately collect and interpret information 
from tribes.  This is especially troublesome in the many parts of the Proposed Rule where the 
EPA merely states that the state should communicate with Tribes and should balance competing 
lines of inquiry.  Consequently, Tribes have little to no water quality data in these critical off-
Reservation areas, and are nearly completely reliant on State water quality data, if States have 
conducted sampling in these critical off-Reservation waters.  Even if we have the opportunity to 
adequately participate in their triennial review process, this level of participation is too 
infrequent for us, making us even more reliant on TEK for these reserved rights areas to fill in 
the data gap.  If Tribes are truly co-managers with the States in these off-Reservation waters as 
the courts have ruled, then the water protection funds Tribes receive must allow for Tribes to 
assist States in monitoring for these off-Reservation waters, and allow for adequate staffing so 
that the water quality protection can be carried out together with the States in protecting our 
common water resources.  If this cannot be achieved, then this process does not differ 
substantially from the current rule or processes undertaken by states, and does not go far enough 
to ensure that Tribal reserved rights are adequately considered in the development of new WQS.  
EPA must acknowledge that the nature and scope of many treaty rights have been the subject of 
sometimes decades-long court battles, and the determination of the scope, location, and manner 
of the exercise of the rights may be controversial and be met with resistance by states.  With this 
in mind, we would like to recommend to the EPA that: 
• 
The final rule should ensure that there is a system by which a minimum threshold for 
state engagement with rights holders is developed, and by which a uniform process for 
consideration of tribal reserved rights is developed.   
• 
The final rule should also create a system by which there is a minimum threshold of 
engagement between EPA and tribes to ensure the EPA retains its federal trust 
responsibility and does not improperly rely on the states.

• 
EPA must require states to communicate early and often with tribes throughout their 
WQS processes. 
• 
The EPA must make clear that competing lines of inquiry must be balanced between the 
states and tribes. 
Finally, we also have concerns that the Federal Register notice is silent on what occurs 
when states and Tribes disagree. The Proposed Rule lacks any clear teeth to ensure that the 
states are giving the appropriate weight to the points of view of Tribes or other rights holders. 
While, ultimately, the EPA must approve state WQS, and these regulations would require Tribal 
reserved rights are considered in the process before new or updated WQS are approved, that is 
not enough. At the least, the final rule should explicitly require states to show how the 
information and data provided by Tribes were considered in the various processes outlined in this 
Proposed Rule. Additionally, the final rule should make clear that the information provided by 
Tribes and other rights holders, specifically including information that was provided through 
TEK processes must be weighted equally to the information provided by states and through 
western scientific processes.

Re: EPA’s proposal to revise the regulations related Clean Water Act (CWA) specific 
to protect “tribal reserved rights”. 
 
Dear Ms. Brundage, 
 
EPA’s proposed regulation clarifies that where tribal reserved rights exist, states must 
account for those rights in revising their designated uses, criteria, and/or antidegradation 
provisions. 
 
The proposal further specifies that WQS must protect unsuppressed use of any reserved 
resources. Determining the unsuppressed level requires considering past, present, and future 
use of the resource, along with what is currently reasonable to achieve for the waterbody.  
 
The proposal would also require that WQS protect the health of the tribal members 
exercising reserved rights to at least the same risk level at which the general population of 
the state would otherwise be protected. EPA anticipates the primary application of this 
provision to be in determining the appropriate cancer risk level when deriving criteria to 
protect human health.  
 
EPA is proposing that state WQS submissions must include documentation of the state’s 
efforts to obtain information about the existence of any applicable tribal reserved rights, 
their current and past use, scope, and nature, as well as the level of water quality that 
protects those rights. Additionally, the rule would require states to re-evaluate whether WQS 
need to be revised to protect any applicable tribal reserved rights at each triennial WQS 
review.  
 
Finally, the proposed rule would require EPA to initiate tribal consultation with the right 
holders when reviewing WQS submissions to determine whether state WQS protect 
applicable reserved rights.

Comments/questions from the Quapaw Nation related to these proposed revisions to 
the CWA: 
1. 
In light of the Supreme Court’s decision in McGirt v. Oklahoma, 207 L. Ed. 2d 985, 
140 S. Ct. 2452 (2020) regarding the status of reservations in Oklahoma, the Quapaw Nation 
(the “Nation”) reserves its rights to protect its water by virtue of our sovereignty as an 
ancient tribal people, which has been recognized and acknowledge by the United States as 
well as Article 25 and 32 of the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous 
Peoples. Aside from an implicit and inherent right, the 1833 Treaty with the Quapaw, 7 Stat. 
424 (May 13, 1833), and the 1867 Treaty with the Seneca, Mixed Seneca, and Shawnee, 
Quapaw, etc., 15 Stat. 513 (Feb. 23, 1867) guaranteed the Quapaw Nation its current home 
as a reservation, which the Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals recently reaffirmed. See 
Oklahoma v. Lawhorn, S-2020-858 (2021 OK CR 37).   
 
a. 
As the Nation’s water rights were never disestablished in treaty or elsewhere, 
the Nation ultimately wants to know how these proposed revisions provide greater 
protection to its water rights? 
 
b. 
Did the EPA recognize and consider the Nation’s water rights as it considered 
the referenced revisions to the CWA?  
 
c. 
In consideration of cases like Winters v. United States, 207 U.S. 564 (1908) 
and Choctaw Nation v. Oklahoma, 397 U.S. 620, 635 (1970), does the EPA currently 
recognize the Nation’s water rights as preserved for purposes of implementing the 
referenced revisions to the CWA? 
 
2. 
The 2005 SAFETEA Rider authorized the state of OK to administer environmental 
regulatory programs in certain areas of “Indian Country”. On October 1, 2020, the EPA 
approved Oklahoma’s SAFETEA request to administer all the State’s EPA-approved 
environmental regulatory programs in the requested areas of Indian country. As requested 
by ODEQ, the EPA’s approval under SAFETEA does not include Indian country lands, 
including rights-of-way running through the same, that: (1) qualify as Indian allotments, the 
Indian titles to which have not been extinguished, under 18 U.S.C. § 1151(c); (2) are held in 
trust by the United States on behalf of an individual Indian or Tribe; or (3) are owned in fee 
by a Tribe, if the Tribe (a) acquired that fee title to such land, or an area that included such 
land, in accordance with a treaty with the United States to which such Tribe was a party, and 
(b) never allotted the land to a member or citizen of the Tribe (collectively “excluded Indian 
country lands”).  This 2020 approval also provided that future revisions or amendments to 
Oklahoma’s approved environmental regulatory programs would extend to the covered 
areas of Indian country (without any further need for additional requests under SAFETEA). 
This approval appears to be in direct opposition to the proposed tribal-related revisions to 
the CWA. For example, how would EPA expect to enforce the new revisions  that would 
require states to re-evaluate whether WQS need to be revised to protect any applicable tribal 
reserved rights at each of Oklahoma’s triennial WQS review? It appears that EPA has 
abrogated their responsibility to approve/disapprove continued delegated authority to  
implement environmental programs (under the CWA, CAA, etc..) through this approval of 
Oklahoma’s SAFETEA request. It is surprising that EPA would concede this authority even 
though SAFETEA does not eliminate, or in any way limit, this authority. The Nation 
requests a written response to this concern, and government-to-government consultation to 
address these issues.

3. 
On December 22, 2021, the EPA proposed to withdraw and reconsider Oklahoma’s 
2020 SAFETEA approval request as it relates to tribal environmental programs. What is the 
status of this withdraw consideration?  
 
4. 
The Nation has internally approved Water Quality Standards(WQS). These standards 
largely mirror the State’s standards; but differ in the Beneficial Use designations of water 
bodies within the reservation. The Nation was working with EPA and in accordance with 
EPA’s requirements,  to establish enforceable WQS until the passing of the SAFETEA in 
2005. When can the Nation expect to continue this process with EPA? Among other benefits 
to public health and environment, establishing WQS that are protective of the Nation and the 
affected communities of Ottawa County would result in significant progress toward the 
Nation’s efforts to accomplish the best possible cleanup of the Tar Creek Superfund site.

On behalf of the states of the Northeast,1 NEIWPCC appreciates the opportunity to submit comments regarding the U.S. 
Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) Clean Water Act (CWA) Water Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions to Protect 
Tribal Reserved Rights.   
 
Established by an Act of Congress in 1947,2 NEIWPCC is a not-for-profit regional commission that helps the states of the 
Northeast preserve and advance water quality. We support state water programs across New England and New York 
responsible for administering programs under the Clean Water Act in five key ways: (1) engaging and convening water 
quality professionals and other stakeholders; (2) implementing and funding research, environmental monitoring, 
restoration, and other on-the-ground projects; (3) training water quality professionals; (4) funding and/or staffing 
programs that engage the public; (5) representing the interests of member states at the local, regional and national level.  
 
States acknowledge the importance of ongoing communications between tribes and EPA regarding Tribal Reserved 
Rights. They appreciate the spirit of the proposed rule but have concerns related to its scope and implementation. 
States would be responsible for carrying out the proposed rule, and it appears that EPA did not conduct appropriate 
outreach directly to states during the development process. States would like a process or statement about how they 
will be included in future conversations relevant to this rule making to facilitate the execution of the rule at the state 
level.   
 
States have long established water quality standards using accepted procedures under EPA guidance. EPA’s current 
regulations do not explicitly require consideration of treaty rights in setting water quality standards. However, EPA has 
tried to incorporate reserved tribal treaty rights and rights provided by and other applicable laws and documents into

Congress under Public Law 80-292, July 31, 1947, with powers and duties relating to the control and reduction of pollution of the interstate 
waters of New England and New York. 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
–2– 
the water quality standards program since 2015.3  EPA’s proposed 2023 Water Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions 
to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights seeks to: 
 
i. amend EPA’s current water quality standard regulations to require states, tribes, and the federal government to 
consider treaty rights when setting water quality standards, and  
 
ii. provide a regulatory framework for setting water quality standards in a manner that “protect(s) aquatic and 
aquatic-dependent resources reserved to tribes through treaties, statutes, executive orders, or other sources of 
Federal law.”   
 
EPA explains that tribal reserved rights may apply to waters in Indian country as well as outside of Indian country, and 
such rights may be express or implied. The proposed rule, if adopted, will have major impacts in states where federally 
recognized tribes hold rights to aquatic or aquatic-dependent resources in waters subject to state water quality 
standards.   
 
State – Tribe Working Relationships 
States would like to acknowledge they each navigate a unique landscape as it relates to their working relationships with 
tribes. Many states have specific settlements with tribes or legal land agreements with tribes, and there is concern 
around the intersection of those unique settlements with this national regulation. For example, in Rhode Island, the 
Narragansett Tribe’s 1,800-acre Settlement Lands are governed by State civil and criminal laws and jurisdiction (25 
U.S.C. 1708(a)) which would include laws governing water quality and the associated regulations. Maine also has a 
nationally unique tribal-state relationship set forth in state and federal laws, including the Maine Implementing Act, 30 
M.R.S. §§ 6201-6214 (2011 & Supp. 2022), and the Maine Indian Land Claims Settlement Act, 25 U.S.C. §§ 1721-1735 
(MICSA). These examples highlight the varied nature of state-tribe interactions. Because of these unique, case-by-case 
conditions, the proposed rule would add regulatory uncertainty to an already complicated legislative landscape. 
 
This point is echoed in the Summary Report of Tribal Consultation for the Proposed Rule: Water Quality Standards 
Regulatory Revisions to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights where commenters asked: “how EPA will ensure the regulation is 
flexible enough to accommodate different treaties and other relevant sources of law.” States would like to know how 
EPA has considered or plans to consider specific settlement acts and other relevant sources of law as they relate to this 
proposed rule.   
 
Similarly, states each navigate unique relationships with state recognized tribes. States would like to know how the 
proposed rule would impact tribes that are recognized at the state level. Are these tribes being considered and how 
should states handle these tribes under the proposed rule? States would like written guidance on any potential impacts 
on state recognized tribes and how to consider their uses in state water quality standards programs.  
 
Identification of Tribal Reserved Rights 
States need more information before fully commenting on the specific text of the proposed rule. This information 
includes but is not limited to, which tribes and a fuller understanding of the rights specifically covered under the 
proposed ruling, the specific boundaries of lands impacted by the rule with reference to relevant mapping tools, which 
waters will be considered and if it is limited to those wholly within trust lands or reservations, and whether this ruling 
extends to water related uses other than fish consumption and foraging. Without this information states are not able to 
 
3 See, Promulgation of Certain Federal Water Quality Standards Applicable to Maine, 81 FR 92466 (December 19, 2016), and Revision of 
Certain Federal Water Quality Criteria Applicable to Washington, 81 FR 85417 (December 28, 2016). Please see Maine’s comments for this 
proposed rule submitted separately for additional details and comments. 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
–3– 
determine how this proposed rule will impact their workload and implementation of water quality standards at the 
state level.  
  
Execution of this proposed rule depends on defining the extent and intricacies of federally recognized tribal reserved 
rights. With this in mind, tribal reserved rights should be identified by the federal agencies with the appropriate 
expertise in advance of propagation of the proposed rule. Federal agencies are in the best position to create a database 
of federal treaties, statutes, executive orders, judicial decisions, and any other sources of federal tribal reserved rights, 
not the individual states. Such a database would address what the tribal reserved rights are, their scope, and to which 
waters they apply. We suggest that the responsible federal agencies update such a database as needed, and that EPA 
shares it early in the states’ triennial review process. This approach would also be consistent with the description of 
EPA’s responsibilities in the preamble.  
 
Defining Tribal Reserved Rights and Unsuppressed Rights 
States would like guidance from EPA on available resources and best practices to gather necessary information about 
current and past uses, scope, and nature of past and current uses which would be necessary under this rule. States 
would also like to know what resources will be allocated by EPA to obtain answers to these questions during the 
implementation process.   
 
The identification of federally recognized tribal reserved rights by the federal agencies should be implemented in the 
proposed rule by adding a provision that EPA will publish a database that identifies, state-by-state, which tribes and 
rights (i.e., the nature and scope of any aquatic and aquatic-dependent resources reserved by each tribe) are covered, 
the affected waterbodies or water segments and the boundaries of any impacted adjacent lands, and clarify the rule’s 
applicability to waterbodies or water segments within and without trust lands and reservations. Also, the rule should 
commit EPA to periodically update the database and create a presumption that a state which bases the incorporation of 
federally recognized tribal reserved rights into its water quality standards triennial review based upon the then current 
federal database has satisfied its obligation to consider changes to those rights since the prior triennial review. 
Implementing this recommendation would require appropriate modifications to 40 CFR 131.6(g)(1), 40 CFR 131.9(b) and 
40 CFR 131.20(a). Barring this, EPA should detail how they intend to assist states with addressing the concerns 
addressed above with identifying tribal reserved rights.  
 
EPA proposes adding a new definition to 40 CFR 131.3 defining “tribal reserved rights” as “any rights to aquatic and/or 
aquatic-dependent resources reserved or held by tribes, either expressly or implicitly, through treaties, statutes, 
executive orders, or other sources of Federal law” but does not define the scope of these rights or provide information 
on how EPA plans to assist states in defining this scope. For example, the term implicitly is subject to interpretation. EPA 
should provide specific examples or activities or resources that have been implicitly determined to be tribal reserved 
rights. To avoid disagreements and disputes over the nature of tribally held rights, the rule should also be limited to 
expressly reserved rights only, as opposed to other kinds of rights. 
 
The proposed rule would require “The exercise of tribal reserved rights unsuppressed by water quality or availability of 
the aquatic or aquatic-dependent resource” but does not define the extent of these unsuppressed rights or how states 
are to determine these unsuppressed rights. On the one hand, the proposed rule at §131.9 would require states “to 
protect: (1) The exercise of tribal reserved rights unsuppressed by water quality or availability of the aquatic or aquatic-
dependent resource,” but on the other hand, the preamble suggests that other factors should be considered in 
determining unsuppressed rights. For example, citing the National Environmental Justice Advisory Committee’s 2002 
report, EPA states that “the unsuppressed level of a resource … will depend on the factors affecting water quality and 
availability of the resources[,]” and that “it may be appropriate to take into consideration both heritage rates of use … 
and factors that have substantially altered the pollutant burden, hydrology, or availability of the resource, such that use 
of the resource at heritage rates is not feasible” Preamble, IV.C.2.ii. Accounting for Suppression Effects. These appear to 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
–4– 
be inconsistent. The proposed rule should include a definition of unsuppressed rights addressing these issues, 
supplemented by written guidance, as appropriate.  
 
The preamble also suggests that unsuppressed rights may vary over time. For example, “the unsuppressed level or use 
of a resource should account for situations where restoration efforts are planned or underway (e.g., efforts to improve 
habitat or reduce contamination), such that it would be reasonable to expect the opportunities for use of the resource 
to increase in the future. In these situations, where supported by available data and information, EPA is proposing to 
require that water quality standards must be set at levels that reflect unsuppressed exercise of the reserved right” 
Preamble, IV.C.2.ii. Accounting for Suppression Effects. EPA should address the implication that if no such restoration 
project is underway, the water quality standards need not reflect unsuppressed exercise of the reserved right which 
appears to contradict the proposed standard set forth in §131.9, quoted above.  
 
EPA guidance cited in the proposal explains that the heritage rate of consumption “is generally extrapolated or 
reconstructed from information available in anthropological or historical literature” and that “[i]n many cases, heritage 
rates may be the only practical way to estimate unsuppressed rates[.]” The proposal explains that the unsuppressed 
analysis “should balance heritage use of a resource with what is currently reasonably achievable for a particular 
waterbody,” but also states that it should consider plans for future restoration activities that could improve current 
conditions. The proposal explains that, in the case of a difference of opinion about the required level of water quality 
necessary to protect a reserved right, “EPA will take action based on the best available information in the same way 
that EPA currently makes [water quality standards] decisions in these circumstances in other contexts, e.g., determining 
whether criteria are scientifically defensible in situations where there is conflicting science, there are gaps in the 
science, and/or there are different conclusions among stakeholders.”   
 
Based on experience, states are concerned that there will be disagreements among states and stakeholders about what 
may be “reasonable” and “achievable currently and in the future.”  States foresee a high likelihood of disputes arising 
given the current requirements for scientific rigor in the water quality standards program, the potential for new 
standards to be developed under this proposal based on reconstructed or extrapolated historical information, and EPA’s 
perceived role as the mediator of such disputes between states and tribes.4 States request that EPA clarify the criteria 
for the states’ decision-making to minimize such disputes. States are unable to accurately assess the impacts of this rule 
without information on these scoping questions and how EPA will support states in determining this scope.   
 
 
 
4 EPA states, “Courts generally adhere to several guiding principles in interpreting treaties and other Federal legal instruments regarding 
Indians tribes known as the ‘‘Indian canons of construction.’’ 87 F.R. 74363.  In accordance with these canons, EPA asserts ‘‘Indian treaties 
are to be interpreted liberally in favor of the Indians, and any ambiguities are to be resolved in their favor.’’ (Citations omitted).  87 F.R. 
74363.  However, in most instances, the state and federal courts have not found the Indian Law Canons to be applicable or determinative 
when deciding legal disputes between the states and tribes about the meaning of settlement language.

The Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation ("Colville Tribes") provides the following 
comments and attached revisions to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's Docket ID No. EPA-
HQ-OW-2021-0791, Proposed Revisions to the Federal Water Quality Standards Regulation to Protect 
Tribal Reserved Rights (Draft Policy). 
The Colville Tribes' response focuses primarily on the demotion of preference of protections and 
consultation requirements with those tribes without treaties. It is disheartening that an agency such as the 
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), takes a position in which gives preferential treatment to 
Tribes with ratified treaties to the detriment of Tribes defined by other trust relationships. The Colville 
Tribes appreciates the ongoing working relationship it has with EPA and respectfully requests that it 
consider the following comments and proposed amendments in order to comply with Executive Order 
13175. 
The Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation consists of twelve tribes whose homelands 
cover much of Eastern Washington. The Colville Tribes have federally recognized and protected rights 
throughout eastern Washington. These rights are protected by statute, agreement, and executive order. 
Pursuant to federal law, these types of rights are exactly the same and to be treated in the same manner as 
rights protected by a treaty. This has been affirmed by the federal courts. 
The proposed revisions continually refer to tribal rights as "Reserved Rights". This term is being 
used in error as reserved rights specifically refer to those rights established through treaty negotiations. 
Reserved rights are not the only federally protected tribal rights. The Colville Tribes have federally 
protected rights based on federal statute, federal executive order, and other federal agreements. While the 
proposed revisions to the Federal Water Quality Standards Regulations make strides towards recognizing 
inherent tribal interests and rights, the language in the proposed document continually gives the 
impression that Tribal Treaty and Reserved Rights are the primary focus to the exclusion of all other 
established tribal rights. The Colville Tribes has affirmed and federally protected rights in its traditional 
territories outside of the Reservation. The Courts have established that there is no difference in rights, 
regardless whether they are held by treaty, statute, executive order, or other legal agreement. 
Additionally, the Colville Tribes is recognized to have cultural interests and ties throughout eastern 
Washington (burial grounds, sacred sites, etc), that have been recognized by federal and state entities. 
The proposed document fails to give equal footing to any of these protected rights or areas, instead 
focusing on those reserved rights derived from a treaty. We request that in the place of language such as, 
Tribal treaty, reserved and similar rights, and the term Protected Tribal Rights be used. We also request 
that instead of using "ceded territories" the language used should be traditional territories.

Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791 
 
RE: EPA proposed rule: Water Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions to Protect Tribal 
Reserved Rights 
 
 
The Leech Lake Band of Ojibwe holds usufructuary rights to hunt, gather, and fish within 
territories ceded in the 1855 Treaty with the Chippewa. Located outside of the current day Leech 
Lake Reservation, many of these waters continue to hold great importance to the Leech Lake 
Band. The Band strongly supports the protection of Tribal Reserved Rights and treaty resources 
and requiring the use of unsuppressed rates of use/consumption for determining water quality 
standards. However, we recommend improvements to the antidegradation standards Option #1. 
Tribes hold a spiritual connection to these lands and waters as well as traditional ecological 
knowledge regarding the natural resources found in their homelands. States have repeatedly 
failed to acknowledge or include input from the Tribes in these decisions, and Tribes must have a 
stronger role in designation of outstanding natural resource waters that protect treaty rights. 
 
Treaty Wild Rice and Antidegradation 
 
The Leech Lake Reservation and the surrounding area are blessed with lakes where Manoomin 
(wild rice) grows. Wild rice is sacred and every fall during the Rice Moon our people gather rice 
both on the Reservation and on lakes in the 1855 Ceded Territory. Wild rice drives our economy 
and provides food security. Anishinaabeg exist because of wild rice, and we have a covenant 
with the Creator to protect it.  
  
The Leech Lake Band of Ojibwe Division of Resource Management purchases unfinished rice 
from our Band members for finishing and resale.  This venture is a business operation, a source 
of income for Tribal harvesters, and a cultural and subsistence food store.  In short, an important 
component of food sovereignty.  The Tribe’s right to harvest wild rice both on and off-
Reservation is protected by Treaties with the United States government. 
 
LEECH LAKE BAND OF OJIBWE 
DIVISION OF RESOURCE MANAGEMENT 

  
 
190 Sail Star Drive NW, Cass Lake, MN 56633 
 
Off-Reservation wild rice lakes have become increasingly important due to climate change and 
drought. If the water levels are too low, the plants may grow, however the beds can be 
inaccessible due to low water levels even by traditional canoe harvesting.  As an example, 
Blackwater Lake immediately to the east of our Reservation is particularly important in low 
water years, like 2021, due to the consistent water levels provided by the Pokegama Dam, 
operated by the Army Corps of Engineers.  
 
Blackwater Lake is an important treaty resource with over 300 acres of wild rice.  Blackwater is 
designated a “Lake of Outstanding Biological Significance” by the MN Department of Natural 
Resources through the Minnesota Biological Survey.1 Blackwater Lake is designated for priority 
protection by the Minnesota Pollution Control Agency under the Mississippi River Headwaters 
Watershed Restoration and Protection Strategy Report.2 Blackwater is also on the DNR List of 
350 Most Important Rice Waters in Minnesota.3   
 
However, Blackwater is not considered an outstanding natural resource water (ONRW) by the 
State of Minnesota. Because of this, the Blackwater wild rice beds, like many others, are 
threatened by development.  For decades the Blackwater has been protected by the large wetland 
buffer upstream from the Boswell coal electrical generating unit.  However, as the Boswell EGU 
anticipates decommissioning, it is seeking to sell off the wetland buffer to industrial 
development. 
 
Impacts of Hydrology and Development 
 
Historically, wild rice was pervasive along this region of the Mississippi River but has since 
declined from the impacts of development, loss of wetlands, and most recently the droughts 
potentially caused by climate change.  The Minnesota Department of Natural Resources has 
documented that hydrological changes and development are the most significant threat to wild 
rice beds.4  
 
Wild rice is a shallow water plant and is sensitive to changes in water levels. Even when the 
water level of a lake remains generally steady, heavy precipitation causes abrupt changes in 
water level that uproot aquatic plants. Natural wild rice is particularly susceptible to uprooting 
during its floating-leaf stage, which occurs in early summer, which is also the time of the largest 
rainfall events in northern Minnesota. Due to the natural buoyancy of the plant, it is at this stage 
of growth that wild rice is most susceptible to uprooting by rapidly rising water levels. Plants can 
be significantly stressed even when they remain rooted. Shoreline development and the removal 
of wetlands eliminates the ability of these areas to retain and absorb stormwater, leading to 
intense stormwater runoff events that raise water levels and uproot wild rice.

biological-signific. See also, https://files.dnr.state.mn.us/eco/sli/blackwaterjaygould_31056100.pdf  
2 https://www.pca.state.mn.us/sites/default/files/wq-ws4-50a.pdf  
3 https://www.eqb.state.mn.us/sites/default/files/documents/DNR%20350%20waters%20list_20181231.pdf  
4 https://files.dnr.state.mn.us/fish_wildlife/wildlife/wildrice/natural-wild-rice-in-minnesota.pdf 

  
 
190 Sail Star Drive NW, Cass Lake, MN 56633 
 
Changes in upstream watersheds reduce the productivity of natural wild rice stands.  Drainage 
ditches and channelization increase the quantity and speed of water moving downstream. The 
resulting peaks in water levels produce abrupt “bounces” or rapid increases in water depth. 
Increased sedimentation caused by drainage and channelization will also bury seeds and reduce 
germination. Wild rice requires high transparency waters to thrive.5   Our projection is that 
development on the shores of Blackwater Lake, with the combination of impervious surfaces and 
stormwater sedimentation impacts, would have the significant negative effects on wild rice beds, 
as they have historically throughout Minnesota’s developed lakes and rivers. 
 
Strengthening Antidegradation Option #1  
 
Our experience in working to protect the Blackwater wild rice beds is that Option #2 will not be 
effective in protecting treaty wild rice.  When faced with the politics of a large economic 
development project, the Minnesota Pollution Control Agency (MPCA) will not consider 
designated uses, alternatives, or treaty rights, in making a 401 certification. Instead, the MPCA 
will start its analysis by finding that allowing lower water quality is necessary to accommodate 
economic development under §131.12(a)(2) so long as the developer incorporates “best 
management practices” for stormwater treatment and purchases credits from a wetland bank.  
Unless high quality waters are protected by designation as a Tier 3 ONRW, they are unlikely to 
receive protection from state agencies.  
 
For this reason, Option #1 will be more protective of treaty wild rice.  However, relying on states 
to designate high quality waters for antidegradation requirements is insufficient.  Like most 
states, Minnesota’s ONRW designations are outdated and inadequate with decades of reluctance 
and neglect.6  This state process will be difficult to change and continue to leave out this 
important consideration unless greater weight is given to treaty rights. 
 
Instead, the final rule should recognize that where high quality waters protect Tribal reserved 
rights, they constitute an ONRW.  This could be accomplished in the same manner as 
§131.12(a)(3) which recognizes “waters of national and state parks and wildlife refuges and 
waters of exceptional recreational or ecological significance.”  Treaty protected waters should be 
in this same category, at a minimum. 
 
This is a specific way to strengthen the antidegradation provisions.  The proposed §131.9(c)(3) 
states: “Use applicable antidegradation requirements consistent with §131.12 to maintain and 
protect water quality that protects Tribal reserved rights.”  We recommend adding to that: 
“Where high quality waters protect Tribal reserved rights, they shall constitute an outstanding 
national resource, and water quality shall be maintained and protected." 
 
The concept is to cross-reference high quality treaty protected waters as Tier 3 ONRW's under 
                                                 
5 See, A. Myrbo, Sulfide Generated by Sulfate Reduction is a Primary Controller of the Occurrence of Wild Rice 
(Zizania palustris) in Shallow Aquatic Ecosystems, 22 September 2017 https://doi.org/10.1002/2017JG003787. 
6 For general discussion of state ONRW designations, see Zellmer, Sandra and Glicksman, Robert, "Using the Public

131.12.  Tribes would still have to nominate, but the additional language would recognize that 
these waters are in a similar category as National Parks or federal wildlife refuges, i.e. very 
strong qualification as Tier 3 ONRW's. 
 
 
 
In addition, a process should be instituted by which Tribes can directly nominate to the EPA 
high-quality waters in areas where they hold usufructuary rights to be designated as ONRWs. 
The process as envisioned in the proposed rule would require Tribes to participate in the states’ 
triennial reviews of water quality standards, put forward nominations to a reluctant state 
bureaucracy, and then follow that triennial review to the EPA’s oversight process. This would 
place a great burden on Tribal natural resource and environmental departments, and risk that 
Tribal nominations of ONRW’s will be lost in the shuffle.  Instead, the EPA’s regional offices 
should seek out nominations from the Tribes and work collaboratively with both Tribes and 
states to ensure that Tribal nominations for ONRW’s are given full consideration. 
 
The Leech Lake Band recommends that in all cases when decisions are made regarding high-
quality water determination, ONRW designation, or anti-degradation decisions, Tribes should be 
consulted and have the opportunity to nominate waters as high-quality or Outstanding Natural 
Resources. 
 
Climate Change, Wild Rice, and Treaty Rights 
 
On November 15, 2021 during the White House Tribal Nations Summit, President Biden 
announced that seventeen federal agencies, including EPA, have formally committed to 
protecting Tribal treaty rights in the Memorandum of Understanding Regarding Interagency 
Coordination and Collaboration for the Protection of Tribal Treaty and Reserved Rights. The 
MOU recognizes that federal agencies “need to consider and account for the effects of their 
actions on the habitats that support treaty-protected rights, including how those habitats will be 
impacted by climate change.” Federal agencies have a responsibility to anticipate the future 
impacts of climate change and incorporate climate adaptation planning into programs, policies, 
rules and operations.   
 
The protection of high quality wild rice waters falls squarely under this provision of the MOU.  
Climate change exacerbates droughts by making them more frequent, longer, and more severe. 
We need our federal partners to help mitigate drought impacts now and into the future by 
protecting existing treaty wild rice. 
 
Treaty Rights and Fish Consumption 
 
As mentioned above, the Leech Lake Band strongly supports requiring the use of unsuppressed 
rates of use/consumption for determining water quality standards. When determining 
unsuppressed rates of consumption, consideration should be given to the operation of dams and 
altered hydrological regimes and the influence such operations have on the growth of wild rice 
and reproduction of fish and mussels. In addition to Tribal Reserved Rights to fish, gather 
aquatic plants, and hunt for aquatic-dependent animals, EPA should also consider ceremonial 

  
 
190 Sail Star Drive NW, Cass Lake, MN 56633 
 
uses. The Leech Lake Band agrees with the use of information sources described for determining 
historic consumption/use rates and would also include reference to Tribal Resolutions regarding 
Tribal fish consumption rates. When conflicts arise between tribes and states regarding the level 
of water quality necessary for protecting Tribal Reserved Rights, EPA should take into 
consideration Traditional Ecological Knowledge/Indigenous Knowledge in addition to other 
resources. 
 
In conclusion, this proposed rule will strengthen the opportunities for members of the Leech 
Lake Band of Ojibwe to continue exercising Tribal Reserved Rights on treaty ceded lands, while 
protecting health, particularly if protected waters are designated as outstanding natural resource 
waters.   
 
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on Water Quality Standards for the protection of 
Tribal Reserved Rights.  We welcome further discussion and engagement on this important 
matter.  Please do not hesitate to contact my staff to continue the conversation and truly import 
change to protect our natural and treaty resources. 
 
 
Regards, 
  
 
Brandy Toft

Mercury in the Fish? 
By Scott Krzanik, Water Resoun-es Specialist 
Jn August, 2000, the Maine Bureau of Health released The Year 2000 Freshwater 
Fish Consumption AdPisoriu percaining co mercury in the fish we ear. This advisory con-
tains important informatio n that affects ANYBODY who eats fish. Mercury can 
remain in the human body for many weeks and up to 2 years in larger fish. It will eventu-
ally be e:\.-pelled from the body through wasce, however, it is imporcant co reduce your ex-
posure co mercury by limiting the consumption of certain fish species as specified in the 
Fish Consumption Advisories. You may ask, "How does mercury find its way into the 
fish we eat?" Lets look at where mercury commonly originates and then follow its path 
through the environment and on its way to humans . 
Mercury occuts nacur.tlly in soil and ceroun rock formations, such as shale. Ir is 
also found in products we use every day such as thermometers, certain batteries, fluores-
cent light bulbs, medical instruments, laboratory equipment, and many electronic devices. 
\'Vhen we throw these produces away, many of 
them end up in municipal incineracors. 
As it bums, this 
mercury vaporizes and enters che atmosphere. When it 
rains or snows, the mercwy is brought back to the earth. 
Naturally occurring mercury leaches out of che soil and 
rock through natural processes and ends up in ground 
and/ or surface water. It also can vaporize when exposed to 
the air and be re-deposited with falling rain or snow. Re-
gardless of the source, mercury in rivers, lakes, and bottom 
sediment is transformed by aquatic organisms into methyl 
mercury, which is highly toxic. Methyl mercury is taken up 
by aquatic life forms such as plankton and fish. As methyl mercury is consumed and 
moves up the food chain through larger and larger organisms, it accumulates in corre-
spondingly higher quantities in the body cissue of fish, for example. When we eat too 
much mercury-contaminated fish, health problems can occur such as numbness, weak-
ness, fatigue, poor coordination, depression, tremors, and irricabilicy. In some cases, eat-
ing excessive amounts of mercury-contaminated fish can lead to birth defects, blindness, 
paralysis, and even death.

How the Fly Saved the River 
An Anishnabeg story 
Many, many years ago when the world was 
new, there was a beautiful river. Fish in 
great numbers lived in this river, and its 
water was so pure and sweet that all the 
animals came there to drink. 
A giant moose heard about the river and he 
too came there to 
drink. But he was 
so big, and he 
drank so much, 
that soon the water 
began to sink 
lower and lower. 
The beavers were 
worried. The water around their lodges was 
disappearing. Soon their homes would be 
destroyed. 
The muskrats were worried, too. What 
would they do if the water vanished? How 
could they live? 
The fish were very worried. The other ani-
mals could live on land if the water dried 
up, but they couldn't. 
Ice Fishing Tips By Dave Joseph 
The ice fishing season will be starting again \'ery 
shortly. Before you set your traps, I would like to re-
mind you of a few things that can make your ice fish-
ing experience safe and more enjoyable. 
• 
Be sure to read the State Ice Fishing regulations 
for the waters that you plan to fish. As the wise 
Judge always says "there is no excuse for igno-
rance of the law." If any o f the regulations are 
confusing be sure to consult with a game warden, 
never j11sl asmme what it means. 
• 
Always dress in layers. Ir is much easier to take 
clothes off and stay warm than to not have 
enough to keep you warm. Cottons are the worst! 
Wear synthetics or wool clothing. 
All the animals tried to think of a way to 
drive the moose from the river, but he was so 
big that they were too afraid to try. Even the 
bear was afraid of him. 
At last the fly said he would try to drive the 
moose away. All the animals laughed and 
jeered. How could a tiny fly frighten a giant 
moose? The fly said nothing, but that day, as 
soon as the moose appeared, he went into ac-
tion. 
He landed on the moose's foreleg and bit 
sharply. The moose stamped his foot harder, 
and each time he stamped, the ground sank 
and the water rushed in to fill it up. Then the 
fly jumped about all over the moose, biting 
and biting and biting until the moose was in a 
frenzy. He dashed madly about the banks of 
the river, shaking his head, stamping his feet, 
snorting and blowing, but he couldn't get rid 
of that pesky fly. At last the moose fled from 
the river, and didn't come back. 
The fly was very proud of his achievement, 
and boasted to the other animals, "Even the 
small can fight the strong if they use 
their brains to think." 
• 
Check the weather forecast before heading out to 
ice fish for the day. As we all know the weather 
can tum on us at anytime during the day. Pack 
plenty food and fluids. Your body will need the 
energy to help you stay warm. 
• 
Always let someone know where you plan to 
fish. 
• 
Remember to get your 2001 fishing/ combination 
license. This sometimes gets overlooked with a 
new year just starting. 
• 
Always remember to heed fish consumption lim-
its (see related mercury article). Just because it's 
winter doesn't mean the fish don't have mercury 
in them. 
Keep the fishing Jines tight and ..:t 
watch for the flags to fly up!

Environmental Practicum 5 
 

 
On June 3rd, the Water Resources Department began collecting and 
analyzing water samples from the Meduxnekeag River Watershed. There are 11 
more sampling sites this year for a total of 23. The sites are located along the 
mainstem, North Branch, South Branch, and 6 tributaries. The water is being 
analyzed for 8 parameters: dissolved oxygen, temperature, E. coli bacteria, 
conductivity, turbidity, pH, alkalinity, and total suspended solids. These are general 
indicators of water quality and will be used to document conditions and changes 
throughout the watershed over time.  
 
In the past, there has been much concern regarding low dissolved oxygen levels, high E. coli numbers, and 
extensive algae blooms along the river. During rain storms there is a lot of sediment transported from fields and 
drained into the river. The work we do is intended to focus our efforts, and those of other organizations 
concerned about the Meduxnekeag River, on locating problem areas and working together to remediate those 
problem areas. By doing this we can only improve the quality of the water for every living thing in the 
watershed. 
 
It has been a long two weeks since we started our early mornings, but everything seems to be working out well. 
We would like to invite anyone interested to join us on our sample collection trips on Tuesdays or Wednesdays 
each week. We leave the office at 4:00 a.m. and return to the lab around 7:00 a.m. If this sounds early to you – 
IT IS !!!  If you can manage to drag yourself out of bed on time and gulp enough coffee, it’s not so bad. We 
have many opportunities to see wildlife that most folks never catch a glimpse of. We love our work and want to 
share those experiences with you all. Just contact the Water Resources Department at 532-4273 ext 212 if you 
wish to join us.

Wildlife Success Story 
With the assistance of the Natural Resource Conservation Service (NRCS) the tribe has been working to reduce 
the amount of runoff from fields into the  nearby Meduxnekeag River.  A number of Nutrient Sediment Control 
Structures (NSCS or collection basins) have been constructed on tribal land. These structures collect melt water, 
rainwater (runoff)  that would normally flow directly into the river, carrying sediment and other debris along with 
it.  These structures have not only  reduced the amount of sediment introduced into the river, it has helped create 
some wildlife habitat for migrating waterfowl and shore birds. 
 
The small ponds, sometimes referred to as vernal pools provide open water for the migrating birds before the 
areas lakes and rivers open up.  This Spring, the 
vernal pools on tribal property have been host to a  
wide variety of ducks, geese and other birds.  
Wood ducks, Mallards, Black ducks, Green 
Winged Teals, Common Pintail,  American 
Wigeon, Canada Geese and Killdeer have all been 
spotted in or near the pools on the Lowery Road. 
  This white throated Canada goose was  seen many times along the  
Lowery Road

Christmas in July 
With warm temperatures complete with blue skies and sunshine the last thing anyone wants to think about is 
winter.  But before we know it it’ll be time to close up the house and wait for all that winter will throw at us. 
But winter means more than snow and ice.  Winter is the perfect time to test your home for Radon. 
 
Radon is a naturally occurring gas found in the soil.  It can collect inside your home to unhealthful levels, es-
pecially during the winter months when your windows and doors are kept closed.  You can’t see or smell ra-
don but prolonged exposure to this gas increases your risk of lung cancer.  You won’t know whether you 
have a radon problem unless you test! 
 
Since we began testing tribal homes for this gas in 1995, we’ve found elevated radon levels in three houses in 
the greater Houlton area.  The Environmental Protection Agency recommends taking action to reduce radon 
in your home if it is 4 pCi/L or greater.  We’ve helped one family reduce their radon levels below this level, 
one family has since moved away (NOT because of radon), and we expect to 
help our third family reduce their radon levels this year.   
 
If your home has not yet been tested contact Sharri Venno at 532-4273 ext. 
215 to arrange for testing.  Testing is really quite painless, all you do is place 
the test kit in your home as instructed, leave it alone for at least 3 months, 
bring the kit in to the office or ask us to collect it.  That’s all there is to it! 
Once your kit is collected we send it off for analysis.  If a problem is detected, 
we will work with you to reduce the radon level in your home.   
 
We have a lot of information available to anyone requesting it.  Some of the 
publications we can provide you include:   
 
 
    
 
 
Radon Facts for Tribal Communities 
 
          Home Buyers and Sellers Guide to Radon 
 
 
Reducing Radon Risks 
 
 
How to Reduce Radon Levels in Your Home 
 
            A Citizen’s Guide to Radon 
 
            Learning About Radon: a part of nature 
 
 
Remember, it’s never too late to take action against Radon.

Through a project funded by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency 
(EPA), employees in the Natural Resources Department are collecting fish 
to  determine the presence and concentration of mercury in fish caught in 
the Meduxnekeag Watershed. 
 
This information will be used to estimate the levels of mercury contamina-
tion in fish populations within the watershed and the potential risk that 
these levels pose to humans and wildlife.  Since statistics show that Native 
American’s eat more wild caught fish than the general population, the 
study of the Meduxnekeag is especially important. 
 
HBMI employees are trained to properly collect, store and transport fish 
samples for analysis.  They are sampling fish from the main stem, North 
and South Branches of the Meduxnekeag River, the Lt. Gordon Manuel Wildlife Management area on the 
south branch, Green Pond, Meduxnekeag (Drews) Lake, Nickerson Lake, B Lake and Number 9 Lake.   
Species that may be collected for analysis include lake, brook, and brown trout; landlocked salmon, burbot, 
large and small mouth bass, chain pickerel, yellow and white perch, suckers and brown bullhead.  Catching 
the numbers and sizes of fish required for the study has proved to be 
quite a challenge.  In the case of  lake trout, the fish must measure 
between 19  -  22 inches, brown trout must measure between 15 - 18 
inches.   
 
If you’d like more information 
about the study or fish 
consumption  advisories please 
don’t hesitate to contact us at   
532-4273.

Low Water in the Meduxnekeag 
 
This Summer has proved to be one of 
the driest in recent memory.  Following 
on the heels of a below normal snowfall 
this past winter, local waterways are 
showing the signs of drought conditions. 
Water levels in the Meduxnekeag River 
are very low and a number of streams 
and brooks have gone dry. 
 
In addition to low water levels, we are 
experiencing a heavy growth of algae in 
the river.  This abundance of algae is 
even visible from the air as shown in the 
aerial photo below. The algae thrives as a 
result of warmer water temperatures and 
an overabundance of phosphorous and 
other nutrients in the water.  A lot of 
these nutrients enter the watershed as  
direct runoff from streets, yards and 
farmland, in addition to being discharged 
from plants and factories along the river.   
 
Times like this help to remind us of the 
importance of water conservation and 
the need to reduce the amount of 
pollutants that enter our lakes and 
rivers.   
  
Aerial photo of HBMI administration 
building and the Meduxnekeag River.  
An overgrowth of algae shows as green 
patches along the river. 
Algae concentration just below the Lowery 
Bridge on the Meduxnekeag River. 
Algae grows in various forms.  Strands 
of algae like the one above can reach 15 
feet or more in length.

Fish Habitat Survey 
In July, the Natural Resources staff took part in a 
fish habitat survey led by Frank Frost, Regional 
Fisheries Biologist for the State of Maine. 
 
The teams set out to map a large segment of the  
Meduxnekeag River to identify areas which provide 
good habitat for local fish populations.  They noted 
information such as water depth, temperature, rate 
of flow, the type of river bottom (rocky or silty), 
the presence or absence of plants in and along the waters 
edge, including riparian buffers, 
streams or tributaries feeding into 
the river, pools, and current or      
potential fish spawning areas.    
 
This information is to be used to 
help determine future fish stocking 
efforts, fish habitat restoration needs and to help restore

Water Resource Techs 
 
It’s hard to believe that our summer water techs Brittney 
London and Danielle Fitzpatrick have left us already.   
 
This year Brittney and Danielle  worked alongside Scott 
Krzanik and Dave Joseph to test and monitor the water 
quality in the  Meduxnekeag River and the surrounding 
tributaries.  Field measurements were taken to record the 
air and water temperature, dissolved oxygen levels as 
well as water depth, which became quite a challenge as 
the  water levels receded due to this summer’s drought.  
Danielle Fitzpatrick in Lab 
Brittney London preparing   
bacteria plates 
Moose Roast Recipe 
 
1– 4 lb moose roast 
     3-4 strips bacon 
 
 
 
2 tbsp chopped onions     1/4 tsp pepper 
 
1 tsp dry mustard 
     1 cup cranberry juice 
 
 
1/4 tsp. ground cloves      2-1/2 cups water  
4 tbsp brown sugar 
     3 tbsp flour  
     
 1 tsp salt 
 
     1/2 tsp cinnamon 
1 cup milk                        1/2 cup white wine vinegar 
 
Remove fat from moose 
and wipe well with clean 
cloth.   
 
Lard the roast as follows: 
 
Cut bacon into 2” strips, pierce the roast with a 
sharp knife at 2” interval and insert bacon into 
holes, place moose into glass or earthenware 
bowl. 
 
Mix the following ingredients and pour over 
roast:: 
Salt,  pepper, cinnamon, cloves,  mustard, brown 
sugar , water and vinegar.  Cover and marinate 
roast in refrigerator for 24 to 48 hours.  Turn 
roast often if marinade does not completely cover 
roast. 
 
Remove roast from marinade and place in cov-
ered roaster at 350 degrees for approx. 1 hour.  
Add onion, cranberry juice and continue cooking 
roast until tender, approx. 1 hour more. 
 
When cooked remove from pan to hot platter.  
At flour to pan drippings and cook for 5 minutes, 
add milk stirring constantly until gravy is at de-
sired thickness. 
 
From Northern Cookbook by Eleanor A. Ellis

The Importance of  Wetlands 
Less than half of the wet-
lands that once existed in the 
United States still remain to-
day.  Presently more than 300,000 acres of wet-
lands are bulldozed in the US each year. The 
subject of wetlands is a touchy one.  Some see 
wetlands as a 
haven for 
wildlife in an 
ever changing 
world, while 
others simply 
see a messy, 
swampy area 
that kills 
trees, breeds 
insects, and 
threatens 
property and 
roads.  Often 
the two sides clash. If one looks a little deeper, 
they’ll find that wetlands mean more than just  
wet land. 
 
Some of the disagreements stem simply from 
the over 50 definitions that exist concerning 
wetland use.  A Natural Research Council 
Committee offered the following definition: “A 
wetland is an ecosystem that depends on con-
stant or recurrent shallow inundation or satura-
tion at or near the surface of substrate”. That 
definition does little to help clarify what a wet-
land is and how we need to treat it.   
 
Essentially  a wetland is usually wet, it will 
probably have standing water or wet soil most 
of the year or it will support plants and soils 
that occur in wet environments.  Wetlands are 
host to approx. 5,000 species of plants, 190 
species of amphibians (frogs, toads etc.) and 
1/3 of the bird species found in the United 
States. 
 
However, most people still see wetlands as eye-
sores, puddles of ooze and 
muck causing problems 
with drainage, and in the 
case of beaver 
ponds, washing 
out roads and 
killing trees and 
vegetation. 
 
But wetlands 
are more than 
just habitat 
for birds, 
bugs, plants 
and other crit-
ters.  Many 
animals like 
the moose, beaver and muskrat rely heavily on wetlands 
for their survival.  Wetlands also help purify groundwa-
ter and stabilize shorelines. Wetland  help filter pollut-
ants thereby improving water quality.  Much of the damage 
in past years from 
the flooding of 
the  Mississippi 
River can be di-
rectly attributed to 
the systematic 
draining of wet-
lands. 
 
Here on tribal 
property, we’ve 
worked to create 
and protect wet-
lands by building 
nutrient sediment control structures and installing a beaver 
deceiver. just to mention a few.  The sediment control 
structures have helped reduce damage from storm water 
and spring runoff that previously had caused a great deal of 
damage to tribal lands and has significantly reduced the 
amount of run off entering the Meduxnekeag River.  These 
collection basins have created temporary ponds, that pro-
vide habitat for migrating ducks and geese in the early 
spring.  Meanwhile the beaver deceiver allows the beaver to 
damn up brooks and streams without causing damage to 
roads. 
 
Next time you see a wetland, please look a little deeper, you 
may be surprised at what you find.  If you’d like more infor-
mation about wetlands or what you can do to help preserve 
or restore wetlands, please feel free to contact this depart-
ment. 
Beaver pond adjacent to HBMI offices 
Migrating ducks and geese on tribal 
lands taking advantage of spring pools 
Beaver deceiver at work on tribal lands 
protecting a tribal road

GRANDMOTHER AUTUMN 
Grandmother Autumn, the one who makes the 
leaves fall, was teaching young autumn girl.  
Grandmother Autumn told the young girl, “It is 
going to be cold, it is time to harvest the gardens 
and to gather many seeds so that they may be 
planted for next year.  Gather traditional medi-
cines and dry them for use in the coming 
year.  Dry the fish when you clean 
them so that you may enjoy them at 
the feasts.  When the hunters have 
returned with their catch, honor the 
catch and use all of the animal not just 
the meat.  You may use the skin, bones, 
teeth, tails and whiskers.  All of it may 
be used throughout the year.  In the eve-
nings enjoy the gift of a warm fire when 
family and friends gather.  After you have en-
joyed the warmth of fire, be sure to extinguish 
the gift of fire so that you may enjoy another 
Moon of Grandmother Autumn, the one who 
makes the leaves fall”.            
Hunting Safety Tips  by Scott Krzanik, Water Resources 
 
Hunting season is upon us – FINALLY!  Bear season is well underway, and 
Grouse (Partridge), Rabbit, and Duck season began on Monday, Oct. 1.  On 
Oct. 27, we can begin hunting deer.  Some people hunt while driving around 
in their vehicles while others pursue animals through the woods on foot.  No 
matter what method you choose, remember to always be safe in your out-
door activities.  Anyone can get lost, hurt, or run out of gas in the middle of 
the woods.  It is your responsibility to handle weapons safely for your sake 
and for others. In addition, here are some safety tips to keep in mind this  
season: 
 
Location:  Tell others where you are going and what time you expect to return.  Nobody will come looking for 
you if they don’t know where you are. 
 
Food and Water:  Bring EXTRA food and water with you.  Keep these items in your vehicle.  Don’t munch on 
your extra food – bring your main meals and snacks for that purpose. 
 
Clothing:  Wear wool and synthetic clothing.  Cotton material retains moisture near your skin and will lead to 
rapid body heat loss.  THIS CAN KILL YOU!!!  Wool and synthetics are easy to come by and can be purchased 
at minimal cost from thrift stores such as the Salvation Army. Don’t forget your hunter orange! 
 
Equipment:  Replace or repair equipment you took out of your pack and used during the winter and summer.  
Don’t find out that your compass or flashlight is missing just when you need it the most. 
 
Stay Alert:  Pay attention to where you are and what you are doing.  If you are tracking an animal be sure to 
mark your trail with crepe paper or flagging tape because animals don’t stay on well-marked trails. 
 
Good luck and have a safe hunting season!

RESULTS OF RADON 
TESTING PROGRAM  
BEGUN IN 1994 
 
Of the 60 homes tested so far: 
The average radon level was:   1.6 pCi/l 
The median radon level was:   0.9 pCi/l 
The lowest radon level was:       0.2 pCi/l 
The highest radon level was:   12.7 pCi/l 
 
Households over the 4 pCi/L action level  -  5 
 
This means that 1 out of every 12 households 
tested had a high level of radon 
 
Radon is a colorless, odorless, radioactive gas that 
occurs naturally in the ground.  Unfortunately, 
sometimes it can build up to unhealthful levels.

Word Search Answers 
Water conservation is a good idea any time by 
doing so you can save money on your water 
and electric bills while protecting water quality. 
Now is a  good time to start conserving water 
by adopting some of the following practices. 
 
Water lawns, trees and shrubs in the early morn-
ing or early evening to avoid excess evaporation.   
Water the lawn only, watch for water on roads, 
sidewalks or driveways. 
Run dishwashers and clothes washers only   
when full. 
Take shorter showers. 
Turn the water faucet off while shaving or  
brushing your teeth. 
Make sure faucets and hoses are turned off   
completely so they don’t drip and waste  water. 
Collect rainwater to water plants & flowers.

and a feasibility study for business development opportunities both on and

A Day for Celebration  
The Natural Resources Department has been taking part in Language Nests 
led by Language Coordinator, Imelda Perley.  At each session the group 
shares language and laughter as Imelda leads us through a little bit of history 
and a little bit of culture on our way to learning the language.   So far none of 
us are fluent speakers but we are all learning to recognize words and speech 
patterns as well as well as developing a greater respect for the Maliseet      
language and culture.

ArcView GIS Training 
In February the Natural Resources department      
underwent in-depth computer training on the use 
of ArcView GIS software. This training was led by 
Judy Colby-George of Spatial Alternatives,        
Yarmouth, Maine. 
 
GIS, which stands for Geographic Information   
Systems, is a powerful tool that can be used for 
mapping out information of all types. In conjunc-
tion with data gathered with our own GPS (Global 
Positioning Systems) equipment and other data-
bases, the department is looking to generate many 
detailed maps of tribal lands and surrounding areas.   
 
This training will enable        
department members to track  
information such as land     
usage, water quality issues, 
fish and wildlife habitat just 
to name a few of its many  
applications.

For creating the great map on page 1.

The Mercury in Fish Tissue study we worked on last summer is approximately 
half over.  We sampled fish from 5 lakes and streams, including the main stem of 
the     Meduxnekeag River, Drew's Lake, Number 9 Lake, Nickerson Lake and 
the south branch impoundment of the Meduxnekeag River.  The fish species 
sampled included brook trout, white perch, smallmouth bass and pickerel.  The 
first batch of fish  samples were tested at the University of Maine at Orono En-
vironmental Chemistry Laboratory.   
 
The average fish sizes and species caught  per body of water are listed below.   
All of the fish sampled to date show some mercury in their tissues, with pickerel 
showing the highest numbers thus far.  Once the sampling is complete we will be 
reporting the results in a later edition of this newsletter. 
 
 
 
 
 
We will be completing the study this field season.  There are a number of locations we have yet to survey  
including Green Pond, B-Lake, as well as the North and South branches of the Meduxnekeag River.

Initial Mercury Fish Study Results  by David Lombard, Forester/Env. Spec. 
Maine’s Safe Eating Guidelines for Freshwater Fish 
The State of Maine has issued  a warning about eating 
freshwater fish and have issued the following safe   
eating guidelines: 
 
B Pregnant and nursing women, women who 
may get pregnant and children under age 8         
Should not eat any freshwater fish from Maine’s 
inland waters.  Except,  for brook trout and     
landlocked salmon, 1 meal per month is safe. 
 
B All other adults and children older than 8 Can 
eat  2 freshwater fish meals per month.  For brook 
trout and landlocked salmon, the limit is 1 meal per 
week. 
The state of Maine has also indicated that fish in 
some Maine waters contain high levels of PCBs, 
Dioxins or DDT in them and have issued addi-
tional consumption advisories for those waters. 
 
This additional information is included in the 
State of Maine Fishing  Regulations booklets as 
well as from their website at   
http://www.state.me.us/dhs/etp   
 
Residents in other areas are encouraged to    
contact their local  Department of Health for 
advisories in their area.
