Re: 
Comments on Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791, Proposed Water 
Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions to Protect Tribal Reserved Rights 
 
Dear Administrator Regan: 
 
The Fond du Lac Band of Lake Superior Chippewa appreciates this opportunity to 
again provide EPA with our comments in support of the agency’s proposed 
rulemaking intended to protect tribal reserved rights under the EPA’s Clean Water 
Act authorities. The Band is a federally recognized Indian tribe, and one of six 
member bands of the Minnesota Chippewa Tribe (“MCT”).  The Band retains 
hunting, fishing, and other usufructuary rights that extend throughout the entire 
northeastern portion of the state of Minnesota under the 1854 Treaty of LaPointe 1, 
through central Minnesota into Wisconsin under the Treaty of St. Peters (1837), and 
across Wisconsin into the upper peninsula of Michigan under the Copper Treaty 
(1842). These rights have been reaffirmed by federal courts, including the US 
Supreme Court.2 Throughout these ceded territories, all signatory Bands have a 
legal interest in protecting natural resources, and all federal agencies share in the 
federal government’s trust responsibility to the Bands to maintain and protect 
those treaty resources.3  
 
Hunting, fishing, trapping and gathering remain an important source of subsistence, 
cultural and religious practices for members of the Fond du Lac Band.  Natural 
resources form the cornerstone of Chippewa traditional lifeways.  Fish, game, and 
plants like Manoomin (wild rice) are vital to meeting the needs of many Band

members for food.  But plants and animals are also relied upon to provide medicines, and 
to meet ceremonial and religious needs that define unique aspects of Chippewa culture.  
The health and welfare of tribal members who rely on these vital resources for sustenance 
and cultural practices is often disproportionately at risk because these resources exist 
within regulatory schemes that have not recognized or protected tribal reserved rights. In 
the Proposed Rule, EPA is for the first time taking significant steps to protect the aquatic 
and aquatic-dependent resources reserved to tribes by proposing revisions to the federal 
water quality standards (WQS) regulations. 
 
As we stated in previous comments, the exercise of these rights requires access to natural 
resources that are not contaminated.4  Treaty rights, environmental health, and tribal 
culture are all interconnected.  Populations with unique connections to the natural 
environment, such as Indian tribes, experience impacts that are too often overlooked.  The 
EPA recognized this in its Final Guidance for Incorporating Environmental Justice Concerns 
in EPA’s NEPA Compliance Analyses (1998): “[A]s a result of particular cultural practices, 
that population may experience disproportionately high and adverse effects.  For example, 
the construction of a new treatment plant that will discharge to a river or stream used by 
subsistence anglers may affect that portion of the population.  Also, potential effects to on-
or off-reservation tribal resources (e.g., treaty-protected resources, cultural resources 
and/or sacred sites) may disproportionately affect the local Native American community 
and implicate the federal trust responsibility to tribes.5   
 
EPA has long recognized the key role that the federal trust responsibility plays in the 
Agency’s planning and decision-making process.  Since 1984, EPA’s Policy for the 
Administration of Environmental Programs on Indian Reservations6 has declared that “EPA 
recognizes that a trust responsibility derives from the historic relationship between the 
Federal Government and Indian Tribes as expressed in certain treaties and Federal Indian 
law.”  The policy further states that “[i]n keeping with that trust responsibility, the Agency 
will endeavor to protect the environmental interests of Indian Tribes when carrying out its 
responsibilities that may affect the reservations.”  One of the guiding principles of EPA’s 
consultation policy is that “EPA recognizes the federal government’s trust responsibility, 
which derives from the historical relationship between the federal government and Indian 
tribes as expressed in certain treaties and federal Indian law.”7  
 
EPA states that “by amending EPA’s WQS regulations, rather than addressing [tribal 
reserved rights] on a case-by-case basis as state WQS are submitted for review . . ., EPA is 
proposing a uniform approach for establishment of WQS where tribal reserved rights apply 
and clearly laying out how EPA will review such WQS.”8 The Band agrees that incorporating

the duty to protect tribal reserved rights into the WQS regulations is the best way to 
achieve clarity, predictability, transparency, and consistency in fulfilling this goal.  
 
The Band supports these proposed revisions. However, as we pointed out in our earlier 
comments for this rulemaking, we recommend clarifying that “…states and EPA must not 
impair tribal reserved rights when establishing, revising, evaluating, implementing, and 
enforcing WQS.  What we have experienced in the state of Minnesota has been a failure, 
for decades, to implement and enforce existing approved water quality standards that are 
intended to protect manoomin, or wild rice, a critically significant cultural and subsistence 
aquatic resource. This deficiency has extended across implementing those standards in 
NPDES permits as numeric pollutant limits, monitoring and assessing state waters for this 
beneficial use, and listing waters as impaired under Section 303(d) when they fail to meet 
WQS. Along with other tribes in the state, we are grateful that the EPA Region 5 office 
recently partially disapproved Minnesota’s 2020 impaired waters list and took over the 
listing of waters impaired for wild rice WQS. As another example, the Band has designated 
our most productive wild rice waters as “Outstanding Reservation Resource Waters”, with 
Tier 3 antidegradation protections under our federally approved WQS. We believe ensuring 
that water quality – specifically high quality waters that support tribally important 
resources – remains sufficient to protect tribal rights to harvest or otherwise access those 
resources necessitates a holistic approach to the implementation of WQS. 
 
Comments on specific provisions of the proposed rule 
 
The key element of EPA’s proposed regulatory initiative is the addition of 40 C.F.R. § 131.9 
to the WQS regulations. That section would require that WQS “protect tribal reserved 
rights applicable to the waters subject to such standards.”9 Notably, the Agency’s revisions 
to § 131.5 make it clear that EPA has the authority and is required to disapprove state WQS 
that do not satisfy this requirement, and must promulgate federal standards that do 
comply. The Band fully supports this long-overdue initiative, and offers the following 
comments and recommendations regarding these provisions and other aspects of the 
proposal to ensure full protection of tribal reserved rights. 
 
1. Section 131.3 (Definitions) 
The Band agrees with EPA’s proposed definition of “tribal reserved rights” in new 40 C.F.R. 
§ 131.3(r) as “rights to aquatic and/or aquatic-dependent resources reserved or held by 
tribes, either expressly or implicitly, through treaties, statutes, executive orders, or other 
sources of Federal law.” We suggest one minor revision: the definition should be prefaced 
with “as used in this Part” or “for purposes of this Part,” because tribal reserved rights are 
broader than aquatic or aquatic-dependent resources. Although those other resources are 
not likely affected by the Clean Water Act and WQS, the regulatory language should be 
clear and accurate.  
                                                             
9 § 131.9(a); see also § 131.5(a)(9). 

4 
 
 
 
 
2. Section 131.5 (EPA Authority) 
EPA itself highlights that this rule is an extension of the agency’s pre-existing obligation 
under the CWA to acknowledge and protect treaty resources in reviewing and approving 
WQS.10 As previously mentioned, the Band strongly supports the proposed requirement 
that WQS must protect tribal reserved rights, § 131.5(a)(9), and that EPA must disapprove 
WQS that do not meet this requirement and promulgate federal standards that do, § 
131.5(b) (emphasis added). The first requirement is the absolute cornerstone of this rule, 
and the second two requirements are clear and necessary actions the agency must take 
under its CWA authorities and trust responsibility to properly implement the rule. 
Our recent, unfortunate experience with Minnesota WQS revisions should be held up as a 
cautionary tale, and a clear example for how important EPA’s role in approving or 
disapproving WQS is. The state of Minnesota recently revised their Class 3 (Industrial 
consumption) and Class 4 (Agriculture and Wildlife) standards for a number of conventional 
pollutants, in some cases withdrawing numeric criteria and replacing them with narrative 
standards. Minnesota tribes strongly and consistently objected to this lowering of water 
quality standards, which included protections for Manoomin or wild rice, a culturally 
significant aquatic plant, and wildlife drinking water (including for traditional subsistence 
species like moose) under Class 4 standards.  
Even after government-to-government consultation with the state, submittal of extensive 
technically supported written comments, and oral testimony to an administrative law 
judge, the state adopted their revisions and submitted them to EPA for approval. At that 
point, despite formal consultation, submittal of additional scientifically-based evidence, 
and expressly communicated tribal objections, EPA approved those revised standards.  
The Band has now been forced to sue EPA.11 In the pending lawsuit, a primary claim is that, 
over tribal objections, neither the state nor the US EPA adequately evaluated or considered 
the impacts of those WQS changes on a treaty-protected uses. This is not just a clear 
example of a broken process—one that the Proposed Rule should clearly and carefully 
remedy—but an action contrary to the CWA itself. 
3. Section 131.6 (Minimum Requirements for WQS Submission) 
The Band generally supports the intent of EPA’s proposed subsection (g), but questions the 
phrasing in the first sentence: information on the scope, nature and current and past use of 
tribal rights holders is said to “aid” EPA in evaluating WQS submissions. But to actually 
incorporate that information provided by a consulting tribe or tribes should be obligatory,  
                                                             
10 87 Fed. Reg. at 74364-65 (“In exercising its CWA section 303(c) authority, EPA has an obligation to ensure that its 
actions are consistent with treaties, statutes, executive orders, and other sources of Federal law reflecting tribal reserved 
rights….Where tribes have reserved rights to aquatic and/or aquatic-dependent resources, protection of such rights falls 
within the ambit of these broad statutory directives and objectives and is consistent with EPA’s longstanding general 
approach to implementing CWA section 303(c), including through adoption and revision of its WQS regulation.”) 
11 See Compl., Grand Portage Band of Lake Superior Chippewa and Fond du Lac Band of Lake Superior Chippewa v. US EPA, et 
al., Case No. 0:22-cv-01783-JRT-LIB (D.Minn. July 14, 2022). 

5 
 
 
 
 
since it is the factual basis for determining in § 131.9 whether the WQS protect reserved 
rights. We also question the ambiguous process suggested by the phrase “as informed by 
the right holders.” The preamble says this “provide[s] a role for right holders” to participate 
in protecting reserved rights. 
 
The current relationships and levels of consultation between states and tribes varies 
considerably across the country. Even where there is expressed policy, such as through 
Executive Orders, for state agencies to consult with tribal nations on issues and actions that 
may affect them, there are often impediments to effective and meaningful consultation. 
Small tribal programs are frequently overwhelmed with the number of requests for 
consultation from federal agencies, and have relatively few resources to support the 
capacity to engage. And it bears mentioning that states simply do not have the trust 
responsibility to sovereign tribes that the federal government has, and that often results in 
either no consultation, notification late in a decision-making process, or an apparent lack of 
consideration of the tribal input provided. For this rulemaking initiative to succeed, there 
must be intentionally designed procedures. 
 
The Band suggests that EPA develop process guidance for these state/tribal interactions, 
and by all means retain the critical EPA-tribal consultation step as state WQS are revised. 
Based upon our extensive experience with providing input to state decision-making, by the 
time the state is ready to submit revised standards to EPA for approval they are heavily 
invested in selecting new criteria and their technical documentation. This puts the burden 
upon tribes to show evidence that the criteria are not adequate to protect treaty resources 
and can exacerbate conflict rather than promote respectful and meaningful state/tribal 
engagement. 
 
Some ways in which EPA could provide clarity and direction would be specifically requiring 
state submissions to define the procedures they used to identify and consult with rights 
holders, describe any substantive suggestions the rights holders made that the state 
ultimately did not adopt, and provide justification for not adopting them. Additionally, EPA 
should ensure states clearly understand and respect tribal requests for confidentiality 
around sensitive tribal information. Tribes have too often experienced degradation or 
destruction of important resources when their location or information about traditional or 
cultural use is made public. 
 
Additionally, the Band strongly recommends that where Traditional Ecological Knowledge 
(TEK) is offered, it will be incorporated as required information in defining the reserved 
right.  EPA has already established a willingness to use TEK in decision-making processes 
such as site assessment, characterization, and cleanup activities of contaminated lands, 12 
and expressly included specific suggestions for and examples of incorporating TEK into 
tribal water quality monitoring programs.13 Incorporation of TEK into §131.6 decision 
                                                             
12 U.S. Environmental Protection Agency; Memorandum “Considering Traditional Ecological Knowledge (TEK) During the 
Cleanup Process (1.3.2017); (https://ww.epa.gov/tribal-lands/considering-traditional-ecological-knowledge-tek-during-
cleanup-process). 
13 Available at https://www.epa.gov/water-pollution-control-section-106-grants/clean-water-act-section-106-tribal-guidance   

6 
 
 
 
 
making must be considered as vital information for state submittals in protecting reserved 
rights. In our experience, TEK and ecological science are often compatible when integrated 
appropriately. 
 
One further tribal concern about sharing information and data with the state is that it 
could be used against a tribe in court proceedings, challenging our reserved rights. This 
scenario is particularly troubling as we consider how a state may approach defining fish 
consumption rates for tribal populations when surveys may not reveal complete or 
accurate information. EPA must acknowledge in this rulemaking that the nature and scope 
of many treaty rights have been the subject of sometimes decades-long court battles, and 
the determination of the scope, location, and manner of the exercise of the rights may be 
controversial and be met with resistance by states.  Or, a state may misinterpret the extent 
of a tribe’s exercise of their treaty harvest rights, and fundamentally, tribes do not want to 
re-adjudicate our reserved rights in court. The Band recommends that 131.6 include clear 
language that any tribally shared information or data will not be used in a manner that 
restricts or challenges their reserved rights where they apply. 
 
Finally, the proposed rule does not identify or provide any resources to assist rights holders 
in participating in state WQS revisions; EPA apparently assumes tribes will be able to 
provide any requested information in a timely manner. Although Fond du Lac has worked 
hard to develop a robust Environmental Program with an effective Office of Water 
Protection that includes delegated jurisdictional authorities under the CWA, we find often 
ourselves at the limits of our personnel and technical capacities. Incorporating the 
evaluation of tribal reserved rights into already-existing state triennial review procedures is 
likely to create complicated and time-consuming processes – and the three states wherein 
the Band holds reserved rights each have independent triennial review schedules. One 
triennial review process itself is a long and complicated process; navigating three will be 
onerous for us to participate in.  The Band has had extensive experience in WQS review, 
including our own triennial review processes, and recognize the amount of work it will take 
to participate effectively.  Taking on the additional responsibilities (legal review, data 
analysis and compilation) to fulfill requests for reserved rights information should suggest 
to EPA the pressing need for additional tribal support, perhaps through discretionary 
funding. 
 
4. Section 131.9 (Protection of Tribal Reserved Rights) 
The Band strongly supports the mandatory language of proposed subsection (a) that WQS 
“must” protect tribal reserved rights, and subsection (c) that WQS “must” designate uses 
and establish appropriate water quality criteria to protect those uses, pursuant to § 131.11. 
We agree that this process might involve creating a new designated use to protect tribal 
reserved rights, perhaps called “supports tribal reserved rights” or simply “tribal reserved 
rights,” with associated water quality criteria for that use, or developing revised criteria to 
protect the reserved right under an existing designated use (i.e., fishing), so long as the 
reserved right’s inclusion is explicit and clearly analyzed. 
 
 

7 
 
 
 
The Band does not, however, support EPA’s proposed interpretation of the requirement in 
§ 131.9(a)(1) that “WQS must protect the exercise of tribal reserved rights unsuppressed 
by water quality or availability of the aquatic or aquatic-dependent resource” as being 
limited to protecting “reasonably anticipated future uses, taking into account factors that 
may have substantially altered a waterbody.”14  
 
Although resources may have been more abundant when the reserved rights were 
established, EPA’s limited interpretation is too restrictive: tribes and other interested 
parties are working toward restoration of those resources, for example by removing dams 
or conducting habitat restoration, which are actions that may not have been “reasonable 
anticipated” yet which shows that “factors that may have substantially altered a 
waterbody” can be changed. There have been extensive tribal efforts in the upper Midwest 
to restore habitat supporting the growth of wild rice. Designating waters for wild rice 
habitat even if some may claim those waters are not “reasonably anticipated” to support it 
is essential to protecting the resource and the tribal reserved rights to gather that 
resource. EPA’s narrow interpretation of this requirement therefore may result in an 
unnecessary diminishment of tribal reserved rights. 
The Band agrees with EPA’s statement that any currently practiced reserved rights are 
“presently attained uses,” that must be treated as designated uses pursuant to 40 C.F.R. § 
131.10(i), and therefore require criteria for protection under 40 C.F.R. 131.12(a)(1). And we 
appreciate that EPA appropriately recognizes that historical land uses have suppressed the 
availability of traditional aquatic resources and the water quality necessary for their 
protection. We fully support EPA’s explicit requirement in § 131.9(a)(1) that WQS must 
protect “unsuppressed” tribal reserved rights.  
Since the Band supports requiring WQS to protect unsuppressed tribal reserved rights, we 
also support adding a provision to § 131.9 requiring the designated use attainability 
analysis (UAA) in § 131.10 to take this requirement into account. See Proposed Rule at 
74372. Otherwise, a finding that a designated use protecting tribal reserved rights is not 
currently feasible under § 131.10 could undermine EPA’s and the states’ obligations to 
protect tribal reserved rights, and would essentially negate the core provisions and 
purpose of § 131.9. A fourth criterion could be added to address this issue under § 131.9(c) 
or as a new subsection § 131.9(d).  
We raise concerns, however, over the determination of level of suppression.  “Proposed 40 
CFR 131.9(a)(1) would require that WQS, to the extent supported by available data and 
information, be established to protect ‘the exercise of the tribal reserved rights 
unsuppressed by water quality or availability of the aquatic or aquatic-dependent 
resource.’’’  Id.  But because the Proposed Rule does not “establish any nationally 
applicable thresholds for unsuppressed levels or use of a resource,” this determination will 
be made on a case-by-case basis.  The supplementary information lays out a balancing test 
for making this determination:  
The unsuppressed level should balance heritage use of a resource with what is  
                                                             
14 Proposed Rule at 74366-67. 

8 
 
 
 
currently reasonably achievable for a particular waterbody. For example, in 
determining the unsuppressed level of a resource for the purpose of establishing 
WQS, it may be appropriate to take into consideration both heritage rates of use of 
that resource and factors that have substantially altered the pollutant burden, 
hydrology, or availability of the resource, such that use of the resource at heritage 
rates is not feasible.15  
This language does not require or provide weight for such a balancing test, and does not 
explain what, exactly, should be taken into consideration.  
Unfortunately, the Federal Register notice is silent on what occurs when states and tribes 
disagree.  The Proposed Rule lacks any teeth to ensure that the states are giving the 
appropriate weight to the points of view of tribes or rights holders.  At minimum, the final 
rule should require states to show how the information and data provided by tribes were 
considered in the various processes outlined in this Proposed Rule (as stated above).  But 
additionally, the final rule should make clear that the information provided by tribes and 
rights holders, specifically including information that was provided through Indigenous 
Knowledge, or TEK, processes, are weighted equally to the information provided by states 
and through western scientific processes.  
Historically, tribes and states have fundamentally differed on how we approach water 
quality management, from considering how climate change will impact water resources, to 
evaluating cumulative impacts.  The often-differing approaches have the potential to lead 
to conflicting data and priorities, as well as different standards for designated uses.  As part 
of its federal treaty obligations and trust responsibility, the EPA must ensure that states do 
not discard or diminish any conflicting data or competing ideologies that come from tribes 
with tribal reserved rights.  This Proposed Rule must make clear how such differences will 
be addressed and resolved; perhaps through a defined dispute resolution process where 
rights holders can request to meet directly with the EPA Administrator to take steps to 
address those disputes, or potentially by EPA utilizing their Conflict Prevention and 
Resolution Center to mediate and resolve disputes. The Band would also anticipate that, in 
some instances, EPA itself may decide to promulgate WQS that are protective of a reserved 
right, as they did when establishing standards to protect subsistence fish consumption in 
several states. 
 
The Band also supports the requirement in § 131.9(c) that WQS must designate uses and 
establish appropriate water quality criteria to protect those uses, pursuant to § 131.11. We 
recognize that this process could involve creating a new designated use to protect the 
tribal reserved right, with associated water quality criteria for that use, or developing 
revised criteria to protect the reserved right under an existing designated use, such as 
fishing, or both of these options. However, the Band maintains that to protect tribal 
reserved rights, the antidegradation requirements referenced in § 131.9(c)(3) should be 
required in addition to the designated uses and water quality criteria required in § 
131.9(c)(1)-(2), not instead of those requirements. In other words, the regulatory text  
                                                             
15 87 Fed.Reg. at 74369 (italics added).   

9 
 
 
 
 
should say “and” instead of “and/or” when listing the requirements in § 131.9(c). The 
antidegradation options of designating Outstanding National Resource Waters (Tier 3 
protection), and to ensure that any lowering of water quality will continue to protect tribal  
reserved rights (Options 1 and 2 in the Proposed Rule at 74371) can both be used to 
support designated uses and related water quality criteria that protect reserved rights. 
 
5. Section 131.20 (State Review and Revision of WQS) 
 
The Band agrees with the inclusion of the new sentence in § 131.20(a) requiring the 
triennial review of WQS to “include evaluating whether there are tribal reserved rights 
applicable to state waters and whether water quality standards need to be revised to 
protect those rights pursuant to § 131.9.” However, the only process identified in the 
Proposed Rule for determining whether the WQS satisfy § 131.9 is the public participation 
required in existing § 131.20(b). The Band requests that EPA include a specific process to 
ensure that states directly ask for and obtain information from right holders as to their 
reserved rights. States must engage in that process while they are reviewing their WQS, 
rather than it falling to EPA to determine whether there are tribal reserved rights at issue 
once the states have already submitted their revised WQS to EPA for review and approval, 
which is when § 131.9(b) comes into play. 
 
We recommend that EPA adopt a process that explicitly requires states to contact all tribes 
with treaty protected rights within their borders, meet with them separately from the 
general public hearing provided in § 131.20, and take their input into account when 
reviewing WQS. In addition, EPA should require states to notify both the tribe or tribes 
affected and EPA if the state disagrees with the tribe’s claim to a reserved right in a 
particular resource.  These additions to the regulation should be mandatory and stringently 
enforced by EPA.  
 
Finally, it is commonly recognized that the triennial review process does not in fact take 
place every three years. To ensure that a review of WQS takes place in a timely fashion in 
response to these revised WQS regulations, another sentence should be added to § 
131.20(a) to require that, within two years of the effective date of this rulemaking, all 
states must review and, if needed, revise their WQS to protect tribal reserved rights. These 
rights, which are protected not only by the Clean Water Act, but also by the Constitution, 
have been neglected far too long. 
 
 
Sincerely, 
                          
 
Nancy Schuldt, Water Projects Coordinator 
Fond du Lac Environmental Program

re: Water Quality Standards Regulatory Revisions To Protect Tribal Reserved

Dear Assistant Administrator Fox, 
The Petroleum Association of Wyoming represents companies involved in all aspects of 
responsible oil and natural gas development in Wyoming, including upstream production, 
oilfield services, midstream processing, pipeline transportation and essential work such as legal 
services, accounting, consulting and more1. Companies operating in the state of Wyoming take 
seriously their duty to attain and keep environmental quality standards, for all land, air and water. 
They have a pragmatic working relationship with the state Department of Environmental Quality 
(DEQ), which fosters a better understanding of federal and state law requirements. Though 
sometimes voluminous, the rules DEQ promulgates outline clear processes for companies to 
follow when developing compliance strategies and, correspondingly, detail enforcement actions 
available to DEQ in the event of noncompliance. The rules are clear and the oil and natural gas 
industry works hard to abide by them. The proposal before us here regarding water and its 
inclusion in Tribal Reserved Rights (TRR) is not clear. It places authorities with the EPA which 
should not be entrusted to it and creates an air of uncertainty about how enforcement may be 
handled. 
Through this action, the EPA is developing a new process to integrate into a state’s framework of 
designating water quality criteria, designated uses and antidegradation requirements during its 
triennial review of water quality standards. The new process is intended to heighten the 
 
1 PAW advocates for oil and gas development that supports sustainable production of Wyoming’s abundant 
resources; fosters mutually beneficial relationships with Wyoming’s landowners, businesses, and communities; and 
upholds the values of science-based, environmental stewardship. Recent studies show this industry supports over 
12,000 jobs in Wyoming and contributes $5 billion in economic activity. Our industry generates significant tax 
revenue to the state of Wyoming, funding state and local government operations, education and public 
infrastructure. Eighty-five percent of the oil and gas companies operating in Wyoming are classified as small 
businesses. 

consideration of TRR when setting those standards. The EPA believes that the current 
framework is insufficient to facilitate appropriate outreach to potentially affected tribes and 
ascertaining how the rights granted to tribes may be impacted by state decision-making. PAW 
asserts that the framework in place provides appropriate outreach to all stakeholders, including 
tribal nations, to provide input for the state’s consideration when setting water quality standards. 
PAW believes this new process may hinder a state’s ability to set appropriate standards by 
directing limited resources towards ambiguous requirements. 
States are required to review their designation of water quality criteria, water uses and 
requirements for antidegradation every three years, known as a triennial review of water quality 
standards. In Wyoming, the DEQ-Water Quality Division initially establishes a work group of 
diverse interests to review the current reports and offer their expertise on any new information 
the DEQ may want to consider. Once the DEQ has finished their internal revisions, those are 
issued for public comment which usually lasts 30-45 days. Next, the revisions and any public 
comments received go to the Waste & Water Quality Advisory Board. The public has an 
opportunity at this forum to again address any concerns and have those incorporated into the 
administrative record. If any deficiencies are identified, the Board has authority to send the 
revisions back to the Division for further consideration. Once passing this step, the revisions and 
public comments go before the Environmental Quality Council, which generally has the same 
authorities as the Board. The revisions then go to the Governor for approval before ultimately 
being sent to the EPA. The EPA, with its oversight role, has a final opportunity to approve or 
disapprove and remand the revisions back to the state.  
This whole process takes a long time, with great consideration to all of the potential uses and 
necessary water quality criteria, and multiple opportunities for public input. PAW believes the 
process currently in place provides every opportunity for any interested stakeholder to submit 
evidence of what a water of the United States designated use should be and the applicable 
associated water quality standard. 
In addition, outside of any formal comment period, PAW has rarely seen an instance where the 
EPA, or certainly the state of Wyoming, has not offered to meet with an interested stakeholder 
on any issue. Regulators are available and willing to meet with people to ensure the regulations 
in place are appropriate. 
The EPA’s proposed new process will inhibit the current framework. To start, the EPA will 
require states to conduct direct outreach to tribal nations with water-related reserved rights in the 
state. However, there is no clearinghouse through which a state can definitively determine which 
tribes have reserved rights within state borders. Boundaries of reserved rights are not always 
clear cut. There is no catalogued library of treaties, federal laws and executive orders detailing 
this information. It will be a difficult task for a state to determine the list of tribes with which it 
must conduct outreach. As written, the consequences of potentially missing outreach to one or 
more tribes opens the entire triennial review process up to disapproval by the EPA. 
The next step would be to define what water-related TRR have been granted through each treaty, 
federal law and executive order. These rights may be express or implied, as acknowledged by the 

EPA. This responsibility will be put on states and tribes, with a hope that expressed and implied 
reserved rights will be agreed upon. But this is no easy exercise. Too often have disagreements 
occurred on defining the extent of rights granted to tribal nations. It is obviously not the intent to 
have disagreement, but states and tribes both have an interest in defending their own rights. Once 
settled, there is no recourse, which heightens the possibility of a contentious process. These 
decisions often go to federal court for deliberation, including all the way to the U.S Supreme 
Court. This stresses state and tribal resources, limiting their capacity to focus on other important 
responsibilities.  
The next layer of uncertainty comes from the lack of clarity regarding the extent to which a state 
must consider TRR downstream, outside of its jurisdictional boundaries. The EPA states that it is 
available to facilitate interaction with tribes with reserved rights in downstream waters. For a 
state like Wyoming, which rests upon the Continental Divide, water travels north through 
Montana, east as far as the Mississippi River, south to the Gulf of Mexico and west to the Pacific 
Ocean. The EPA provides no guidance for states to consider when determining the proportion to 
which their water quality standards influence reserved rights, perhaps to tribes thousands of 
river-miles downstream. 
In addition to these concerns, if finalized, the EPA will expand its jurisdiction by anointing itself 
as decider of tribal reserved right. This is due to the fact that, through its oversight authority, the 
EPA will be the entity with final say on whether a state appropriately considered its water quality 
standards effects on TRR. To make that determination, the EPA would have to decide the 
breadth of each right granted to each tribe. The EPA was not granted this responsibility, nor does 
it have the capacity or expertise to make such determinations. 
This all matters to oil and gas companies operating in Wyoming because they are required to 
maintain water quality standards based on designated uses. Each operation with a point source 
discharge is permitted before that activity can occur. If water quality criteria, designated uses or 
antidegradation requirements change, that may require the state to amend an operator’s permit to 
reflect the new standard. Companies appreciate this process and comply accordingly. Yet now, 
the EPA’s process will incorporate uncertainty into this regulatory program. At too many points 
during this new process, disagreements can occur about whether a state met with all necessary 
tribes and whether a state appropriately considered TRR when setting water quality standards. 
The EPA’s heightened oversight authority in this area may lead to more instances of the EPA 
disapproving state revisions or could lead to more instances of litigation. The pendulum of water 
quality standards may swing until a final decision is made in federal court. All the while, 
companies may have invested in new discharge technologies to comply with standards that 
ultimately weren’t appropriate for a water body.  
PAW does appreciate the responsibility of all three entities – tribal governments, the federal 
government and state governments – to work collaboratively to ensure the actions of one do not 
affect the jurisdiction of another. PAW suggests that if the EPA does take action on this subject, 
it should remove the asserted disapproval and enforcement concepts if a state inadvertently fails 
to identify all tribes, reserved rights and water quality standard’s effects on those. PAW believes 
that a simplified but more deliberate effort for states to attempt to identify and consider rights 

granted to tribes within its boundaries would suffice. Doing so will foster more robust outreach 
to tribal nations, while not straining the overall effort.

Colin McKee

Submitted via: https://www.regulations.gov/ 
Michael S. Regan, Administrator 
Environmental Protection Agency 
1200 Pennsylvania Avenue, N.W. 
Washington, DC 20460 
RE: 
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's proposed Water Quality Standards Regulatory 
Revisions To Protect Tribal Reserved Right, EPA Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791 
Dear Administrator Regan: 
On behalf of my office and the Oklahoma Department of Environmental Quality, please accept the 
following comments in response to EPA's Proposed Water Quality Standards Regulatory 
Revisions To Protect Tribal Reserved Rights, EPA Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0791, 87 
Fed. Reg. 74,361 (Dec. 5, 2022). The proposed rule, if fmalized, would have a substantial impact 
on the State of Oklahoma. As such, the opportunity to provide comments on the proposed rule, as 
well as EPA's consideration of said comments, is greatly appreciated. 
As an initial matter, the precise relationship between water quality standards and reserved rights 
is unclear. However, the State of Oklahoma recognizes and appreciates the need, and without 
question shares the desire, to protect water rights and beneficial uses of water, including tribal 
reserved rights. Nevertheless, as drafted, the proposed rule would be essentially impossible to 
successfully implement in our State, and would undoubtedly and inappropriately, provide an 
opportunity for the federalization of Water Quality Standards in Oklahoma. Consequently, for the 
reasons detailed below, the State of Oklahoma requests that EPA not fmalize the proposed rule. 
Determination of Reserved Rights 
It appears that the intended purpose of the proposed rule is to ensure that reserved rights are 
adequately preserved and protected by new or existing Water Quality Standards. 
A key 
requirement in the proposal is that States gather information and determine the nature and extent 
of reserved rights impacted by such Water Quality Standards. First and foremost, it does not 
appear that EPA has the authority to make a determination related to reserved rights, let alone the 
ability to delegate such authority to the States. Notwithstanding this lack of authority, prior to 
considering the role that Water Quality Standards play in protecting and preserving reserved rights 
(and definitely prior to determining that new and existing Water Quality Standards must 
1 

affirmatively demonstrate that such reserved rights are adequately protected), the reserved rights 
shouldfirst be determined or adjudicated kv a court of competent jurisdiction. As EPA recognized 
in the proposed rule, determining the nature and extent of a reserved right requires an incredibly 
complex analysis. As defined in the proposed rule, a reserved right includes "any rights to aquatic 
and/or aquatic-dependent resources reserved or held by tribes, either expressly or implicitly, 
through treaties, statutes, executive orders, or other sources of Federal law." 87 Fed. Reg. at 
74,362. The sources of Federal law that establish reserved rights do not typically lay out the 
precise nature and extent of the reserved right, but instead require a determination of the nature 
and extent of the right necessary to satisfy the purpose of the reservation. Every element of the 
proposed definition requires an extremely complex analysis: "any rights;" "aquatic and/or aquatic-
dependent resources;" "reserved or held;" "expressly or implicitly;" and "through treaties, statues, 
executive orders, or other sources of Federal law." 
To further complicate the determination, the proposed rule also provides that the States must 
determine what constitutes the unsuppressed use of any reserved resources (unsuppressed by water 
quality or availability), which requires the consideration of past, present, and future uses (which 
in turn requires taking "into account factors that may have substantially altered a waterbody."). 87 
Fed. Reg. at 74,367. This type of determination is difficult anywhere (as evidenced by the 
enormous number of State and Federal court cases dealing with such adjudications) and would be 
especially challenging in Oklahoma considering that 39 federally recognized tribal nations are 
located within the State's exterior boundaries and that Indian country in Oklahoma ranges from 
reservations to over one hundred thousand acres of tribal trust land scattered across the State. 
Determining the nature and extent of the reserved rights applicable to each tribal nation would be 
especially difficult considering that any such reserved rights were likely created through separate 
and distinct treaties, statutes, executive orders, and/or other sources of Federal law. 
Primary Role of States in Protecting Water Quality 
Considering the geographic extent of Oklahoma's unique jurisdictional situation, each statewide 
Water Quality Standard could potentially implicate reserved rights involving all 39 federally 
recognized tribal nations in Oklahoma. In addition, it appears that the proposed rule would also 
require the State to determine that all existing Water Quality Standards are adequately protective 
of all reserved rights during the required triennial review, and that such a determination would 
have to reoccur every three years. See 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,367 (Pursuant to the proposed rule, when 
conducting the triennial review of existing Water Quality Standards, States are required to "include 
an evaluation of whether there are tribal reserved rights applicable to waters subject to the state's 
WQS and whether WQS need to be revised to protect those rights."). The complexity of 
determining the nature and extent of reserved rights makes any single determination made by a 
State vulnerable to challenge by EPA or a third-party. When the number of new and existing 
Water Quality Standards is multiplied by the number of tribal nations potentially holding reserved 
rights in Oklahoma, the resulting number of complex and potentially controversial reserved rights 
determinations all but guarantees that the State would face difficult challenges to the nature and 
extent determination alone. The likelihood of challenge becomes even greater considering that 
each one of those determinations would likely need to be reviewed and updated every three years. 
These vulnerabilities will exist even before the State makes the difficult determinations related to 
the quality of water necessary to protect and preserve the reserved rights. 
2 

Again, the sheer number of court cases involving the determination of reserved rights demonstrates 
the difficulty involved in making such determinations, as well as the likelihood that any such State 
determination would be vulnerable to an infinite number of potential challenges. If, as proposed, 
such a determination is considered by EPA to be a prerequisite to developing approvable Water 
Quality Standards, then the challenge of any such determination is all but guaranteed and would 
be a potential justification for EPA to disapprove any related standard developed by the State, 
which would likely result in the federalization of Water Quality Standards in Oklahoma. In other 
words, requiring such a challenging determination to occur as part of the Water Quality Standards 
promulgation process, provides EPA with much geater discretion in determining that a State's 
standard is insufficient. The proposed rule recognizes that EPA must promulgate a Federal Water 
Quality Standard if it believes a State standard does not adequately protect a reserved right. 
Moreover, the complexity of such a determination would also bring the process of developing and 
promulgating new and revised Water Quality Standards to a halt. Failing to meet the required 
timelines could, in and of itself, provide a justification for EPA to federalize Water Quality 
Standards in Oklahoma. As stated by EPA in the proposed rule, "[s]hould a state fail to meet this 
tight timeline, EPA would be obligated to promulgate WQS for the state." 87 Fed. Reg. at 74,363. 
Mandating a determination that results in making a State's ability to successfully promulgate 
Water Quality Standards so vulnerable to challenge would be inconsistent with Congress' intent 
that the States are charged with the primary responsibility and right to prevent, reduce, and 
eliminate water pollution and to plan the development and use of water resources within their 
boundaries. See 33 U.S.C. § 1251(b) ("It is the policy of the Congress to recognize, preserve, and 
protect the primary responsibilities and rights of States to prevent, reduce, and eliminate pollution, 
to plan the development and use (including restoration, preservation, and enhancement) of land 
and water resources."). 
Burden on State Resources and Uncertain Regutatory Process 
Determining reserved rights is not typically a State environmental agency responsibility. 
Generally, State environment agencies do not have the expertise or personnel necessary to conduct 
the required complex reserved rights determinations. The creation of such a new and expansive 
responsibility would place a significant burden on already strained State resources. The potential 
impact on State resources from an unfunded federal mandate such as that required in the proposed 
rule cannot be overstated. In addition to the strain on State resources, the uncertainty related to 
determining the nature and extent of all reserved rights that must be protected in new and existing 
Water Quality Standards would result in a corresponding uncertainty to the adequacy of existing 
water quality discharge permits and the availability of new or modified discharge permits. This 
uncertainty would place a significant burden on the State water agencies and the regulated 
community. . 

Conclusion 
As mentioned above, the State of Oklahoma appreciates the opportunity to comment on the 
proposed rule. Furthermore, the State strongly supports the protection of water rights and 
beneficial uses of water; however, the proposed rule, as drafted, is unworkable and would likely 
result in the federalization of Water Quality Standards in Oklahoma. Consequently, the State 
requests that EPA not finalize the proposed rule. 
Sincerely, 
Ken McQueen 
Secretary of Energy & Environment

Dear Administrator Regan:  
 
The Petroleum Alliance of Oklahoma (The Alliance) appreciates this opportunity to provide 
comments on the above-captioned rulemaking.  The Alliance represents more than 1,400 
individuals and member companies and their tens of thousands of employees in the upstream, 
midstream, and downstream sectors and ventures ranging from small, family-owned businesses to 
large, publicly traded corporations. Our members produce, transport, process and refine the bulk of 
Oklahoma’s crude oil and natural gas. 
 
The Alliance acknowledges the states’ role in establishing and regularly reviewing water 
quality standards for waters within each state’s external boundaries.  Those standards form the basis 
for other Clean Water Act programs, such as water-quality-based effluent limitations and section 
401 and 404 permits.  Clearly, these are critical responsibilities under the Clean Water Act and the 
State of Oklahoma has a robust program in place to meet the state’s water quality obligations.  
Similarly, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) must acknowledge the State of Oklahoma’s 
existing unique, complex legal framework as it relates to tribes.  Thirty-nine Native American tribes 
call Oklahoma home. The Alliance appreciates and values what American Indians and tribes 
contribute to the state’s economy, culture and diversity.  The tribes are a vital part of our state. 
Oklahoma’s non-Indians and tribal members alike share a common interest in economic prosperity. 
 
 
However, The Alliance has a number of concerns about this proposed rulemaking.  
Fundamentally, we question EPA’s authority to promulgate this rule that requires determination of 
tribal reserved rights and delegates these responsibilities to the various states.  These rights can only 
be adjudicated by federal courts; EPA has no implied or explicit congressional grant of authority to 
engage in such a practice.  To the extent EPA has the authority to adopt and implement this rule, we 
believe it necessary to remind the agency of how the Safe, Accountable, Flexible, Efficient 
Transportation Equity Act of 2005 (SAFETEA) limits EPA’s authority and delegation of 
environmental protection responsibilities in Oklahoma.   
 
 
Moreover, if the agency proceeds with this rule, the financial impact to state water quality 
programs such as Oklahoma’s will be substantial.  The work program outlined by the proposed rule 
will demand a significant investment of human resources and time – far more significant than EPA 

 
 
 
2 
 
appears to acknowledge.  Then, the proposed rule anticipates an EPA review of the work done by 
the state, effectively duplicating the effort to establish treaty-based water quality standards.  The 
agency’s tentative decision that this new rule will not impose an unfunded mandate on states like 
Oklahoma is far off the mark.   
 
Finally, EPA’s proposal will have significant and profound impacts on all Oklahoma 
citizens, surrounding states, and our members.  For all of these reasons, we call on EPA to 
reconsider the basis for this rule and withdraw it. 
 
I. 
EPA LACKS THE LEGAL AUTHORITY TO ADOPT THIS RULE 
In the preamble to this proposed rule, EPA cites instances where federal courts have found 
that a treaty, statute, or executive order expressly or impliedly reserved certain rights to certain 
Indian tribes.  United States v. Winans, 196 U.S. 371 (1905), may be the progenitor of the line of 
cases finding that tribes may reserve certain rights when treating with the United States.  The 
decisions in Winters v. United States, 207 U.S. 564, 576 (1908), United States v. Washington, 520 
F.2d 676, 687 (9th Cir. 1975), cert denied 423 U.S. 1086, 96 S. Ct. 877 (1976), and Sohappy v. 
Smith, 302 F. Supp. 899 (D. Or. 1969) reflect the line of federal court decisions supporting the 
express or implied reservation of certain rights.  
The Alliance takes no issue with these decisions, nor with decisions confirming that treaties 
and similar agreements represent the supreme law of the land.  See., e.g., Skokomish Indian Tribe v. 
United States, 410 F.3d 506, 512 (9th Cir. 2005).  However, we note that every case to which EPA 
cites is a decision of the federal judiciary recognizing tribal rights, including implied and express 
reserved rights.  EPA does not – and cannot – cite to any authority enabling a federal agency to 
supplant the judicial role in interpreting treaties, statutes, executive orders, and other devices for 
entering into agreements with Indian tribes.  It is unclear whether EPA is proposing to require 
states, and ultimately the EPA, to interpret treaties and similar documents to determine whether 
they convey reserved rights.  If that is EPA’s intention, then the agency is acting outside its 
statutory and Constitutional powers. 
 
The Alliance is concerned that it appears EPA has arrogated upon itself not only the power 
to determine whether such reserved rights exist, as well as their scope and breadth, but that EPA 
believes it may delegate that same authority to state governments.1  In the long line of cases cited 
by the EPA, and in the discussion found in the preeminent authority on Indian law, there is no hint 
that a federal agency may determine or delegate such a profound responsibility to state 
governments.2  COHEN’S HANDBOOK OF FEDERAL INDIAN LAW, (Neil Jessup Newton ed., 2012).   
 
 
1 EPA has often stated that as a general rule it will not recognize state jurisdiction over federal regulatory programs in 
Indian country.  
2 While we firmly believe Oklahoma is capable of carrying out this responsibility with integrity and fairness, we find it 
particularly ironic that EPA proposes to delegate this responsibility to the entities that, more often than not, have 
questioned tribal reserved rights claims, e.g., United States v. Washington, 853 F.3d 946, 966, (9th Cir. 2017), aff’d , 138 
S.Ct.1832 (per curiam). 

 
 
 
3 
 
Finally, we also note that section 518 of the Clean Water Act authorizes EPA to treat 
eligible tribes with Indian reservations as a state (treatment as a state, or TAS) for purposes of 
administering section 303 of the Act.3  No other provision of the Act speaks to the EPA’s authority 
with respect to tribal rights on or off reservation.  Those statutory provisions imply the absence of 
other authority in this regard and that EPA’s proposal here falls outside its authority. 
 
It is on these bases we challenge the EPA’s authority to adopt this rule.  EPA should 
withdraw the proposed rule. 
 
II. 
SAFETEA OF 2005 LIMITS EPA’S AUTHORITY 
In addition to questioning EPA’s legal authority for the proposed rule, The Alliance believes 
EPA has failed to take into account the unique and complex landscape that exists in Oklahoma.   
Section 10211 of SAFETEA4 clarified and streamlined the State of Oklahoma’s role in managing 
virtually all environmental media within the state’s exterior borders. 
Subsection (a) of Section 10211 provides that if the EPA Administrator has approved 
regulatory programs submitted by the State of Oklahoma for implementation of federal 
environmental programs in non-Indian country, then upon request of the State, the Administrator 
shall approve the State to administer the State programs within certain areas of Indian country.  
Significantly, SAFETEA does not provide EPA Administrator discretion to consider the merits or 
circumstances of the State request or to impose conditions on approval; if the State’s request falls 
within the statute’s parameters, then the Administrator must grant the State’s request. It is virtually 
a ministerial task on the Administrator’s part. 
On July 22, 2020, the Governor of Oklahoma duly requested approval under Section 
10211(a) of SAFETEA to administer in Indian country those environmental programs that had 
previously been approved by EPA for application outside Indian country.5 In a letter to the 
Governor dated October 1, 2020, the Administrator acknowledged that despite its general practice 
with respect to Indian country, EPA must apply the statutory mandate embodied by SAFETEA6 and 
grant the Governor’s request.  The EPA Administrator’s approval applied to all of the State of 
Oklahoma’s existing EPA-approved regulatory programs, including, but not limited to, water 
quality standards and implementation plans7 and national pollutant discharge elimination system 
programs8 of the CWA implemented by a range of state agencies.9

III. 
THE PROPOSED RULE WILL HAVE A SIGNIFICANT  
IMPACT ON OKLAHOMA 
Assuming for the purposes of this discussion that there may be reserved rights in Oklahoma, 
the proposed rule would require states such as Oklahoma to dedicate significant new resources to 
developing water quality standards for the state’s numerous water bodies.  It appears that EPA 
minimizes the scope and depth of those new program requirements. 
First, as just noted, states would be required to evaluate whether there are tribal reserved 
rights applicable to waters subject to state water quality standards.  EPA does not explain how 
Oklahoma would make such a decision in the absence of judicial decrees affirming such rights.   
Second, states such as Oklahoma would have to collect information about the scope, nature, 
and current and past use of tribal activities as informed by the tribes.  In doing so, the state would 
be required not only to consult with tribes but also to consult other sources of information regarding 
potential reserved rights, including information about the geographic scope of any such rights, plus 
relevant information about the level of water quality needed to preserve the potential reserved 
rights.  Determining the level of water quality necessary to protect any aquatic dependent resource 
or users would require the state to weigh multiple lines of evidence.  That could include fish 
consumption surveys, studies of heritage fish consumption rates, reports on pollutant levels that 
could adversely affect the aquatic-related resource, and monitoring data reflecting current and 
historic water quality.

In a remarkable understatement, EPA acknowledges this may involve a “complex inquiry.”  
In Oklahoma, it would require the state to canvas 39 federally recognized tribes and virtually every 
water course in the state.  Moreover, EPA concedes in its Economic Analysis11 that determining the 
geographical location and scope of tribal reserved rights, the scope and nature of aquatic and 
aquatic-dependent resources, and whether those resources are protected by existing water quality 
standards could require a “detailed legal and scientific analysis.” 
Third, in cases where water quality is lower than necessary to allow for tribes to fully 
exercise their reserved rights, states such as Oklahoma would be required to establish water quality 
standards to protect potential reserved rights “unsuppressed by water quality or availability of the 
aquatic or aquatic dependent resource.”  This alone would demand a significant investment of 
human and taxpayer resources.  Many states, including Oklahoma, would have to start their 
inquiries from zero. 
In addition, states like Oklahoma would have to conduct enhanced coordination with 
surrounding states.  For example, surface water flowing from one state into another that may impact 
a tribe’s reserved right would provide its own unique set of challenges. 
The materials above represent a brief summary of the task that EPA seeks to impose upon 
states.  In a state such as Oklahoma, with 39 federally recognized tribes, it would demand a 
significant dedication of resources aside from the regular water quality work performed by state 
agencies.  It also would involve the state in reconciling competing claims among tribes on the same 
water courses, an inevitable occurrence.  EPA offers no guidance on how a state would reconcile 
different tribes’ claims on the same water course; indeed, that is not a state’s role.  Of course, it 
would immerse the state in an entirely new endeavor of seeking to define not only the existence of 
reserved rights but also their scope and breadth.  All of this has immense implications for state 
management not only of water quality, but also state allocation of water resources.   
Over the course of decades, states such as Oklahoma have developed complex, sophisticated 
statutory and successful regulatory programs for water resource allocation.  The proposed rule 
threatens to violate section 33 U.S.C. § 1251(b), which restates Congress’s policy to recognize, 
preserve, and protect the primary responsibilities of states to plan for the development and use of 
land and water resources. 
It is important to note that withdrawal of this proposal does not diminish tribes’ ability to 
provide input into the State of Oklahoma’s regulatory water program.  Tribes, as with any other 
citizen in the state, are always allowed to engage in the state’s rulemaking actions as provided by 
well-established Oklahoma laws, regulations, processes, and procedures.  For all of these reasons, 
in addition to the legal and policy concerns outlined above, the Alliance urges EPA to withdraw this 
proposed rule.

IV. 
EPA’S SUBSEQUENT REVIEW WOULD DUPLICATE THE  
STATES’ WORK AND ANALYSIS 
As we explained above, setting water quality standards that comport with tribal reserved 
rights would be a substantial undertaking in any state but even more so in Oklahoma, which is 
home to 39 federally recognized tribes.  Yet after setting water quality standards as part of each 
triennial review, EPA would then initiate its own consultation with tribes to determine whether 
applicable reserved rights are protected.  “This consultation will inform EPA’s determination 
pursuant to 40 CFR 131.5(a)(9) as to whether [water quality standards] protect tribal reserved 
rights, where applicable.”  87 Fed. Reg. 74361, 74,372 (Dec. 5, 2022).  In addition, EPA explains in 
the preamble to the proposed rule that in this consultation process EPA would seek “information 
and input regarding applicable tribal reserved rights.”  Id. 
It appears that in reviewing state water quality standards adopted pursuant to this rule, EPA 
would duplicate much of the work done by states in identifying tribal water rights as well as their 
scope and breadth, in combination with EPA’s review based on other criteria.  We presume that in 
order to assure itself that states have appropriately identified tribal rights, EPA will necessarily have 
to examine treaties and other similar documents, as well as other historical materials, in some detail.  
The states will already have done so.  Even after the states have engaged in a challenging and 
demanding process, EPA may second-guess or even deny the state’s water quality standards.  EPA 
should explain the need for this duplicative exercise.   
 
V. 
EPA’s ECONOMIC ANALYSIS GRAVELY UNDERESTIMATES THE 
FINANCIAL IMPACTS OF THESE NEW RULE 
 
In the preamble to the proposed rule and in the Economic Analysis, EPA concedes the need 
for a detailed legal and scientific analysis of not only the existence, scope, and extent of reserved 
rights, but also of the extant water quality and the water quality needed to sustain water dependent 
species.  In addition, the agency anticipates states may need to make changes in their water quality 
regulatory program, including potential rulemakings to update designated uses, adopt new or 
modified water quality criteria, and even add waters to the list of Outstanding National Resource 
Waters.12  In fact, EPA remarks that “States may incur costs for rulemaking activities such as 
reviewing existing WQS in relation to protection of tribal reserved rights; collecting data; 
performing technical, economic, and legal analysis of proposed WQS changes; developing 
proposed WQS regulation revisions; engaging in stakeholder outreach and the public comment 
process; and promulgating final regulations.”13 
 
EPA also acknowledges that tribes may have claims to different types of resources that 
require different levels of water quality.  As a result, states may have to update their water quality 
standards in “stages,” focusing on protection of different resources at different times.  Or in other 
words, the process EPA is proposing could stretch out over multiple triennial reviews.14  In 
addition, EPA’s Economic Analysis concedes that “[t]he cost of resources required to collect data 
and perform analyses is unknown. The number of analyses will depend on the number of [water 
 
12 Economic Analysis at 6. 
13 Id. 
14 Id. 

 
 
 
7 
 
quality standard] changes needed to protect reserved rights and the sufficiency of existing, readily 
available data on the scope of the right(s) and level of water quality necessary to protect those 
rights.”15 
Despite explaining the potential challenges to implementing this new rule and identifying a 
number of unknowns, EPA estimated that the total cost per state to comply with the proposed rule 
would max out at $98,911.  In its view, if all 50 states had to engage in this exercise the costs would 
not exceed a total of just under $5 million. 
It is possible that Oklahoma could simply report there are no adjudicated express or implied 
treaty rights to water-dependent species. That may well be the case.  But if EPA declines to accept 
that response, Oklahoma will have to review materials applicable to as many as 39 federally 
recognized tribes with potential competing claims to the same or multiple water bodies.  Perhaps at 
that point, Oklahoma could again report that there are no adjudicated express or implied treaty 
rights to water-dependent species in the state.  Were EPA to again reject that response, and if 
Oklahoma had to conduct the study and analysis required by this rule, that likely could not be 
completed for under $5 million. 
There are, thus, two salient problems with EPA’s proposal.  First, it fails to explain what 
kind of inquiry states must pursue in cases where there are or may be no adjudicated express or 
implied treaty rights to water-dependent species.  Second, EPA has grossly underestimated the costs 
to states associated with complying with this rule.   
Under those circumstances, this proposal unequivocally would constitute an unfunded 
mandate. 
 
VI. 
CONCLUSION 
For the reasons discussed above, we request EPA withdraw this rule.  The Alliance 
appreciates the opportunity to provide comments to the EPA on the proposed rule.  If you have 
questions, please contact me at angie@okpetro.com or 405-601-2124.

Dear Administrator Regan: 
The Lac du Flambeau Band of Lake Superior Chippewa Indians ("Lac du Flambeau 
Tribe") is a federally-recognized Indian Tribe, centered within the Lac du Flambeau Reservation 
located in Vilas, Oneida and Iron Counties in Northern Wisconsin. The Lac du Flambeau Tribe 
also retains interest in ceded lands in Wisconsin, Michigan and Minnesota; these lands were 
ceded to the United States government in the Treaties of 1837, 1842 and 1854. 
Waaswagoning, or Place of the Torch, later named Lac du Flambeau by French fur-
traders, the main village sits at the northern point of Flambeau Lake. Kiishkiman moved the band 
into this area after overpowering the Dakota, Sac, and Fox tribes in the 1700s. While there was 
one main village, Waaswagoning, small villages were established throughout the area. At 
Waaswagoning the Ojibwe were still living• a semi-nomadic life, moving seasonally to gather 
where the wild harvest was most abundant but returning to the village throughout the year. 
Currently, there are just over 4000+ enrolled Anishinaabe members of the Lac du 
Flambeau Tribe with numerous descendants. They currently are maintaining their hunting, 
fishing and gathering way of life in a manner that can be sustained for seven generations. By 
hunting, fishing and gathering, they can meet the cultural, subsistence, economic, medicinal and 
spiritual needs of the cornmunity. In order to be able to continue to hunt, fish and gather, there 
needs to be clean, healthy and abundant natural resources, especially water resources, available. 
The Federal Government is obligated to fulfill the treaty rights by providing clean, healthy 
natural resources to meet the needs and requirements of the Tribes. 
Water is as fundamental as blood in your veins, we cannot survive without it. The Tribe 
cannot overemphasize enough on how important clean water is in order to meet their cultural, 
subsistence, economic, medicinal and spiritual needs.
